summary.en: Gases have widely spaced molecules with negligible intermolecular attractions, giving them indefinite shape and volume, high compressibility, continuous mobility, diffusion, effusion, pressure, and low density.
summary.ur: گیسوں کے مالیکیولز کے درمیان وسیع خلا ہوتا ہے جس کی وجہ سے ان کی غیر معینہ شکل، لچکدار دباؤ، ڈفیوژن اور کم کثافت ہوتی ہے۔
summary.ps: غازونه نه ټاکلې بڼه او نه حجم لري، مالیکولونه یې خپاره دي او لوړ نفوذ او ټیټ کثافت لري.

subtopics.name: Indefinite Shape, Volume, Compressibility, and Mobility
subtopics.desc: Because intermolecular forces are extremely weak and intermolecular spaces are huge (molecules occupy only ~0.1% of total gas volume), gases do not possess fixed shape or fixed volume; they expand to fill any container completely. Compressibility: When external pressure is applied, empty intermolecular spaces are reduced, bringing molecules closer together. Mobility: Gas molecules possess high kinetic energy and move constantly in random straight lines, colliding with each other and container walls.
subtopics.sciNote: Point to remember: Gases can be compressed easily because gas molecules are separated by distances much greater than their molecular diameters.
subtopics.sq: Why are gases highly compressible compared to liquids and solids?

mcq.q: Gases are highly compressible because of:

subtopics.name: Diffusion, Effusion, Pressure, and Density
subtopics.desc: Diffusion: The spontaneous mixing of gas molecules by random motion and collision to form a homogeneous mixture (e.g. perfume scent spreading across a room). Lighter gases diffuse faster than heavier gases (Graham's Law). Effusion: The escape of gas molecules through an extremely tiny pinhole into a space of lower pressure without collisions (e.g. air leaking from a punctured tire). Pressure: Force exerted per unit area by colliding gas molecules on container walls: P = F / A. SI unit is Pascal (1 Pa = 1 N/m2; 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101,325 Pa). Density: Gases have very low densities (expressed in g/dm3 or g/L), approximately 1000 times less than liquids.
subtopics.sciNote: Gas density increases with cooling (contracts volume) and decreases with heating (expands volume).
subtopics.sq: Differentiate between diffusion and effusion of gases with examples.

mcq.q: The spontaneous mixing of gas particles to form a homogeneous mixture is called:

summary.en: Gas laws describe relationships between pressure, volume, and temperature: Boyle's Law (P vs V at constant T) and Charles's Law (V vs T at constant P) leading to the absolute Kelvin temperature scale.
summary.ur: گیسوں کے قوانین: بوائل کا قانون (حجم اور پریشر کا معکوس تعلق) اور چارلس کا قانون (حجم اور ٹمپریچر کا راست تعلق)۔
summary.ps: د غازونو قوانین: د بویل قانون (د حجم او فشار معکوس تړاو) او د چارلس قانون (د حجم او تودوخې مستقیم تړاو).

subtopics.name: Boyle's Law and Experimental Verification
subtopics.desc: In 1662, Robert Boyle stated: 'The volume of a given mass of a dry gas is inversely proportional to its pressure at constant temperature.' Mathematically: V proportional to 1/P, or P x V = k (constant). Therefore: P1 x V1 = P2 x V2. If pressure is doubled, the gas volume is halved. Experimental Verification: A gas sample in a cylinder fitted with a movable frictionless piston at constant temperature shows that doubling the weight (pressure) from 1 atm to 2 atm reduces volume from 2.0 dm3 to 1.0 dm3, keeping P x V = 2.0 atm.dm3 constant.
subtopics.sciNote: A plot of P versus V produces a hyperbolic curve called an Isotherm (at constant temperature).
subtopics.sq: State Boyle's Law and write its mathematical equation.

mcq.q: According to Boyle's law, when the pressure of a gas is tripled at constant temperature, its volume becomes:

subtopics.name: Charles's Law and Absolute Zero
subtopics.desc: In 1787, J.A.C. Charles stated: 'The volume of a given mass of a dry gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature at constant pressure.' Mathematically: V proportional to T, or V / T = k (constant). Therefore: V1 / T1 = V2 / T2 (where T is in Kelvin). Kelvin scale: T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15. Absolute Zero: If a plot of volume versus temperature is extrapolated to zero volume, it intersects the temperature axis at -273.15 °C (0 Kelvin). Absolute zero is the theoretical lowest attainable temperature where all molecular motion ceases.
subtopics.sciNote: Why must temperatures always be converted to Kelvin in gas law calculations? Because volume cannot be proportional to a scale containing zero degrees or negative numbers like Celsius.
subtopics.sq: State Charles's Law and explain the concept of absolute zero.

summary.en: Liquids possess definite volume but indefinite shape. Key properties include evaporation (endothermic surface phenomenon causing cooling), vapour pressure (dynamic equilibrium), and boiling point dependent on external pressure.
summary.ur: مائعات کا معینہ حجم مگر غیر معینہ شکل ہوتی ہے۔ اہم خصوصیات میں بخارات بننا (ٹھنڈک پیدا کرنا)، ویپر پریشر اور نقطہ کھولاؤ شامل ہیں۔
summary.ps: مایعات ټاکلی حجم لري خو ټاکلې بڼه نه لري، تبخیر، د بخار فشار او د جوش ټکی د دوی مهمې ځانګړتیاوې دي.

subtopics.name: Evaporation and Cooling Effect
subtopics.desc: Evaporation is the spontaneous escape of high kinetic energy molecules from the surface of a liquid into the vapour state at any temperature. It is a continuous surface phenomenon. Cooling Effect: As high-energy molecules leave the surface, the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid molecules decreases, causing the liquid's temperature to drop. Hence, evaporation causes cooling (e.g. sweating, spirit/alcohol evaporating on skin). Factors affecting evaporation: (1) Surface area (larger area -> faster evaporation); (2) Temperature (higher temp -> faster); (3) Intermolecular forces (weaker forces -> faster).
subtopics.sciNote: Why do we feel cool under a fan when sweating? The air flow sweeps away saturated water vapours, accelerating the rate of sweat evaporation and absorbing body heat.
subtopics.sq: Explain why evaporation causes cooling.

mcq.q: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon that occurs at:

subtopics.name: Vapour Pressure and Dynamic Equilibrium
subtopics.desc: When a liquid is kept in a closed container, molecules evaporate to form vapour. Some vapour molecules collide with liquid surface and condense back into liquid. Eventually, the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation, establishing Dynamic Equilibrium: Liquid <=> Vapour. Vapour Pressure is the pressure exerted by vapours in dynamic equilibrium with their liquid at a given temperature in a closed container. Factors affecting vapour pressure: (1) Nature of liquid (weaker intermolecular forces -> higher VP; ether > alcohol > water); (2) Temperature (VP increases exponentially with temperature); (3) Size of molecules. Vapour pressure does NOT depend on liquid volume or container surface area.
subtopics.sciNote: Dynamic equilibrium means both forward (evaporation) and reverse (condensation) processes occur simultaneously at exactly equal rates.
subtopics.sq: Define vapour pressure and dynamic equilibrium.

mcq.q: The vapour pressure of a liquid in a closed container depends upon:

subtopics.name: Boiling Point and External Pressure
subtopics.desc: The Boiling Point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external atmospheric pressure. At this temperature, bubbles of vapour form throughout the bulk liquid and rise to the surface. Relationship with External Pressure: When external pressure increases, more heat is required to raise the liquid's vapour pressure to match it, raising the boiling point (e.g. pressure cooker operates at ~2 atm, water boils at ~120 °C, cooking food rapidly). Conversely, when external pressure decreases (at high altitudes like Murree or Mount Everest, atmospheric pressure is ~0.7 atm), water boils at a lower temperature (~92 °C), taking much longer to cook food.
subtopics.sciNote: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level (1 atm = 760 mmHg), at 98 °C in Murree, and at 70 °C on Mount Everest (atmospheric pressure ~250 mmHg).
subtopics.sq: Why does it take longer time to cook food at high altitudes (mountains)?

summary.en: Solids possess definite shape and definite volume due to strong intermolecular forces locking particles in fixed positions, giving high rigidity, high density, and sharp melting points.
summary.ur: ٹھوس اشیاء کی معینہ شکل اور حجم ہوتا ہے، ان کے ذرات مضبوط قوتوں کے باعث لرزشی حرکت کرتے ہیں جس سے ان کی کثافت زیادہ اور پگھلاؤ کا نقطہ مخصوص ہوتا ہے۔
summary.ps: جامدات ټاکلې بڼه او ټاکلی حجم لري، او د ذرو د کلکو اړیکو له امله لوړ کثافت او ټاکلی ویلې کېدو ټکی لري.

subtopics.name: Rigidity, Density, and Melting Point
subtopics.desc: Rigidity: In solids, constituent particles (atoms, ions, or molecules) are held firmly in fixed positions by strong intermolecular forces; particles cannot slide or move freely, only vibrating around mean positions. Melting Point: The temperature at which a solid is converted into a liquid under 1 atm pressure, where solid and liquid phases coexist in dynamic equilibrium: Solid <=> Liquid. Density: Solids have the highest densities among the three states of matter because particles are packed together with minimal intermolecular spaces.
subtopics.sciNote: Ice is an unusual solid that is less dense than liquid water due to an open cage-like hexagonal hydrogen-bonded structure.
subtopics.sq: Define melting point and explain why solids are rigid.

mcq.q: In solid state, particles can only perform:

summary.en: Solids are categorized into Crystalline (regular geometric arrangement, sharp MP) and Amorphous (random arrangement, soften over range). Allotropy is the existence of an element in multiple crystalline forms.
summary.ur: ٹھوس اشیاء کی اقسام: قلمی (کرسٹلائن) اور غیر قلمی (امارفوس)؛ ایلوٹروپی کسی عنصر کا ایک سے زائد قلمی اشکال میں پایا جانا ہے۔
summary.ps: د جامداتو ډولونه: کرسټالي او بې بڼې (امورفوس)؛ ایلوټروپي د یو عنصر په مختلفو کرسټالي بڼو کې شتون دی.

subtopics.name: Crystalline vs Amorphous Solids
subtopics.desc: Crystalline Solids: Solids in which particles are arranged in a definite, repeating three-dimensional geometric pattern. They have sharp and characteristic melting points, clear cleavage planes, and regular crystal faces (e.g. Sodium chloride NaCl, Diamond, Ice, Sucrose). Amorphous Solids: Solids lacking an orderly three-dimensional repeating arrangement ('amorphous' = shapeless). Particles are randomly arranged. They do not have sharp melting points; instead, they gradually soften over a wide range of temperatures (e.g. Glass, Plastic, Rubber, Pitch).
subtopics.sciNote: Glass is often considered a supercooled liquid because its disordered molecular structure resembles a liquid frozen in place.
subtopics.sq: Differentiate between crystalline and amorphous solids with examples.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT an amorphous solid?

subtopics.name: Allotropy and Transition Temperature
subtopics.desc: Allotropy is the existence of a chemical element in more than one physical or crystalline form in the same physical state. Allotropes possess identical chemical properties but different physical properties. Reasons for Allotropy: (1) Different number of atoms in a molecule (e.g. Oxygen O2 and Ozone O3); (2) Different arrangement of atoms/molecules in crystal lattices. Allotropes of Carbon: Diamond (tetrahedral sp3, hardest natural substance, non-conductor), Graphite (hexagonal layers sp2 with delocalized pi-electrons, slippery lubricant, electrical conductor), and Buckyballs (Fullerenes C60, cage-like soccer ball). Allotropes of Sulphur: Rhombic (octahedral S8) and Monoclinic (needle-shaped S8). Transition Temperature: The temperature at which two allotropic forms of an element coexist in dynamic equilibrium: Rhombic Sulphur <=> Monoclinic Sulphur at 95.5 °C.
subtopics.sciNote: Above 95.5 °C, rhombic sulphur transforms into monoclinic sulphur; below 95.5 °C, monoclinic sulphur reverts back to rhombic.
subtopics.sq: Define allotropy and transition temperature with an example.

mcq.q: The transition temperature between rhombic and monoclinic sulphur is:

mcqs.q: The spontaneous mixing of particles is called:
mcqs.exp: Diffusion is the spontaneous mixing of particles by random thermal motion from higher concentration to lower concentration until homogeneous.

mcqs.q: Which statement for the particles of solid is NOT correct?
opts: They are arranged in regular pattern
There is very little space between the particles
Force of attraction between particles are strong
mcqs.exp: Particles in a solid do not move at great speed or travel translatory distances; they can only vibrate about their fixed lattice positions.

mcqs.q: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to:
mcqs.exp: At sea level, standard atmospheric pressure is 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa. A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals this external pressure.

mcqs.q: The vapour pressure of a liquid increases with the:
mcqs.exp: As temperature increases, molecules acquire higher kinetic energy to overcome intermolecular forces and escape into vapour phase, increasing vapour pressure.

mcqs.q: Water normally boils at 100 °C but it is possible to boil at 50 °C. Which variable would you have to change to do this?
mcqs.exp: Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals external pressure. If external pressure is reduced in a vacuum container to ~92.5 mmHg, water boils at 50 °C.

mcqs.q: The vapour pressure of a liquid in a closed container depends upon:
opts: Both surface area and amount of liquid
mcqs.exp: Vapour pressure depends only on the nature of the liquid and temperature. It is independent of liquid volume and container surface area.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is NOT an example of an amorphous solid?
mcqs.exp: Glucose (C6H12O6) forms crystalline solids with an ordered three-dimensional lattice and sharp melting point (146 °C), unlike amorphous glass, rubber, or plastic.

mcqs.q: At freezing point, which one of the following coexists in dynamic equilibrium?
mcqs.exp: At the freezing (melting) point, the rate of liquid freezing equals the rate of solid melting: Liquid <=> Solid.

mcqs.q: Ink spreads in water because of:
mcqs.exp: Ink dye particles move spontaneously from higher concentration into regions of lower water concentration via diffusion.

mcqs.q: What will be the pressure of a gas if the volume of the gas at 2 atmospheres is increased from 1.5 dm3 to 3 dm3?
mcqs.exp: By Boyle's Law: P1 x V1 = P2 x V2 => 2 atm x 1.5 dm3 = P2 x 3 dm3 => P2 = 3.0 / 3 = 1.0 atm.

sq.q: Can you give reason why it takes longer time to cook at high altitude?
sq.ans: At high altitudes (e.g. Murree, Gilgit), atmospheric pressure is significantly lower than 1 atmosphere (760 mmHg). Because boiling point depends directly on external atmospheric pressure, water boils at a lower temperature (e.g. ~92 °C in Murree, ~70 °C on Mount Everest). Since boiling water absorbs and delivers less heat energy to the food, cooking takes a much longer time.

sq.q: Glass softens over a wide range of temperature. Ice melts at a specific temperature. Explain the reason for this difference.
sq.ans: Ice is a crystalline solid with an orderly, repeating three-dimensional lattice held by uniform hydrogen bonds; all bonds require the exact same energy to break, giving ice a sharp and specific melting point (0 °C). Glass is an amorphous solid with randomly arranged molecules and non-uniform bond lengths/strengths; weaker bonds break at lower temperatures while stronger bonds break at higher temperatures, causing glass to soften gradually over a wide range.

sq.q: Explain why it happens that on a hot summer day when there is sweat on the body of a person, one feels cool under fast moving fan?
sq.ans: Evaporation is a cooling process because high-energy molecules escape into vapour, leaving lower-energy molecules behind. Fast-moving air from the fan rapidly sweeps away the humid boundary layer of water vapour surrounding the body, accelerating the rate of sweat evaporation and drawing latent heat of vaporization away from the skin.

sq.q: Why are the densities of gases lower than that of liquids?
sq.ans: Density is mass per unit volume (d = m / V). In gases, molecules are separated by extremely large intermolecular distances and occupy vast volumes (molecules account for only ~0.1% of gas volume). In liquids, molecules are closely packed with minimal empty space. For the same mass, gas occupies roughly 1000 times greater volume, making gas density ~1000 times lower than liquid density.

sq.q: What is the relationship between the atmospheric pressure and boiling point of a liquid?
sq.ans: Boiling point is directly proportional to external atmospheric pressure. When atmospheric pressure increases (such as inside a pressure cooker), vapour pressure must reach a higher value to equal it, so the boiling point rises. When atmospheric pressure decreases (such as at high altitudes), vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure at a lower temperature, so the boiling point drops.

sq.q: Why a gas is compressible?
sq.ans: In the gaseous state, there are enormous empty spaces between gas molecules (intermolecular distances are about 10 times the diameter of the molecules themselves). When external pressure is applied, these empty spaces are compressed, bringing molecules closer together without molecular distortion.

sq.q: Calculate the final pressure of a sample of gas that is changed at constant temperature to 14.3 dm3 from 7.55 dm3 at 828 torr.
sq.ans: Given: P1 = 828 torr, V1 = 7.55 dm3, V2 = 14.3 dm3, T = constant. Using Boyle's Law: P1 x V1 = P2 x V2 => P2 = (P1 x V1) / V2 = (828 torr x 7.55 dm3) / 14.3 dm3 = 6251.4 / 14.3 = 437.16 torr.

sq.q: Calculate the final volume at 302 K of a 5.41 dm3 sample of gas originally at 353 K if the pressure does not change.
sq.ans: Given: V1 = 5.41 dm3, T1 = 353 K, T2 = 302 K, P = constant. Using Charles's Law: V1 / T1 = V2 / T2 => V2 = (V1 x T2) / T1 = (5.41 dm3 x 302 K) / 353 K = 1633.82 / 353 = 4.62 dm3.

sq.q: Calculate the initial volume at 0 °C of a sample of gas that is changed to 731 cm3 by cooling to -14 °C at constant pressure.
A sample of a gas at room temperature occupies 0.80 dm3 at 1.5 atm. What will be its volume when the pressure of the gas is raised to 2.1 atm?
sq.ans: Given: V1 = 0.80 dm3, P1 = 1.5 atm, P2 = 2.1 atm, T = constant. Using Boyle's Law: P1 x V1 = P2 x V2 => V2 = (P1 x V1) / P2 = (1.5 atm x 0.80 dm3) / 2.1 atm = 1.20 / 2.1 = 0.571 dm3.

lq.q: Define Boyle's law and verify it experimentally.
lq.ans: Definition: Robert Boyle (1662) stated that: 'The volume of a given mass of a dry gas is inversely proportional to its pressure provided the temperature remains constant.' Formula: V proportional to 1/P => P x V = k (constant), or P1 x V1 = P2 x V2. Experimental Verification: Take a cylinder equipped with a frictionless movable piston containing a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature (25 °C). Step 1: Place a 1 atm weight; volume is 2.0 dm3 (P x V = 1 x 2 = 2.0 atm.dm3). Step 2: Increase pressure to 2 atm by adding weight; volume shrinks to 1.0 dm3 (P x V = 2 x 1 = 2.0 atm.dm3). Step 3: Increase pressure to 3 atm; volume contracts to 0.67 dm3 (P x V = 3 x 0.67 = 2.0 atm.dm3). Graph: A plot of P versus V yields a smooth hyperbolic curve (isotherm), verifying Boyle's law.

lq.q: Differentiate between: (a) Evaporation and Boiling, (b) Effusion and Diffusion of gases, (c) Condensation and Evaporation.
lq.ans: (a) Evaporation vs Boiling: Evaporation occurs at all temperatures, is a quiet surface phenomenon, and causes cooling. Boiling occurs only at a specific fixed temperature (when vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure), involves the whole bulk liquid with bubble formation, and maintains constant temperature. (b) Effusion vs Diffusion: Diffusion is the mixing of gas molecules through random collisions in all directions into open spaces. Effusion is the escape of gas molecules one by one through a microscopic pinhole into an evacuated or low-pressure chamber without inter-molecular collisions. (c) Condensation vs Evaporation: Evaporation is the conversion of liquid into gas with absorption of heat (endothermic). Condensation is the conversion of gas into liquid with release of heat (exothermic).

lq.q: Define the term allotropy with examples. Explain the three allotropic forms of carbon in detail.
lq.ans: Definition: Allotropy is the phenomenon in which an element exists in more than one physical or crystalline form in the same physical state, having identical chemical properties but different physical structures. Allotropic Forms of Carbon: 1) Diamond: Carbon atoms are sp3 hybridized, forming a rigid three-dimensional tetrahedral network with strong covalent bonds. It is the hardest known natural substance, has a very high melting point (3550 °C), and is an electrical insulator (no free electrons). 2) Graphite: Carbon atoms are sp2 hybridized, arranged in flat two-dimensional hexagonal planar sheets. Layers are held by weak van der Waals forces and slide past each other easily, making graphite soft, slippery, and useful as a solid lubricant. Delocalized pi electrons allow it to conduct electricity. 3) Buckyballs (Fullerenes / C60): Discovered in 1985, consists of 60 carbon atoms bonded in alternating hexagons and pentagons forming a hollow cage-like sphere resembling a soccer ball. Used in nanotechnology and superconductivity.

lq.q: What are solids? Differentiate between amorphous and crystalline solids.
lq.ans: Solids are states of matter having definite shape and definite volume due to strong cohesive intermolecular forces holding particles in fixed positions. Comparison: 1) Arrangement of Particles: Crystalline solids possess a regular, repeating, highly ordered three-dimensional geometric arrangement (crystal lattice). Amorphous solids have particles randomly scattered without long-range geometric order. 2) Melting Points: Crystalline solids have sharp, distinct melting points (e.g. ice at 0 °C, NaCl at 801 °C). Amorphous solids soften gradually over a broad temperature range (e.g. glass, plastic). 3) Cleavage: Crystalline solids cleave cleanly along smooth crystal faces. Amorphous solids break irregularly with curved, rough conchoidal fractures. 4) Examples: Crystalline = NaCl, diamond, quartz, sucrose; Amorphous = window glass, rubber, plastics, paraffin wax.

lq.q: Define Charles's law and verify it graphically and diagrammatically.
lq.ans: Definition: J.A.C. Charles (1787) stated that: 'The volume of a given mass of a dry gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature on the Kelvin scale at constant pressure.' Formula: V proportional to T => V / T = k => V1 / T1 = V2 / T2. Graphical Verification: Plotting gas volume (y-axis) against temperature in Celsius (x-axis) produces a straight line. If extrapolated backward to zero volume (V=0), the line intersects the temperature axis at -273.15 °C. This temperature is designated as 0 Kelvin (Absolute Zero). Diagrammatic Verification: A gas sample at constant pressure in a cylinder with a movable piston expands when heated (molecules gain kinetic energy and strike the piston harder) and contracts when cooled, maintaining V/T constant.

subtopics.name: Solution and Aqueous Solution
subtopics.desc: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more chemically non-reacting substances whose composition can be varied within certain limits. A solution containing two components is called a Binary Solution. Aqueous Solution: A solution in which water acts as the solvent (e.g. table salt in water, sugar syrup). Water is termed the 'Universal Solvent' because its high polarity (delta+ H, delta- O) and high dielectric constant allow it to dissolve a wide variety of ionic compounds and polar covalent substances.
subtopics.sciNote: Point to remember: In a true solution, solute particles are molecular or ionic in size (< 1 nm) and do not settle under gravity.

subtopics.name: Solute and Solvent
subtopics.desc: Solute: The component of a solution present in smaller quantity that gets dissolved (e.g. salt, sugar, iodine). Solvent: The component of a solution present in larger quantity that dissolves the solute and determines the physical state of the solution (e.g. water, alcohol, benzene). If components are in equal amounts, water is conventionally considered the solvent.
subtopics.sciNote: In soft drinks, water is the solvent, while carbon dioxide gas, sugar, citric acid, and flavorings are solutes.

subtopics.name: Saturated, Unsaturated, and Supersaturated Solutions
subtopics.desc: Unsaturated Solution: A solution that contains less amount of solute than that required to saturate it at a given temperature; it can dissolve more solute. Saturated Solution: A solution that contains the maximum amount of solute that can be dissolved in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature. Undissolved solute exists in dynamic equilibrium with dissolved solute: Undissolved Solute <=> Dissolved Solute. Supersaturated Solution: A solution that contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at that temperature. Prepared by heating a saturated solution, dissolving additional solute, and gently cooling it undisturbed. It is unstable; dropping a tiny seed crystal causes excess solute to crystallize out immediately.
subtopics.sciNote: A supersaturated sodium thiosulfate (hypo) or sodium acetate solution crystallizes rapidly into a solid mass upon scratching or adding a crystal.

subtopics.name: Dilute vs Concentrated Solutions
subtopics.desc: Dilute Solution: A solution containing a relatively small amount of solute dissolved in a large quantity of solvent (e.g. 5 g salt in 1 liter of water). Concentrated Solution: A solution containing a relatively large amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent (e.g. 300 g salt in 1 liter of water). Dilution does not change the total moles of solute; it only increases the solvent volume.
subtopics.sciNote: Concentration is a relative qualitative description; molarity and percentage provide precise quantitative measurements.

subtopics.desc: Gaseous Solutions: (1) Gas in Gas: Air (O2 in N2); (2) Gas in Liquid: CO2 dissolved in water (carbonated soda); (3) Gas in Solid: H2 gas adsorbed on Palladium metal. Liquid Solutions: (4) Liquid in Gas: Fog, mist, clouds (water vapour in air); (5) Liquid in Liquid: Alcohol in water, vinegar (acetic acid in water); (6) Liquid in Solid: Dental amalgam (liquid mercury dissolved in solid silver). Solid Solutions: (7) Solid in Gas: Smoke, dust particles in air; (8) Solid in Liquid: Sugar or salt dissolved in water, sea water; (9) Solid in Solid: Metal alloys such as Brass (Zinc in Copper), Bronze (Tin in Copper), and 22-carat gold (Copper in Gold).

subtopics.name: Percentage Composition (% m/m, % m/v, % v/m, % v/v)
subtopics.desc: (1) % m/m: Mass of solute in grams dissolved in 100 g of solution = (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 100. (2) % m/v: Mass of solute in grams dissolved in 100 cm3 of solution = (mass of solute / volume of solution) x 100. (3) % v/m: Volume of solute in cm3 dissolved in 100 g of solution = (volume of solute / mass of solution) x 100. (4) % v/v: Volume of solute in cm3 dissolved in 100 cm3 of solution = (volume of solute / volume of solution) x 100.

subtopics.name: Molarity (M) and Dilution Formula
subtopics.desc: Molarity (M) is defined as the number of moles of solute dissolved in one cubic decimeter (1 dm3 or 1 Liter) of solution. Formula: Molarity (M) = (Moles of solute) / (Volume of solution in dm3) = (Mass of solute in g / Molar mass of solute) x (1000 / Volume of solution in cm3). Units: mol/dm3 or M. Dilution Formula: When a concentrated solution of molarity M1 and volume V1 is diluted with solvent to a new volume V2, the resulting molarity M2 is calculated by: M1 x V1 = M2 x V2.
subtopics.sciNote: To prepare a 1.0 M solution of NaOH, dissolve 40.0 g of pure NaOH in distilled water and make total volume exactly 1000 cm3 (1 dm3) in a volumetric flask.

summary.en: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute in grams that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature. Governed by 'Like Dissolves Like', solute-solvent interactions, and temperature.
summary.ur: حل پذیری (سولیوبلٹی) 100 گرام سالونٹ میں حل ہونے والی سلوٹ کی زیادہ سے زیادہ مقدار ہے۔ 'ایک جیسی چیز ایک جیسی کو حل کرتی ہے' اور ٹمپریچر اس پر اثر انداز ہوتے ہیں۔

subtopics.name: Definition and 'Like Dissolves Like' Principle
subtopics.desc: Solubility is defined as the number of grams of solute dissolved in 100 g of solvent to prepare a saturated solution at a specific temperature. General Principle: 'Like Dissolves Like' — (1) Polar substances dissolve in polar solvents (e.g. ionic salts NaCl, KNO3 and polar compounds HCl dissolve readily in polar water); (2) Non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents (e.g. grease, benzene, oil, and naphthalene dissolve in non-polar ether, CCl4, gasoline); (3) Non-polar substances do NOT dissolve in polar solvents (e.g. oil does not mix with water).
subtopics.sciNote: Solute-solvent interactions require attractive forces between solute and solvent particles to be stronger than solute-solute and solvent-solvent attractions.

subtopics.name: Effect of Temperature on Solubility
subtopics.desc: (1) Endothermic Dissolution (heat is absorbed): If heat is absorbed during solution formation (e.g. KNO3, NH4Cl, KCl), solubility increases with rising temperature. (2) Exothermic Dissolution (heat is released): If heat is released during solution formation (e.g. Ce2(SO4)3, Li2SO4), solubility decreases with rising temperature. (3) Negligible Heat Change: For some salts like NaCl, dissolution involves almost no heat exchange; solubility remains virtually constant across temperature changes.
subtopics.sciNote: Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen gas than warm water; thermal pollution reduces dissolved O2, endangering aquatic life.

topics.title: Comparison of Solution, Colloid, and Suspension

summary.en: Mixtures are differentiated by particle size: True Solutions (< 1 nm, homogeneous, clear, no Tyndall effect), Colloids (1 to 1000 nm, false solutions, show Tyndall effect), Suspensions (> 1000 nm, heterogeneous, opaque, settle on standing).
summary.ur: سلوشن (سائز 1 نینو میٹر سے کم)، کولائیڈ (1 سے 1000 نینو میٹر، ٹنڈال ایفیکٹ) اور سسپنشن (1000 نینو میٹر سے زیادہ، تلچھٹ بن جاتی ہے) کا موازنہ۔
summary.ps: د محلول، کولایډ او تعلیق (سسپنشن) پرتله: د ذرو اندازه، د رڼا خوریدل (ټینډال اغیز) او د چاڼ کېدو وړتیا.

subtopics.name: True Solutions, Colloids, and Suspensions
subtopics.desc: True Solution: Homogeneous mixture of solute particles < 1 nm diameter. Solute particles do not settle down, pass through filter paper, and do not scatter light (transparent, e.g. salt in water). Colloid (False Solution): Heterogeneous system where dispersed particles range between 1 nm and 1000 nm. Particles do not settle down under gravity, pass through ordinary filter paper, and scatter a beam of light making its path visible (Tyndall Effect). Examples: Milk, fog, mayonnaise, jelly, blood. Suspension: Heterogeneous mixture of visible particles > 1000 nm diameter. Particles settle down on standing under gravity, can be separated by ordinary filtration, and do not show Tyndall effect (they reflect or block light). Examples: Chalk in water, sand in water, milk of magnesia, muddy river water, paints.
subtopics.sciNote: Why do paints need thorough stirring before use? Paints are suspensions; dense pigment particles settle to the bottom over time.
subtopics.sq: What is the Tyndall Effect and why do colloids show it while true solutions do not?

mcqs.q: Which of the following solution is more concentrated?
mcqs.exp: A 1.0 M solution contains the highest number of moles (1.0 mol) of solute per dm3 of solution, making it the most concentrated.

mcqs.q: Milk is an example of:
mcqs.exp: Milk is a colloidal emulsion containing fat droplets and protein particles (1–1000 nm) dispersed in water.

mcqs.q: Water droplet in air is an example of which type of solution?
mcqs.exp: Liquid water droplets (solute) suspended in atmospheric gas (solvent) constitute a liquid-in-gas solution (e.g. fog, mist).

mcqs.q: When there is a low concentration of solute in a solution, it is known as:
mcqs.exp: A solution containing a relatively small proportion of solute relative to solvent is termed dilute.

mcqs.q: What is the molarity of a NaNO3 solution made by diluting 250.0 cm3 of a 1.60 M solution to a final volume of 400 cm3?
mcqs.exp: Using dilution formula M1 x V1 = M2 x V2: 1.60 M x 250 cm3 = M2 x 400 cm3 => M2 = 400 / 400 = 1.00 M.

mcqs.q: What is the concentration, in % mass by volume (m/v) of a solution containing 15.0 g KCl in 600.0 cm3 solution?
mcqs.exp: % m/v = (mass of solute in g / volume of solution in cm3) x 100 = (15.0 / 600.0) x 100 = 2.50%.

mcqs.q: When KCl dissolves in water, the following will be produced:
mcqs.exp: Potassium chloride is an ionic compound that dissociates in water into potassium cations (K+) and chloride anions (Cl-).

mcqs.q: 2 moles of Na2SO4 are dissolved in one dm3 of solution. Molarity of solution is:
mcqs.exp: Molarity = moles / volume in dm3 = 2 moles / 1 dm3 = 2 M.

mcqs.q: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved in:
mcqs.exp: By standard IUPAC definition, Molarity is moles of solute dissolved per 1 cubic decimeter (1 dm3 or 1 L) of solution.

mcqs.q: The molarity of a NaOH solution prepared by dissolving 4 g of it in 250 ml water is:
mcqs.exp: Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g/mol. Moles = 4 / 40 = 0.1 mol. Volume = 250 cm3 = 0.25 dm3. Molarity = 0.1 / 0.25 = 0.4 M.

sq.q: Is seawater a solution? How would you prove with a simple experiment whether it is pure water or a solution?
sq.ans: Yes, seawater is a homogeneous liquid solution containing various dissolved mineral salts (solutes) in water (solvent). Experiment: Place a sample of seawater in an evaporating dish and heat it gently over a burner until all liquid boils off. A white crystalline residue of salts (NaCl, MgCl2) will remain in the dish, whereas pure water evaporates completely without leaving any solid residue.

sq.q: A bottle in a drug store contains a label '3 percent hydrogen peroxide'. What does it mean?
sq.ans: It means that the solution contains 3 grams of pure hydrogen peroxide (H2O2 solute) dissolved in enough water to make 100 cm3 of total antiseptic solution (3% mass by volume, m/v), or 3 cm3 of pure H2O2 in 100 cm3 of solution (% v/v).

sq.q: Classify the following as a solution, colloid or suspension and explain why: (i) Milk, (ii) Hot cup of tea, (iii) Orange juice with pulp, (iv) Mayonnaise, (v) Listerine mouthwash, (vi) Milk of Magnesia, (vii) Cheese, (viii) Mist, (ix) Bottled water.
sq.ans: True Solutions: Hot cup of tea, Listerine mouthwash, Bottled water (homogeneous, clear, particles < 1 nm, no Tyndall effect). Colloids: Milk, Mayonnaise, Cheese, Mist (particle sizes 1–1000 nm, do not settle under gravity, exhibit Tyndall effect). Suspensions: Orange juice with pulp, Milk of Magnesia (heterogeneous, visible particles > 1000 nm that settle upon standing and can be separated by filtration).

sq.q: Why we stir paints thoroughly before using it?
sq.ans: Paint is a suspension containing insoluble pigment particles and binders suspended in a liquid solvent. Because suspension particles are large (> 1000 nm) and dense, gravity causes them to settle out to the bottom of the can over time. Thorough stirring redisperses the pigment particles uniformly to ensure consistent color and coverage.

sq.q: Why suspensions and solutions do not show Tyndall Effect, while colloids do?
sq.ans: True solutions do not show Tyndall effect because their solute particles are smaller than 1 nm, which is too small to scatter visible light wavelengths. Colloids have particle sizes between 1 and 1000 nm, which are comparable to visible light wavelengths and effectively scatter light beams. Suspensions do not show a continuous Tyndall path because their large particles (> 1000 nm) either block or reflect light rather than scattering it.

sq.q: What is the molarity of a solution composed of 5.85 g of potassium iodide (KI) dissolved in enough water to make 0.125 dm3 of solution?
sq.ans: Given: Mass of KI = 5.85 g. Molar mass of KI = 39.1 (K) + 126.9 (I) = 166.0 g/mol. Moles of KI = 5.85 / 166.0 = 0.03524 mol. Volume of solution = 0.125 dm3. Molarity (M) = Moles / Volume = 0.03524 mol / 0.125 dm3 = 0.281 M.

sq.q: How many moles of H2SO4 are present in 0.500 dm3 of 0.150 M H2SO4 solution?
sq.ans: Given: Molarity = 0.150 M, Volume = 0.500 dm3. Formula: Moles = Molarity x Volume (dm3) = 0.150 mol/dm3 x 0.500 dm3 = 0.075 moles of H2SO4.

sq.q: Suppose you wanted to dissolve 40.0 g NaOH in enough H2O to make 6.00 dm3 of solution. (a) What is the molar mass of NaOH? (b) What is the molarity of this solution?
sq.ans: (a) Molar mass of NaOH = 23 (Na) + 16 (O) + 1 (H) = 40.0 g/mol. (b) Moles of NaOH = 40.0 g / 40.0 g/mol = 1.00 mol. Volume = 6.00 dm3. Molarity = 1.00 mol / 6.00 dm3 = 0.166 M.

sq.q: What is the molarity of a solution of 14.0 g NH4Br in enough H2O to make 150 cm3 of solution?
sq.ans: Given: Mass of NH4Br = 14.0 g. Molar mass of NH4Br = 14 + 4(1) + 79.9 = 97.9 g/mol. Moles = 14.0 / 97.9 = 0.143 mol. Volume = 150 cm3 = 0.150 dm3. Molarity = 0.143 mol / 0.150 dm3 = 0.953 M.

sq.q: Suppose you want to produce 1.00 dm3 of 3.5 M solution of H2SO4. (a) What is the solute? (b) What is the solvent? (c) How many grams of solute are needed to make this solution?
sq.ans: (a) Solute = Sulphuric acid (H2SO4). (b) Solvent = Water (H2O). (c) Moles needed = Molarity x Volume = 3.5 mol/dm3 x 1.00 dm3 = 3.5 moles. Molar mass of H2SO4 = 2(1) + 32 + 4(16) = 98 g/mol. Mass of solute = Moles x Molar mass = 3.5 mol x 98 g/mol = 343 g.

lq.q: Define solution. Explain types of solution on the basis of states of matter.
lq.ans: Definition: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more chemically non-reacting substances whose proportions can be varied within certain limits. Nine Types of Solutions: 1) Gas in Gas: Air (O2, CO2, Ar in N2 gas). 2) Gas in Liquid: Aerated carbonated soda drinks (CO2 in water). 3) Gas in Solid: Hydrogen gas adsorbed on Palladium metal surface. 4) Liquid in Gas: Fog, mist, aerosol sprays (liquid water droplets in air). 5) Liquid in Liquid: Vinegar (acetic acid in water), alcohol in water. 6) Liquid in Solid: Dental amalgams (liquid mercury in silver-tin alloy). 7) Solid in Gas: Airborne smoke and dust in atmosphere. 8) Solid in Liquid: Sugar in water, saline solution (NaCl in water). 9) Solid in Solid: Metal alloys like Brass (Cu + Zn), Bronze (Cu + Sn), and steel (Fe + C).

lq.q: (a) Discuss the solubility of a substance. (b) Explain the factors that are responsible for the solubility of a substance.
lq.ans: (a) Solubility: Defined as the maximum mass of solute in grams that can dissolve in 100 grams of a given solvent at a specific temperature to produce a saturated solution. (b) Factors Affecting Solubility: 1) Nature of Solute and Solvent ('Like Dissolves Like'): Polar and ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents (e.g. NaCl in water) because dipole-ion attractive forces overcome crystal lattice forces. Non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents (e.g. naphthalene in benzene). Non-polar solutes do not dissolve in polar solvents (oil in water). 2) Solute-Solvent Interactions: Dissolution occurs only if attractive forces between solute and solvent molecules are stronger than the internal solute-solute and solvent-solvent attractions. 3) Temperature: For endothermic dissolution (e.g. KNO3, NH4NO3), solubility increases with temperature. For exothermic dissolution (e.g. Ce2(SO4)3, Li2CO3), solubility decreases with rising temperature. For salts with near-zero heat of solution (e.g. NaCl), temperature has virtually no effect.

lq.q: (a) What is the difference between a concentrated and a dilute solution? Give examples of each. (b) Differentiate between unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions.
lq.ans: (a) Dilute vs Concentrated: A dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute dissolved in a large quantity of solvent (e.g. 5 g table salt in 1 liter water). A concentrated solution contains a large amount of solute dissolved in a solvent (e.g. 300 g salt in 1 liter water). (b) Saturation Classification: Unsaturated Solution: Contains less solute than its maximum saturation capacity at that temperature; it can dissolve more solute. Saturated Solution: Contains the maximum amount of dissolved solute in dynamic equilibrium with undissolved solute at a specific temperature. Supersaturated Solution: Contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at that temperature; prepared by cooling a warm saturated solution gently. Highly unstable; adding a seed crystal induces rapid crystallization of excess solute.

lq.q: Describe one way to prove that a mixture of sugar and water is a solution and that a mixture of sand and water is not a solution.
lq.ans: Proof by Filtration and Tyndall Effect: 1) Filtration Test: Pour both mixtures through filter paper set in glass funnels. For the sugar-water mixture, the entire liquid passes through cleanly; no residue is left on the filter paper because sugar molecules (< 1 nm) are smaller than filter pores. For the sand-water mixture, sand particles (> 1000 nm) are trapped on the filter paper as residue, while clear water passes as filtrate. 2) Light Beam (Tyndall) Test: Pass a flashlight beam through both mixtures. Sugar-water is transparent and does not scatter light (the beam path is invisible inside the liquid). Sand-water is opaque/turbid, settling down upon standing. This conclusively proves sugar-water is a true solution and sand-water is a suspension.

lq.q: Explain the following concentration units: (a) Percentage composition, (b) Molarity.
lq.ans: (a) Percentage Composition: Expresses parts of solute per 100 parts of solution. Four variations: 1) % m/m = (mass of solute in g / mass of solution in g) x 100; 2) % m/v = (mass of solute in g / volume of solution in cm3) x 100; 3) % v/m = (volume of solute in cm3 / mass of solution in g) x 100; 4) % v/v = (volume of solute in cm3 / volume of solution in cm3) x 100. (b) Molarity (M): Number of moles of solute dissolved in 1 dm3 (1000 cm3 or 1 Liter) of solution. Formula: M = (mass of solute in g / molar mass of solute) x (1000 / volume of solution in cm3). Dilution Equation: When solvent is added to dilute a solution, moles of solute remain constant: M1 x V1 = M2 x V2.

subtopics.name: Classical Concepts (Oxygen and Hydrogen Transfer)
subtopics.desc: Classical definitions: (1) Oxidation: Addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen from a substance (e.g. 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO; CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O; H2S + Cl2 -> 2HCl + S, where H2S loses hydrogen and is oxidized). (2) Reduction: Addition of hydrogen or removal of oxygen from a substance (e.g. CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, where CuO loses oxygen and is reduced; N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, where N2 gains hydrogen).
subtopics.sciNote: Oxidation and reduction always occur simultaneously; one cannot happen without the other. Such mutually occurring processes are called Redox Reactions.

subtopics.name: Modern Electronic Concept (LEO says GER)
subtopics.desc: Modern electronic definition: (1) Oxidation is the Loss of Electrons (LEO): An atom, ion, or molecule loses one or more electrons, accompanied by an increase in oxidation number (e.g. Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-; Fe2+ -> Fe3+ + e-). (2) Reduction is the Gain of Electrons (GER): An atom, ion, or molecule gains one or more electrons, accompanied by a decrease in oxidation number (e.g. Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu; Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-). Overall Redox: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu (Zn is oxidized; Cu2+ is reduced).
subtopics.sciNote: Mnemonic rule: LEO (Loss of Electrons is Oxidation) and GER (Gain of Electrons is Reduction).

topics.title: Oxidation State and Rules for Assigning Oxidation Numbers

summary.en: The oxidation number is the formal apparent electrical charge assigned to an atom in a compound according to a set of international rules.
summary.ur: آکسیڈیشن نمبر وہ ظاہری برقی چارج ہے جو کسی مالیکیول یا کمپاؤنڈ میں کسی ایٹم کو مخصوص قواعد کے تحت دیا جاتا ہے۔

subtopics.name: Rules for Assigning Oxidation Numbers
subtopics.desc: IUPAC Rules: (1) Free/uncombined elements have oxidation number = 0 (e.g. Na, H2, O2, P4, S8). (2) In simple monoatomic ions, oxidation number equals ion charge (Na+ = +1, Ca2+ = +2, Al3+ = +3, Cl- = -1, O2- = -2). (3) Hydrogen is always +1 in compounds, except in binary metal hydrides where it is -1 (NaH, CaH2). (4) Oxygen is always -2, except in peroxides where it is -1 (H2O2, Na2O2), superoxides where it is -1/2 (KO2), and in OF2 where it is +2. (5) Fluorine is always -1 in all compounds. (6) In neutral compounds, the algebraic sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms equals 0 (e.g. in H2SO4: 2(+1) + S + 4(-2) = 0 => S = +6). (7) In polyatomic ions, the algebraic sum equals the ion's charge (e.g. in SO4 2-: S + 4(-2) = -2 => S = +6; in MnO4-: Mn + 4(-2) = -1 => Mn = +7).
subtopics.sciNote: Determining oxidation states allows chemists to identify which species is being oxidized and which is being reduced in complex reactions.

summary.en: An oxidizing agent oxidizes another substance and itself gets reduced (gains electrons). A reducing agent reduces another substance and itself gets oxidized (loses electrons).

subtopics.name: Definitions and Identification in Chemical Reactions
subtopics.desc: Oxidizing Agent (Oxidant): A species that brings about oxidation by accepting electrons from another substance; its own oxidation state decreases (e.g. O2, Cl2, KMnO4, K2Cr2O7, HNO3, concentrated H2SO4). Reducing Agent (Reductant): A species that brings about reduction by donating electrons to another substance; its own oxidation state increases (e.g. electropositive metals like Na, K, Zn, Fe, and non-metals like C, CO, H2S). In 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl: Sodium loses electrons (reducing agent); Chlorine gains electrons (oxidizing agent).
subtopics.sciNote: Point to remember: Non-metals have high electronegativities and act as oxidizing agents, whereas metals have low ionization energies and act as reducing agents.

summary.en: Electrochemical cells convert between electrical and chemical energy: Electrolytic Cells (non-spontaneous, external battery drives chemical reaction) and Galvanic / Voltaic Cells (spontaneous chemical reaction generates electricity).

subtopics.name: Electrolytes and Electrolytic Conduction
subtopics.desc: An electrolyte is a chemical substance which conducts electricity in molten state or aqueous solution due to the migration of mobile ions, accompanied by chemical decomposition. Types: (1) Strong Electrolytes: Ionize completely in water to produce high ion concentration; conduct electricity strongly (e.g. NaCl, HCl, NaOH, H2SO4); (2) Weak Electrolytes: Ionize only partially in water (e.g. CH3COOH, NH4OH, H2CO3); conduct weakly; (3) Non-Electrolytes: Substances that dissolve without producing ions; do not conduct electricity (e.g. sugar, urea, glucose, benzene, alcohol).
subtopics.sciNote: Metallic conduction occurs via free electrons without chemical decomposition; electrolytic conduction occurs via mobile ions with chemical decomposition.
subtopics.sq: Why is NaOH a strong electrolyte while NH4OH is a weak electrolyte?

subtopics.name: Electrolytic Cells
subtopics.desc: An electrolytic cell is a device in which electrical energy supplied by an external direct-current (DC) power source drives a non-spontaneous chemical redox reaction (Electrolysis). Construction: An electrolytic tank containing an electrolyte, immersed with two electrodes: (1) Anode (connected to battery's positive terminal; oxidation occurs: 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-); (2) Cathode (connected to battery's negative terminal; reduction occurs: Na+ + e- -> Na). Electrons travel from anode to cathode through the external circuit.
subtopics.sciNote: In both electrolytic and galvanic cells: Oxidation ALWAYS occurs at the Anode (An Ox), and Reduction ALWAYS occurs at the Cathode (Red Cat).
subtopics.sq: Describe the construction and working of an electrolytic cell.

subtopics.name: Galvanic (Voltaic) Cells and the Daniell Cell
subtopics.desc: A galvanic (voltaic) cell is an electrochemical device that converts chemical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. The classic example is the Daniell Cell: Construction: Two half-cells: (1) Zinc half-cell: A Zinc strip immersed in 1.0 M ZnSO4 solution (Anode: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-, oxidation); (2) Copper half-cell: A Copper strip immersed in 1.0 M CuSO4 solution (Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, reduction). The two half-cells are joined internally by a Salt Bridge (an inverted U-tube containing an inert electrolyte gel like KCl or KNO3 in agar-agar) and externally by a wire through a voltmeter. Overall Cell Reaction: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) -> Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s); Cell potential E_cell = +1.10 Volts. Function of Salt Bridge: (1) Completes electrical circuit; (2) Maintains electrical neutrality by allowing ions to migrate between half-cells.
subtopics.sciNote: Electrons flow from zinc anode to copper cathode through the external wire, while conventional current flows from copper to zinc.
subtopics.sq: State the two main functions of the salt bridge in a Daniell cell.

summary.en: Industrial electrochemistry enables large-scale production of essential chemicals: Down's Cell (extraction of sodium from molten NaCl), Nelson's Cell (manufacture of NaOH and Cl2 from brine), and copper refining.
summary.ur: صنعتی الیکٹرو کیمسٹری: ڈاؤنز سیل (پگھلے ہوئے نمک سے سوڈیم کی تیاری)، نیلسنز سیل (کاسٹک سوڈا NaOH اور کلورین کی تیاری) اور تانبے کی صفائی۔

subtopics.name: Down's Cell (Extraction of Sodium Metal)
subtopics.desc: Sodium metal is commercially extracted by the electrolysis of molten anhydrous NaCl in Down's Cell. Calcium chloride (CaCl2) is added to lower the melting point of NaCl from 801 °C to about 600 °C. Construction: Circular steel shell lined with firebricks. Central graphite anode surrounded by a cylindrical steel wire gauze cathode. An iron wire gauze separates anode and cathode to prevent newly formed sodium and chlorine from recombining. Electrode Reactions: At Anode: 2Cl-(l) -> Cl2(g) + 2e- (chlorine gas escapes via dome); At Cathode: 2Na+(l) + 2e- -> 2Na(l). Molten sodium is lighter than the molten electrolyte, floats to the top, and is collected in an inverted reservoir under kerosene oil.
subtopics.sciNote: Why is CaCl2 mixed with NaCl in Down's cell? Pure NaCl melts at 801 °C; adding CaCl2 lowers the operating temperature to 600 °C, conserving energy and preventing sodium vaporization.
subtopics.sq: Write the electrode reactions occurring in Down's cell for sodium extraction.

subtopics.name: Nelson's Diaphragm Cell (Manufacture of NaOH)
subtopics.desc: Caustic soda (Sodium hydroxide, NaOH) is manufactured on a commercial scale by the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (Brine) in Nelson's Diaphragm Cell. Construction: A U-shaped perforated steel cathode lined inside with an asbestos diaphragm (separates anode and cathode compartments, preventing Cl2 from reacting with NaOH). A titanium or graphite anode dips into the central brine solution. Electrode Reactions: At Anode: 2Cl-(aq) -> Cl2(g) + 2e- (chlorine gas is collected at top); At Cathode: 2H2O(l) + 2e- -> H2(g) + 2OH-(aq) (water is reduced because H+ has higher discharge potential than Na+). The OH- ions combine with remaining Na+ ions to form NaOH solution, which drips through the perforated cathode into a lower catch basin. Overall Reaction: 2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) + H2(g).
subtopics.sciNote: Three commercially valuable chemicals are co-produced in Nelson's cell: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), Chlorine (Cl2), and Hydrogen (H2).
subtopics.sq: Write the balanced chemical reactions that occur in Nelson's Diaphragm Cell.

subtopics.name: Electrolytic Refining of Copper
subtopics.desc: Impure 'blister copper' (obtained from smelting, ~98% pure) is electrochemically refined to 99.99% pure copper. Setup: Anode = Thick slab of impure blister copper; Cathode = Thin sheet of 99.99% pure copper; Electrolyte = Acidified copper sulphate (CuSO4 + H2SO4) solution. Reactions: At Anode: Cu(impure) -> Cu2+(aq) + 2e- (copper dissolves into solution; impurities like Au, Ag, Pt settle below the anode as valuable 'anode mud'); At Cathode: Cu2+(aq) + 2e- -> Cu(pure) (pure copper deposits onto the thin cathode sheet).
subtopics.sciNote: High-purity copper (> 99.95%) is mandatory for electrical wiring because even trace impurities drastically impair electrical conductivity.

summary.en: Corrosion is the slow, spontaneous electrochemical destruction of metals by environmental moisture and oxygen. Prevention includes barrier coatings, galvanizing, tin plating, and cathodic sacrificial protection.
summary.ur: زنگ لگنا (کوروشن) نمی اور آکسیجن کی موجودگی میں دھاتوں کی تباہی کا الیکٹرو کیمیکل عمل ہے۔ بچاؤ: رنگ و روغن، گیلوانائزنگ، ٹن پلیٹنگ اور کیتھوڈک پروٹیکشن۔
summary.ps: زنګ وهل د لوندوالي او اکسیجن په شتون کې د فلزاتو ویجاړیدل دي. مخنیوی: رنګ کول، ګالوانایز کول، قلعي کول او کاتودي ساتنه.

subtopics.name: Mechanism of Rusting of Iron
subtopics.desc: Corrosion is defined as the slow and continuous eating away of a metal by the chemical or electrochemical action of its surrounding environment (moisture and atmospheric oxygen). Rusting of Iron Mechanism: When a drop of water containing dissolved oxygen contacts an iron surface with structural strains or impurities, a miniature galvanic cell is set up: (1) Anodic Region: Iron is oxidized into Fe2+ ions: 2Fe(s) -> 2Fe2+(aq) + 4e-. (2) Cathodic Region: Released electrons migrate through the iron to a region rich in oxygen and moisture, reducing dissolved O2 in acidic moisture (from CO2 forming H2CO3): O2(g) + 4H+(aq) + 4e- -> 2H2O(l). (3) Rust Formation: The Fe2+ ions react further with oxygen and water: 4Fe2+(aq) + O2(g) + (4+2x)H2O(l) -> 2Fe2O3.xH2O(s) + 8H+(aq). Rust is porous, flaky hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3.xH2O) which falls away, continuously exposing fresh iron underneath until complete destruction occurs.
subtopics.sciNote: Both oxygen (O2) and moisture (water) are absolutely essential for rusting; iron does not rust in dry air or boiled oxygen-free water.
subtopics.sq: Why are both oxygen and moisture essential for the rusting of iron?

subtopics.name: Methods of Corrosion Prevention
subtopics.desc: Methods include: (1) Barrier Coatings: Applying paint, grease, oil, or enamel to physically block oxygen and water contact; (2) Alloying: Mixing iron with Chromium and Nickel to form Stainless Steel (forms a self-healing, non-porous Cr2O3 oxide film); (3) Galvanizing (Zinc Coating): Dipping iron into molten zinc. Zinc (E° = -0.76 V) is more electropositive than iron (E° = -0.44 V). Even if the zinc coating is scratched, zinc acts as a sacrificial anode, oxidizing preferentially and protecting the underlying iron; (4) Tin Plating (Tin Cans): Coating iron with tin (used in food cans). Tin protects only as long as the layer is unbroken; once scratched, iron is more electropositive than tin and rusts even faster than unplated iron; (5) Cathodic Protection: Connecting underground iron pipelines or ship hulls to more active sacrificial metal blocks (Magnesium or Zinc), making the pipeline the cathode.
subtopics.sciNote: Why is zinc used for galvanizing roofing sheets while tin is used for food containers? Zinc protects iron even after scratching, but zinc salts are toxic; tin is non-toxic for food storage.

subtopics.name: Electroplating (Cr, Ag, Sn)
subtopics.desc: Electroplating is the process of depositing a thin, adhering protective layer of a superior metal onto an inferior base metal using electrolytic action. Objectives: (1) Corrosion protection; (2) Attractive, decorative finish. General Setup: (1) Anode = Pure sheet of the coating metal (e.g. Silver, Chromium, Nickel); (2) Cathode = The base metal article to be plated (cleaned thoroughly with acid and alkali); (3) Electrolyte = A soluble salt solution of the coating metal (e.g. AgNO3 + NaCN for silver plating; Cr2(SO4)3 for chromium plating). During electrolysis, anode metal dissolves into solution as cations and deposits uniformly as a bright metallic layer onto the cathode article.
subtopics.sciNote: Chromium plating on steel requires an undercoat of copper or nickel because chromium does not adhere directly to steel surfaces.

Reduction occurs at the anode only

mcqs.exp: In all electrochemical cells (both electrolytic and galvanic), oxidation strictly occurs at the anode (An Ox) and reduction at the cathode (Red Cat).

opts: It is oxidized as it gains electrons
It is oxidized as it loses electrons
It is reduced as it gains electrons
It is reduced as it loses electrons
mcqs.exp: A reducing agent loses electrons and therefore undergoes oxidation.

opts: From the anode to the cathode through the external circuit
From the anode to the cathode through the salt bridge

mcqs.exp: Electrons are liberated at the anode by oxidation and travel through the external metal wire to the cathode where reduction consumes them.

sq.q: Indicate which element is reduced in the following reactions: (a) 2FeCl3 + H2 -> 2FeCl2 + 2HCl, (b) 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.
sq.ans: (a) In 2FeCl3 + H2 -> 2FeCl2 + 2HCl: Iron (Fe) changes from oxidation state +3 in FeCl3 to +2 in FeCl2 (gain of 1 electron); hence, Iron (Fe) is reduced. (b) In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O: Oxygen (O) changes from oxidation state 0 in elemental O2 to -2 in H2O (gain of electrons); hence, Oxygen (O) is reduced.

sq.q: What is the oxidation number of silver on each side of the following equation: 4Ag(s) + O2(g) -> 2Ag2O(s)?
sq.ans: On the reactant (left) side: Silver exists in its free uncombined elemental state, so its oxidation number is 0. On the product (right) side in Ag2O: Oxygen has an oxidation state of -2; therefore, 2(Ag) + (-2) = 0 => 2(Ag) = +2 => Ag = +1. Silver is oxidized from 0 to +1.

sq.q: Why NaOH is a strong but NH4OH is weak electrolyte?
sq.ans: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is an ionic compound that ionizes almost completely (100%) in aqueous solution into Na+ and OH- ions, delivering a very high concentration of mobile charge carriers (strong electrolyte). Ammonium hydroxide (NH4OH) is a weak base that ionizes only slightly (~1-2%) in water (NH4OH <=> NH4+ + OH-), leaving most molecules unionized and conducting current weakly.

sq.q: How to prevent corrosion? Enlist few of the methods.
sq.ans: 1) Applying protective barrier coatings: Paint, grease, enamel, or plastic coating. 2) Alloying: Making Stainless Steel (Fe + Cr + Ni). 3) Metallic coatings: Galvanizing (coating with zinc) or Tin plating. 4) Cathodic protection: Connecting underground iron pipes to a sacrificial anode of Magnesium or Zinc. 5) Electroplating: Electrolytic deposition of corrosion-resistant metals like Chromium, Nickel, or Silver.

sq.q: Write chemical reactions that occur in Nelson's cell.
sq.ans: In Nelson's Diaphragm Cell (electrolysis of aqueous NaCl brine): Ionization: 2NaCl -> 2Na+ + 2Cl-; 2H2O <=> 2H+ + 2OH-. At Anode (Oxidation): 2Cl-(aq) -> Cl2(g) + 2e-. At Cathode (Reduction): 2H+(aq) + 2e- -> H2(g), or 2H2O(l) + 2e- -> H2(g) + 2OH-(aq). Solution Combination: 2Na+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) -> 2NaOH(aq). Overall Balanced Reaction: 2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) + H2(g).

sq.q: Write one example from daily life which involves the oxidation-reduction reaction.
sq.ans: Cellular Respiration in human bodies: Glucose reacts with inhaled oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water, and biological energy (ATP): C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + Energy. Carbon in glucose is oxidized (from 0 to +4 in CO2), and oxygen is reduced (from 0 in O2 to -2 in H2O). Other examples: Rusting of iron cars/gates and combustion of natural gas (methane) in stoves.

sq.q: Assign oxidation numbers to each atom in the following compounds: (a) HI, (b) PBr3, (c) CaCO3, (d) H3PO4, (e) As2O3, (f) H2SO4.
Why O2 is necessary for rusting?
sq.ans: In the electrochemical mechanism of rusting, iron acts as the anode and dissolves by losing electrons: 2Fe -> 2Fe2+ + 4e-. For this oxidation to proceed, an electron acceptor must be present at the cathodic site to consume these electrons. Dissolved oxygen (O2) acts as the essential oxidizing agent (depolarizer) by undergoing reduction in moisture: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O. Furthermore, O2 subsequently oxidizes Fe2+ to Fe3+ to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust Fe2O3.xH2O). Without O2, the cathodic reaction stalls, halting rust formation.

sq.q: Sketch the Daniel cell, labeling the cathode, anode and the direction of flow of the electrons.
sq.ans: Description of sketch: Left beaker: Zinc strip (Anode, -) immersed in 1.0 M ZnSO4 solution (Oxidation: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-). Right beaker: Copper strip (Cathode, +) immersed in 1.0 M CuSO4 solution (Reduction: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu). Connecting wire with Voltmeter joins Zn to Cu; electrons flow from Zinc Anode to Copper Cathode through the external wire. Inverted U-tube Salt Bridge containing agar gel and KCl links both beakers (K+ migrates to cathode, Cl- to anode) to maintain ionic electrical neutrality.

sq.q: Write down some possible uses of an electrolytic cell.
sq.ans: 1) Extraction of highly reactive metals from molten salts (e.g. Sodium in Down's cell, Aluminium in Hall-Héroult cell, Magnesium). 2) Commercial manufacture of industrial chemicals (NaOH, Cl2 gas, H2 gas in Nelson's cell). 3) Electrolytic refining and purification of crude metals (e.g. Copper, Silver, Gold). 4) Electroplating of base metals with protective or decorative coatings (Chromium, Silver, Nickel, Tin). 5) Production of anodized aluminium.

lq.q: (a) What is electroplating? (b) Distinguish between the nature of the anode and cathode in such a process. Describe electroplating of chromium or silver on steel.
lq.ans: (a) Electroplating: Electroplating is the electrochemical process of depositing a thin, uniform, tightly adherent layer of a superior, corrosion-resistant metal (e.g. silver, gold, chromium, tin, nickel) onto the surface of an inferior base metal (e.g. steel, iron, copper) using electrolysis. (b) Nature of Electrodes: Anode: Made of a pure sheet of the metal to be deposited (e.g. pure silver Ag or chromium Cr); it dissolves during electrolysis, continually replenishing the metal ions in the electrolyte. Cathode: Made of the thoroughly cleaned metallic article to be coated (e.g. steel spoon or car bumper); metal cations from the electrolyte migrate to it and deposit as a solid metallic film. Example (Silver Plating): The object (spoon) is cleaned with caustic alkali and acid, then hung as the cathode. A pure silver plate is used as the anode. The electrolyte is an aqueous solution of silver cyanide Na[Ag(CN)2] or AgNO3 with sodium cyanide. Reactions: At Anode: Ag(s) -> Ag+(aq) + e- (silver dissolves); At Cathode: Ag+(aq) + e- -> Ag(s) (pure silver deposits onto the spoon). Result is an attractive, lustrous, corrosion-resistant silver-plated spoon.

lq.q: Differentiate between the processes of oxidation and reduction. Write an equation to illustrate each.
lq.ans: Comprehensive Comparison: 1) Oxygen Concept: Oxidation is the addition of oxygen: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Reduction is the removal of oxygen: CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O. 2) Hydrogen Concept: Oxidation is the removal of hydrogen: H2S + Cl2 -> 2HCl + S. Reduction is the addition of hydrogen: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. 3) Electronic Concept: Oxidation is the Loss of Electrons (LEO): Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e-, or Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-. Reduction is the Gain of Electrons (GER): Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, or Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-. 4) Oxidation State: Oxidation causes an increase in oxidation number (e.g. Fe2+ (+2) to Fe3+ (+3)). Reduction causes a decrease in oxidation number (e.g. Mn (+7) in KMnO4 to Mn (+2) in MnSO4). Combined equation: Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s), where Zinc is oxidized (0 to +2) and Copper is reduced (+2 to 0).

lq.q: (a) What is corrosion? Explain rusting of iron as an example of corrosion. (b) Differentiate between electrolytic cell and voltaic cell.
lq.ans: (a) Corrosion & Rusting: Corrosion is the slow and spontaneous destruction of metals due to chemical or electrochemical reactions with their ambient environment (oxygen and moisture). Rusting of Iron: Iron surfaces with scratches, dents, or impurities set up galvanic micro-cells. At Anodic Site: Iron metal oxidizes: 2Fe(s) -> 2Fe2+(aq) + 4e- (E° = +0.44 V). The released electrons flow through the conductive iron to an oxygen-rich region. At Cathodic Site: In the presence of moisture and dissolved atmospheric CO2 (acting as H+ electrolyte), oxygen is reduced: O2(g) + 4H+(aq) + 4e- -> 2H2O(l). The generated Fe2+ ions diffuse through the moisture droplet, react further with dissolved O2: 4Fe2+(aq) + O2(g) + (4 + 2x)H2O(l) -> 2Fe2O3.xH2O(s) (Rust) + 8H+(aq). Because rust is flaky and porous, it peels off, continuously exposing underlying iron until the metal is destroyed. (b) Electrolytic vs Voltaic Cell: 1) Energy Conversion: Electrolytic cell converts electrical energy into chemical energy; Voltaic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy. 2) Spontaneity: Electrolytic reaction is non-spontaneous and requires an external battery; Voltaic reaction is spontaneous and produces electric voltage. 3) Electrode Charges: Electrolytic: Anode is positive (+), Cathode is negative (-); Voltaic: Anode is negative (-), Cathode is positive (+). 4) Salt Bridge: Voltaic cells use a salt bridge; simple electrolytic cells do not require a salt bridge.

lq.q: Discuss the method of recovering / extracting metal from its ore using Down's cell.
lq.ans: Extraction of Sodium Metal in Down's Cell: 1) Principle: Electrolysis of molten (fused) anhydrous sodium chloride (NaCl). 2) Operating Conditions: Pure NaCl has a very high melting point of 801 °C. To make the process commercially viable, Calcium chloride (CaCl2) is added in a ratio of ~1:2, which depresses the melting point down to about 600 °C. 3) Cell Construction: A cylindrical steel vessel lined with refractory firebricks. A large central graphite carbon rod serves as the anode (+). It is surrounded by an annular iron or steel cylinder serving as the cathode (-). A cylindrical steel wire gauze diaphragm separates anode and cathode to keep molten sodium and chlorine gas apart. 4) Electrode Reactions: Ionization: 2NaCl(l) -> 2Na+(l) + 2Cl-(l). At Anode (+): 2Cl-(l) -> Cl2(g) + 2e- (chlorine gas rises and is collected via an inverted nickel hood). At Cathode (-): 2Na+(l) + 2e- -> 2Na(l) (molten sodium metal forms as a liquid). 5) Collection: Molten sodium has a density (0.97 g/cm3) lower than the molten salt mixture (approx 2.0 g/cm3). It floats to the surface and rises through a vertical pipe into an external collecting vessel, where it is drained and packaged under mineral oil.

lq.q: Discuss the preparation of Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) from Brine along with diagram and reactions at cathode and anode.
lq.ans: Preparation of NaOH in Nelson's Diaphragm Cell: 1) Raw Material: Brine (saturated aqueous solution of sodium chloride, ~25% NaCl). 2) Cell Construction: A U-shaped perforated steel cathode lined on the inside with a porous asbestos diaphragm. A titanium or graphite anode hangs suspended inside the U-tube immersed in brine. The outer casing has an exit pipe for hydrogen and a collection catch basin at the bottom. 3) Working Mechanism: Brine enters the anode compartment. The asbestos diaphragm allows liquid and positive Na+ ions to slowly seep through to the cathode by hydrostatic pressure, while keeping generated Cl2 gas away from OH- ions. 4) Electrode Reactions: In aqueous solution: 2NaCl -> 2Na+ + 2Cl-; 2H2O <=> 2H+ + 2OH-. At Anode (+): Chloride ions discharge preferentially: 2Cl-(aq) -> Cl2(g) + 2e- (collected at upper gas outlet). At Cathode (-): Water molecules / hydrogen ions discharge preferentially over Na+ due to lower reduction potential: 2H2O(l) + 2e- -> H2(g) + 2OH-(aq) (hydrogen gas escapes via upper cathode pipe). Formation of NaOH: Hydroxide ions (OH-) combine with Na+ ions in the catholyte: Na+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> NaOH(aq). The solution of NaOH containing some unreacted NaCl drips through the perforations into the catch basin and is concentrated by fractional crystallization to obtain pure solid flakes of caustic soda (NaOH).

definitions.def: The branch of chemistry that deals with the relationship between electricity and chemical reactions, and their interconversion.
The process involving loss of electrons, loss of hydrogen, or addition of oxygen, resulting in an increase in oxidation state.
The process involving gain of electrons, gain of hydrogen, or removal of oxygen, resulting in a decrease in oxidation state.
A chemical species that accepts electrons from another reactant and undergoes reduction itself.
A chemical species that donates electrons to another reactant and undergoes oxidation itself.
A chemical substance whose aqueous solution or molten liquid conducts electric current by the movement of ions.
An electrochemical cell that produces electricity spontaneously from an internal chemical redox reaction.
An electrochemical cell that uses an external electric current to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.
The slow, continuous eating away of metals through electrochemical oxidation by environmental agents (oxygen and moisture).
The process of coating iron or steel with a protective layer of zinc to prevent rusting by sacrificial protection.

summary.en: Metals are elements with low ionization energies that readily lose valence electrons to form electropositive cations (M -> M+ + e-). They are lustrous, malleable, ductile, and excellent electrical/thermal conductors.

subtopics.name: Physical Properties of Metals
subtopics.desc: Key physical characteristics: (1) Metallic Luster: Freshly cut metal surfaces have a characteristic shine because mobile valence electrons reflect incident light; (2) High Thermal and Electrical Conductivity: Free delocalized electrons transfer heat and electric charge rapidly; (3) Malleability: Ability to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets (Gold is the most malleable metal); (4) Ductility: Ability to be drawn into thin wires (1 g of gold can be drawn into a wire 2 km long); (5) High Melting and Boiling Points (except Mercury, which is a liquid at room temperature; Gallium and Cesium melt in hand); (6) High Density and Sonorous nature (ring when struck).
subtopics.sciNote: Point to remember: Mercury (Hg) is the only metal that exists in the liquid state at room temperature.

subtopics.name: Chemical Properties and Electropositive Character
subtopics.desc: Electropositive Character (Metallic Character): The tendency of an atom to lose its valence electrons and form a positive cation: M -> M+ + e- (monovalent), M -> M2+ + 2e- (divalent), M -> M3+ + 3e- (trivalent). Metals react with oxygen to form Basic Oxides (e.g. 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO; MgO + H2O -> Mg(OH)2 which turns red litmus blue). Trend in Periodic Table: Electropositivity decreases across a period from left to right (due to higher nuclear charge and decreasing atomic size) and increases down a group from top to bottom (due to increasing atomic size and shielding effect).
subtopics.sciNote: Alkali metals (Group 1) are the most electropositive elements in the periodic table.

subtopics.name: Alkali Metals (Group 1: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs)
subtopics.desc: Characteristics: Valence configuration ns1; very low ionization energies (Li = 520, Na = 496 kJ/mol); soft enough to be cut with a knife; low densities (Li, Na, K float on water). They never occur free in nature because of intense reactivity; stored under kerosene oil to prevent reaction with atmospheric moisture and oxygen. Reactions: (1) With Water: React violently, releasing hydrogen gas and forming strong alkaline hydroxides: 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g) + Heat. (2) With Oxygen: Form normal oxides, peroxides, and superoxides: 4Li + O2 -> 2Li2O (monoxide); 2Na + O2 -> Na2O2 (sodium peroxide); K + O2 -> KO2 (potassium superoxide). (3) With Halogens: Form ionic halides: 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl.
subtopics.sciNote: Why is sodium kept stored under kerosene oil? Sodium reacts vigorously and exothermically with moisture and oxygen in the air, catching fire.

subtopics.name: Alkaline Earth Metals (Group 2: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba)
subtopics.desc: Characteristics: Valence configuration ns2; harder and denser than alkali metals; higher melting and boiling points; higher ionization energies (Be = 899, Mg = 738 kJ/mol). Less reactive than alkali metals. Reactions: (1) With Water: Beryllium does not react with water; Magnesium reacts only with steam (Mg + H2O(steam) -> MgO + H2); Calcium reacts slowly with cold water: Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2. (2) With Oxygen: Form normal basic oxides upon heating: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO; 2Ca + O2 -> 2CaO. (3) With Halogens: Form ionic dihalides: Mg + Cl2 -> MgCl2; Ca + Cl2 -> CaCl2.

subtopics.name: Inertness of Silver (Ag), Gold (Au), and Platinum (Pt)
subtopics.desc: Noble Metals: Transition metals that show little or no chemical reactivity under ordinary conditions. They do not react with atmospheric oxygen, water, moisture, or non-oxidizing dilute acids (HCl, H2SO4). Silver (Ag): Lustrous white metal, highest electrical and thermal conductivity of all metals; used in jewelry, silverware, photography (AgBr), and mirrors. Tarnishes slowly due to atmospheric H2S forming black Ag2S. Gold (Au): Highly unreactive, yellow lustrous metal; unaffected by single acids, dissolves only in 'Aqua Regia' (a 3:1 mixture of concentrated HCl and HNO3). Platinum (Pt): Silver-white metal, extremely resistant to corrosion, high melting point (1772 °C); used in fine jewelry, automotive catalytic converters, laboratory crucibles, and chemotherapy drugs (Cisplatin).
subtopics.sciNote: Aqua Regia ('Royal Water') dissolves gold and platinum by generating nascent chlorine: HNO3 + 3HCl -> NOCl + 2H2O + 2[Cl].

subtopics.name: The Carat System of Gold Purity
subtopics.desc: Pure gold (100% Au) is designated as 24 Carats. However, pure 24-carat gold is too soft to withstand wear and cannot hold gemstones securely in jewelry. Therefore, it is alloyed with copper or silver to increase hardness: (1) 24 Carat Gold = 24/24 parts gold (100% pure); (2) 22 Carat Gold = 22 parts pure gold + 2 parts copper/silver (91.6% pure gold), ideal for traditional jewelry; (3) 18 Carat Gold = 18 parts pure gold + 6 parts copper/silver (75% pure gold), used in diamond rings and watches.
subtopics.sciNote: Carat formula: Percentage of Gold = (Carat Number / 24) x 100%.

summary.en: Non-metals are electronegative elements that gain electrons to form anions. Halogens (Group 17: F2, Cl2, Br2, I2) are powerful oxidizing agents whose reactivity decreases down the group, giving rise to displacement reactions.

subtopics.name: Physical and Chemical Properties of Non-Metals
subtopics.desc: Physical Properties: Exist in all three states of matter at room temperature: Gases (H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, noble gases), Liquid (Bromine Br2), Solids (Carbon, Sulphur, Phosphorus, Iodine); poor conductors of heat and electricity (except Graphite); non-malleable, brittle as solids, dull appearance (except Iodine and Diamond which are lustrous). Chemical Properties: High electronegativities; gain electrons to form anions: X + e- -> X-; form acidic or neutral covalent oxides (e.g. CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3, turns blue litmus red; SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4; NO and CO are neutral).
subtopics.sciNote: Bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.

subtopics.name: Halogens and Displacement Reactions
subtopics.desc: The Halogens (Group 17: Fluorine F2 pale yellow gas, Chlorine Cl2 greenish-yellow gas, Bromine Br2 reddish-brown liquid, Iodine I2 dark purple-black solid): Have 7 valence electrons (ns2 np5) and need only 1 electron to complete their octet. They are the most reactive non-metals and strong oxidizing agents. Relative Oxidizing Power: Decreases down Group 17: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. Halogen Displacement Reactions: A more reactive halogen (higher in the group) will displace a less reactive halogen (lower in the group) from its aqueous halide solution: (1) Cl2(g) + 2KBr(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + Br2(l) (Chlorine displaces Bromine); (2) Cl2(g) + 2KI(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + I2(s) (Chlorine displaces Iodine); (3) Br2(l) + 2KI(aq) -> 2KBr(aq) + I2(s) (Bromine displaces Iodine); (4) Iodine cannot displace Chlorine or Bromine (I2 + 2KCl -> No Reaction).
subtopics.sciNote: Halogen displacement is an analytical test to identify halide ions in laboratory qualitative analysis.

topics.title: Daily Life Applications of Metals and Non-Metals

summary.en: Metals (Iron, Aluminum, Copper, Sodium, Magnesium, Calcium) and Non-Metals (Oxygen, Nitrogen, Chlorine, Carbon, Hydrogen) play vital roles in construction, transport, electronics, agriculture, and human physiology.
summary.ur: دھاتیں اور غیر دھاتیں تعمیرات، نقل و حمل، بجلی، زراعت، ادویات اور انسانی زندگی کے نظام میں بنیادی کردار ادا کرتی ہیں۔

subtopics.name: Applications of Major Metals and Non-Metals
subtopics.desc: Metals: (1) Iron (Fe): Structural steel for bridges, buildings, railways; central atom in blood hemoglobin; (2) Aluminum (Al): Aircraft bodies, window frames, high-voltage transmission cables, cooking foil (lightweight and corrosion-resistant); (3) Copper (Cu): Electrical wiring, electric motors, water pipes, coinage; (4) Sodium (Na): Yellow vapor street lamps, heat exchanger in nuclear reactors; (5) Magnesium (Mg): Flares, fireworks, lightweight alloys (Magnalium), antacid medicine (milk of magnesia); (6) Calcium (Ca): Bones, teeth, cement, mortar, limestone. Non-Metals: (1) Oxygen (O2): Respiration in living organisms, combustion, steel manufacturing, hospital oxygen cylinders; (2) Nitrogen (N2): Inert food packaging (chips bags), synthesis of ammonia (Haber process) for urea fertilizers; (3) Chlorine (Cl2): Municipal water disinfection, PVC plastics, bleaching powder; (4) Carbon (C): Fossil fuels, graphite electrodes, diamond cutting tools, carbon fiber in aerospace.
subtopics.sciNote: Hemoglobin contains iron (Fe2+) to transport oxygen in blood; chlorophyll in green plants contains magnesium (Mg2+) to capture sunlight for photosynthesis.
