part1_Bair_e_Roma.heading: The Purchase of Bair-e-Roma
part1_Bair_e_Roma.text:
Arabia is a desert land where water is scarce. Even if water is found, it is not always suitable for drinking. In olden days people had to travel long distances to fetch water and sometimes they had to remain without it for a day or even more. When Hazrat Muhammad (SAW) migrated to Medina, there was only one well of sweet water in town. It was called Bair-e-Roma. The well was owned by a Jew who sold its water at a high price. The companions of Rasool (SAW) were generally poor and found it hard to get water. One day they came to Hazrat Muhammad (SAW) and apprised him about their condition. Hazrat Muhammad (SAW) was sitting in the Masjid at that time and many of his companions were there. He looked around and said, 'Is there anyone here who would like to purchase paradise for himself in return for Bair-e-Roma?'

Hazrat Usman (RA) stood up and went out quietly. He went to the Jew and offered to buy the well from him. The Jew did not agree to sell it at first, but then he thought it to be more profitable to make Hazrat Usman (RA) a partner as he was a rich businessman. He, therefore, agreed to sell half of his share in the well to Hazrat Usman (RA) for twelve thousand dirhams (silver coins). It was agreed that Hazrat Usman (RA) would receive all the income from the well for one day and the Jew for the next.

Hazrat Usman (RA) returned to the Masjid and offered his share in the well to Hazrat Muhammad (SAW). It was proclaimed in Medina that everyone could carry as much water, free of cost, as he/she liked, on the day appointed for Hazrat Usman (RA). The Muslims as well as the Jews made full use of Hazrat Usman's (RA) generosity and carried enough water to last for the next day as well. The Jew learnt a bitter lesson. Whereas he had hoped to make more money, he made none at all. He went to Hazrat Usman (RA) and offered to sell the other half of the well also. Hazrat Usman (RA) could have refused to buy it, for the Muslims had no longer any difficulty, but such was his generosity that he paid the Jew whatever he asked for his share. The well was dedicated as an endowment to the people of Medina. The well exists in Medina to this day and is known as Bair-e-Usman or Usman's well.

part2_The_Famine.heading: The Relief during Famine
part2_The_Famine.text:
During the days of Caliph Umar (RA) a famine broke out in Arabia. Hazrat Umar (RA) was greatly distressed. He did all he could to lessen the hardships of the people. All the food that was brought into Medina was purchased by the Caliph for the Bait-ul-Mal and distributed among the people. One day he learnt that a thousand camel-load of flour belonging to Hazrat Usman (RA) had reached Medina. Hazrat Umar (RA) went to him straight away and offered to buy the entire stock from him at a handsome profit. Hazrat Usman (RA), however, turned down the offer and said, 'I have another buyer who is offering me much more.'

The Caliph said, 'I can offer you 50% profit.' Hazrat Usman (RA) still declined. Hazrat Umar (RA) raised his offer higher, but Hazrat Usman (RA) did not agree and said, 'I have a buyer who is offering me even more.' The Caliph offered to pay three times the price of the flour, then four times and even five times. Hazrat Usman (RA) rejected all these offers. Hazrat Umar (RA) got up angrily and said, 'Usman, why have you become so hard-hearted now, whereas you used to be generous in the days of Hazrat Muhammad (SAW)?' He answered, 'I am only doing business and I would sell my goods to the one who would give me the greatest profit.' The Caliph raised his offer higher and higher until he was willing to pay nine times the price of the flour as profit.

Hazrat Usman (RA) then stood up calmly and said, 'Umar, I have already sold my stock. The buyer is Allah who has promised to pay me at least ten times the price as profit and may raise it to seventy or even seven hundred times. Go and distribute the flour among the people in the name of Allah.' The Caliph was so touched by the generosity of Hazrat Usman (RA) that he wept. He then embraced him and begged forgiveness for the harsh words he had used earlier. Then the food was distributed among the people happily and generously.

shortQuestions.q: Why did Hazrat Umar weep?
shortQuestions.a: Hazrat Umar (RA) wept because he was deeply touched by the extraordinary generosity, selflessness, and piety of Hazrat Usman (RA), who donated a thousand camel-loads of flour for the sake of Allah to feed starving people rather than selling it for huge earthly profits.

shortQuestions.q: Why did the Jew agree to Hazrat Usman's offer?
shortQuestions.a: The Jew agreed to sell half of his share in the well because Hazrat Usman (RA) was a very wealthy and respected merchant. The Jew calculated that partnering with Hazrat Usman (RA) would bring more customers and yield greater financial profits.

shortQuestions.q: What simple steps can you incorporate into your life to foster generosity?
shortQuestions.a: We can foster generosity by sharing our pocket money with the needy, volunteering our time to teach or help others, sharing food with neighbors, donating unused clothes and books, and offering emotional support and kind words to those in distress.

shortQuestions.q: How did the Jew learn a bitter lesson?
shortQuestions.a: On the day allocated to Hazrat Usman (RA), people took enough water free of cost to last for two days. Consequently, nobody came to buy water from the Jew on his turn. Having earned nothing, the Jew realized his greed had failed and was compelled to sell the remaining half of the well to Hazrat Usman (RA).

shortQuestions.q: What is the role of generosity in Islamic history?
shortQuestions.a: Generosity is one of the foundational pillars of Islamic society. It fosters social equality, relieves suffering during crises, establishes trust and brotherhood among Muslims, and strengthens the community through charitable endowments (Waqf) and Zakat.

shortQuestions.q: Service to humanity is liked by Allah. Elaborate.
shortQuestions.a: Islam teaches that the best among people are those who benefit others. When a person feeds the hungry, relieves hardships, or provides water to the thirsty, Allah multiplies their reward tenfold to seven hundred times and grants them high stations in Paradise.

shortQuestions.q: What did Hazrat Usman do when Hazrat Muhammad (SAW) said: 'Is there anyone here who would like to purchase paradise for himself in return for Bair-e-Roma?'
shortQuestions.a: Hazrat Usman (RA) stood up quietly, left the mosque, went directly to the Jew who owned Bair-e-Roma, and negotiated to purchase half of the well for twelve thousand dirhams, subsequently buying the other half and dedicating it as an endowment for all people.

shortQuestions.q: Why did Hazrat Usman keep on rejecting the offer of Hazrat Umar?
shortQuestions.a: Hazrat Usman (RA) kept rejecting Hazrat Umar's offers because he had already struck a deal with Allah Almighty, who promised a profit of at least ten times, up to seventy or seven hundred times, by distributing the grain freely to the starving public in His name.

shortQuestions.q: Identify a real life situation / problem that could be improved with generosity and how will you display personal generosity to that situation/problem?
shortQuestions.a: Poverty and malnutrition among street children is a major issue in our society. This can be improved by establishing free meal centers and educational sponsorships. Personally, I can donate a portion of my monthly allowance and dedicate weekends to tutoring underprivileged children in my locality.

b. make a bargain with the owner of the well

essayGenerosity.title: Generosity
essayGenerosity.text: Generosity is one of the noblest human virtues. It means being sympathetic towards someone in order to be helpful, being kind and encouraging, and sharing one's money, time, and energy with others to make their lives better without expecting anything in return. In Islam, generosity holds a supreme position, exemplified by the holy Prophet Muhammad (SAW) and his companions. Hazrat Usman (RA) demonstrated supreme generosity by purchasing the well of Bair-e-Roma for public use and donating a thousand camel-loads of food during a severe famine in Medina. True generosity does not depend on wealth alone; sharing a comforting word, smiling at someone, or lending a helping hand to an underprivileged person is equally generous. When individuals practice generosity, poverty is reduced, social harmony flourishes, and humanity becomes united in compassion and love.

writing.summary: The lesson 'The Two Bargains' highlights the unmatched generosity of Hazrat Usman (RA) through two historical incidents. First, when Muslims migrated to Medina, sweet drinking water was scarce and a Jew sold water from Bair-e-Roma at exorbitant prices. At the Prophet's (SAW) call, Hazrat Usman bought half the well for 12,000 dirhams and allowed everyone free access. The Jew, unable to sell water, was forced to sell the remaining half to Hazrat Usman, who dedicated it as an eternal endowment. Second, during a devastating famine in Caliph Umar's reign, Hazrat Usman imported a thousand camel-loads of flour. Rejecting Caliph Umar's offer of huge profits, he declared that he had traded with Allah, who promised a return of ten to seven hundred times, and distributed the entire stock free to the suffering people.

engChapters.title: Hope is the Thing with Feathers

poet.name: Emily Dickinson
poet.bio: Emily Dickinson is considered one of the most original 19th-century American poets. She was born in Amherst, Massachusetts, to a family well known for supporting the local college. Her mother was a religious, hardworking housewife. Emily was educated at Amherst Academy. She lived a secluded life. Her works have been a source of much comfort to distressed hearts. 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers' is such an example. She died at the age of fifty-five.

poem: “Hope” is the thing with feathers -
That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words -
And never stops - at all -
And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -
And sore must be the storm -
That could abash the little Bird
That kept so many warm -
I’ve heard it in the chilliest land -
And on the strangest Sea -
Yet - never - in Extremity,
It asked a crumb - of me.

shortQuestions.q: What is the implicit and explicit meaning of the poem 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers'?
shortQuestions.a: Explicitly, the poem describes a little feathered bird that perches in the soul, sings a ceaseless wordless melody, braves fierce storms, and never asks for a single crumb of food. Implicitly, the poem is an extended metaphor representing hope as an eternal, resilient spiritual force within the human heart that comforts us in our darkest hours without ever demanding anything in return.

shortQuestions.q: What is the theme of the poem 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers'?
shortQuestions.a: The central theme is the resilience, immortality, and selflessness of hope. Hope is an invincible presence residing within the human spirit that remains strongest during periods of pain, adversity, and despair.

shortQuestions.q: How does the bird react to hardships in the poem 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers'?
shortQuestions.a: The bird reacts to hardships with remarkable resilience and courage. Instead of fleeing or going silent, its song sounds 'sweetest in the Gale.' It continues to sing and provide warmth, refusing to be abashed even by the fiercest storms.

shortQuestions.q: Discuss how 'Hope' and 'the Thing with Feathers' are similar.
shortQuestions.a: Both hope and a bird are delicate yet resilient, possess wings to lift human spirits above despair, sing continuously to bring comfort, and survive in harsh, stormy weather. Like a gentle bird perching on a bough, hope perches quietly inside the soul.

shortQuestions.q: What does the poem reveal about hope?
shortQuestions.a: The poem reveals that hope is universal, unconditional, and completely selfless. It is available to everyone everywhere—even in the 'chilliest land' and 'strangest Sea'—and never asks for even a 'crumb' in payment.

shortQuestions.q: What do you understand by 'And sore must be the storm'?
shortQuestions.a: It means that a storm (trial, tragedy, or grief) would have to be extraordinarily harsh, severe, and catastrophic to crush or silence the resilient little bird of hope that has kept so many souls warm.

shortQuestions.q: Do you like this poem? Why?
shortQuestions.a: Yes, I like this poem immensely because of its uplifting imagery and positive message. Emily Dickinson's portrayal of hope as a singing bird brings deep psychological comfort and motivates us never to despair during difficult times.

shortQuestions.q: Read the first stanza of the poem and write: Which abstract noun is described as having living characteristics? What living characteristics does this item have?
shortQuestions.a: The abstract noun is 'Hope'. It is given living avian characteristics: having feathers, perching (landing) in the human soul, and singing a perpetual wordless tune without ever stopping.

mcqs.q: The Poet's comparison of hope to a bird is made in the form of:
mcqs.ans: d. metaphor

mcqs.q: The poet uses the words 'gale' and 'storm' as metaphor. What do these words represent?
options: d. times of success and growth
mcqs.ans: b. hard or painful times

mcqs.q: 'Hope is helpful in times of pain, sorrow and difficulty'. Which of the following lines from the poem best support this statement?
options: a. 'Hope' is the thing with feathers - That perches in the soul -
b. And sings the tune without the words - And never stops - at all -
c. And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard - And sore must be the storm -
d. Yet - never - in Extremity, It asked a crumb - of me.
mcqs.ans: c. And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard - And sore must be the storm -

mcqs.q: The poet says that 'And sings the tune without the words'. Why does the bird of hope sing in a tune that has no words?
options: a. To emphasize that hope does not need to be put into words to be felt
b. To point out that it is very difficult for people to express whether they feel hopeful or not
c. To suggest that people are unable to understand the feeling of hope
d. To indicate that people who are always hopeful are also often forgetful
mcqs.ans: a. To emphasize that hope does not need to be put into words to be felt

mcqs.q: What does the word 'abash' mean in the poem?
mcqs.ans: d. to silence / embarrass

writing.summary: In the poem 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers', Emily Dickinson uses an extended metaphor to compare hope to a resilient little singing bird. This bird perches within the human spirit and sings an unending tune that requires no words. Hope is universal, enduring across the chilliest lands and strangest seas, yet it remains completely selfless, never asking for anything in return.

engChapters.title: The Fantastic Shoemaker
engChapters.author: Waheedullah

reading.story:
I first met him in my youthful days in the holy month of Ramazan, when my father took me to his shop for a pair of new shoes for the coming Eid. His shop was in a small but busy street of Qissa Khwani Bazar. A monstrous size black 'Peshawari Chappal' overhung on the faint coloured wooden door of his shop. The inside of the shop was as quiet and serene as that of a sacred holy place. There were some old wooden stools and in the window some pairs of shoes were visible. A big smooth square-shaped stone, a heavy wooden mallet, an awl and a three-legged anvil were on the right side of the shop. The rest was as barren as a desert because he made only those pairs of shoes that were ordered. At the far end wall of the shop was hanging a small signboard showing 'Zarin Gul Brothers'.

The shoes that Zarin Gul made never failed to fit the feet and they lasted extraordinarily longer than usual. To make shoes — such shoes as he made — seemed to me then and seems to me now, mysterious and wonderful. I still remember my hesitant remarks, while stretching out to him my youthful foot: 'Isn't it awfully hard to make shoes in such tough conditions?' The serpentine wrinkles wriggled on his smiling face and he answered, 'It is an art!'

Zarin Gul's remarks about shoe-making and their suitability to different people were so authoritative and final that nobody dared reject them. My father, though chieftain of the area, would accept his views about a particular pair of shoes with a brisk nod. It was not possible to go to him often because there was something in his shoes that was beyond the temporary. It would not be wrong to say that durability was stitched into them.

I cannot forget that day on which I had to say to him, 'Zarin Gul Kaka, my last pair of shoes makes a creaking sound, you know.' He looked at me with strange looks as if expecting me to withdraw the statement and then said, 'It shouldn't have creaked.' 'It did, I am afraid,' I said with a quivering tone. At that he lowered his eyes, as if hunting for the memory of those pair of shoes. I really felt sorry that I mentioned this petty thing, which looked to him so serious and grave. 'Send them back,' he said, 'I will look at them. Some shoes are bad from birth. If I can do nothing with them, I will give back the amount you paid for them.'

Then I went abroad to pursue my higher studies and career and could not have the opportunity to meet Zarin Gul, the fantastic shoemaker, for several years. After several years I returned to Peshawar. And the first shop I went to was my old friend Zarin Gul's. I had left a man of fifty; I came back to one of sixty-five, worn and torn like an overused pair of shoes. He shook his bony hand with me, but the grip of his hand was as tight as it was many years ago. At first, he did not know me. But when I got myself introduced, his brooded eyes sparkled with a smile. 'Do you want any shoes?' he asked. 'I can make them quickly, because I have plenty of free time.'

Then he looked at my 'branded shoes' and said, 'Those are not my shoes.' His tone was not one of anger, or of sorrow, not even of contempt, but there was in it something quiet that froze my blood. He put his hand down and pressed a finger on the place where my left shoe was not quite comfortable. 'It hurts you there,' he said. 'Do the big shoe-making companies have no self-respect?' And then he spoke bitterly against the big multinationals that have extended their tentacles to the shoe-making trade. He told me how these companies had hired the craftsmen of the shoe-making trade. 'These big firms use their hands, not their brain or experience.' I asked Zarin Gul Kaka why he didn't join these big firms if his trade was not doing well. His reply was crisp and blunt, 'I am an artist, not a machine who will blindly follow their irrational and stupid dictations. They get it all,' he continued, 'by advertisement, not by work, and presently we have no work.'

Looking at his crumpled leathered face, I saw things I had not noticed before, bitter things and bitter struggle. His face and voice made so deep an impression on me that during the next few minutes I ordered many pairs. I wanted to make him advance payment but he refused, though he badly needed money, by saying, 'Pay it when the shoes are ready to deliver.'

A week later, I came to where his shop had been. I was surprised to see that the monstrous size black 'Peshawari Chappal' was no more hanging on the wooden door of his shop. A big size signboard displaying the name of a famous shoe-brand was hanging on his shop. I went in and said, 'Zarin Gul Kaka?' 'No sir,' a smartly dressed young man replied, 'No, but we can attend to anything with pleasure; we've taken the shop over.' 'Yes, yes,' I said, 'but where is Zarin Gul Kaka?' 'Oh!' he answered, 'dead.' 'Dead! But I have to receive the shoes that I ordered last week.' 'Ah!' he said, 'poor old man starved himself. Slow starvation, doctor called it! He never gave himself time to eat; never had a penny in the house. All went in rent and leather.'

As I was coming back with a heavy heart, the words of Zarin Gul, the fantastic shoemaker, were tinkling in my mind: 'Do the big shoe-making companies have no self-respect?'

shortQuestions.q: Why is Zarin Gul different from other businessmen?
shortQuestions.a: Zarin Gul is different because he views shoe-making as an art rather than a commercial trade. He never made shoes in advance or for display, used only high-grade leather, crafted shoes exclusively on custom order, guaranteed perfect fit and unmatched durability, and refused to compromise on quality for profit or advertising.

shortQuestions.q: How did the author come in touch with the Zarin Gul Brothers?
shortQuestions.a: The author came in touch with Zarin Gul Brothers in his youthful days during the holy month of Ramazan, when his father took him to Zarin Gul's shop in Qissa Khwani Bazar to order a pair of new shoes for the upcoming Eid festival.

shortQuestions.q: Describe the shoemaker and his shop.
shortQuestions.a: The shop was located in a narrow, bustling street of Qissa Khwani Bazar. It had a faint wooden door overhung by a huge black Peshawari chappal and a signboard reading 'Zarin Gul Brothers'. Inside, it was as quiet and serene as a sacred place, furnished with old wooden stools, a smooth stone, a wooden mallet, an awl, and a three-legged anvil. Zarin Gul was a dedicated craftsman with a lean, wrinkled face, bony hands with a firm grip, and eyes that reflected intense commitment to his art.

shortQuestions.q: What were Zarin Gul's priorities in making shoes?
shortQuestions.a: Zarin Gul's highest priorities were impeccable quality, comfort, durability, and artistic integrity. He prioritized crafting shoes that fitted the customer's foot perfectly and lasted extraordinarily long over commercial advertising, rapid mass production, or easy money.

shortQuestions.q: What is the setting of the story?
shortQuestions.a: The story is set in the historic and vibrant Qissa Khwani Bazar in Peshawar, Pakistan, inside the modest, tranquil workshop of the traditional shoemaker Zarin Gul.

shortQuestions.q: What is the conflict about in the story?
shortQuestions.a: The central conflict is between authentic traditional craftsmanship and modern commercial industrialization. It pits the dedicated artisan Zarin Gul, who values quality and integrity, against giant multinational corporations that rely on flashy advertisements, mass production, and cheap labor despite producing inferior shoes.

shortQuestions.q: What was the author's opinion about Zarin Gul as a shoemaker?
shortQuestions.a: The author considered Zarin Gul a true artist and a 'fantastic shoemaker' whose craftsmanship was mysterious and wonderful. He admired his unwavering honesty, authoritative expertise, and uncompromising dedication to his craft.

shortQuestions.q: Why did the author visit the shop after a long time?
shortQuestions.a: The author had gone abroad for many years to pursue his higher education and professional career. Upon returning to Peshawar, he visited Zarin Gul's shop out of nostalgic respect and affection for the master craftsman.

shortQuestions.q: What was Zarin Gul's complaint against 'big firms'?
shortQuestions.a: Zarin Gul complained that big multinational firms lacked self-respect and took away all business through misleading advertisements rather than genuine workmanship. He pointed out that they hired craftsmen to work blindly with their hands without utilizing brains or real experience, leaving genuine independent artists without work.

shortQuestions.q: Retell the story in the form of a dialogue.
shortQuestions.a:
Author: 'Peace be upon you, Zarin Gul Kaka. Do you recognize me?'
Zarin Gul: 'Yes, my boy! Welcome back. Your branded shoes... they are not mine. They hurt your left foot right here, don't they?'
Author: 'Indeed they do! Why didn't you join one of the big shoe firms, Kaka?'
Zarin Gul: 'I am an artist, not a machine! Those big companies have no self-respect. They get customers by flashy advertisement, not by good work. We have no work left.'
Author: 'Please make me several pairs! Let me pay in advance.'
Zarin Gul: 'No, pay only when they are delivered.'
(A week later)
Young Shopkeeper: 'The old man is dead, sir. Doctor called it slow starvation. He spent all his money on rent and fine leather, never keeping a penny to eat.'

grammar.title: Sentence Structure: Clauses, Simple, Compound, and Complex Sentences

definitions.independentClause: An independent clause contains a subject and a predicate and expresses a complete thought. It can stand alone as a sentence (e.g., 'I like spaghetti.').
definitions.dependentClause: A dependent clause contains a subject and a verb but does not express a complete thought. It cannot stand alone and depends on an independent clause (e.g., 'Although I like spaghetti...').
definitions.simpleSentence: A simple sentence consists of only one independent clause with a single subject and predicate.
definitions.compoundSentence: A compound sentence contains at least two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or a semicolon.
definitions.complexSentence: A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent (subordinate) clause connected by a subordinating conjunction (e.g., because, although, since, when, if).

writing.summary: In 'The Fantastic Shoemaker' by Waheedullah, the author reminisces about Zarin Gul, a master shoemaker in Peshawar's Qissa Khwani Bazar who treated shoe-making as an art. His custom-made Peshawari chappals were famed for perfect fit and exceptional durability. After returning from studies abroad years later, the author found Zarin Gul aged and struggling. Large multinational companies had monopolized the market through aggressive advertising, pushing traditional craftsmen out of work. Despite starving and unable to pay shop rent, Zarin Gul refused to compromise his artistry or work for commercial firms. A week after the author placed an order for several pairs, he discovered that Zarin Gul had died of slow starvation, having spent his last pennies on leather and rent rather than food.

storyBeginning.story: It was a stormy night. Saad was sleeping in his bedroom. All of a sudden, a violent crash of thunder rattled the window panes and plunged the entire neighborhood into darkness. A chilling gust of wind blew the curtains wildly. Saad sat upright, his heart pounding like a hammer. Through the torrential rain outside, he heard a faint, persistent scratching sound at the front door. Grabbing his rechargeable flashlight, he cautiously crept down the creaking staircase. Every shadow on the wall seemed like a crouching phantom. Gathering his courage, he unlocked the door and pulled it open. To his immense relief, shivering on the wet doormat was a soaked, frightened little puppy whining for shelter. Saad smiled, wrapped the little creature in a dry towel, and brought it inside, grateful that the terrifying storm had brought a loyal new companion into his life.

engChapters.title: Technology in Everyday Life

reading.introduction: The role of technology in our daily lives is undeniable. Technology plays a vital role and it has added convenience to our lives. From kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, to any other place of home or office, technological equipment is present in different forms and manifestations. In today's dynamic world, life without technology is very strenuous if not impossible. The offshoots of technological development have stretched out to diverse fields of health, communication, agriculture, architecture, engineering, and transportation systems. The significance of technology will get more intelligible if we dwell on its main areas:

sections.title: Health Sciences and Medicine
sections.text: Technology has been of great use in the health sciences industry. Modern electronic equipment has been discovered which has improved the quality of treatment people receive at health institutions as well as increasing their survival chances from various ailments. Another notable advance is that it has enabled doctors to discover most health problems while they are still in the developing stages, and treat them before they develop into advanced stages.

sections.title: Communication Across the Globe
sections.text: Communication across the globe is now easy. The invention and use of the internet has changed the world into a global village. People hailing from different geographical regions can virtually communicate through video calls, e-mails, as well as many social media platforms. Business owners have realized the power of using the internet to reach more customers easily by creating business websites where customers click on items to buy them in the comfort of their homes. In the past communication was limited to letter writing and waiting for postal services. Today technology has made communications instant. Now you can draft a business message and email it or fax it in a second without delays. The recipient gets the message and replies instantly. Similarly, the telephone has evolved over decades into portable cellular phones coupled with extraordinary entertainment features.

sections.title: Elimination of Paperwork and Virtual Storage
sections.text: Another importance of technology in our daily lives is that it has eliminated the bulkiness associated with paperwork. With technology, information can now be stored virtually in various storage devices such as compact disks, flash drives, and microchips. More so, the information stored in these technological devices is secured with passwords and encryption codes known only to the proprietors of the information, making it a far better and safer way of storing confidential data.

sections.title: Agricultural Industry and Biotechnology
sections.text: We cannot fail to mention that technology has been of great benefit to the agricultural industry. It is now possible to determine climatic changes as well as climatic conditions that favor various plants. Likewise, today it is possible to grow crops in a desert by use of agricultural biotechnology. With biotechnology, plants have been engineered to survive in drought conditions. Through genetic engineering, scientists have managed to introduce traits into existing genes with the goal of making crops resistant to droughts, pests, and diseases.

sections.title: Controlling and Harnessing Natural Forces
sections.text: Natural forces affect and disrupt human life and daily economic activities. For example, floods wash away farmlands and homes, carrying away fertile topsoil and disrupting crop growth. Fires burn buildings and forests. However, technology has enabled humans to build large dams which can harbor excess flood water and use that water to generate clean hydroelectric power. Also, fire is tamed to heat our homes and process industrial materials. Wind is being harnessed with turbines to generate electricity. We have converted solar energy into electrical power that lights up homes and runs businesses.

sections.title: Fast and Efficient Transportation
sections.text: Transportation is one of the basic areas of technological activity. Both businesses and individuals have benefitted from new technologies in the travel industry. 'Time is money', so we must have fast and efficient means of transport. Imagine life without well-developed transportation systems! Transportation is just as essential as food, clothing, and shelter. It has become a basic need because we use advanced transport means like cars, high-speed bullet trains, and airplanes to commute to work, transport raw materials and finished goods, go shopping, and visit friends and families across continents in a matter of hours.

shortQuestions.q: What is the role of technology in daily life?
shortQuestions.a: Technology plays an indispensable role in daily life by adding immense convenience, speed, and efficiency. It facilitates every sector, from domestic appliances in the home to advanced medicine, global communication, agriculture, security, and transport.

shortQuestions.q: Discuss how you use technology at home and in your personal life.
shortQuestions.a: At home, I use smartphones and computers to attend online classes, research educational topics, and communicate with friends and family. My family uses refrigerators, microwave ovens, washing machines, and air conditioners to make daily chores effortless.

shortQuestions.q: How does technology help transportation?
shortQuestions.a: Technology has revolutionized transportation by introducing fast, safe, and comfortable vehicles like modern cars, bullet trains, cargo ships, and aeroplanes. It saves precious time, facilitates rapid global trade, and connects distant parts of the world in hours.

shortQuestions.q: What is the importance of technology in agriculture?
shortQuestions.a: Technology enables farmers to forecast weather, analyze soil quality, and cultivate drought-resistant and pest-resistant crops through genetic engineering and biotechnology. It also allows desert farming through automated drip irrigation systems.

shortQuestions.q: How is communication made easy?
shortQuestions.a: Communication is made effortless through the internet, emails, instant messaging, smartphones, and video calls. These tools have eliminated geographic boundaries, converting the world into a connected global village where information travels in milliseconds.

shortQuestions.q: What is the impact of technology on medicine?
shortQuestions.a: Technology has revolutionized medicine by introducing sophisticated diagnostic tools (like MRI, CT scans, and ultrasound), robotic surgical instruments, and genetic therapies. These innovations allow early disease detection, increase survival rates, and improve patient care.

shortQuestions.q: Does technology impact culture and society? How?
shortQuestions.a: Yes, technology profoundly impacts culture and society. It fosters cross-cultural exchange and global awareness through social media and digital entertainment, while also changing traditional communication habits, lifestyle patterns, and work culture.

essayDiscovery.title: A Great Scientific Discovery of the 21st Century: Artificial Intelligence and Smartphones
essayDiscovery.text: The 21st century has witnessed revolutionary technological and scientific breakthroughs, among which Artificial Intelligence (AI) and modern smartphones stand out as the most transformative. In earlier times, computers were bulky machines confined to research laboratories. Today, a pocket-sized smartphone contains millions of times more processing power than the computers that landed Apollo 11 on the moon. Combined with Artificial Intelligence, smartphones can translate languages in real time, diagnose illnesses through digital imaging, facilitate global video conferencing, and automate complex tasks. AI algorithms optimize agricultural crop yields, monitor climate change, and steer autonomous electric vehicles. This discovery has democratized knowledge, allowing students anywhere in the world to access libraries and educational courses freely. AI and smart mobile technology have redefined human capability, inaugurating a truly connected global civilization.

engChapters.title: Safety First
engChapters.theme: Health, Emergency Preparedness and First Aid

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: Assalam-o-Alaikum my dearest friend! Where were you yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: Wa Alaikum Assalam! I attended a First Aid class yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: Really? What is first aid? What did you learn?

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: First aid is the help given to a sick or injured person until full medical treatment is available. First aid is about using your common sense in ways that will keep that person safe without doing harm.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: You mean if a friend has an accident or someone collapses perhaps from a heart attack, then the first person there will be the first aider or the person who will help the casualties till help arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: Yes, my dear friend.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: It's a great idea for older children and adults to do a first aid course so that they know what to do to help others. Tell me more, what else did you learn?

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: A lot of stuff. We were taught to have a first aid kit at home, school, and work place.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: What is a first aid kit? What should I keep in my first aid kit?

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: A basic first aid kit may contain: adhesive plasters in a variety of different sizes and shapes; small, medium and large sterile gauze dressings; at least two sterile eye dressings; triangular bandages; crepe rolled bandages; safety pins; disposable sterile gloves; tweezers; scissors; and essential medicines.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: When and where do you use a first aid kit?

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: Make sure you know how to use all the items in your kit, especially the medications. Train others in your family to use the kit. You may be the one who needs first aid.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: You are right, just having a first aid kit is not enough. One must know how to use it.

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: Exactly, first aid is all about what to do in emergency situations. For example, what should you do if you burn yourself on a hot stove?

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: My grandma says that you should put butter on a burn.

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: No! That's the worst thing to do!

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: Oh. Then maybe you should put ice on the burn.

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: No, the first thing you should do when you get a minor burn is run cool (not cold) water over the burn area for about 20 minutes. Later, cover it with a sterile, non-adhesive bandage or clean cloth.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: How about this? What should you do if someone is choking?

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: First you should make sure they are really choking. If they can't speak or breathe, you wrap your arms around the person quickly from behind and pull inwards and upwards with your fist (Heimlich maneuver). The air that is forced up dislodges the object. Do not hit them blindly on the back because that might lodge the object deeper into their throat.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: Similarly, what would you do if someone cuts his arm and is bleeding?

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: Take a deep breath to calm down a little. Call the emergency phone number for help, and in the meanwhile put a clean cloth over the wound, apply firm direct pressure, and elevate the injured limb above heart level.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: Great. My grandfather is elderly. God forbid if he gets a heart attack, what should I do?

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: Call medical help as soon as possible. In the meanwhile, you need to ease the strain on his heart, so make him as comfortable as possible. A half-sitting position, with his head and shoulders supported and his knees bent, is best.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: That is good information, otherwise we normally make the patient lie down. Please tell me another thing: often when we play in the sun or accidentally get hit, the nose bleeds. What should be done in that case?

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: Sit the person up straight and tilt their head slightly forward. Apply finger and thumb pressure on the soft part of the nostrils below the bridge of the nose for at least 10 minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: Wow! There is so much to learn. I think I need to take this class.

dialogue.speaker: Asim
dialogue.text: Everyone should take a first aid class. Thank you for all the information. Allah Hafiz.

dialogue.speaker: Babar
dialogue.text: Allah Hafiz.

shortQuestions.q: What is first aid?
shortQuestions.a: First aid is the immediate assistance and temporary care given to a sick or injured person until full professional medical treatment becomes available. Its aim is to preserve life, prevent condition worsening, and promote recovery.

shortQuestions.q: Discuss a situation in which you provided first aid to someone.
shortQuestions.a: Once during a school football match, my classmate scraped his knee badly and was bleeding. I immediately washed the wound with clean water, applied antiseptic liquid, pressed a sterile gauze pad to stop the bleeding, and bandaged it neatly.

shortQuestions.q: What will you do if someone cuts his foot and is bleeding?
shortQuestions.a: I will remain calm, call for emergency medical help, place a sterile cloth or gauze pad directly over the wound, apply firm continuous pressure to stop bleeding, and elevate the foot above heart level.

shortQuestions.q: You're having lunch with a friend and he begins to choke on some food. How can you help?
shortQuestions.a: I will quickly check if he can cough or speak. If his airway is blocked, I will stand behind him, wrap my arms around his waist, place a fist above his navel, and deliver quick inward and upward abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) to dislodge the trapped food.

shortQuestions.q: A passenger travelling in bus with you is complaining of breathlessness and a tight pain in the chest. You suspect a heart attack. What should you do?
shortQuestions.a: I will alert the driver to stop near the nearest hospital or call an ambulance immediately. Meanwhile, I will seat the passenger in a comfortable half-sitting position with head and shoulders supported and knees bent to reduce strain on the heart, loosen tight clothing, and keep him calm.

pastaParagraph.text: Pasta, a large family of shaped, dried wheat pasta, is a basic staple in many countries. Its origins are obscure. Rice pasta were known very early in China; pasta made of wheat were used in India and Arabia long before they were introduced into Europe in the 11th or 12th century. According to legend, Marco Polo brought a pasta recipe with him from Asia in 1295. Pasta quickly became a major element in the Italian diet, and its use spread throughout Europe. Pasta is made from durum wheat flour, which makes a strong, elastic dough. Hard durum wheat has the highest wheat protein value. The flour is mixed with water, kneaded to form a thick paste, and then forced through perforated plates or dies that shape it into one of more than 100 different forms.

essayNaturalDisaster.title: Natural Disasters and Disaster Management
essayNaturalDisaster.text: Natural disasters are catastrophic environmental events caused by nature's powerful forces, such as earthquakes, floods, tsunamis, hurricanes, and droughts. They cause devastating loss of human lives, destruction of infrastructure, and severe economic setbacks. In Pakistan, recurrent floods and devastating earthquakes, such as the 2005 Kashmir earthquake and the 2010/2022 floods, have displaced millions. While natural disasters cannot be prevented, their impact can be greatly mitigated through effective disaster management, early warning systems, strict building codes, and community emergency preparedness. Training citizens and students in first aid, evacuation drills, and emergency rescue creates resilient communities capable of surviving unforeseen calamities.

writing.schoolPreparedness: Schools must establish comprehensive disaster preparedness plans. Every school should have functional fire extinguishers on every floor, clearly marked emergency exit routes, and well-stocked first aid kits. Teachers and students should participate in regular earthquake and fire evacuation drills. Emergency contact numbers for rescue services (like Rescue 1122), ambulances, and fire brigades must be prominently displayed across all classrooms.

engChapters.title: The Old Woman
engChapters.theme: Old Age, Dignity, Peace and Respect for Elders

poet.name: Joseph Campbell
poet.bio: Joseph Campbell was born in 1906 in White Plains, New York. He earned fame as a writer, poet, and athlete (being among the fastest half-mile runners in the world). The poem 'The Old Woman' describes the serene beauty, quiet dignity, and spiritual peace of an elderly woman who has fulfilled all her earthly responsibilities.

poem: As a white candle
In a holy place,
So is the beauty
Of an aged face.
As the spent radiance
Of the winter sun,
So is a woman
With her travail done,
Her brood gone from her,
And her thoughts as still
As the waters
Under a ruined mill.

shortQuestions.q: Who does the poet praise in the poem 'The Old Woman'? Explain how.
shortQuestions.a: The poet praises an elderly woman in her old age. He celebrates her spiritual beauty, quiet grace, and dignified serenity after a long lifetime of maternal sacrifice and hard labor.

shortQuestions.q: What does 'a white candle' represent in the poem 'The Old Woman'?
shortQuestions.a: 'A white candle in a holy place' represents purity, holiness, devotion, peace, and spiritual illumination. It signifies that the aged woman's face reflects a sacred life lived in righteousness.

shortQuestions.q: What is the message in the poem 'The Old Woman'? Explain briefly.
shortQuestions.a: The message is that old age is not ugly or useless; rather, it possesses a sublime, peaceful, and sacred beauty. Elders who have dedicated their youth to raising families deserve our utmost reverence, love, and respect.

shortQuestions.q: Why does the poet compare old woman to a 'white candle in a holy place', 'the winter sun' and 'the water under a ruined mill' in the poem 'The Old Woman'?
shortQuestions.a: He compares her to a 'white candle' to highlight her pure spiritual sanctity; to 'the winter sun' to portray her gentle, soothing, spent radiance after a lifetime of fiery labor; and to 'waters under a ruined mill' to symbolize her absolute inner calm, stillness, and meditative tranquility now that life's frantic wheel has stopped.

shortQuestions.q: Do you like this poem 'The Old Woman'? Why?
shortQuestions.a: Yes, I like this poem deeply because of its gentle similes, serene tone, and profound appreciation for elderly mothers and grandmothers who have sacrificed their youth for their children.

shortQuestions.q: What words in the poem help establish imagery?
shortQuestions.a: Words such as 'white candle', 'holy place', 'aged face', 'spent radiance', 'winter sun', and 'waters under a ruined mill' evoke vivid visual and sensory imagery of light, warmth, and tranquil stillness.

shortQuestions.q: How many lines and stanzas are there in this poem?
shortQuestions.a: The poem consists of 12 lines divided into 3 quatrains (four-line stanzas).

mcqs.q: The poet's comparison of old woman to a 'white candle' is made in the form of:
mcqs.ans: b. simile

options: a. The old woman is weak but with rich experience of life
b. The old woman is strong and with wide experience of life
c. The old woman is symbol of beauty and sunshine
d. The old woman is symbol of success and growth
mcqs.ans: a. The old woman is weak but with rich experience of life

options: b. her children gone (grown up and moved away)
mcqs.ans: b. her children gone (grown up and moved away)

mcqs.q: The poet says that 'As the waters under a ruined mill'. What does it mean?
options: a. To emphasize that there is steadiness, stillness and peace in the life of an old woman
b. To point out that it is very difficult for old women to show whether they feel confident or not
c. To suggest that old women do not usually have feelings
d. To indicate that wide range of experience is an extra ornament in the life of old lady
mcqs.ans: a. To emphasize that there is steadiness, stillness and peace in the life of an old woman

mcqs.q: What does 'travail done' mean based on the poem?
options: a. Difficulties of an old woman neither vanished nor run away
b. Laborious life and hard work of an old woman are completed
c. Calmness and wisdom in the life of an old woman
d. Natural beauty vanished in an old woman
mcqs.ans: b. Laborious life and hard work of an old woman are completed

writing.paraphraseStanza1: Just as a pure white candle glows with serene, sacred reverence in a holy place of worship, similarly an elderly person's face possesses a holy and dignified beauty.
writing.paraphraseStanza3: Now that her children have grown up and left home, her mind is perfectly at rest and tranquil, just like the quiet, motionless waters resting beneath an abandoned water mill.
writing.summary: In the poem 'The Old Woman', Joseph Campbell paints an affectionate, respectful portrait of elderly motherhood. Through three evocative similes, he describes the beauty of old age. First, an aged face is compared to a white candle burning in a holy temple, signifying purity and spiritual sanctity. Second, the woman whose lifelong labors are finished is likened to the gentle, spent glow of the winter sun. Finally, with her children grown and independent, her thoughts are as serene and calm as still waters beneath an old, resting watermill.

essayRespectElders.title: Appreciating and Respecting Elders
essayRespectElders.text: Respecting elders is one of the highest moral virtues instilled by religion and society. Our parents, grandparents, and teachers dedicate their youth, energy, and resources to nurturing us, protecting us, and preparing us for life. As they grow old and frail, they deserve our deepest appreciation, patience, and affection. Showing respect involves listening to their wisdom, speaking to them with gentleness, assisting them with daily tasks, and spending quality time in their company. In Islam, serving elderly parents is directly linked to earning Allah's pleasure and Paradise. By honoring our elders, we preserve family harmony and cultivate a compassionate society.

engChapters.title: Letter to the Newspaper Editor
engChapters.theme: Media Literacy, Civic Awareness and Formal Correspondence

letter.senderAddress: House B-106, Shah Jahan Complex, Shami Road, Peshawar.
letter.recipient:
The Editor,
The Frontier Post,
Peshawar.
body: The media has the power of educating people, the good and the bad. Since it affects the eyes, the ears and the mind simultaneously, nothing can overcome the influence of the media. The media should perform a noble mission of enlightening people and discourage sectarian, communal and divisive trends. Through your esteemed paper, I would like to highlight the bright and dark sides of the media and request the related authorities to boost the positive influences and curb the negative impacts of media on the general communities.

Firstly, the term media is derived from medium, which means carrier or channel. Media denotes an item specifically designed to reach a large audience or viewers. The term was first used with the advent of newspapers and magazines. However, with the passage of time, the term broadened by the inventions of radio, TV, cinema and internet.

Secondly, in the world of today, media has become almost as necessary as food and clothing. It is true that media is playing an outstanding role in strengthening society. Its duty is to inform, educate and entertain the people. It helps us know current situations around the world. The media has a strong social and cultural impact upon society. Because of its inherent ability to reach a large number of the public, it is widely used to convey messages to build public opinion.

Thirdly, the original idea behind the creation of various 'media means' was to entertain the masses. Radio, TV, cinema and magazines spend most of their resources targeting entertaining programs. Every year billions are traded in the entertainment industry. Another primary role of media today is to inform people about latest happenings. Media covers weather, politics, health, finance, science, and sports. Dedicated news channels enable people to watch news whenever and wherever they want.

Fourthly, media is the overseer of the political system. If it plays its role honestly, it is a powerful force in building the nation. It brings the common man close to their leaders and details major political decisions. Hence people can better understand their rights and make informed choices. As the power of media is huge, it can be used to educate people at very low cost across the country.
Moreover, various agencies utilize media to broadcast weather warnings, storm alerts, epidemics, and train/flight schedules. Almost all businesses use media advertising to promote goods and services.

Lastly, even though there are lots of plus points, there are also serious disadvantages. Media often promotes commercialism and induces baseless ideas through sensational advertisements, forcing people into buying substandard products. Sometimes media creates unnecessary sensation and distortion of truth to boost ratings. Because of its vast power, media can make or break reputations.
In perspective of the above actualities, it is trusted that the Government and media organizations will promote constructive broadcasting and curb sensationalism.
letter.subscription:
Thanking you in anticipation.
Sincere regards,
Abrar Khan

shortQuestions.q: What is media? Explain with references from text.
shortQuestions.a: The word 'media' is derived from 'medium', meaning a carrier or channel. In the text, it denotes channels of communication—including newspapers, magazines, radio, television, cinema, and the internet—specifically designed to inform, educate, entertain, and reach large audiences simultaneously.

shortQuestions.q: What is meant by misuse of media? How can it be stopped?
shortQuestions.a: Misuse of media means broadcasting false news, spreading sectarian and divisive hate, distorting facts for cheap sensationalism, and advertising substandard or harmful products. It can be stopped through strict regulatory monitoring (such as PEMRA), ethical journalism codes, and consumer awareness.

shortQuestions.q: How should students take benefits from internet and avoid its bad effects?
shortQuestions.a: Students should use the internet for research, educational lectures, learning new skills, and reading digital libraries. They can avoid bad effects by limiting screen time, avoiding inappropriate content, and steering clear of time-wasting social media addictions.

shortQuestions.q: Do you think television is useful source of information? Why?
shortQuestions.a: Yes, television is a highly useful source of information because it combines audio and visual elements simultaneously. It provides live news coverage, scientific documentaries, educational programs, and weather alerts accessible even to illiterate citizens.

shortQuestions.q: How can media bring about religious harmony?
shortQuestions.a: Media can foster religious harmony by discouraging sectarianism, promoting shared universal values of tolerance and brotherhood, highlighting interfaith dialogues, and showcasing positive stories of communal cooperation.

shortQuestions.q: Find out transitional devices in the text.
shortQuestions.a: Transitional devices used in the letter include: 'Firstly', 'Secondly', 'Thirdly', 'Fourthly', 'Moreover', 'Lastly', 'Hence', 'However', and 'In perspective of'.

Respected Sir,
With due respect, I beg to submit that a fine of Rs. 200 was imposed upon me for being absent from school for three consecutive days last week. I could not attend school because I was suffering from severe viral fever, and a medical certificate from the doctor is attached herewith.

engChapters.title: Biodiversity in Pakistan

reading.text:
Pakistan is blessed with several natural beauties including indigenous wildlife, beautiful mountains of the Himalayas, deserts of Cholistan and Thar, man-made forests like Changa Manga forest, as well as several natural resources from the Balochistan trails. It also holds the second tallest mountain in the world, K-2, which is a really challenging tourist attraction for mountaineers. Four seasons bloom each year to their fullest, and an average rainfall of 12-14 inches per year makes Pakistan a fertile agricultural land.

But despite its enormous beauty, a number of animal and plant species are threatened or endangered due to over-exploitation and loss of natural habitat. Rapid human population growth is increasing pressure on the country's natural resources. Increased poverty has forced rural people to exploit biodiversity at unsustainable rates. Factors like deforestation, overgrazing, soil erosion, salinity and water-logging are posing major threats to the remaining biodiversity of the country. The continuing loss of habitat, with its associated flora and fauna, will have serious implications for the nation's natural and agricultural ecosystems.

The best known of Pakistan's endangered mammals is the snow leopard, which makes its home in the mid-level elevations of the Himalayas. Threatened by poaching and loss of habitat, the snow leopard is iconic among endangered species in the Himalayan Range. In the lower subtropical regions of Pakistan, small populations of leopards still exist. Other endangered land mammals in Pakistan include: the Asian elephant; hog deer; Asiatic wild ass; woolly flying squirrel; Kashmir musk deer; and the fishing cat. Markhor, the national animal, is on the brink of extinction, too. This wild goat is classified as 'near threatened' by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

The bird most at risk of extinction in Pakistan is the red-headed vulture. Another vulture species found in the region, the Egyptian vulture, is also globally endangered. Another, the white-headed duck, maintains a population stronghold in Pakistan as it declines in other countries.

Similarly, the Indus River dolphin is a freshwater-dwelling cetacean species found in the Indus River. There is a serious threat to this species because of the water regulatory barrages constructed on the Indus River. Shortage of water and water diversion to meet agricultural needs have resulted in the extirpation of the Indus River dolphin from much of its historical range. Accidental mortality of Indus River dolphins is attributed to entanglements in fishing nets as by-catch, unsustainable fishing practices, and entrapment in irrigation canals. Contamination of river water due to agrochemicals and industrial waste significantly contributes to the deterioration of the dolphin's core habitats.

Likewise, Balochistan's juniper forests in Ziarat are one of the most extensive and oldest juniper ecosystems in the world. They provide habitats to many unique birds, mammals, and plant species. Juniper is an extremely slow-growing species, attaining only one-inch diameter growth in 50 years. Unfortunately, this national heritage is facing a grave threat from a parasitic disease caused by dwarf mistletoe.

In this backdrop, the government of Pakistan has shortlisted national parks for biodiversity conservation, including Lal Suhanra National Park (Bahawalpur), Kirthar National Park (Sindh), Khunjerab National Park (Northern Areas), Chiltan Hazarganji National Park (Balochistan), Margalla Hills National Park (Islamabad), and Chitral Gol National Park (KPK). Further, Pakistan has 14 National Parks, 99 Wildlife Sanctuaries, and 96 Game Reserves. Kirthar National Park holds the distinction of being the first Pakistani park on the UN list of protected areas.

shortQuestions.q: Describe the natural beauty of Pakistan.
shortQuestions.a: Pakistan is blessed with diverse natural landscapes ranging from the majestic snow-capped Himalayan and Karakoram peaks (including K-2) to the golden deserts of Thar and Cholistan, lush fertile agricultural plains, ancient juniper forests in Ziarat, man-made forests like Changa Manga, and scenic coastlines along the Arabian Sea.

shortQuestions.q: How can we preserve Pakistan's fauna and flora?
shortQuestions.a: We can preserve flora and fauna by banning illegal poaching and deforestation, expanding national parks and wildlife sanctuaries, controlling industrial effluent discharges into rivers, eradicating plant parasites like dwarf mistletoe, and engaging local communities in sustainable conservation programs.

shortQuestions.q: Name some endangered species in Pakistan.
shortQuestions.a: Endangered mammals include the snow leopard, Markhor (national animal), Indus River dolphin, Kashmir musk deer, hog deer, Asiatic wild ass, woolly flying squirrel, and fishing cat. Endangered birds include the red-headed vulture, Egyptian vulture, and white-headed duck.

shortQuestions.q: Search the internet and find about the endangered peacocks.
shortQuestions.a: The Indian peafowl (peacock) in Pakistan's Tharparkar desert faces threats from viral Newcastle disease (Ranikhet), extreme drought, loss of indigenous acacia trees, and illegal hunting. Conservation drives focus on vaccination and habitat restoration.

shortQuestions.q: How can we contribute as individuals to save nature?
shortQuestions.a: Individuals can plant native trees, reduce water wastage, avoid single-use plastics, refrain from hunting wild animals, dispose of trash responsibly, and spread ecological awareness among peers.

shortQuestions.q: What type of challenges is Pakistan facing while preserving nature?
shortQuestions.a: Key challenges include rapid population growth, poverty, lack of financial resources, limited technical capacity, illegal poaching, deforestation, climate change, and weak enforcement of environmental laws.

persuasiveEssay.title: Preservation of Nature: An Urgent Imperative
persuasiveEssay.text: Nature provides humanity with air to breathe, water to drink, fertile soil to grow food, and life-saving medicinal plants. Yet, modern industrialization and reckless human exploitation are driving species toward catastrophic extinction. In Pakistan, iconic creatures like the snow leopard, Markhor, and Indus River dolphin are threatened due to habitat destruction and pollution. Conserving nature is not a luxury; it is a prerequisite for human survival. Protecting forests prevents devastating floods and mitigates global warming, while maintaining biodiversity preserves ecosystem equilibrium. Governments, civil societies, and individuals must unite to enforce conservation laws, plant millions of trees, and safeguard our planet for future generations.

writing.chitralDescription: Chitral Valley, nestled in the Hindukush mountain range of northern Pakistan, is a wonderland of snow-clad peaks, gushing glacial streams, and vibrant cultures. Dominated by the majestic Tirich Mir (7,708 m), the valley is home to the unique Kalash people who celebrate ancient festivals with traditional dance and colorful attire. The fragrant walnut orchards and terraced fields offer a tranquil escape, making Chitral a treasure of Pakistani biodiversity.

engChapters.title: Abou Ben Adhem
engChapters.theme: Humanism, Love for Mankind and Divine Pleasure (Huqooq-ul-Ibad)

poet.name: James Henry Leigh Hunt
poet.bio: James Henry Leigh Hunt (1784–1859) was an eminent English poet, critic, and essayist. 'Abou Ben Adhem' is his most celebrated poem, embodying the spiritual truth that true love of God is expressed through genuine, selfless love and service to fellow human beings.

poem: Abou Ben Adhem (may his tribe increase!)
Awoke one night from a deep dream of peace,
And saw, within the moonlight in his room,
Making it rich, and like a lily in bloom,
An angel writing in a book of gold: —
Exceeding peace had made Ben Adhem bold,
And to the presence in the room he said,
"What writest thou?" — The vision raised its head,
And with a look made of all sweet accord,
Answered, "The names of those who love the Lord."
"And is mine one?" said Abou. "Nay, not so,"
Replied the angel. Abou spoke more low,
But cheerly still; and said, "I pray thee, then,
Write me as one that loves his fellow men."
The angel wrote, and vanished. The next night
It came again with a great wakening light,
And showed the names whom love of God had blest,
And lo! Ben Adhem's name led all the rest.

shortQuestions.q: Why was Abou Ben Adhem's name on top of the list?
shortQuestions.a: Abou Ben Adhem's name was at the top of the list because he loved and served his fellow human beings selflessly. God loves those most who love and care for His creation.

shortQuestions.q: What is the main idea of the poem?
shortQuestions.a: The central idea is that service to humanity (Huqooq-ul-Ibad) is the highest and truest form of divine worship. Loving one's fellow men earns the highest love and blessings of Almighty God.

shortQuestions.q: Describe the character of Abou Ben Adhem in your own words.
shortQuestions.a: Abou Ben Adhem is a pious, humble, peace-loving, and compassionate man. When told his name was not among those who love God, he remained cheerful and humbly requested to be recorded as a lover of mankind, demonstrating pure unselfish devotion.

shortQuestions.q: Write down the implied and explicit meanings of the poem.
shortQuestions.a: Explicitly, the poem tells the story of Abou waking up, conversing with an angel writing in a golden book, asking to be listed as a lover of men, and finding his name leading the blessed list the next night. Implicitly, it conveys that ritualistic worship without compassion for humanity is incomplete; genuine love for God is proven through empathy and service to mankind.

shortQuestions.q: Mention the other words used by the poet to refer to the angel.
shortQuestions.a: The poet refers to the angel as 'the presence in the room' and 'the vision'.

shortQuestions.q: Give brief description of the angel in Abou Ben Adhem.
shortQuestions.a: The angel appeared radiant and peaceful in the moonlight like a lily in bloom, holding a golden book and pen, possessing a demeanor of sweet accord, benevolence, and celestial light.

mcqs.q: Abou Ben Adhem's room looked beautiful and bright because of:

c. the blooming lilies in the room

writing.paraphraseStanza1: Abou Ben Adhem awakened one night from a serene, peaceful slumber and noticed his room illuminated by bright moonlight resembling a blooming lily. Within this radiance, he saw a divine angel writing in a book of gold.
writing.paraphraseStanza3: The angel wrote down Abou's humble request and vanished. The following night, the angel reappeared accompanied by an immense heavenly light, displaying the names of those blessed with God's love; and remarkably, Abou Ben Adhem's name led all the rest.
writing.summary: In 'Abou Ben Adhem', Leigh Hunt narrates an inspiring encounter between the pious Abou and a celestial angel writing the names of those who love the Lord in a golden book. When Abou learns his name is not in the book, he humbly requests the angel to record him as someone who loves his fellow human beings. The next night, the angel returns with a glorious divine light and reveals that Abou's name leads the list of those whom God's love has blessed. The poem conveys the sublime moral that true devotion to God lies in loving and serving mankind.

essayHuqooqUlIbad.title: Huqooq-ul-Ibad (Rights of Fellow Human Beings)
essayHuqooqUlIbad.text: In Islam, human duties are divided into two categories: Huqooq-ullah (Rights of Allah) and Huqooq-ul-Ibad (Rights of Human Beings). While Allah may forgive shortcomings in personal worship through His infinite mercy, He has declared that violations of the rights of fellow beings will not be pardoned until the aggrieved person forgives. Huqooq-ul-Ibad encompasses respecting parents, caring for orphans, assisting the impoverished, treating neighbors with kindness, and being honest in all dealings. The Holy Prophet Muhammad (SAW) taught that the best among Muslims is the one who benefits people the most. Serving humanity is the true essence of religion and the surest path to divine grace.

reading.theme: Simplicity & Humility

passages.heading: Ingrained Traits of Humility and Equality
passages.text: Humility and simplicity were ingrained traits of Hazrat Muhammad's (PBUH) personality. He (PBUH) never made people feel small, unwanted or embarrassed. He (PBUH) urged his followers to live decently and kindly. He (PBUH) would sit wherever there was a place available in an assembly and never sought a prominent or elevated place. He (PBUH) never wore anything that could distinguish him from his companions. He (PBUH) would meet the affluent and the impoverished alike and never made distinction on the basis of caste, creed and colour. People who did not know him could not tell him apart from the rest of his comrades.

summary.en: Humility and simplicity were natural qualities of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH). He treated the rich and the poor equally without discrimination of caste or creed, dressing and sitting just like his companions.
summary.ur: عاجزی اور سادگی رسول اللہ ﷺ کی شخصیت کے بنیادی اوصاف تھے۔ آپ ﷺ امیر اور غریب دونوں سے یکساں طور پر ملتے تھے اور لباس یا بیٹھنے میں ساتھیوں سے کوئی امتیاز پسند نہیں فرماتے تھے۔

passages.heading: Simplicity is Part of Faith
passages.text: Abu Umamah bin Tha'labah (RA) reported, "The Companions of The Rasool of Allah mentioned the life of the world before him. He (PBUH) said, 'Do you not hear? Do you not hear? Simplicity (in life) is part of faith, simplicity is part of faith'."¹

summary.en: Abu Umamah (RA) reported that when worldly luxuries were discussed, the Holy Prophet (PBUH) emphasized twice that simplicity in life is an essential part of faith.
summary.ur: حضرت ابو امامہ بن ثعلبہؓ سے روایت ہے کہ جب دنیاوی زندگی کا ذکر ہوا تو رسول اللہ ﷺ نے دو مرتبہ ارشاد فرمایا: سادگی ایمان کا حصہ ہے، سادگی ایمان کا حصہ ہے۔

passages.heading: Austere Diet and Barley Bread
passages.text: In lifestyle, diet and manners, he was simple and humble. Sahl Ibn Sa'ad, one of Muhammad's (PBUH) companions, said, "The Rasool of Allah did not see bread made from fine flour from the time Allah sent him (as a Rasool) until he died".²

summary.en: Sahl Ibn Sa'ad (RA) related that throughout his prophetic mission until his death, the Holy Prophet (PBUH) never consumed bread made from refined flour.
summary.ur: حضرت سہل بن سعدؓ نے فرمایا کہ نبوت سے وصال تک رسول اللہ ﷺ نے کبھی چھنے ہوئے باریک آٹے کی روٹی نہیں دیکھی۔

passages.heading: Bedding of Leather and Date-Palm Fiber
passages.text: Similarly, Aa'isha (RA) said, "The mattress of the Rasool (PBUH), on which he slept, was made of leather stuffed with the fibre of date tree".³

summary.en: Hazrat Aa'isha (RA) described the Prophet's (PBUH) modest bed: a leather casing stuffed with coarse fibers of the date palm tree.
summary.ur: حضرت عائشہؓ فرماتی ہیں کہ رسول اللہ ﷺ کا بستر چمڑے کا تھا جس کے اندر کھجور کے درخت کے ریشے بھرے ہوئے تھے۔

passages.heading: No Worldly Wealth Left Behind
passages.text: Amr Ibn Al-Hareth (RA), one of Hazrat Muhammad's (PBUH) companions, said that when the Rasool (PBUH) died, he left neither money nor anything else except his white riding mule, his arms, and a piece of land which he left to charity.⁴

summary.en: At his passing, the Prophet (PBUH) left behind no dirhams or dinars, leaving only a white mule, his weapons, and a plot of land donated as charity.
summary.ur: حضرت عمرو بن حارثؓ فرماتے ہیں کہ وصال کے وقت رسول اللہ ﷺ نے درہم و دینار نہیں چھوڑے، سوائے ایک سفید خچر، ہتھیار اور ایک قطعہ زمین کے جسے صدقہ کر دیا گیا۔

passages.heading: Personal Chores, Visiting the Sick, and Digging the Trench
passages.text: Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) lived this hard life till he died although the Muslim treasury was at his disposal, the greater part of the Arabian Peninsula was Muslim, and the Muslims were victorious after eighteen years of his mission. Despite his responsibilities as a Nabi, a teacher, a statesman, and a judge, Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) used to milk his goat⁵, mend his clothes, repair his shoes⁶ and help with the household work⁷. He (PBUH) used to visit ailing persons and exhorted all Muslims to do likewise⁸. He (PBUH) also helped his companions in digging a trench by moving sand with them⁹. Whenever he (PBUH) visited a person he would first greet him and then take his permission to enter the house. He (PBUH) advised the people to follow this etiquette and not to get annoyed if anyone declined to give permission, for it was quite likely the person concerned was busy otherwise and did not mean any disrespect.

summary.en: Despite governing Arabia, the Prophet (PBUH) personally milked goats, repaired clothes and shoes, assisted at home, visited the sick, carried earth to dig trenches, and taught flawless visiting manners.
summary.ur: تمام تر حکومتی اور عدالتی ذمہ داریوں کے باوجود آپ ﷺ نے اپنے کپڑے اور جوتے خود گانٹھے، بکری دوہی، خندق کی کھدائی میں مٹی اٹھائی اور بیمار پرسی و اجازت طلبی کے آداب سکھائے۔

passages.heading: Handshake Etiquette and Attentive Listening
passages.text: Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) was always the first to greet another and would not withdraw his hand from a handshake till the other man withdrew his. If one wanted to say something in his ears, he would not turn away till one had finished.

summary.en: He was always first to offer greetings, never released a handshake until the other person released first, and listened intently when whispered to.
summary.ur: آپ ﷺ سلام میں ہمیشہ پہل فرماتے، مصافحہ کے دوران اپنا ہاتھ پہلے نہیں چھوڑتے تھے اور کان میں بات کرنے والے کی بات ختم ہونے تک توجہ سے سنتے تھے۔

passages.heading: Reverence for Foster Mother and Foster Sister
passages.text: Anas (RA), one of Hazrat Muhammad's (PBUH) companions said that there was no person whom they loved more than the Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH), yet when he came to them, they did not stand up for him because he (PBUH) hated their standing up for him.¹⁰ He (PBUH) would himself, however, stand up when any dignitary came to him. He (PBUH) had stood up to receive the wet nurse who had reared him in infancy and would spread his own sheet for her. His foster sister was given similar treatment.¹¹

summary.en: The Prophet (PBUH) disliked people standing up for him, yet he stood up with profound respect and spread his own sheet for his foster mother and foster sister.
summary.ur: آپ ﷺ نے اپنے لیے احتراما کھڑے ہونے کو ناپسند فرمایا، مگر اپنی رضاعی والدہ اور رضاعی بہن کی آمد پر خود کھڑے ہو کر ان کے لیے اپنی چادر بچھائی۔

passages.heading: Affectionate Respect for Hazrat Fatima (RA)
passages.text: Similarly, Hazrat Aa'isha (RA) has narrated: "I have never encountered anyone that had emulated the Rasool (PBUH) in manner, likeness and speech more than Fatima (RA). When she came in to visit him (the Rasool) he got up to (welcome) her, took her by the hand, kissed her and made her sit where he was sitting; and when he (PBUH) went in to visit her, she got up to (welcome) him, took him by the hand, kissed him, and made him sit where she was sitting".¹² He avoided sitting at a prominent place in a gathering, so much so that people coming in had difficulty in spotting him and had to ask who the Rasool (PBUH) was.

summary.en: Hazrat Fatima (RA) emulated the Prophet (PBUH) in manner and speech. Whenever they visited one another, each stood up, took the other by the hand, kissed with warmth, and offered their seat.
summary.ur: حضرت عائشہؓ فرماتی ہیں کہ حضرت فاطمہؓ طور طریقوں اور گفتگو میں رسول اللہ ﷺ کے سب سے زیادہ مشابہ تھیں۔ ملاقات کے وقت دونوں ایک دوسرے کے لیے کھڑے ہوتے اور عزت سے اپنی جگہ بٹھاتے۔

passages.heading: Collecting Firewood and Rejecting Privileges
passages.text: Once Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) was travelling with his companions and when it was time to have the food prepared, he asked them to slaughter a sheep. A man said, "I will slaughter it." Another one said, "I will skin it out." A third one said, "I will cook it." So the Rasool of Allah (PBUH) said, "I will collect wood for fire." They said, "No, we will suffice you that work." "I know that you can do it for me, but I hate to be privileged. Allah hates to see a slave of His, privileged to others." So he went and collected fire-wood.¹³

summary.en: While travelling, the companions divided the cooking duties. The Prophet (PBUH) insisted on gathering firewood, declaring that Allah dislikes seeing a servant treated as privileged above his brothers.
summary.ur: ایک سفر میں جب صحابہ کرام نے کھانا تیار کرنے کے کام بانٹے تو رسول اللہ ﷺ نے ایندھن جمع کرنے کی ذمہ داری لی اور فرمایا کہ اللہ اپنے بندے کو دوسروں سے ممتاز اور مراعات یافتہ دیکھنا پسند نہیں کرتا۔

passages.heading: Eradicating Ostentation and Embracing Humility
passages.text: Our beloved Rasool Hazrat Mohammad (PBUH) was endowed with impeccable qualities from which we can learn a lot to improve our lifestyle. Humbleness and simplicity were some of his many qualities. By adopting the sunnah of simplicity and humility, we can eradicate the social evils like ostentation, haughtiness, arrogance and pride. Regrettably, we squander our hard-earned resources on unwanted luxurious items simply to gratify our sense of pride and superiority over others. If we make simplicity and humility a part of our personality, our social behaviour will be considerate and genuine, our happiness will be unadulterated and we will not recoil our heads in pride but bow them in humility and affection.

summary.en: By adopting the Sunnah of simplicity and humility, society can eradicate ostentation and arrogance, avoid wasting resources on luxury, and achieve genuine, considerate human relationships.
summary.ur: سنتِ نبوی ﷺ کے مطابق سادگی اور عاجزی اپنا کر ہم نمود و نمائش اور تکبر کا خاتمہ کر سکتے ہیں، فضول خرچی سے بچ سکتے ہیں اور مخلصانہ و مہربان معاشرہ تشکیل دے سکتے ہیں۔
