questions.q: What is meant by simplicity and humility?
questions.ans: Simplicity refers to leading an unpretentious, modest, and austere life free from luxury, ostentation, and wasteful extravagance. Humility means acknowledging one's human limitations, showing deep respect and kindness to everyone regardless of social status, and refusing to consider oneself superior, privileged, or elevated above other human beings.

questions.q: Describe in a few sentences, the life style of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) in the light of the text that you have read.
questions.ans: Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) led an exceptionally simple and humble lifestyle. He slept on a coarse leather mattress stuffed with the fibers of the date tree and never ate bread made of fine flour. Despite governing the Arabian Peninsula with the state treasury at his disposal, he performed his own domestic chores, milked his goat, mended his clothes, repaired his shoes, and helped dig trenches alongside his companions. At his passing, he left neither dirhams nor dinars, leaving only his white riding mule, arms, and a plot of land donated to charity.

questions.q: How can simplicity and humility do away with the culture of extravagance and waste?
questions.ans: Simplicity and humility curb the urge to indulge in showy displays and competitive consumption. When people adopt humility, they stop squandering hard-earned resources on unwanted luxury items simply to gratify feelings of false pride and superiority over others. This redirects resources toward real societal necessities, eliminates financial anxiety, and establishes an egalitarian culture of contentment and mutual care.

questions.q: Read the last paragraph of the lesson, "Simplicity and humility of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH)" with comprehension and write down the main idea and supporting details of the paragraph.
questions.ans:
• Main Idea: Adopting the Sunnah of simplicity and humility is vital to eradicating damaging social vices and fostering authentic, affectionate human relations.
• Supporting Details:
  1. Humbleness and simplicity can eradicate social evils such as ostentation, haughtiness, arrogance, and pride.
  2. People regrettably squander their hard-earned wealth on unnecessary luxuries simply to gratify pride and superiority.
  3. Incorporating simplicity and humility into our character makes our social behaviour considerate and genuine, keeps our happiness unadulterated, and makes us bow our heads in affectionate humility rather than pride.

questions.q: How did Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) treat his foster sister?
questions.ans: Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) treated his foster sister with the highest reverence, honor, and deep affection. Just as he stood up to welcome the wet nurse (Halima Sadia) who reared him in infancy and spread his own blessed sheet for her to sit upon, he gave the exact same honorable, affectionate, and dignified treatment to his foster sister.

mcqs.q: The mattress on which Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) slept was made of leather, stuffed with the fibre of date tree. This shows that he (PBUH):
mcqs.exp: Textbook Exercise B.1 confirms option (b): his bedding reflected his conscious choice to lead an austere and simple life.

mcqs.q: The word that is opposite in meaning to affluent is:
mcqs.exp: Textbook Exercise B.2 confirms option (d): 'affluent' means having wealth, so its direct antonym is 'poor'.

mcqs.q: According to the text Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) and Hazrat Fatima (RA) greeted each other _______ way.
mcqs.exp: Textbook Exercise B.3 confirms option (a): both got up to welcome the other, took each other by the hand, kissed, and seated the other in their own place.

mcqs.q: The word closest in meaning to impoverished is:
mcqs.exp: Textbook Exercise B.4 confirms option (a): 'impoverished' means very poor or without money.

mcqs.q: According to the text of the lesson Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) used to milk his goat, this shows that:
opts: the Rasool (PBUH) liked the milk of goats
the Rasool (PBUH) did not like milking of goat by other people
humility was essential part of the Rasool's (PBUH) character
mcqs.exp: Textbook Exercise B.5 confirms option (c): performing routine domestic chores demonstrated that humility was an essential, inherent part of the Prophet's character.

vocabulary.title: Dictionary Study: Guide Words, Entry Words & Pronunciation Keys
vocabulary.instruction: Use dictionaries to locate guide words, entry words, choose appropriate word definitions, and identify pronunciations through pronunciation keys (Book p. 7):

items.definition: Important, well-known, or easily seen; standing out from surroundings.
items.example: He never sought a prominent or elevated seat in any assembly.

items.definition: To kill an animal for food or butchering purposes.
items.example: He asked the traveling companions to slaughter a sheep for dinner.

items.definition: The quality of having a modest or low view of one's importance; freedom from pride.
items.example: Humility and simplicity were ingrained traits of Hazrat Muhammad's personality.

items.definition: The state or character of being humble, unpretentious, and respectful toward others.
items.example: Humbleness in power is the truest mark of righteous character.

items.definition: A person considered to be important because of high rank or official position.
items.example: The Prophet (PBUH) would stand up courteously whenever any dignitary visited him.

items.definition: Denoting family relationship formed by care, upbringing, or nursing rather than blood.
items.example: The Prophet (PBUH) received his foster sister with tender love and honor.

grammar.topic: Types of Nouns: Countable, Uncountable, Abstract, Material & Collective (Exercise A)
grammar.rule: Nouns name persons, places, things, ideas, or qualities. Countable nouns can be enumerated with plurals; Uncountable nouns cannot be counted in units; Abstract nouns name intangible feelings, concepts, or states; Material nouns denote raw substances or physical matters; Collective nouns name groups.
examples: Countable: tables, companions, goats, shoes
Uncountable: sugar, honey, sand, flour
Abstract: success, bravery, simplicity, humility
Material: leather, wood, water, iron
Collective: assembly, army, family, flock

exercises.q: "Success" is an example of: a) countable noun, b) uncountable noun, c) abstract noun, d) material noun
exercises.ans: c) abstract noun (names an intangible state or quality of accomplishment).

exercises.q: "Sugar" is an example of: a) countable noun, b) uncountable noun, c) abstract noun, d) collective noun
exercises.ans: b) uncountable noun (a substance that cannot be enumerated as individual units).

exercises.q: "Honey" is an example of: a) countable noun, b) uncountable noun, c) abstract noun, d) collective noun
exercises.ans: b) uncountable noun (a liquid substance that is non-countable without a container measure).

exercises.q: "Bravery" is an example of: a) countable noun, b) uncountable noun, c) abstract noun, d) material noun
exercises.ans: c) abstract noun (names a moral quality or human virtue).

exercises.q: "Tables" is an example of: a) countable noun, b) uncountable noun, c) abstract noun, d) collective noun
exercises.ans: a) countable noun (plural form of an individual physical object that can be counted).

grammar.rule: Most English nouns form their plural by adding -s or -es, but irregular nouns change vowels, take Greek/Latin endings, mutate endings (-fe to -ves), or retain identical singular and plural forms.
examples: person → persons / people
woman → women
child → children
knife / shelf → knives / shelves
phenomenon → phenomena
fish → fish (or fishes for distinct species)

exercises.q: These (person) are protesting against the president.
exercises.ans: persons / people

exercises.q: The (woman) over there want to meet the manager.
exercises.ans: women

exercises.q: My (child) hate eating pasta.
exercises.ans: children

exercises.q: The (student) are doing the exercise right now.
exercises.ans: students

exercises.q: The (fish) I bought is in the fridge.
exercises.ans: fish

exercises.q: Where did you put the (knife) which were on the (shelf)?
exercises.ans: knives, shelves

exercises.q: (Piano) are expensive.
exercises.ans: Pianos

exercises.q: These (phenomenon) are not fully understood.
exercises.ans: phenomena

grammar.topic: Nouns that Change Meaning in the Plural Form (Exercise C)
grammar.rule: Certain nouns acquire a completely different meaning when used in the plural form rather than simply representing multiple units (e.g. arm = body limb; arms = weapons).
examples: good (virtue/benefit) vs goods (merchandise/commodities)
wood (material from trees) vs woods (forest)
spectacle (notable display/sight) vs spectacles (eyeglasses)
character (moral nature) vs characters (letters/alphabet symbols)
manner (method/way) vs manners (polite social etiquette)
force (physical power) vs forces (military troops)

exercises.q: good – goods: Show difference in meaning using both singular and plural in sentences.
exercises.ans: Singular: He dedicated his entire life to doing good for humanity. | Plural: The heavy truck transported manufactured goods to Karachi harbor.

exercises.q: wood – woods: Show difference in meaning using both singular and plural in sentences.
exercises.ans: Singular: Teak wood is famous for making durable household furniture. | Plural: The weary travelers pitched their tents at the edge of the dark woods.

exercises.q: spectacle – spectacles: Show difference in meaning using both singular and plural in sentences.
exercises.ans: Singular: The sunset over the Himalayan peaks was a breathtaking spectacle. | Plural: Grandfather cannot read the daily newspaper without his spectacles.

exercises.q: character – characters: Show difference in meaning using both singular and plural in sentences.
exercises.ans: Singular: Integrity and honesty are the hallmarks of a righteous character. | Plural: The Chinese writing system consists of thousands of distinct characters.

exercises.q: manner – manners: Show difference in meaning using both singular and plural in sentences.
exercises.ans: Singular: The scientist solved the complex equation in an innovative manner. | Plural: Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) taught his companions courteous table manners.

exercises.q: force – forces: Show difference in meaning using both singular and plural in sentences.
exercises.ans: Singular: Friction is the opposing force that slows down moving vehicles. | Plural: The national armed forces defended the frontier with great bravery.

grammar.rule: A Noun Phrase consists of a noun (the headword) accompanied by its modifiers (determiners, adjectives, prepositional phrases) that functions collectively as a single noun in a sentence (as subject, direct object, or prepositional object).
examples: "The wicked man" (determiner + adjective + noun = subject)
"poor people" (adjective + noun = object)
"dark stables" (adjective + noun = prepositional object)

exercises.q: Identify the noun phrases in: 'He wished to talk to his manager.'
exercises.ans: Noun phrase: 'his manager' (possessive determiner + noun; functions as object of the preposition 'to').

exercises.q: Identify the noun phrases in: 'The wicked man loves getting poor people into trouble.'
exercises.ans: Noun phrases: 'The wicked man' (subject), 'poor people' (object of gerund 'getting'), 'trouble' (object of preposition 'into').

exercises.q: Identify the noun phrases in: 'The poor man wanted to pay back every penny he owed.'
exercises.ans: Noun phrases: 'The poor man' (subject), 'every penny he owed' (direct object noun phrase modified by relative clause).

exercises.q: Identify the noun phrases in: 'All the kids were sleeping.'
exercises.ans: Noun phrase: 'All the kids' (predeterminer + determiner + noun; functions as grammatical subject).

exercises.q: Identify the noun phrases in: 'Horses prefer living in dark stables.'
exercises.ans: Noun phrases: 'Horses' (subject noun), 'dark stables' (adjective + noun; object of preposition 'in').

grammar.rule: A Noun Clause is a dependent clause containing a subject and a predicate that functions as a noun within a sentence. In indirect questions and noun clauses, statement word order (Subject + Verb) must be followed rather than inverted question word order (Auxiliary + Subject).
examples: Correct: Jamal asked me where his wallet was. (NOT: where was his wallet)
Correct: I don't know how many children he has. (NOT: how many children does he have)
Correct: What she said was sad. (Subject noun clause)

exercises.q: Jamal asked me _______ ? a) where was his wallet, b) where his wallet was
exercises.ans: b) where his wallet was (indirect question uses statement order: wh-word + subject + verb).

exercises.q: I couldn't tell him _______. a) where was I, b) where I was
exercises.ans: b) where I was (dependent noun clause uses subject 'I' followed by verb 'was').

exercises.q: I don't know _______. a) how many children he has, b) how many children does he have
exercises.ans: a) how many children he has (statement order is required in a subordinate noun clause).

exercises.q: _______ is not important. a) How close we are, b) How close are we
exercises.ans: a) How close we are (functions as the subject of the main verb 'is').

exercises.q: _______ was sad. a) What did she say, b) What she said
exercises.ans: b) What she said (noun clause functioning as subject of the sentence).

writing.summary: This lesson from the KPK Class 10 English textbook highlights the sublime traits of simplicity and humility ingrained in the personality of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH). He treated the affluent and impoverished alike, never wore distinguishing attire, and disliked when companions stood up in his honor. In his diet and domestic life, he was extraordinarily modest: he never tasted bread made of fine flour and slept on a leather mattress stuffed with coarse date-palm fibers. When he passed away, he left no money, but only a white mule, his weapons, and land donated to charity. Despite governing Arabia, he milked goats, mended clothes and shoes, helped dig trenches, and greeted everyone first. During journeys, he collected firewood himself to avoid privileged treatment. The lesson urges us to embrace the Sunnah of simplicity and humility to eradicate pride, ostentation, and extravagance.

essay.title: Pride Makes Us Artificial and Humility Makes Us Real
essay.text: Pride is a deceptive veneer that forces individuals into an artificial posture, while humility anchors the human soul in authentic truth. When pride takes root in human hearts, people squander their hard-earned wealth on extravagant luxuries simply to flaunt social superiority and project an illusion of importance. Such ostentation produces shallow, pretentious relationships where individuals are valued for outward ornaments rather than inner virtue. In stark contrast, humility strips away pretense and reveals the genuine human being. Humility allows a person to acknowledge their human limitations, respect the dignity of fellow creatures, and lead a purposeful life marked by compassion and simplicity. Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH), the supreme leader of Arabia, proved through his impeccable life that the highest human nobility lies in humility: he milked his own goats, mended his own shoes, slept on coarse palm-fiber mats, and gathered firewood alongside his companions. When we emulate this sublime Sunnah, our conduct becomes considerate and genuine, our happiness becomes unadulterated, and we replace arrogant pride with affectionate humility.

reading.title: The Champions
reading.theme: Intercultural Harmony, Loyalty & True Friendship
reading.author: Adapted from 'Amigo Brothers' by Piri Thomas (with slight modifications to suit social and cultural sensitivities)
reading.preReading:
Look at the picture and guess what the story is about.
1. What do you see in the picture?
2. Which sport do you think is being played?
3. What qualities are needed to become a good sports person?

passages.heading: Bosom Friends and Lyarite Brothers
passages.text: Ahmad Ali and Gul Sher were classmates studying in grade ten in a government school, situated in the impoverished neighbourhood of Lyari, Karachi. They were so together in friendship that they felt themselves to be brothers. They had known each other since childhood, growing up on the lower Eastern side of Lyari River. Gul Sher was fair, lean, and lanky; his family had moved from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to Karachi before his birth. Ahmad Ali was Sheedi, dark, short, and husky. Gul Sher's hair was always falling over his eyes, while Ahmad Ali wore his black hair in a natural Afro style.

summary.en: Ahmad Ali and Gul Sher were two devoted teenage friends from Lyari, Karachi who grew up together like brothers despite different ethnic origins.
summary.ur: احمد علی اور گل شیر لیاری، کراچی کے دو قریبی دوست تھے جو مختلف نسلی پس منظر کے باوجود بچپن سے سگے بھائیوں کی طرح ساتھ پلے بڑھے۔

passages.heading: Shared Passion and Legendary Boxing Idols
passages.text: Each youngster had a dream of someday becoming a lightweight boxing champion of the world. To achieve this cherished dream, they would strive hard day and night. Early morning sunrises would find them running along the River Lyari. They would attend the boxing club daily without any break. They had a collection of pictures of famous boxers like Joe Louis, Evander Holyfield, Rocky Marciano, Joe Frazier, Muhammad Ali and Mike Tyson; cut out from old newspapers and magazines. If asked a question about any given fighter, they would immediately zip out from their memory ranks, divisions, weights, records of fights, knockouts, technical knockouts, and draws or losses.

summary.en: Both boys shared a passionate ambition to become world lightweight boxing champions, training relentlessly along the Lyari River and memorizing stats of boxing legends.
summary.ur: دونوں نوجوانوں کا خواب تھا کہ وہ دنیا کے لائٹ ویٹ باکسنگ چیمپئن بنیں۔ اس مقصد کے لیے وہ دریائے لیاری کے کنارے سخت مشق کرتے اور مشہور باکسروں کی تاریخ زبانی یاد رکھتے۔

passages.heading: Contrasting Styles: The Tall Boxer and the Muscular Slugger
passages.text: Each had fought many fights and had won medals. They were equally good boxers. The difference was in their boxing style: Gul's lean form and long reach made him the better boxer, while Ali's short and muscular frame made him the better slugger. Whenever they had met in the ring for a friendly fight, it had always been hot and close. Now they were fighting from two different poles—for the National Boxing Championship and the winner of the final was to represent the country in the World Lightweight Boxing Championship. After a series of bouts, the two friends were scheduled to meet each other, just two weeks away.

summary.en: Gul was a tactical boxer with long reach, while Ali was a hard-hitting slugger. After winning elimination bouts, the two best friends qualified to fight each other in the national final.
summary.ur: گل شیر لمبی پہنچ والا ماہر باکسر تھا جبکہ احمد علی طاقتور گھونسے برسانے والا سلگر۔ دونوں نے تمام مقابلے جیت لیے اور اب فائنل میں ایک دوسرے کے مدمقابل تھے۔

passages.heading: The Rising Wall of Friendship and Unspoken Tension
passages.text: The two boys continued to run together, but even when talking with each other, they both had sensed that a wall was rising between them. One morning less than a week before the fight, they met as usual for their daily workout along the river's edge. Gul glanced at Ali who kept his eyes steadfastly straight ahead, pausing from time to time to throw fists at an imaginary jaw. After a mile or so, Ali puffed and said, "Let's stop for a while, bro. I think we both got something to say to each other." Gul nodded. It was not natural to be acting as though nothing unusual was happening when two star players and bosom friends were going to fight each other within a few short days.

summary.en: As the final match drew near, an awkward psychological distance emerged between the friends during their daily workout.
summary.ur: مقابلے کے قریب آتے ہی دونوں کے درمیان ایک نامعلوم تناؤ اور دوری پیدا ہو گئی جس پر انہوں نے باہمی گفتگو کرنے کا فیصلہ کیا۔

passages.heading: The Honest Talk by the Lyari River
passages.text: They rested their elbows on the railing separating them from the river. Ali broke the silence. "Man, I don't know how to come out with it." Gul helped. "It's about our fight, right?" "Yeah, right. In fact, since we found out it was going to be me and you, I've been awake at nights, pulling punches on you, trying not to hurt you." "Same here. It is natural to think about the fight. I mean, we both are outstanding fighters, and we both want to win. But only one of us can win. There is no draw in the elimination." Ali tapped Gul gently on the shoulder. "I don't mean to sound like I'm bragging, bro. But I want to win, fair and square." Gul nodded quietly. "Yeah. We both know that in the ring the better man wins. Friend or no friend, brother or no..." They shook hands and departed to confront each other in the ring.

summary.en: They frankly discussed their anxieties, agreeing that inside the ring they must fight honestly as professional competitors without holding back.
summary.ur: انہوں نے دریا کے کنارے اعتراف کیا کہ وہ دونوں ایک دوسرے کو زخمی کرنے سے ڈر رہے تھے، مگر طے پایا کہ رنگ کے اندر دونوں پوری دیانتداری سے لڑیں گے۔

passages.heading: Sleepless Nights and Heavy Doubts
passages.text: Walking the streets had not relaxed Ali; the more he thought about the fight the more perplexed he felt. Lost in thoughts, he let himself quietly into his apartment and went straight to bed, falling into a restless and fitful sleep with sounds of the gong for Round One. When Gul reached home, he made his way to the rooftop. In the quiet early dark, he peered below where the lights of the city blinked, and the sounds of cars mingled with the shout and the laughter of children in the street. He was passing some heavy time on his rooftop. How would the coming fight affect his relationship with Ali?

summary.en: Both boys endured restless, agonizing hours contemplating the possible impact of the fight on their lifelong bond.
summary.ur: دونوں دوستوں نے بے چین اور فکرمند راتیں گزاریں اور سوچتے رہے کہ اس مقابلے کا ان کی دوستی پر کیا اثر پڑے گا۔

passages.heading: Entering the Ring: The Crowd and the Announcer
passages.text: As the two climbed into the ring, the crowd exploded with a roar. Gul and Ali both bowed gracefully and then raised their arms in acknowledgment. Gul turned slowly and his eyes met Ali's. Suddenly Ali's left eye winked and Gul responded. Bong, bong, bong! The roar turned to stillness. "Ladies and Gentlemen," the announcer spoke slowly. "Now the moment we have all been waiting for—the main event between two fine young fighters. In this corner, weighing 131 pounds, Ahmad Ali. And in this corner, weighing 133 pounds, Gul Sher Khan. The winner will represent Pakistan in World Boxing Championship in the Lightweight Category. There will be no draw. May the best man win!"

summary.en: The stadium was packed with enthusiastic fans as the announcer introduced Ahmad Ali and Gul Sher Khan for the national title fight.
summary.ur: شائقین کے پرجوش نعروں کے دوران رنگ میں اعلان ہوا کہ جیتنے والا عالمی باکسنگ چیمپئن شپ میں پاکستان کی نمائندگی کرے گا۔

passages.heading: Round One: Piston Jabs and Punishing Body Blows
passages.text: "BONG! BONG! ROUND ONE!" Ali and Gul turned and faced each other squarely in a fighting pose. Ali wasted no time. He came in fast, head low, half hunched toward his right shoulder, and lashed out with a straight left. He missed a right cross as Gul slipped the punch and countered with one-two-three lefts that snapped Ali's head back, sending a mild shock coursing through him. If Ali had any small doubt about their friendship affecting their fight, it was completely dispelled. Gul's left hand was like a piston pumping jabs one right after another with seeming ease. Ali bobbed and weaved and threw occasional punches with his right. He ducked a short right and missed a left hook. Ali trapped him against the ropes just long enough to pour some punishing rights and lefts to Gul's hard midsection. Bong! Round one came to conclusion.

summary.en: Round One was explosive: Gul landed swift combinations while Ali cornered Gul against the ropes with punishing body punches.
summary.ur: پہلے راؤنڈ میں گل شیر نے پسٹن کی طرح تیز گھونسے مارے جبکہ علی نے اسے رسیوں کے سہارے دبا کر پیٹ پر زوردار وار کیے۔

passages.heading: Round Two: Fierce Exchanges and Shaken Legs
passages.text: Both Lyarite brothers froze their punches well on its way, sending up a roar of approval for good sportsmanship. No sooner did Round two begin than Ali was off his stool and rushed at Gul like a bull, sending a hard right to his head. A bead of water exploded from Gul's long hair. Lights suddenly exploded inside Ali's head as Gul slipped the blow and hit him with a piston-like left to Ali's chin. Cheering and yelling broke out in the stadium when Gul's crushing blow momentarily unbalanced Ali's legs. Neither fighter was giving an inch. Suddenly a short right punch struck Gul squarely on the chin. His long legs turned to jelly, and his arms flailed out desperately. Ali, grunting like a bull, threw wild punches from every direction. Gul felt dizzy, disoriented, bobbed and weaved, evading most of the blows. Ali lashed back with a haymaker but at the same instant, his eye caught another left hook from Gul. Ali swung out, trying to clear the pain. In a fog, he heard the roaring of the crowd, who seemed to have gone insane. His head cleared to hear the bell sound at the end of the round.

summary.en: Round Two saw dramatic turns: Ali attacked like a raging bull, but Gul struck back fiercely, leaving both fighters staggered yet unyielding.
summary.ur: دوسرے راؤنڈ میں گھمسان کا رن پڑا، دونوں کے گھونسے اتنے کاری تھے کہ دونوں کے قدم لڑکھڑائے لیکن کوئی پیچھے نہ ہٹا۔

passages.heading: Round Three: The Savage Toe-to-Toe Finale
passages.text: Bong! Round three—the final round. Up to now it had been pretty much even. But everyone knew there could be no draw, and that this round would decide the winner. This time, to Ali's surprise, it was Gul Sher who came out fast, charging across the ring. Ali braced himself but couldn't ward off the barrage of punches. Gul drove Ali hard against the ropes. The crowd got frenzied. So far the two had fought with courage and bravery. Ali tapped his gloves and commenced his attack anew. Gul, throwing boxer's caution to the wind, jumped in to meet him. Both pounded away. Neither gave an inch, and neither fell to the canvas. Ali's left eye was tightly closed. Coral red blood poured from Gul's nose. They fought toe-to-toe. The sounds of their blows were loud in contrast to the silence of the crowd. The referee was stunned by their savagery.

summary.en: The final round was a furious toe-to-toe battle with Ali's eye swollen shut and blood streaming from Gul's nose as the referee watched in awe.
summary.ur: تیسرا راؤنڈ انتہائی خطرناک اور برابری کا تھا؛ علی کی آنکھ سوج چکی تھی اور گل کی ناک سے خون بہہ رہا تھا مگر دونوں بغیر رکے لڑتے رہے۔

passages.heading: The Embrace of True Champions
passages.text: Bong! Bong! Bong! Bell sounded over and over again. Ali and Gul were past hearing. Their blows continued to pound on each other like hailstones. Finally the referee and the two trainers pried Ali and Gul apart. Cold water was poured over them to bring them back to their senses. They looked around and then rushed toward each other. A cry of alarm surged through the stadium. Was this a fight to the death instead of a boxing match? The fear soon gave way to wave upon wave of cheering as the two Lyarite brothers embraced at the conclusion of the final round. No matter what the decision, they knew they would always be champions to each other.

summary.en: When separated by the referee, instead of attacking, the two boys rushed into an emotional embrace, earning thunderous ovations from the crowd.
summary.ur: گھنٹی بجنے کے بعد جب ریفری نے دونوں کو الگ کیا تو وہ آپس میں لڑنے کے بجائے گلے مل گئے جس پر سارا اسٹیڈیم تالیوں سے گونج اٹھا۔

passages.heading: Walking Away Hand in Hand: The True Victory
passages.text: Bong! Bong! Bong! "Ladies and Gentlemen. The winner and champion of the grand finale is..." The announcer turned to point to the winner and found himself alone. Arm in arm, the champions had already left the ring.

summary.en: Before the announcer could declare who won on points, both champions had already walked away arm in arm, proving friendship is supreme.
summary.ur: اس سے پہلے کہ فاتح کا باضابطہ اعلان ہوتا، دونوں چیمپئن ایک دوسرے کے کندھوں پر ہاتھ ڈال کر رنگ سے باہر جا چکے تھے۔

glossary.sentence: Gul Sher was fair, lean, and lanky, which gave him an exceptional reach in boxing.

glossary.sentence: Ahmad Ali was a proud young Sheedi boy from Lyari with natural Afro hair.

glossary.sentence: Ali's short and husky build made him a formidable inside slugger.

glossary.meaning: Excessively proud and boastful talk about one's achievements or possessions.
glossary.sentence: Ali assured Gul that he wasn't bragging, but simply meant to give his very best.

glossary.sentence: The sharp clang of the ringside gong announced the start of Round One.

vocabulary.title: Boxing Terminology & Idiomatic Sports Expressions
vocabulary.instruction: Study the specialized boxing terms and idioms used by the author to create realistic narrative tension.

items.definition: A wild, swinging punch delivered with maximum force and body momentum, capable of knocking an opponent out.
items.example: Ali lashed back with a vicious haymaker, but Gul slipped underneath it.

items.definition: A defensive boxing maneuver where the fighter rhythmically bends down and sways side-to-side to evade straight punches.
items.example: Gul bobbed and weaved smoothly, frustrating Ali's offensive charges.

items.definition: A quick, sharp, straight punch thrown with the leading fist while keeping the body balanced.
items.example: Gul's left hand was like a mechanical piston pumping rapid jabs.

items.definition: Holding back strength or refraining from striking with full force; metaphorically, withholding honest criticism.
items.example: Neither fighter pulled punches; both fought with complete honesty.

items.definition: A formal competitive match or contest between two boxers or wrestlers.
items.example: After winning a series of gruelling bouts, the two friends reached the finals.

items.definition: A boxer who relies on sheer physical strength and devastating knockout punches rather than subtle footwork.
items.example: Ali was an aggressive slugger whose close-range punches packed immense power.

questions.q: What is the significance of the title 'The Champions'?
questions.ans: The title 'The Champions' is deeply symbolic and thematic. It demonstrates that genuine champions are not defined merely by judges' scorecards, medals, or championship belts, but by the moral height of their character, loyalty, and sportsmanship. By fighting with complete honesty and then walking away arm in arm before hearing the verdict, Ahmad Ali and Gul Sher proved that their brotherly love was far superior to selfish victory. Both boys were true champions of the human spirit.

questions.q: What was the dream of Ahmad Ali and Gul Sher?
questions.ans: The shared dream of Ahmad Ali and Gul Sher was to become the Lightweight Boxing Champions of the world. To achieve this lifelong goal, they dedicated themselves to rigorous daily training, running along the Lyari River at dawn, attending the boxing gym without missing a single session, and collecting pictures and statistics of boxing legends like Muhammad Ali and Joe Louis.

questions.q: Why was the fight so important for both Ali and Gul Sher?
questions.ans: The fight was critically important because it was the grand finale of the National Boxing Championship. The winner was guaranteed to represent Pakistan at the World Lightweight Boxing Championship. For two impoverished boys from Lyari, this contest was their golden gateway to international acclaim, professional glory, and escaping poverty.

questions.q: How did the two friends fight? Describe in your own words in five sentences.
questions.ans:
1. Both boys fought with fierce professional intensity and bravery, never pulling a single punch.
2. In the opening round, Gul landed crisp, piston-like left jabs while Ali retaliated with punishing hooks to Gul's midsection.
3. The second round turned into an explosive exchange where crushing blows wobbled both fighters' legs and tested their endurance.
4. In the final round, they battled toe-to-toe with relentless ferocity, with Ali's eye swollen shut and blood streaming from Gul's nose.
5. When the final bell sounded, they immediately cast aside hostility and embraced warmly in deep mutual respect.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the characters of Ali and Gul.
questions.ans:
• Ahmad Ali: A dark, short, and muscularly built Sheedi youth wearing an Afro hairstyle. As a boxer, he was a compact 'slugger' specializing in explosive infighting, crushing hooks, and unrelenting forward pressure.
• Gul Sher Khan: A fair, lean, and lanky youth whose family hailed from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. As a boxer, he utilized his height and long reach to fight tactically from a distance with sharp jabs and elusive footwork.
• Common Character: Both were honest, hardworking, fiercely competitive inside the ring, yet bound by unconditional love and supreme loyalty outside it.

questions.q: Is there any conflict in the story? If yes, describe it in detail.
questions.ans:
Yes, the story contains both internal (psychological) and external (physical) conflicts:
• Internal Conflict: Both boys were tormented by the painful dilemma of having to fight their closest friend. They spent sleepless nights worrying that the brutal rivalry of the championship bout might permanently rupture their brotherhood.
• External Conflict: The physical conflict unfolded in the boxing ring during three savagely contested rounds where each fighter had to summon his greatest physical power and skill against his best friend.

questions.q: What was the effect of the fight on the relationship of the two friends?
questions.ans: The fight strengthened and elevated their relationship rather than harming it. Because both boys fought with unreserved courage and total honesty, neither felt resentful or cheated. Their emotional embrace immediately following the final bell proved that their bond of brotherhood was completely immune to the pressures of competition.

questions.q: Keeping in view the relationship of the two friends, is it easier or harder for them to fight each other? Support your answer by giving references from the text.
questions.ans:
It was immensely harder for them to fight each other. The text illustrates their deep emotional agony:
1. 'They both had sensed that a wall was rising between them' as the match date drew near.
2. Ali confessed, 'Since we found out it was going to be me and you, I've been awake at nights, pulling punches on you, trying not to hurt you.'
3. Gul spent 'heavy time on his rooftop' agonizing over how the fight would affect their friendship.
4. Ali endured a 'restless and fitful sleep' troubled by the psychological burden of facing his brother in the ring.

questions.q: Are you satisfied with the ending? Support your response with cogent arguments.
questions.ans: Yes, I am thoroughly satisfied with the ending. Having the two friends walk away arm-in-arm before the official decision was announced provides a masterful resolution to the central conflict. It asserts that human love and loyalty are infinitely more valuable than sports trophies. Leaving the winner anonymous highlights that both boys were champions of sportsmanship, dignity, and brotherhood.

mcqs.q: "Gul's lean form and long reach made him better boxer." This statement means that Gul was a better boxer because:
opts: he was short, big with long arms
he was tall, skinny with long arms
he was short, skinny with long arms
he was high, well-built with short arms
mcqs.exp: 'Lean' means slim or skinny, and 'long reach' refers to having tall stature with long arms, giving a distinct boxing advantage.

mcqs.q: "Ali was dark, short and husky." In this sentence the phrase "short and husky" means:
opts: thick and strong / small and well-built
mcqs.exp: 'Husky' describes a person who is solidly built, strong, and muscular despite being shorter in height.

mcqs.q: They both sensed that a wall was rising between them. This statement means:
opts: they were climbing higher on the wall of fame
communication gap and psychological distance were increasing between them
they were getting closer to each other
they decided to construct a physical partition
mcqs.exp: A 'wall rising between them' is a metaphor for awkward psychological reserve, emotional barrier, and declining open communication.

mcqs.q: They could not win the contest individually in the ring because:
opts: they were afraid of each other
they realised that boxing is not a good sport
friendship was greater than winning the fight
mcqs.exp: Their supreme loyalty and love made individual victory irrelevant; brotherhood transcended the athletic trophy.

mcqs.q: Ali had restless and fitful sleep on the night before the fight because:
opts: he had quarrelled with Gul Sher
he was challenged by Gul Sher
he had fallen ill on that particular night
he was disturbed about the effects of the forthcoming fight on their friendship
mcqs.exp: Ali was deeply troubled by the fear of hurting his dearest friend and damaging their lifelong brotherhood.

grammar.topic: Articles: Definite, Indefinite, and Zero Article (Exercise A)
grammar.rule: Articles define whether a noun is specific or unspecific. Use 'a' before singular countable nouns starting with a consonant sound, 'an' before vowel sounds, and 'the' when referring to a specific, previously mentioned, or unique noun. Use no article (zero article) before proper nouns, abstract qualities, and plural/uncountable nouns used in general.
examples: Ahmad is an athlete (unspecific singular countable).
The boxing ring in Lyari was packed (specific known location).
Sportsmanship is vital (zero article for abstract concept).

exercises.q: My mother is ______ doctor and my father is ______ author.
exercises.ans: a / an (doctor begins with a consonant sound /d/; author begins with a vowel sound /ɔː/).

exercises.q: Tariq recommended ______ good dentist, but ______ dentist doesn't have any openings for two months.
exercises.ans: a / the (first mention is indefinite 'a good dentist'; second mention refers to the specific known dentist).

exercises.q: Do you have ______ broom? I dropped ______ piece of cake, and I need to clean it up.
exercises.ans: a / a (both nouns are singular countable items mentioned generally).

exercises.q: Do you have ______ dictionary? I don't have one, and I need to look up ______ word.
exercises.ans: a / a (both nouns are indefinite, non-specific countable items).

exercises.q: Do you have ______ passport? You need ______ passport to travel outside of ______ country.
exercises.ans: a / a / the (a passport = any valid passport; the country = specific native country one resides in).

grammar.rule: Supply 'a', 'an', 'the', or 'x' (no article) depending on specific reference, general category, or geographical convention.
examples: Ancient Greece (zero article with ancient historical countries).
The first Olympic games (ordinal numbers require 'the').

exercises.q: Boxing was originated in Ancient Greece [____] and has been [____] popular sport ever since, especially for men. Lately, however, it has been [____] major health fitness trend for women. In ancient Greece boxing was in [____] first Olympic games. In [____] sport, they never used gloves. Professional boxing is [____] excellent career. [____] boxer's aim is to land as many punches on [____] opponent as possible. For most of [____] 20th century, boxing attracted huge fan and media attention.
exercises.ans: x (Ancient Greece) / a (popular sport) / a (major health trend) / the (first Olympic games) / the (sport) / an (excellent career) / A (boxer's aim) / the (opponent) / the (20th century).

grammar.rule: Personal pronouns take different forms according to person (first, second, third), number (singular, plural), gender (masculine, feminine, neuter), and grammatical case (subjective, objective, possessive).
examples: Subjective: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
Objective: me, you, him, her, it, us, them
Possessive: my/mine, his, her/hers, its, our/ours, their/theirs

exercises.q: My name is Sonia. (He / I / She / We) love my family.
exercises.ans: I (first-person singular subject pronoun matching 'my family').

exercises.q: I met Sonia yesterday. (Her / She / They / Him) made me laugh.
exercises.ans: She (third-person singular feminine subject pronoun replacing Sonia).

exercises.q: At the left, you can see Saad. (He / Him / That / She) is my brother.
exercises.ans: He (third-person singular masculine subject pronoun referring to Saad).

exercises.q: Birds flap (it / his / their / those) wings.
exercises.ans: their (third-person plural possessive determiner agreeing with plural 'Birds').

exercises.q: My grandparents live in Karachi. (Them / They / Their / He) visit us.
exercises.ans: They (third-person plural subject pronoun referring to grandparents).

exercises.q: Lubna, Laila and Tahira were cross because (them / he / they / it) had waited ages for the bus.
exercises.ans: they (plural subject pronoun replacing compound subject Lubna, Laila, and Tahira).

exercises.q: Palwasha watched the children carefully as (them / he / they / it) crossed the road.
exercises.ans: they (plural subject pronoun referring to children).

exercises.q: Hold the bag please while I put the shopping in (him / it / she / them).
exercises.ans: it (singular neuter object pronoun referring to 'the bag').

grammar.topic: Relative Pronouns: Who, Which, Whose (Exercise B)
grammar.rule: Relative pronouns introduce relative clauses. Use 'who' for persons (as subject), 'whom' for persons (as object), 'whose' for possession, and 'which' for animals, objects, and non-human concepts.
examples: The boy who boxed bravely (person).
The trophy which they contested (thing).
The girl whose car broke down (possession).

exercises.q: I talked to the girl ______ car had broken down in front of the shop.
exercises.ans: whose (shows possession of the car by the girl).

exercises.q: Mr. Tariq, ______ is a taxi driver, lives on the corner.
exercises.ans: who (refers to a human subject Mr. Tariq).

exercises.q: I live in a house in Naran, ______ is in Northern Pakistan.
exercises.ans: which (refers to a place / non-human antecedent 'Naran' or 'house').

exercises.q: This is the girl ______ comes from Swat.
exercises.ans: who (refers to a female person as subject).

exercises.q: That's Naeem, the boy ______ has just arrived at the airport.
exercises.ans: who (refers to the boy as subject).

exercises.q: This is a detective novel ______ you might like.
exercises.ans: which (refers to a thing / book).

exercises.q: Here are the keys ______ you were searching for.
exercises.ans: which (refers to objects / keys).

exercises.q: Those ______ haven't paid their fee should do so at once.
exercises.ans: who (refers to plural persons as subject).

grammar.rule: An indefinite pronoun refers to non-specific people, objects, or quantities. Singular: everybody, anybody, nobody, someone, each, either, neither, everything. Plural: few, many, several, both. Variable: some, all, any, none.
examples: Everybody cheered for the champions.
Nobody knew who would win.

exercises.q: Underline the indefinite pronoun in: 'Everybody enjoys a good movie.'
exercises.ans: Indefinite pronoun: 'Everybody' (singular indefinite pronoun).

exercises.q: Underline the indefinite pronoun in: 'Does anybody have the time?'
exercises.ans: Indefinite pronoun: 'anybody' (singular indefinite pronoun used in questions).

exercises.q: Underline the indefinite pronoun in: 'Nobody knows the trouble I've seen.'
exercises.ans: Indefinite pronoun: 'Nobody' (negative singular indefinite pronoun).

exercises.q: Underline the indefinite pronouns in: 'The secret was known by few. / The secret was known by many.'
exercises.ans: Indefinite pronouns: 'few' and 'many' (plural indefinite pronouns referring to unspecified numbers of people).

exercises.q: Underline the indefinite pronoun in: 'Calculus is too hard for some.'
exercises.ans: Indefinite pronoun: 'some' (indefinite pronoun indicating an unspecified portion).

exercises.q: Underline the indefinite pronoun in: 'Surely you recognize somebody.'
exercises.ans: Indefinite pronoun: 'somebody' (singular indefinite pronoun).

exercises.q: Underline the indefinite pronoun in: 'He's not a liar. I'm sure everything he said was true.'
exercises.ans: Indefinite pronoun: 'everything' (singular indefinite pronoun referring to all statements).

grammar.rule: An antecedent is the noun or noun phrase to which a pronoun refers. A pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number, person, and gender.
examples: Asma played with her dollhouse (Antecedent: Asma -> Pronoun: her).
Classmates chose their topic (Antecedent: Classmates -> Pronoun: their).

exercises.q: Identify pronoun and antecedent: 'Asma often played with her dollhouse.'
exercises.ans: Antecedent: Asma | Personal pronoun: her

exercises.q: Identify pronoun and antecedent: 'Neither Danish nor Waseem will have trouble finding information for their report.'
exercises.ans: Antecedents: Danish, Waseem | Possessive pronoun: their (or his in formal usage)

exercises.q: Identify pronoun and antecedent: 'Each of the boys refused help saying that they would proofread the report on their own.'
exercises.ans: Antecedent: Each (of the boys) | Pronouns: they, their (or he / his in formal prescriptive grammar)

exercises.q: Identify pronoun and antecedent: 'Tania needs a result card of her grades.'
exercises.ans: Antecedent: Tania | Pronoun: her

exercises.q: Identify pronoun and antecedent: 'One of the girls left her sweater in the bus.'
exercises.ans: Antecedent: One (of the girls) | Pronoun: her

exercises.q: Choose correct pronoun agreement: 'Each man must do what (he, they) feel(s) is right.'
exercises.ans: he feels (singular pronoun 'he' agrees with singular distributive subject 'Each man').

exercises.q: Choose correct pronoun agreement: 'Everybody in the lab was ready to complete (her, their) assignment.'
exercises.ans: her / his (singular indefinite pronoun 'Everybody' formally takes a singular possessive determiner).

exercises.q: Choose correct pronoun agreement: 'No one wants to admit (his, their) weaknesses.'
exercises.ans: his (or his/her) (singular indefinite pronoun 'No one' takes singular pronoun).

writing.summary: In 'The Champions', adapted from Piri Thomas's celebrated short story, two lifelong teenage friends from Lyari, Karachi—Ahmad Ali, a muscular Sheedi slugger, and Gul Sher Khan, a tall, tactical boxer from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa—share an ambition to become world lightweight boxing champions. When both qualify for the national finals where only one can advance to represent Pakistan globally, a painful emotional barrier arises between them. Fearing their bond might suffer, they frankly promise to fight with complete honesty inside the ring. On fight night, before an ecstatic crowd, the two friends unleash three savage, punishing rounds of relentless combinations, refusing to concede an inch despite battered eyes and bleeding noses. However, when the final bell rings and trainers separate them, the two brothers immediately rush into an affectionate embrace. Before the announcer can declare the winner on points, Ali and Gul leave the ring arm-in-arm, proving that their brotherhood is the ultimate victory.

essay.title: Is Boxing Too Brutal for Youth? Reflections on 'The Champions'
essay.text: The story 'The Champions' presents a profound dual perspective on whether boxing is too violent a sport for young people. On one hand, the narrative graphically depicts the brutality of combat sports: swollen eyes, bleeding noses, bruised midsections, and dazed senses as two teenage boys exchange devastating blows that turn their legs to jelly. The visceral violence illustrated in the third round demonstrates why critics argue that combat sports expose developing youth to severe neurological and physical harm. On the other hand, the story demonstrates that the discipline of boxing cultivated deep mutual respect, physical resilience, dedication, and sportsmanship in Ahmad Ali and Gul Sher. Rather than producing hatred or malice, the sport taught them courage and self-control. Most remarkably, their bond survived the ultimate physical contest: they discarded the glory of victory and walked out arm-in-arm, illustrating that character and sportsmanship can transcend physical violence.

dialogue.title: Dialogue Between Ahmad Ali and Gul Sher After Leaving the Ring
dialogue.text:
Ali: (Wiping sweat and smiling through a swollen eye) Bro, you hit like a runaway truck in that second round! My ribs are singing a symphony!
Gul: (Laughing as he holds an ice pack to his nose) Look who's talking! That right hook of yours in round three turned the stadium into spinning lights! I thought the ceiling was collapsing on me.
Ali: You know what, Gul? When the bell rang, I didn't care about the judges' scorecards or the trip abroad. All I cared about was that you were still my brother.
Gul: (Puts his arm around Ali's shoulder) We won something much bigger than a metal trophy tonight, Ali. In the eyes of Lyari and each other, we'll always be the real champions.

translationUrdu.english: Ahmad Ali and Gul Sher were classmates studying in grade ten in a government school, situated in the impoverished neighbourhood of Lyari, Karachi.
translationUrdu.urdu: احمد علی اور گل شیر لیاری، کراچی کے پسماندہ علاقے میں واقع ایک سرکاری اسکول کی دسویں جماعت میں ہم جماعت تھے۔

translationUrdu.english: They were so together in friendship that they felt themselves to be brothers.
translationUrdu.urdu: وہ دوستی میں اتنے یکجان تھے کہ خود کو سگے بھائی محسوس کرتے تھے۔

translationUrdu.english: Each youngster had a dream of someday becoming a lightweight boxing champion of the world.
translationUrdu.urdu: ہر نوجوان کا خواب تھا کہ وہ کسی دن دنیا کا لائٹ ویٹ باکسنگ چیمپئن بنے۔

translationUrdu.english: Arm in arm, the champions had already left the ring.
translationUrdu.urdu: ایک دوسرے کے بازو میں بازو ڈالے چیمپئن پہلے ہی رنگ سے باہر جا چکے تھے۔

poet.name: Langston Hughes
poet.bio: Langston Hughes was born on February 1, 1902, in Joplin, Missouri. Hughes published his first book in 1926. He went on to write countless works of poetry, prose and plays, as well as a popular column for the Chicago Defender. He died on May 22, 1967.

reading.title: Dreams
reading.theme: Ambition & Hope
reading.author: Langston Hughes (1902–1967)
reading.preReading:
Think and answer the pre-reading questions:
1. What are dreams?
2. What would your life be like if you had no dreams for your future?

passages.heading: Stanza 1: The Broken-Winged Bird
passages.text:
Hold fast to dreams
For if dreams die
Life is a broken-winged bird
That cannot fly.

summary.en: The poet implores the reader to cling tightly to dreams, warning that without them life becomes helpless and grounded like a bird with a shattered wing.
summary.ur: شاعر خوابوں اور مقاصد کو مضبوطی سے تھامنے کی تلقین کرتا ہے کیونکہ اگر خواب ختم ہو جائیں تو زندگی ایک ٹوٹے ہوئے پروں والے پرندے کی مانند بے بس ہو جاتی ہے۔

passages.heading: Stanza 2: The Barren, Frozen Field
passages.text:
Hold fast to dreams
For when dreams go
Life is a barren field
Frozen with snow.

summary.en: The poet repeats the urgent call to preserve dreams, comparing a dreamless life to a desolate, icy field incapable of bearing life or harvest.
summary.ur: شاعر دوبارہ تاکید کرتا ہے کہ خوابوں کو تھامے رکھو، ورنہ زندگی برف سے جمے ہوئے اس بنجر کھیت جیسی ہو جائے گی جس میں کوئی فصل نہیں اگ سکتی۔

passages.heading: About the Poet (Langston Hughes)
passages.text: Langston Hughes was born on February 1, 1902, in Joplin, Missouri. Hughes published his first book in 1926. He went on to write countless works of poetry, prose and plays, as well as a popular column for the Chicago Defender. He died on May 22, 1967.

summary.en: Biographical context of the prominent American poet, novelist, and playwright of the Harlem Renaissance.
summary.ur: مشہور امریکی شاعر اور ادیب لینگسٹن ہیوز کا تعارف جن کی شاعری امید اور جدوجہد کا استعارہ ہے۔

glossary.meaning: Hold something tightly, firmly, and tenaciously without letting go.
glossary.sentence: Hold fast to your noble principles in times of adversity.

glossary.meaning: (Of land) too poor to produce much or any vegetation; bleak, sterile, and lifeless.
glossary.sentence: Without water, the fertile valley turned into a barren desert.

glossary.meaning: An area of open land, especially one planted with crops or pasture.
glossary.sentence: The farmers plowed the wide field before the onset of monsoon rains.

glossary.meaning: Turned into ice or covered with frost as a result of extreme cold; rigid and motionless.
glossary.sentence: The lake remained completely frozen throughout the sub-zero winter.

vocabulary.title: Poetic Figurative Analysis & Textual Evidence
vocabulary.instruction: Explain the inferred meaning of each phrase using evidence directly from the poetic context.

items.definition: A bird unable to take flight; metaphorically signifies a human spirit deprived of soaring potential, freedom, and self-actualization.
items.example: Life without aspiration is reduced to a broken-winged bird.

items.definition: Sterile soil incapable of germinating seeds; represents an empty existence that produces no creative achievements or spiritual fruits.
items.example: A mind devoid of hope resembles a barren field.

items.definition: Chilled into paralysis and lifeless stillness; conveys the emotional coldness, stagnation, and desolation of despair.
items.example: The winter cold left the landscape frozen with snow.

items.definition: To maintain an unshakeable grip with perseverance and determination.
items.example: Hold fast to dreams despite discouraging circumstances.

questions.q: What is the theme of the poem?
questions.ans: The central theme of 'Dreams' is the supreme vital importance of holding onto hopes, ideals, and ambitions. Langston Hughes asserts that dreams give purpose, vitality, and direction to human existence. Without dreams, life loses its beauty and becomes spiritually crippled and dead.

questions.q: How important do you think dreams are? Explain.
questions.ans: Dreams are indispensable to human life because they serve as the internal engine of motivation, innovation, and perseverance. They inspire individuals to overcome daunting obstacles, endure suffering, and strive for self-improvement. Without dreams, human history would lack progress, art, science, and the inspiration to rise above mediocrity.

questions.q: Identify an example of a word or phrase that is repeated in the poem and explain why the poet makes this repetition.
questions.ans: The phrase 'Hold fast to dreams' is repeated at the start of both Stanza 1 and Stanza 2. The poet uses this refrain (anaphora) to emphasize urgency and reinforce his central command. By repeating this admonition, Hughes ensures that the message resonates forcefully with the reader as an uncompromisable priority.

questions.q: Identify an example of personification. Explain what is being personified.
questions.ans: In Stanza 1, the poet personifies dreams in the line 'For if dreams die' and in Stanza 2 'For when dreams go'. Here, 'dreams' (which are abstract mental thoughts and aspirations) are given the biological attributes of living organisms that can perish ('die') or depart ('go'). This highlights that dreams possess a delicate life of their own that must be nourished and protected.

questions.q: Identify lines containing metaphors. What ideas are being conveyed by these metaphors?
questions.ans:
The poem contains two central metaphors:
1. 'Life is a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly' (Stanza 1): Directly equates a dreamless life to an injured bird. It conveys the idea of tragic helplessness, frustration, and the inability to achieve one's natural soaring potential.
2. 'Life is a barren field / Frozen with snow' (Stanza 2): Directly equates life without dreams to a bleak, ice-bound wasteland. It conveys total sterility, spiritual coldness, emotional stagnation, and hopelessness.

questions.q: List the alliterative words from the poem 'Dreams'.
questions.ans:
The alliterative phrases in the poem include:
• 'dreams die' (repetition of the initial consonant sound /d/).
• 'broken-winged bird' (repetition of the consonant sound /b/).
• 'frozen / field' (subtle consonant harmony in /f/).

questions.q: How is imagery used in this poem?
questions.ans:
Hughes masterfully employs visual and tactile imagery to evoke vivid emotional contrasts:
• Visual imagery of a 'broken-winged bird' struggling helplessly on the dirt evokes intense pity and sorrow.
• Tactile and visual imagery of a 'barren field frozen with snow' evokes biting cold, desolate gray emptiness, and total absence of warmth or life. These stark images contrast powerfully with the unspoken warmth and freedom that dreams provide.

questions.q: What is the mood of this poem? How does it make you feel?
questions.ans: The mood of the poem is solemn, cautionary, yet deeply motivating and urgent. It evokes a poignant awareness of human vulnerability while instilling a fierce, renewed determination to cling tenaciously to one's highest life goals regardless of difficulties.

mcqs.q: The phrase 'hold fast to dreams' means:
opts: don't do anything just dream day and night
day dreaming is good for health
dreaming will make your holding power strong
stick fast to your ambition in life
mcqs.exp: 'Hold fast' is an idiomatic expression meaning to grip tightly, persevere, and adhere steadfastly to your ambitions.

mcqs.q: In the line 'life is a broken-winged bird', the poet uses the technique of:
mcqs.exp: The line is a direct comparison equating 'life' to a 'broken-winged bird' without using 'like' or 'as', which is the definition of a metaphor.

mcqs.q: In the line 'life is a barren field', the phrase 'a barren field' is an example of:
mcqs.exp: Equating life to a barren field without comparative conjunctions constitutes a metaphor.

mcqs.q: According to the poet, life without dreams is:
mcqs.exp: The imagery of an injured bird and a frozen barren field depicts an existence that is sterile, hollow, and bleak.

mcqs.q: According to 'Dreams', what will happen if our dreams die?
opts: Life will be easier to handle
Life will appear as it is
mcqs.exp: Without dreams, life loses meaning, mobility, and vitality, descending into hopeless stagnation.

grammar.rule: A transitive verb requires a direct object to complete its meaning (Subject + Verb + Direct Object). An intransitive verb does not require a direct object; the action stops with the subject or is modified by an adverbial (Subject + Verb + Adverbial/None).
examples: Transitive: I watched a movie (movie = direct object).
Intransitive: The child gurgles (no object needed).
Intransitive: The birds are flying (action does not pass to an object).

exercises.q: Choose the sentence that does NOT have an intransitive verb: a) I watched a movie. b) The child gurgles. c) She sobs. d) The baby cried.
exercises.ans: a) I watched a movie ('watched' is transitive taking the direct object 'a movie'; the others are intransitive).

exercises.q: Choose the sentence that does NOT have a transitive verb: a) I presented a bouquet. b) He waved his arm. c) She understood my question. d) She laughed heartily.
exercises.ans: d) She laughed heartily ('laughed' is intransitive; 'heartily' is an adverb of manner, not an object).

exercises.q: Choose the sentence that does NOT have a transitive verb: a) We showed her the flower vase. b) The grocer is selling vegetables. c) The birds are flying. d) The coach advised me to practice daily.
exercises.ans: c) The birds are flying ('flying' takes no direct object and is intransitive).

exercises.q: Choose the sentence that does NOT have an intransitive verb: a) The customer is buying pancakes. b) The customer is buying this afternoon. c) They were crying all day long. d) Akbar is jogging.
exercises.ans: a) The customer is buying pancakes ('buying' has direct object 'pancakes').

exercises.q: Choose the sentence that does NOT have a transitive verb: a) She cut the cake. b) They climbed the hill. c) Arman telephoned Tariq. d) Asma shouted in the class.
exercises.ans: d) Asma shouted in the class ('shouted' is intransitive; 'in the class' is a prepositional phrase of place).

exercises.q: Choose the sentence that does NOT have an intransitive verb: a) The student is answering questions. b) Akbar is jogging at this moment. c) She sleeps too much. d) He complains frequently.
exercises.ans: a) The student is answering questions ('answering' is transitive with direct object 'questions').

grammar.topic: Present Participle and Past Participle (Exercises A & B)
grammar.rule: A participle is a verbal that functions as an adjective or forms compound tenses. The Present Participle ends in -ing (active meaning). The Past Participle typically ends in -ed, -en, -t, -d (passive/completed meaning). Participle clauses allow two related sentences to be combined concisely.
examples: Prepared by the chef, the meal was delicious (Past participle).
We met a boy carrying a heavy bag (Present participle clause).

exercises.q: Put verb in correct participle: '(prepare) by the best cook in town, the meal was sheer poetry.'
exercises.ans: Prepared (past participle indicating passive condition).

exercises.q: Put verb in correct participle: 'After (study) all day, her head was aching in the evening.'
exercises.ans: studying (present participle used after preposition 'after').

exercises.q: Put verb in correct participle: '(lie) on the sofa, they were watching TV.'
exercises.ans: Lying (present participle showing simultaneous active state).

exercises.q: Put verb in correct participle: 'Everybody was (shock) to hear the news.'
exercises.ans: shocked (past participle acting as predicate adjective).

exercises.q: Put verb in correct participle: 'Before (leave) the house, I always check if all lights are switched off.'
exercises.ans: leaving (present participle following preposition).

exercises.q: Combine using participles: 'The house was decorated with lights. It looked beautiful.'
exercises.ans: Decorated with lights, the house looked beautiful.

exercises.q: Combine using participles: 'The robbers saw the policeman. They ran away.'
exercises.ans: Seeing the policeman, the robbers ran away.

exercises.q: Combine using participles: 'I found the door open. I went inside.'
exercises.ans: Finding the door open, I went inside.

exercises.q: Combine using participles: 'The police saw the body. It was floating down the river.'
exercises.ans: The police saw the body floating down the river.

grammar.topic: Clauses: Main, Subordinate, and Relative Clauses
grammar.rule: A Main (Independent) Clause contains a subject and verb and expresses a complete thought. A Subordinate (Dependent) Clause begins with a subordinating conjunction (because, if, when, although) and cannot stand alone. A Relative (Adjective) Clause begins with a relative pronoun (who, whom, whose, which, that) or relative adverb (where, when, why) and modifies a noun.
examples: Independent: I don't like Mondays.
Subordinate: Because the test was so difficult, none passed.
Relative: Isn't that the woman who lives across the road?

exercises.q: Classify clause: 'Isn't that the woman who lives across the road from you?'
exercises.ans: Relative clause ('who lives across the road from you' modifies 'woman').

exercises.q: Classify clause: 'Because the test was so difficult, none of the students got a very good grade.'
exercises.ans: Subordinate (dependent) clause ('Because the test was so difficult').

exercises.q: Classify clause: 'She is very fit because she goes running every day.'
exercises.ans: Subordinate (dependent) clause ('because she goes running every day').

exercises.q: Classify clause: 'The police said the accident that happened last night was unavoidable.'
exercises.ans: Relative clause ('that happened last night' modifies 'accident').

exercises.q: Classify clause: 'I don't like Mondays.'
exercises.ans: Main (independent) clause (expresses a complete standalone thought).

exercises.q: Classify clause: 'Have you seen those people who we met on holiday?'
exercises.ans: Relative clause ('who we met on holiday' modifies 'people').

exercises.q: Classify clause: 'Can you tell me why you said that?'
exercises.ans: Subordinate noun clause functioning as the direct object of tell.

exercises.q: Classify clause: 'You shouldn't believe everything that you read in the newspaper.'
exercises.ans: Relative clause ('that you read in the newspaper' modifies 'everything').

exercises.q: Classify clause: 'If you help me, I will help you!'
exercises.ans: Subordinate conditional clause ('If you help me').

writing.summary: In the lyric poem 'Dreams', Langston Hughes delivers a passionate plea to cherish and guard one's aspirations. Through two succinct four-line stanzas, he warns against abandoning dreams. In the first stanza, he compares a life devoid of dreams to a broken-winged bird that cannot fly, emphasizing that without dreams, the human spirit is crippled, grounded, and stripped of its natural potential to soar. In the second stanza, he portrays a dreamless existence as a barren field frozen with snow, illustrating coldness, spiritual sterility, and absolute desolation. The poem powerfully concludes that dreams are the life-giving force of human ambition and happiness.

essay.title: A Dream Doesn't Become Reality Through Magic: It Takes Sweat, Determination and Hard Work
essay.text: Every transformative breakthrough in human civilization originated as a dream in an inspired mind. However, visionary ideas remain inert fantasies unless they are converted into tangible reality through unyielding labor, sweat, and perseverance. As Colin Powell famously observed, success requires relentless commitment rather than wishing upon stars. History is replete with icons who turned dreams into monuments of human achievement through grueling struggle. Thomas Edison endured thousands of failed experiments before illuminating the world with the electric bulb. Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah transformed the dream of an independent Pakistan into a political reality against colossal odds through intellectual discipline and unshakeable fortitude. Obstacles, setbacks, and discouragements are inevitable in any worthwhile endeavor. Those who hold fast to their dreams while willingly investing sweat, discipline, and sustained sacrifice ultimately conquer adversity and transform aspirations into enduring triumph.

reading.title: Population Growth and its Impact on Environment
reading.theme: Environmental Protection, Resource Depletion & Public Health
reading.author: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Textbook Board (Referencing UN FAO & World Bank Reports)
reading.preReading:
Look at the mind-map to predict the theme of the lesson:
Population Growth → Increased Needs → Environmental Destruction → Increased Consumption → Declining Resources → Scarcity and Poverty → Migration → Discrimination & Conflict.

passages.heading: Global Demographic Projections and Resource Pressure
passages.text: Population growth has direct impact on the environment. An increase in population means an increase in consuming more resources and producing vast quantities of waste materials. Presently seven billion and six hundred million people live in this world. It is estimated that world's population will reach 9.2 billion by 2050. The impact of so many people on our environment will be consumption of resources like land, food, water, fossil fuel and production of waste materials like garbage, greenhouse gases and water and air pollutants. Experts in the field of population and environment worry that this unchecked population growth may result in environmental catastrophe.

summary.en: Global population is projected to reach 9.2 billion by 2050, triggering massive increases in consumption of food, water, and fossil fuels, alongside alarming waste production.
summary.ur: دنیا کی آبادی 2050 تک 9.2 ارب تک پہنچنے کا امکان ہے، جس سے خوراک، پانی اور ایندھن کا استعمال بے پناہ بڑھ جائے گا اور ماحولیاتی تباہی کا خطرہ پیدا ہوگا۔

passages.heading: The Menace of Deforestation and Biodiversity Loss
passages.text:
At the moment, issues of ground show that the environment is suffering because of overpopulation. Increase in population has resulted in a higher demand for arable land, pastures and timber for the growing demands of population. More people have moved to cities, adding pressure on urban environments. More unwanted materials are thrown away every day, adding to the crust of garbage-mounds. The picture of growing population and its impact will become more vivid if we dwell on this problem in some detail.

The conversion of forested areas to non-forest land for uses such as arable land, pasture, ranches, or urban use is called deforestation. Deforestation can lead to several imbalances in the environment and results in decrease in habitat and biodiversity. Ranches and agricultural activities are a few of the causes of deforestation. Forests cover 30% of the earth's land. According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), an estimated 18 million acres (7.3 million hectares) of forest are lost each year. Agriculture, urbanization, poverty, over-population and unequal land access are the main causes of man-made deforestation. If the current rate of deforestation continues, it will take less than 100 years to destroy all rainforests on the earth.

summary.en: Overpopulation drives rampant deforestation, destroying 18 million acres of forest each year according to the UN FAO, threatening complete rainforest extinction within a century.
summary.ur: بڑھتی ہوئی آبادی کے باعث جنگلات کی کٹائی جاری ہے؛ اقوام متحدہ کے مطابق ہر سال 1.8 کروڑ ایکڑ جنگلات ختم ہو رہے ہیں جو حیاتیاتی تنوع کے لیے بڑا خطرہ ہے۔

passages.heading: Urbanization, Industrialization, and the Anthropocene Epoch
passages.text:
Urbanization is a process whereby populations move from rural to urban areas, enabling cities and towns to grow. It can also be termed as the progressive increase of the number of people living in towns and cities. Experts think that future world population growth will be concentrated in towns and cities. Much of urban migration is driven by rural populations' desire for the advantages that urban areas offer. Urban advantages include greater opportunities to receive higher education, healthcare, and specialized services such as entertainment. Urban people change their environment through their consumption of food, energy, water, and land.

Industrialization began during the Industrial Revolution in the 18th century, when workers moved towards manufacturing jobs and agriculture became less dominant. Industrialisation has had the most severe impact on environment. Huge quantities of pollutants are being let out into the air, water, and land by various industries. Industrialization produces a greater amount of waste, both directly as a result of production of goods and indirectly through disposal of those goods once their purpose has been served.

Industrialisation and urbanization are the major causes of waste production. As the world's population has grown and become more urban and affluent, waste production has risen tenfold. Every year we dump a massive 2.12 billion tons of waste. By 2025 it will become double its present production. Rubbish is being generated faster than other environmental pollutants, including greenhouse gases. Plastic clogs the world's oceans and rivers, causing flooding and toxic contamination. The impact of human actions is so enormous that scientists use the term 'Anthropocene epoch' for our era, denoting the dominant influence of human activities on earth's ecosystems.

summary.en: Urbanization and industrial manufacturing generate 2.12 billion tons of waste annually, choking oceans with plastic and inaugurating the human-dominated Anthropocene epoch.
summary.ur: شہری پھیلاؤ اور صنعتی سرگرمیوں سے سالانہ 2.12 ارب ٹن کچرا پیدا ہو رہا ہے جس سے سمندر پلاسٹک سے آلودہ ہو رہے ہیں اور اس دور کو 'اینتھروپوسین' یعنی انسانی غلبے کا دور کہا جاتا ہے۔

passages.heading: Earth's Carrying Capacity and Sustainable Solutions
passages.text:
As the world population continues to grow, more people will use more resources and generate more waste. But how many people can earth support? In the view of scientists, the figure ranges from 500 million to more than one trillion. This range is called 'the carrying capacity of earth'. Whether the earth's carrying capacity is 500 million or one trillion, we still must respect the finite boundaries of nature.

To restore balance between population growth and environmental limitations, there is no single easy solution. All options must be part of the solution. First of all, we should educate people about their consumption actions and their effects on the environment. Moreover, we need to assess our consumption patterns. We need to reduce the amount of resources we consume: take shorter showers to conserve water; say no to single-use plastics; buy less and recycle our waste. If millions around the world adopt conservation and manage the growth of population, we will have the opportunity to lead an enjoyable and full life, and our future generations will find earth a place worth living.

summary.en: Earth's carrying capacity is finite; overcoming the crisis requires civic education, curtailing over-consumption, curbing plastic waste, and stabilizing population growth.
summary.ur: زمین کی وسائل فراہم کرنے کی صلاحیت محدود ہے۔ اس مسئلے کے حل کے لیے عوام میں آگاہی، فضول خرچی کا خاتمہ، پانی و بجلی کی بچت اور پلاسٹک کا بائیکاٹ ناگزیر ہے۔
