questions.q: Why is there no single and easy solution to the problem of population growth and its impact on environment?
questions.ans: There is no single and easy solution because population growth and environmental degradation are deeply interconnected with complex economic, social, cultural, and technological factors. Addressing the crisis requires multifaceted strategies simultaneously: widespread public education, family planning, restructuring wasteful industrial production, transitioning to clean renewable energy, strictly regulating plastic waste, and overhauling individual consumption lifestyles across all socioeconomic classes.

questions.q: How is the carrying capacity of earth affected?
questions.ans: The carrying capacity of earth—the maximum population size that the planet's ecosystems can indefinitely support—is severely depleted by over-consumption, deforestation, industrial pollution, and soil degradation. When humans consume groundwater, topsoil, fisheries, and fossil fuels faster than nature can replenish them, and dump 2.12 billion tons of waste that nature cannot assimilate, the earth's biological productive capacity shrinks, reducing its ability to sustain future generations.

questions.q: Why does population growth directly affect the environment?
questions.ans: Population growth directly affects the environment because every additional human being requires food, fresh drinking water, housing, energy, clothing, and transportation. Fulfilling these biological and social needs necessitates clearing natural forests for agriculture, extracting non-renewable minerals and fuels, diverting river water, and generating domestic garbage and greenhouse gas emissions that alter planetary climate patterns.

questions.q: Analyse any passage of the text 'Population Growth and its Impact on Environment' and identify key idea and its supporting details.
questions.ans:
• Passage Analysed: Paragraph 2 (Deforestation).
• Key Idea: Rampant deforestation driven by population pressure is causing catastrophic ecological destruction.
• Supporting Details:
  1. The conversion of forest land to arable fields, pasture, and housing strips away animal habitats and shatters biodiversity.
  2. Forests cover 30% of global land, yet the UN FAO estimates that 18 million acres (7.3 million hectares) are demolished annually.
  3. If current logging and clearing rates persist, all rainforests could vanish in less than a century.

questions.q: Locate examples from the text that support your opinion.
questions.ans:
The text provides concrete empirical evidence that underscores the ecological emergency:
1. Global population will expand from 7.6 billion to 9.2 billion by 2050, compounding demand for finite resources.
2. Over 18 million acres of forest are leveled each year for agriculture and urbanization.
3. Human societies dump 2.12 billion tons of waste annually, a figure projected to double by 2025.
4. Non-biodegradable plastics clog rivers and oceans, leading to catastrophic urban flooding and marine toxicity.

questions.q: Keeping in view the population and the environment of your area, do you agree or not with the content of the lesson? Support your view with solid arguments.
questions.ans: I wholeheartedly agree with the lesson. In our local Pakistani cities (such as Peshawar, Lahore, and Karachi), rapid population growth and rural-to-urban migration have visibly overwhelmed urban systems. Fertile agricultural outskirts have been converted into concrete housing schemes, municipal drainage lines are choked with polythene bags causing monsoon urban flooding, drinking water tables have plunged hundreds of feet due to excessive tube-well extraction, and winter air quality reaches hazardous AQI levels due to vehicular emissions and brick kilns.

mcqs.q: Experts in the field worry that this unchecked population growth may result in environmental catastrophe. In this sentence the word 'unchecked' means:
mcqs.exp: 'Unchecked' means not held back, unrestrained, or continuing without regulation or limits.

mcqs.q: Presently, according to the textbook, how many people live in this world?
opts: seven billion and six hundred million
nine billion and two hundred million
mcqs.exp: The textbook explicitly documents that 'Presently seven billion and six million people live in this world' with projections reaching 9.2 billion by 2050.

mcqs.q: According to the United Nations FAO, how much forest is lost each year?
mcqs.exp: The UN FAO data cited in the text specifies that 18 million acres (7.3 million hectares) of forests are lost annually.

mcqs.q: According to the text, the term 'the carrying capacity of earth' means:
opts: the total volume of pollutants let out into the atmosphere
the maximum population size of a species that the environment can sustain indefinitely
the dominant influence of human activities on ecosystems
the net difference between annual birth rates and death rates
mcqs.exp: Ecological carrying capacity is defined as the maximum population of a species that an ecosystem can support without environmental degradation.

mcqs.q: The issue of population growth and environment is an urgent challenge for:
opts: poor, developing and advanced nations alike
mcqs.exp: Because planetary ecosystems, oceans, and atmospheres are shared, environmental collapse impacts developing and developed nations alike.

grammar.rule: English verbs conjugate into twelve tenses indicating time of action (Past, Present, Future) and aspect (Simple, Continuous, Perfect, Perfect Continuous). Rewrite sentences by substituting auxiliary verbs and main verb forms.
examples: Simple Present: He does his work with diligence.
Simple Future: I will follow his instructions.
Present Continuous: That is being interesting.

exercises.q: He will do his work with diligence. (Change to Simple Present)
exercises.ans: He does his work with diligence.

exercises.q: I followed his instructions. (Change to Simple Future)
exercises.ans: I will follow his instructions.

exercises.q: That will be interesting. (Change to Present Continuous)
exercises.ans: That is being interesting.

exercises.q: I will not allow this to happen. (Change to Simple Past)
exercises.ans: I did not allow this to happen.

exercises.q: He worked very hard. (Change to Future Continuous)
exercises.ans: He will be working very hard.

exercises.q: I will never raise any demand. (Change to Present Perfect)
exercises.ans: I have never raised any demand.

exercises.q: He is crying at the top of his voice. (Change to Past Perfect)
exercises.ans: He had cried at the top of his voice.

exercises.q: We buy vegetables from the market. (Change to Present Perfect)
exercises.ans: We have bought vegetables from the market.

grammar.rule: Use past and past perfect verb forms to maintain narrative coherence when describing past sequences of events.
examples: Things got so bad recently (past simple).
He had loved (past perfect for action prior to another past event).

exercises.q: Fill in the correct forms: 'My friend, Hashim, has always been fat, but things (get) so bad recently that he had to go on a strict diet which forbade most of the food he (love): butter, potatoes, rice, chocolate, and sweets. Yesterday, I (pay) him a visit. I (ring) the bell and was not surprised to see Hashim as fat as ever. He (lead) me to his room and hurriedly (put) a parcel on the desk. When I (ask) him what he (hide), he (smile) guiltily and (show) me the contents: five large bars of chocolate!'
exercises.ans: got / had loved / paid / rang / led / put / asked / was hiding (or had hidden) / smiled / showed

grammar.topic: Present Perfect Continuous vs Past Perfect Continuous (Exercises C & D)
grammar.rule: Use Present Perfect Continuous (has/have been + verb-ing) for an action that began in the past and is still ongoing or has immediate present results. Use Past Perfect Continuous (had been + verb-ing) for an ongoing action that occurred before another specific point in the past.
examples: I have been waiting for two hours (still waiting now).
They had been waiting for two hours before the train arrived (completed prior to past arrival).

exercises.q: Where have you been? We (had been waiting / have been waiting) for you for ages.
exercises.ans: have been waiting (the waiting is connected to the present arrival of the person).

exercises.q: He hasn't decided on a career yet, but he (has been thinking / had been thinking) about it lately.
exercises.ans: has been thinking ('lately' indicates present relevance).

exercises.q: After she (has been playing / had been playing) tennis for ten years, she joined a squash team.
exercises.ans: had been playing (the action occurred and continued prior to joining the squash team in the past).

exercises.q: Nabeel has never had an accident and he ______ (drive) for ten years.
exercises.ans: has been driving (action began in the past and continues into the present).

exercises.q: They eventually found the dog after they ______ (search) for it all night.
exercises.ans: had been searching (searching preceded finding in the past).

exercises.q: How long ______ your father ______ (work) for the company when he retired?
exercises.ans: had your father been working (action ongoing prior to past retirement).

exercises.q: Correct the error: 'Jameela has lost weight. She had been dieting for months now.'
exercises.ans: Correction: 'She has been dieting for months now.' ('now' requires present perfect continuous).

exercises.q: Correct the error: 'Everything was white when we woke up because it has been snowing all night.'
exercises.ans: Correction: '...because it had been snowing all night.' ('was white' sets past time frame).

writing.summary: This informative lesson examines the disastrous environmental consequences of unchecked global population growth, which is projected to expand from 7.6 billion to 9.2 billion by 2050. Fulfilling the demands of billions requires catastrophic deforestation—clearing over 18 million acres of forest annually for agriculture, cattle ranching, and urban sprawl. As populations migrate from rural areas to cities in pursuit of education and jobs, municipal infrastructure collapses under mountains of trash. Global human activities produce 2.12 billion tons of refuse each year, with non-biodegradable plastics choking marine life and drainage networks. These unprecedented human footprints have inaugurated what geologists term the 'Anthropocene epoch'. Because earth possesses a finite ecological 'carrying capacity', the lesson urges global conservation education, reduction of individual consumption, curtailment of single-use plastics, and responsible family planning to secure a viable habitat for future generations.

essay.title: Causes and Effects of the Rapid Growth of Urban Population
essay.text:
Urbanization is one of the defining social and demographic phenomena of the twenty-first century. As populations across the developing world surge, rural dwellers migrate en masse into metropolitan centers, transforming sprawling villages into crowded megacities. Examining the underlying causes and subsequent environmental effects of this rapid urban expansion reveals one of humanity's most pressing challenges.

The principal cause of urban migration is the sharp economic disparity between neglected rural hinterlands and bustling cities. Rural agriculture often suffers from unpredictable climatic droughts, low wages, and primitive technology, leaving younger generations with limited financial mobility. In contrast, urban centers offer diversified employment opportunities in manufacturing, commerce, and digital services. Additionally, cities provide vastly superior access to higher educational institutions, modern specialized hospitals, electricity, clean water, and cultural entertainment. People willingly migrate to urban centers in pursuit of upward social mobility.

However, the sudden influx of millions of citizens triggers catastrophic environmental and municipal consequences. First, rapid urban growth results in unplanned, hazardous sprawl. Prime agricultural lands and forests surrounding cities are leveled and paved over with asphalt and concrete to construct commercial plazas and housing colonies. This permanent loss of greenery eliminates carbon sinks and causes severe urban heat-island effects.

Furthermore, urban municipal infrastructure invariably buckles under rapid demographic pressure. Waste generation skyrockets; cities generate billions of tons of solid trash that municipal services fail to collect or treat, resulting in smoldering open dumps that release carcinogens. Millions of private automobiles congest roads, choking the atmosphere with toxic emissions and particulate matter that produce hazardous seasonal smog. Finally, untreated industrial effluents and municipal sewage are dumped directly into natural rivers, destroying aquatic life and contaminating drinking groundwater aquifers.

In conclusion, while urban centers remain the engines of economic development, their uncontrolled expansion threatens the ecological viability of our planet. Governments must implement proactive urban planning, decentralize economic opportunities to secondary towns, invest heavily in mass public transit, enforce zero-waste recycling, and protect surrounding arable land. Only through balanced and sustainable development can modern cities provide prosperity without destroying the natural environment.

eng10Chapters.name: The Great Masjid of Cordoba and Iqbal
eng10Chapters.title: The Great Masjid of Cordoba and Iqbal
eng10Chapters.theme: Places of historical and cultural importance; Islamic civilization and spiritual renewal
slos: Read critically to understand the historical, architectural, and spiritual legacy of Muslim civilization in Al-Andalus (Spain).
Analyze Allama Iqbal's philosophical concept of 'Ishq' (divine creative passion and moral excellence) as expressed in his poetry.
Identify and explain architectural and cultural terminology: gold tesserae, horseshoe arches, Kufic calligraphy, vegetal motifs, Iberian Peninsula.
Demonstrate accurate usage of various types of adjectives: demonstrative, proper, indefinite, and quantitative.
Apply correct degrees of adjectives (positive, comparative, superlative) with regular and irregular variations.

reading.title: The Great Masjid of Cordoba and Iqbal
reading.theme: Islamic Heritage, Architectural Splendor & Spiritual Renewal
reading.author: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Textbook Board (with references to Allama Iqbal's 'Masjid-e-Qurtuba')
reading.preReading:
Look at the picture and guess what the lesson is about:
1. Have you seen pictures of famous historical mosques?
2. What architectural features distinguish Islamic monuments?
3. Why did Allama Iqbal compose a monumental poem on a mosque in Spain?

passages.heading: Historical Emergence of Cordoba and Islamic Spain
passages.text: The Iberian Peninsula, situated at the southwestern tip of Europe, was transformed by the arrival of Muslims in 711 AD under Tariq bin Ziyad. The historic city of Cordoba emerged as the radiant jewel of Al-Andalus and the capital of the Umayyad dynasty founded by Abd al-Rahman I in 756 AD. In Cordoba, he attempted to recreate the grandeur and cultural elegance of Damascus. While the rest of Europe languished in the Dark Ages, Muslim Spain shone as a glittering beacon of science, medicine, philosophy, literature, and architectural brilliance. Libraries, universities, hospitals, paved and illuminated streets made Cordoba the cultural capital of the medieval world.

summary.en: Cordoba became the cultural and scientific capital of Europe under Umayyad Muslim rule following Tariq bin Ziyad's arrival in 711 AD.
summary.ur: 711ء میں مسلمانوں کی آمد کے بعد قرطبہ علم و حکمت کا عالمی مرکز بنا اور اندلس میں اندھیروں میں ڈوبے یورپ کے لیے ایک روشن مینار ثابت ہوا۔

passages.heading: Architectural Marvel of the Prayer Hall
passages.text:
The most consummate and accomplished structure of the Masjid is its prayer hall. Begun in 784 AD by Abd al-Rahman I and expanded by subsequent rulers, the hall is erected with 857 majestic columns of jasper, onyx, marble, and granite from which sprout an amazing forest of two-tiered symmetrical arches. These double arches are composed of alternating keystones of red brick and white stone, creating a rhythmic chromatic effect and an impression of infinite spatial depth. The multiplicity of the columns in the prayer hall so amazed Allama Iqbal that he expressed his feelings in these memorable words:

'Your foundations are lasting, your columns countless,
Like the profusion of palms in the plains of Syria.'

summary.en: The vast prayer hall features 857 marble columns and two-tiered red-and-white horseshoe arches that reminded Iqbal of Syrian palm forests.
summary.ur: مسجد کا وسیع نماز ہال 857 سنگِ مرمر کے ستونوں اور سرخ و سفید مہرابی محرابوں پر مشتمل ہے جس کے حسن نے علامہ اقبال کو مسحور کر دیا۔

passages.heading: The Splendor of the Mehrab and Kufic Calligraphy
passages.text: The focal point in the prayer hall is the famous horseshoe-arched Mehrab and the sacred Qibla wall. The arch and the Qibla wall of the Mehrab are decorated with the inscription of two lines of calligraphy in ornate Kufic style both on the top and on either side of the arch. The mosaic of the two lines of calligraphy has a deep blue background with shimmering gold lettering. The dome above the Mehrab is constructed with crisscrossing ribs that form an intricate radial star pattern, clad with dazzling Byzantine gold tesserae—individual glass cubes sandwiching pure gold leaf that produce an ethereal golden luster. Stylized vegetal motifs and geometric arabesques cover every surface, symbolizing the eternal and unsearchable infinity of Allah.

summary.en: The Mehrab is adorned with brilliant gold tesserae mosaics, intricate ribbed domes, and blue-and-gold Kufic Quranic calligraphy.
summary.ur: محراب کو سونے کے شیشے کی ٹائلوں، نیلے و سنہری کوفی خطاطی اور نفاست سے بنے ہندسی اور نباتاتی نقش و نگار سے سجایا گیا ہے۔

passages.heading: Allama Iqbal's Spiritual Pilgrimage and the Philosophy of Ishq
passages.text:
In 1931, during his visit to Europe for the Round Table Conferences, Allama Muhammad Iqbal was granted special permission by the Spanish government to offer prayers inside the Masjid of Cordoba—the first Muslim prayer heard within its walls since 1492. Iqbal was so moved by the magnificence of the masjid that he saw in its stones the living traces of the 'Ishq' of those who built it.

Ishq, according to Iqbal, is not mere romantic infatuation; it is the burning divine desire, selfless dedication, and moral passion to achieve perfection and self-realization in accordance with the teachings of Islam. It was this transformative spiritual energy that inspired early Muslims to construct everlasting monuments of faith, intellect, and justice. Iqbal immortalized this experience in his celebrated philosophical masterpiece poem 'Masjid-e-Qurtuba' in Bal-e-Jibril:

'Yet there exists a hue of eternity in this imprint
The one that has been completed by some man of God;
The action of the Man of God gets accelerated with Ishq,
The essence of life is Ishq, death is forbidden for it.'

Iqbal attributed the eternal majesty of the Masjid to this intense spiritual fire: 'Your grandeur and beauty manifest the man of God; he is eminent and handsome, you too are eminent and handsome.' For Iqbal, the monument stands as an enduring call for the moral awakening and renaissance of the Muslim Ummah.

summary.en: In 1931, Allama Iqbal visited the mosque and penned his immortal poem 'Masjid-e-Qurtuba', identifying the monument as the ultimate manifestation of 'Ishq'.
summary.ur: 1931ء میں علامہ اقبال نے مسجدِ قرطبہ میں تاریخی نماز ادا کی اور اپنی شاہکار نظم لکھی جس میں مسجد کو 'مردِ مومن' کے لازوال 'عشق' کا شاہکار قرار دیا۔

questions.q: What was the historical background of the Great Masjid of Cordoba?
questions.ans: Following the Muslim conquest of Spain in 711 AD led by Tariq bin Ziyad, Abd al-Rahman I established the independent Umayyad Emirate of Cordoba in 756 AD. In 784 AD, he purchased land and commenced construction of the Great Mosque to rival the mosques of Damascus and Baghdad. Expanded across two centuries by Abd al-Rahman II, Al-Hakam II, and Al-Mansur, the mosque became the spiritual and political heart of Islamic Al-Andalus, symbolizing a golden era of scientific enlightenment and religious tolerance.

questions.q: Describe the architecture of the prayer hall of the Great Masjid of Cordoba.
questions.ans: The prayer hall is a breathtaking architectural wonder supported by 857 slender columns of jasper, onyx, granite, and marble. Above these columns rise two-tiered superimposed horseshoe arches built of alternating red brick and white limestone. This revolutionary double-tiered design provided extraordinary ceiling height, improved ventilation and acoustics, and created an unforgettable chromatic impression of an endless forest of arches.

questions.q: How did Allama Iqbal define 'Ishq' in relation to the Masjid of Cordoba?
questions.ans: Iqbal defined 'Ishq' as the supreme master passion of the human spirit—a burning, selfless love for the Divine, coupled with continuous creative action, moral excellence, and the pursuit of ideal perfection. In his poem 'Masjid-e-Qurtuba', Iqbal asserts that all transient material creations perish with time, but monuments and deeds forged through genuine 'Ishq' receive the enduring stamp of eternity.

questions.q: What, in your opinion, is the significance of the Masjid of Cordoba to present day Muslims?
questions.ans: To contemporary Muslims, the Masjid of Cordoba serves as a magnificent testament to the intellectual heights, aesthetic sophistication, and cultural tolerance achieved by Muslim civilization. It inspires modern believers to transcend intellectual complacency, embrace scientific innovation, cultivate artistic mastery, and rekindle the spiritual vigor that once illuminated world history.

questions.q: Why did Iqbal greatly appreciate a faraway Masjid in Spain, when there were superb buildings of the Muslim era in Sub-Continent?
questions.ans: While Iqbal deeply admired Mughal monuments in the Subcontinent, the Masjid of Cordoba held unique philosophical pathos for him. It stood in a land where Muslim political dominance had completely vanished centuries prior, yet its stones still radiated the unmistakable spiritual presence and 'Ishq' of the believers who erected it. It served as a powerful historical mirror reflecting both the tragic consequences of moral decline and the latent potential for cultural renaissance.

mcqs.q: After the fall of Muslims in Spain, the Masjid was converted into a cathedral. This shows that Muslims were overthrown by:
mcqs.exp: Following the fall of Cordoba in 1236 and Granada in 1492, Christian Spanish monarchs conquered Al-Andalus and converted the mosque into a Catholic cathedral.

mcqs.q: According to Allama Iqbal, we can achieve the master passion (Ishq) again if we enkindle in ourselves:
opts: an exalted state of moral and spiritual character
mcqs.exp: In Iqbal's philosophy, Ishq is cultivated through spiritual purification, moral discipline, and selfless devotion to Allah's guidance.

mcqs.q: "It was an era when the Iberian Peninsula was glittering with the progress and advancement of the Muslim civilization." In this sentence the word 'glittering' is used as:
mcqs.exp: 'Glittering' metaphorically compares cultural and scientific flourishing to radiant light or glowing jewels.

mcqs.q: The most consummate and accomplished structure of the Masjid of Cordoba is:
mcqs.exp: The textbook explicitly identifies the magnificent prayer hall with its two-tiered arches and 857 columns as the most consummate structure.

mcqs.q: The mosaic calligraphy around the Mehrab is inscribed in which historic Arabic script?
mcqs.exp: The inscriptions decorating the arch and Qibla wall of the Mehrab were executed in archaic and ornate Kufic calligraphy.

grammar.rule: Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns. Demonstrative adjectives (this, that, these, those) point out specific items. Indefinite adjectives (few, several, many, some) modify nouns non-specifically. Adjectives modifying pronouns qualify indefinite pronouns.
examples: Can you see that plane? ('that' is a demonstrative adjective modifying 'plane').
He identified the red one ('red' is an adjective modifying pronoun 'one').
The brave few fought the war ('brave' modifies pronoun 'few').

exercises.q: 'Can you see that plane?' — Which type of adjective is the word 'that'?
exercises.ans: Demonstrative adjective (points out a specific distant object).

exercises.q: 'He was asked to spot the car that crashed and he identified the red one.' — Which type of adjective is 'red'?
exercises.ans: An adjective that modifies the indefinite pronoun 'one'.

exercises.q: 'The brave few fought the war.' — Which type of adjective is 'brave'?
exercises.ans: An adjective that modifies the pronoun 'few' (acting as noun).

grammar.rule: Adjectives have three degrees: Positive (base form), Comparative (comparing two entities, adding -er or 'more'), and Superlative (comparing three or more, adding -est or 'most').
examples: big → bigger → biggest
beautiful → more beautiful → most beautiful
good → better → best
dangerous → more dangerous → most dangerous

exercises.q: My house is ______ (big) than yours.
exercises.ans: bigger (comparative degree followed by 'than').

exercises.q: This flower is ______ (beautiful) than that one.
exercises.ans: more beautiful (comparative degree for multi-syllable adjective).

exercises.q: This is the ______ (interesting) book I have ever read.
exercises.ans: most interesting (superlative degree preceded by 'the').

grammar.rule: When multiple adjectives precede a noun, English follows a standard conventional sequence: Opinion → Size → Physical Quality → Age → Shape → Color → Origin → Material → Purpose → Noun.
examples: An incredible (opinion), brand-new (age), huge (size), Italian (origin) ocean liner.
A pair of nice (opinion), new (age), red (color) rain boots.
A huge (size), old (age), round (shape), red (color) box.

writing.summary: This lesson details the historical, architectural, and spiritual glory of the Great Masjid of Cordoba in Andalusia (Spain) and explores its profound philosophical resonance in the thought of Allama Muhammad Iqbal. Founded in 784 AD by Abd al-Rahman I, the mosque stood as the architectural crown of Muslim Spain during an era when Cordoba led Europe in science, arts, and enlightenment. Its hypostyle prayer hall showcases 857 columns of marble and jasper supporting a dizzying forest of two-tiered red-and-white horseshoe arches, while its radiant Mehrab is embellished with Byzantine gold tesserae and blue-and-gold Kufic Quranic calligraphy. When Allama Iqbal visited Cordoba in 1931 and offered historical prayers, he was deeply inspired by the monument's timeless spiritual majesty. In his immortal Urdu poem 'Masjid-e-Qurtuba', Iqbal characterized the mosque as the physical embodiment of 'Ishq'—the burning divine love and creative dedication of the Man of God. The monument stands today as an enduring reminder of Islamic civilizational genius and an inspiring summons for intellectual and spiritual rebirth.

essay.title: A Comparison and Contrast: The Great Masjid of Cordoba and the Badshahi Masjid of Lahore
essay.text:
The Great Masjid of Cordoba in Spain and the Badshahi Masjid in Lahore, Pakistan, stand as two of the most sublime architectural masterworks of Islamic civilization. Though constructed centuries apart in radically different geographical and cultural landscapes—one in Moorish Al-Andalus during the eighth century and the other under Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb in the seventeenth century—both monuments celebrate the timeless spiritual ideals and engineering genius of Muslim builders.

Architecturally, the two mosques present fascinating contrasts in structural design and spatial philosophy. The Masjid of Cordoba is celebrated for its vast, low-ceilinged hypostyle prayer hall, where 857 slender columns of jasper, onyx, and marble create an endless interior forest of two-tiered, red-and-white horseshoe arches. Its orientation emphasizes introspective, rhythmic infinity within an enclosed sanctuary. In contrast, the Badshahi Masjid in Lahore exemplifies Mughal monumental grandeur, characterized by a colossal open sandstone courtyard capable of accommodating 100,000 worshippers, flanked by four soaring 176-foot minarets and three majestic, bulbous white marble domes. While Cordoba's aesthetic relies on intricate Byzantine gold tesserae, horseshoe arches, and geometric Kufic calligraphy, Badshahi Masjid showcases red ochre sandstone richly embellished with white marble floral inlays, arched cusped squinches, and sweeping Persian vaults.

Culturally and historically, both sanctuaries carry immense emotional and spiritual weight. The Masjid of Cordoba, converted into a Catholic cathedral following the Reconquista, inspired Allama Iqbal's most profound philosophical reflections on the impermanence of empires and the eternity of deeds performed through divine 'Ishq'. Badshahi Masjid remains an active sanctuary of living faith, where the calls to prayer and recitation of the Quran have resounded uninterrupted for more than three centuries.

In conclusion, while Cordoba's mosque represents the intimate Moorish jewel of medieval European Islam and Badshahi Masjid embodies the monumental majesty of the Mughal Empire, both sanctuaries stand as immortal testaments to the supreme artistic and spiritual heights of the Muslim Ummah.

poet.name: Angela Morgan
poet.bio: Angela Morgan was born in 1875 in Washington, D.C. Her given name at birth was Nina Lillian, which she later changed to Angela. Her career as a writer started as a journalist for the Chicago and New York newspapers before World War I. Her most productive years were from 1914–1940. Morgan's pieces were published in major magazines. She also wrote fourteen books of poetry and stories. She passed away on January 24, 1957, in New York.

reading.title: In Spite of War
reading.theme: Optimism, Hope & Nature's Triumphant Renewal
reading.author: Angela Morgan (1875–1957)
reading.preReading:
Look at the pictures and predict the theme of the poem:
1. When human beings wage war, how does nature respond?
2. What gives human beings hope in the darkest moments of tragedy?

passages.heading: Stanza 1: Blooming Flowers Amid Suffering and Wrath
passages.text:
In spite of war, in spite of death,
In spite of all man's suffering,
Something within me laughs and sings
And I must praise with all my breath.
In spite of war, in spite of hate,
Lilacs are blooming at my gate,
In spite of war, in spite of wrath,
"Courage!" the morning-glory saith;
And just to live is so divine
When pansies lift their eyes to mine.

summary.en: Despite wartime hatred and slaughter, blooming lilacs, courageous morning-glories, and pansies inspire the poet to celebrate the sacred gift of life.
summary.ur: جنگ، نفرت اور تباہی کے باوجود دروازے پر کھلنے والے پھول اور صبح کی رونق شاعرہ کے دل میں جینے کی خوشی اور شکر گزاری پیدا کرتے ہیں۔

passages.heading: Stanza 2: The Eternal Air and Nature's Unstoppable Splendor
passages.text:
The clouds are vying with the sea,
The leaves are tripping in the tree;
That naught is real but what is fair,
That everywhere and everywhere
A glory liveth through the air.
Though guns may roar and cannon boom,
Roses are born and gardens bloom;
My spirit still may catch its flame
At that same torch whence poppies came.

summary.en: While cannons roar, dancing leaves and newborn roses affirm that goodness and divine beauty outlive human violence.
summary.ur: توپوں کی گھن گرج کے باوجود باغوں میں گلاب کھلتے ہیں اور فطرت کی خوبصورتی ثابت کرتی ہے کہ اصل سچائی حسن اور زندگی ہی ہے۔

passages.heading: Stanza 3: Awakening from the Nightmare to Divine Ecstasy
passages.text:
Where morning's altar whitely burns
Lilies may lift their silver urns
In spite of war, in spite of shame.
And in my ear, a whispering breath:
"Wake from the nightmare! Look and see
That life is naught but ecstasy
In spite of war, in spite of death!"

summary.en: The poem culminates in a triumphant inner awakening, bidding mankind to banish the nightmare of war and realize that life itself is pure ecstasy.
summary.ur: شاعرہ انسان کو جنگ کے خوفناک خواب سے جاگنے کا پیغام دیتی ہے کیونکہ زندگی کی اصل حقیقت خوشی اور لازوال روحانی مسرت ہے۔

vocabulary.title: Emotional Connotations: Positive vs Negative Words
vocabulary.instruction: Distinguish between words evoking feelings of life, beauty, and optimism versus those evoking destruction and despair.

items.definition: Words evoking joy, life, and natural splendor: praise, blooming, courage, divine, fair, glory, ecstasy, flame.
items.example: "Lilacs are blooming at my gate" evokes renewal, warmth, and unquenchable vitality.

items.definition: Words evoking violence, destruction, and human malice: war, death, suffering, hate, wrath, guns, cannon boom, shame, nightmare.
items.example: "Though guns may roar and cannon boom" evokes the grim terror of mechanized warfare.

questions.q: What are the things that thrive despite the ravages of war?
questions.ans: Despite the horrors of war, nature continues its glorious, uninterrupted cycle: fragrant lilacs bloom at the gate, morning-glories unfold, pansies turn their faces to the light, clouds soar over the sea, tree leaves dance in the breeze, vibrant roses are born in gardens, poppies flame in fields, and lilies lift their silver blossoms to the dawn.

questions.q: What are some of the different words and images used in the poem that convey the emotion of loss?
questions.ans: The poet conveys the grim reality of loss and devastation through poignant words and stark auditory imagery: 'war', 'death', 'man's suffering', 'hate', 'wrath', 'shame', 'guns roar', 'cannon boom', and 'nightmare'. These harsh expressions evoke the terror, agony, and destruction inflicted by human combat.

questions.q: In the poem 'In Spite of War', there are several examples of personification. Identify two examples of personification: explain what is being personified and how in each example.
questions.ans:
1. '"Courage!" the morning-glory saith': The morning-glory flower is personified as a brave counselor speaking words of fortitude and courage to the suffering human heart.
2. 'When pansies lift their eyes to mine': Pansies are personified with human facial features ('eyes') capable of gazing up tenderly at the poet with affectionate companionship.

questions.q: Make a list about the tone of the poem 'In Spite of War' and explain how those words tell us what the tone is. Use examples from the poem to back up your reasoning.
questions.ans: The tone of the poem is overwhelmingly optimistic, celebratory, resilient, and ecstatic. Words such as 'laughs and sings', 'praise', 'divine', 'fair', 'glory', 'bloom', and 'ecstasy' establish this tone. Even when acknowledging that 'guns may roar and cannon boom', the poet's spirit catches flame from nature, asserting that war is merely a temporary human nightmare, while beauty and life are eternal realities.

questions.q: What is the theme of the poem?
questions.ans: The central theme of the poem is the ultimate supremacy of nature, life, and spiritual beauty over human destructiveness and violence. Angela Morgan declares that while man-made wars bring horrific suffering and death, nature's divine renewal cannot be extinguished. Human souls must find courage in nature's enduring cycles and awaken from despair to celebrate life as divine ecstasy.

mcqs.q: According to the poet Angela Morgan, life is the name of:

mcqs.exp: The poem maintains a fiercely optimistic and celebratory stance, refusing to yield to despair despite the horrors of war.

mcqs.q: In the line '"Courage!" the morning-glory saith', the poetic device employed is:
mcqs.exp: Giving the morning-glory flower the human ability to speak ('saith') is an example of personification.

mcqs.q: What blossoms at the gate in spite of war and hate?
mcqs.exp: The text states: 'In spite of war, in spite of hate / Lilacs are blooming at my gate'.

mcqs.q: The phrase 'morning's altar whitely burns' uses imagery of which sense?
mcqs.exp: The glowing white dawn described as a burning altar is a striking visual image.

grammar.rule: An Adjective Phrase is a group of words that functions as an adjective by modifying a noun or pronoun. Unlike an adjective clause, it does not contain a subject and a finite verb.
examples: An elephant with a white skin (phrase modifying 'elephant').
A crown made of gold (phrase modifying 'crown').
Wild beasts in small cages (phrase modifying 'beasts').

grammar.rule: An Adjective Clause is a dependent clause that begins with a relative pronoun (who, whom, whose, which, that) or relative adverb (where, when, why) and modifies a preceding noun or pronoun (its antecedent).
examples: The dog that barked loudly kept us awake ('that barked loudly' modifies 'dog').
This is the town where I was born ('where I was born' modifies 'town').

writing.summary: In 'In Spite of War', American poet Angela Morgan delivers a passionate hymn to the indomitable power of nature and the resilience of the human spirit. Written during an era plagued by mechanized global conflict, the poem directly confronts the devastating reality of war, suffering, hatred, and death. However, rather than succumbing to grief, the poet proclaims that a divine vitality laughs and sings within her soul. While cannons roar and guns thunder across battlefields, nature proceeds with its glorious, unthwarted work: lilacs bloom at the gate, morning-glories whisper courage, pansies look upward with affection, leaves dance, and delicate roses blossom. Nature's unquenchable radiance proves that goodness and beauty are the true enduring realities of the universe. In the poem's stirring climax, an inner voice commands humanity to awaken from the dark nightmare of war and realize that life itself is divine ecstasy.

essay.title: Paraphrase of Selected Stanza from 'In Spite of War'
essay.text:
Stanza: '"Courage!" the morning-glory saith; / When pansies lift their eyes to mine / And just to live is so divine.'

Paraphrase: In these uplifting lines, the poet portrays nature as an active, comforting companion. The brightly blooming morning-glory flower appears to address the human soul directly, urging it to remain brave and steadfast amidst tragedy. Simultaneously, the humble pansies lift their velvety petals like gentle eyes gazing with tenderness into the poet's own. In the presence of such delicate natural affection, the mere experience of drawing breath and being alive feels profoundly sacred, filling the human heart with gratitude that easily overcomes the darkness of human violence.

passages.heading: The Peaceful Province and the Tyrant's Cruel Decree
passages.text: Once there lived at the foot of a mountain a poor farmer and his aged, widowed mother. They owned a bit of land that supplied them with food. They both led a humble and peaceful life. Shinano, the province where they lived, was governed by a despotic leader who, though a skilled warrior, had a great and cowardly terror of anything suggestive of failing health and strength. This caused him to send out a cruel proclamation: the entire province was given strict orders to immediately put to death all the aged people. The days were barbarous, and the custom of abandoning aged people in mountains was not uncommon. The poor farmer loved his mother with tender reverence, and the cruel decree filled his heart with profound grief.

summary.en: A tyrannical governor of Shinano province, terrified of old age and weakness, orders that all elderly people be immediately put to death.
summary.ur: شنانو کے ظالم حکمران نے بڑھاپے اور کمزوری کے خوف سے حکم جاری کیا کہ ریاست کے تمام بوڑھے لوگوں کو پہاڑوں پر چھوڑ کر ہلاک کر دیا جائے۔

passages.heading: The Journey up Mount Obatsuyama
passages.text:
With many deep and sorrowful sighs, the son prepared for what at that time was considered the kindest mode of death. Just at sunset, when his day's work was ended, he took quantities of unwhitened rice, cooked it, dried it, and tied it in a square cloth. Lifting the bundle along with a gourd filled with cool, sweet water, he lifted his helpless old mother onto his back and started on his painful journey up the steep mountain.

The road was long and steep; the narrow path was crossed and recrossed by many paths made by hunters and woodcutters. In some places, they were lost and confused, but he gave no heed. One path or another, it mattered not for him. On he went, climbing blindly upward, ever upward towards the high bare summit of what was known as Obatsuyama, the mountain of the 'abandoning of the aged'.

summary.en: With a heavy heart, the farmer carries his mother on his back toward the desolate summit of Obatsuyama, the mountain of the abandoned.
summary.ur: نوجوان کسان بوجھل دل کے ساتھ اپنی بوڑھی ماں کو پیٹھ پر اٹھا کر اوباتسویاما یعنی 'بوڑھوں کو لاوارث چھوڑنے کے پہاڑ' کی طرف روانہ ہوا۔

passages.heading: The Mother's Sacrificial Trail of Twigs
passages.text:
The eyes of the old mother still had light in them, and they noted the reckless hastening of her son from one unfamiliar path to another. Her loving heart grew anxious because her son did not know the mountain's paths and his return alone in the dark might be fraught with perils. She stretched forth her hand to snap twigs from bushes as they passed by. She quietly dropped a handful of twigs every few steps as they climbed up. Thus the narrow trail behind them was dotted at frequent intervals with tiny piles of broken twigs.

At last the summit was reached. Weary and heart-sick, the youth gently released his burden and prepared a place of comfort as his last duty to the one who had nurtured him. He gathered fallen pine needles to make a soft cushion, spread his coat over it, and wrapped his mother tenderly. With tearful eyes and an aching heart, he bowed low to say farewell. But the mother's gentle voice spoke words of self-effacing guidance: 'My son, your path downward is dark and perilous. Look carefully and follow the path dotted with twigs; they will guide you safely back to our home.'

summary.en: Even while facing death, the mother lovingly broke twigs along the trail to ensure her son would not lose his way returning home.
summary.ur: اپنی موت کے وقت بھی ماں نے راستے میں ٹہنیاں توڑ کر گرائیں تاکہ واپسی پر اس کا بیٹا اندھیرے میں راستہ نہ بھٹک جائے۔

passages.heading: The Repentance and Secret Sanctuary
passages.text:
The son looked back at the path and then at the poor, gnarled hands of his mother, scratched and soiled from snapping the branches for his safety. His heart broke within him. Bowing to the ground, he cried aloud: 'Oh, honorable mother, your kindness breaks my heart! I will not leave you. Together we will follow the path of twigs, and together we will die!'

Once more he shouldered his mother and hastened down the path through the shadows to his humble thatched hut. Beneath the kitchen floor, he had a secret closet where food was stored. There he gently concealed his mother, providing her with everything she needed, watching and fearing constantly lest she be discovered. Months passed in safety, and the son cared for her with unwavering devotion.

summary.en: Moved to tears by his mother's unconditional love, the son refuses to abandon her, brings her home secretly, and hides her in a concealed closet.
summary.ur: ماں کی بے لوث محبت دیکھ کر بیٹے کی چیخ نکل گئی؛ وہ ماں کو واپس لے آیا اور کچن کے خفیہ تہہ خانے میں چھپا کر اس کی خدمت کرنے لگا۔

passages.heading: The Governor's Challenge: A Rope of Ashes
passages.text:
Time passed, and the despotic governor again sent forth an impossible mandate to intimidate his subjects: he demanded that the people of Shinano present him with a rope of ashes. The entire province was plunged into despair. Who could weave a rope out of ashes? In deep sorrow, the farmer confided the tyrant's impossible order to his hidden mother.

'Wait, my son,' she replied gently. 'I will think.' The next day, she instructed him: 'Make a rope of tightly twisted straw, stretch it straight upon a row of flat stones, and burn it on a calm, windless night.' The son followed her advice precisely. When the straw burned down, there lay upon the flat stones a perfect, intact rope of white ashes, holding its shape without crumbling.

The farmer presented the rope of ashes to the governor. The tyrant marveled at the feat and demanded to know who had conceived such extraordinary wisdom. The youth bowed low and truthfully confessed the whole story—how he had hidden his aged mother and how her lifelong wisdom had solved the riddle.

summary.en: When the governor demands an impossible rope of ashes, the wise mother reveals the secret of burning twisted straw on flat stones.
summary.ur: جب گورنر نے راکھ کی رسی بنانے کا ناممکن مطالبہ کیا، تو عقل مند ماں نے تنکوں کی بٹی ہوئی رسی کو پتھروں پر جلا کر راکھ کی ہو بہو رسی تیار کروائی۔

passages.heading: The Abolition of the Proclamation and the Crown of Snow
passages.text:
The governor listened in silence, deeply moved by the son's filial devotion and the mother's profound sagacity. He meditated on the truth and exclaimed: 'Shinano needs more than the physical strength of youth. Ah, that I should have forgotten the well-known saying: With the crown of snow, there cometh wisdom!'

That very hour, the cruel decree was abolished forever. The governor recognized the irreplaceable value of elder citizens in guiding society with their accumulated experience. The farmer brought his beloved mother out into the sunshine without fear, and the aged people of Shinano were honored with respect and reverence ever after.

summary.en: Realizing that 'with the crown of snow comes wisdom', the governor permanently abolishes the cruel decree and honors the elderly.
summary.ur: گورنر نے تسلیم کیا کہ 'سفید بالوں کے ساتھ دانائی آتی ہے'؛ اس نے ظالمانہ قانون منسوخ کر دیا اور بزرگوں کو عزت و تکریم دینے کا اعلان کیا۔

vocabulary.title: Literary Context Clues & Archaic Idioms
vocabulary.instruction: Study the metaphorical expressions and archaic vocabulary featured in the folktale.

items.definition: A poetic metaphor for white or silver hair resulting from old age, symbolizing lifelong wisdom and experience.
items.example: "With the crown of snow, there cometh wisdom" reminds us that age brings irreplaceable insight.

items.definition: Ruling with absolute, unlimited, tyrannical power and cruelty.
items.example: The despotic ruler enforced arbitrary laws that oppressed his citizens.

items.definition: Brown, unpolished rice eaten by poor rural peasants.
items.example: He prepared a simple meal of unwhitened rice for their journey.

items.definition: Citizens living under the rule of a sovereign monarch or governor.
items.example: The governor ordered his subjects to solve the riddle of the rope of ashes.

questions.q: Why did the farmer decide to take his mother to the summit?
questions.ans: The farmer decided to carry his mother to the summit of Mount Obatsuyama because the tyrannical governor of Shinano had issued a strict, merciless proclamation ordering all elderly citizens to be put to death immediately. Fearing the cruel and barbarous execution methods of the governor's soldiers, the son sorrowfully chose to carry his mother to the mountain summit to give her what was then considered the gentlest and most peaceful passing.

questions.q: Why did the son hide his mother in the closet?
questions.ans: After realizing the boundless depth of his mother's love—who snapped twigs to guide his safe return even while facing her own death—the son could not bear to abandon her. He brought her back down to his hut and hid her in a concealed underground storage closet beneath the kitchen floorboards to protect her from the governor's soldiers.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'with the crown of snow, there cometh wisdom!' mean?
questions.ans: The proverb means that old age—symbolized by white or silver hair like a 'crown of snow'—brings profound wisdom, judgment, and practical knowledge accumulated through decades of living. True sagacity and life insight belong to the elderly, whose experience is vital to guiding the community.

questions.q: What is the theme of 'The Aged Mother'?
questions.ans: The central theme of the story is the sacred bond of filial devotion, maternal selflessness, and the indispensable value of senior citizens to society. It highlights that elderly parents must not be discarded as burdens; rather, their accumulated experience and wisdom are essential pillars of a compassionate civilization.

questions.q: What is the climax of the story 'The Aged Mother'?
questions.ans: The climax occurs on the bare summit of Obatsuyama when the mother gently reveals to her son that she has left a trail of broken twigs so he will not get lost on his return. This overwhelming act of maternal sacrifice shatters the son's resolve to obey the law, prompting him to defy the ruler and risk his own life to save his mother.

questions.q: How did the farmer disclose his secret?
questions.ans: When the governor demanded to know where the humble farmer had obtained the extraordinary wisdom to make a rope of ashes, the farmer refused to claim credit dishonestly. He bowed low and courageously disclosed the complete truth: that he had kept his aged mother hidden in defiance of the law, and that she was the true source of the ingenious solution.

questions.q: What are the challenges faced by the farmer and his mother?
questions.ans: The farmer and his mother endured extreme poverty, surviving on a meager plot of land. They faced the constant terror of the governor's death decree, the harrowing physical journey up the mountain trails, the psychological agony of imminent abandonment, and months of claustrophobic confinement in a dark closet in constant fear of discovery.

questions.q: What is the setting of the story?
questions.ans: The story is set in ancient feudal Japan in the mountainous, rural province of Shinano, primarily around the farmer's humble thatched hut at the mountain base and the steep, rugged, forest-covered trails of Mount Obatsuyama.

questions.q: Why did the leader issue the proclamation?
questions.ans: The governor issued the cruel decree because, despite being a skilled warrior, he possessed a cowardly, irrational dread of physical weakness, sickness, and aging. He viewed the elderly as useless burdens who contributed nothing to physical labor or military combat.

questions.q: How does the poor youth feel about the proclamation?
questions.ans: The proclamation filled the youth's heart with sorrow, anguish, and despair. He revered his mother tenderly, and the thought of causing her death tore him apart, forcing him into deep moral agony.

questions.q: How did the mother help her son safely return from the mountain?
questions.ans: Observing that her son was hurrying blindly along unfamiliar mountain paths in distress, the mother selflessly snapped twigs from overhanging roadside bushes and dropped them every few steps. This created a visible trail of white wood markings that guided the son safely back down the mountain through the darkness.

mcqs.q: The governor of Shinano issued the cruel decree ordering all aged people to be put to death because:
opts: the province was facing a severe famine
he had a great and cowardly fear of failing health and old age
the elderly refused to pay agricultural taxes
the province lacked land for housing
mcqs.exp: The text states that the leader 'had a great and cowardly terror of anything suggestive of failing health and strength'.

mcqs.q: The son decided to take his mother back down to his hut because:
opts: the mountain was too cold for him to stay
she demanded to return home immediately
the governor had already cancelled the decree
he was deeply moved by the selfless pains she took to guide him safely back home
mcqs.exp: Seeing his mother's scratched hands and realizing she thought only of his safety broke his heart and made him refuse to abandon her.

mcqs.q: The ancient saying 'With the crown of snow, there cometh wisdom' means that:
opts: kings who wear silver crowns are always wise
wisdom comes with age and life experience (white hair)
snow in winter enhances human intelligence
mcqs.exp: The 'crown of snow' is a metaphor for gray or white hair, symbolizing that wisdom is gained through years of lived experience.

mcqs.q: How did the wise mother solve the riddle of the rope of ashes?
opts: By mixing ashes with sticky river mud
By burning a twisted straw rope stretched upon flat stones on a windless night
By weaving horsehair with white chalk
By collecting white ashes from the mountain peak
mcqs.exp: She instructed her son to twist straw into a rope, lay it on flat stones, and burn it on a still night so the ash retain the rope's exact shape.

mcqs.q: 'His demand was that his subjects should present him with a rope of ashes.' The word 'subjects' in this context means:
opts: the citizens / people governed by the ruler
mcqs.exp: In a political/monarchical context, 'subjects' refers to the residents or citizens under a sovereign's rule.

grammar.topic: Modal Verbs and Their Functions (Exercise A)
grammar.rule: Modal auxiliary verbs (can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would, need) express grammatical mood: ability, possibility, permission, obligation, necessity, advice, or willingness.
examples: Can you help me? (Inquiring about willingness / informal request).
You needn't take your umbrella (Lack of necessity).
Could you say it again? (Polite request).
It might be Anam's (Possibility).

exercises.q: 'Can you help me with this exercise?' — The modal verb expresses: a) ability b) willingness / request c) possibility d) permission
exercises.ans: b) to express or inquire about willingness / polite request.

exercises.q: 'You needn't take your umbrella. It isn't raining.' — The modal verb expresses: a) prohibition b) obligation c) lack of necessity d) ability
exercises.ans: c) expressing lack of necessity.

exercises.q: 'Could you say it again more slowly?' — The modal verb expresses: a) a polite request b) past ability c) obligation d) suggestion
exercises.ans: a) to make a polite request.

exercises.q: 'The weather will be hot enough to go to the beach this weekend.' — The modal expresses: a) intention b) a prediction c) habitual action d) permission
exercises.ans: b) to make a prediction about the future.

exercises.q: 'You don't look well. You ______ see a doctor.' (Advice) a) are to b) could c) need to d) should
exercises.ans: d) should (expresses moral or medical advice).

exercises.q: '______ you take a message please?' (Request) a) May b) Could c) Shall d) Need
exercises.ans: b) Could (polite request form).

exercises.q: 'Whose book is this? I am not sure. It ______ be Anam's.' (Possibility) a) might b) should c) must d) would
exercises.ans: a) might (expresses uncertain possibility).

grammar.topic: Regular and Irregular Past Tense Narrative Verbs (Exercise B)
grammar.rule: Regular verbs form the simple past by adding -ed or -d (brush → brushed, enter → entered). Irregular verbs change root vowels or alter endings unpredictably (get → got, have → had, go → went, take → took, eat → ate).
examples: Regular: He brushed his teeth and combed his hair.
Irregular: He got up at 7 o'clock and had a shower.

exercises.q: Conjugate into Simple Past: 'Yesterday Tahir (get) up at 7 o'clock. He (have) a shower and (put) on clean clothes. Then he (have) breakfast. At half past seven he (go) into the bathroom, (brush) his teeth and (comb) his hair. After that he (put) on his shoes and (leave) his home. He (take) the bus and (get) off in front of the school. He (enter) his classroom just in time. The teacher (teach) from 8 a.m. to 1:35 p.m. Then he (be) very hungry. He (hurry) home and (eat) lunch.'
exercises.ans: got / had / put / had / went / brushed / combed / put / left / took / got / entered / taught / was / hurried / ate

writing.summary: In the moving Japanese folktale 'The Aged Mother', adapted by Matsuo Basho, the cruel governor of Shinano province decrees that all elderly citizens must be put to death due to his cowardly fear of infirmity. A loving young farmer tearfully carries his widowed mother up the rugged slopes of Mount Obatsuyama to abandon her to a gentle death. Along the arduous climb, the mother selflessly snaps branches and drops twigs along the path so her son will not lose his way returning home in the dark. Deeply moved by this supreme demonstration of maternal love, the son refuses to leave her. He carries her back down, concealing her in a secret closet under his kitchen floor. When the governor later challenges the province to produce an impossible 'rope of ashes', the mother's wisdom guides the son to burn twisted straw on flat stones on a windless night. Presenting the flawless rope of ashes, the youth courageously confesses his secret. Amazed by her genius, the governor repents, acknowledging that 'with the crown of snow comes wisdom', permanently repealing the cruel decree and restoring honor to all elderly citizens.

essay.title: Respect for Parents and Senior Citizens in Modern Society
essay.text: The Japanese folktale 'The Aged Mother' delivers a timeless moral message on the sanctity of parents and the invaluable role of senior citizens. In contemporary consumerist societies, there is an alarming tendency among modern youth to regard aging parents as financial or social liabilities, overlooking the immense sacrifices made in raising them. Senior citizens possess a lifetime of accumulated wisdom, moral patience, and practical insight that no textbook or algorithm can replicate. True civilizational maturity is demonstrated not by the speed of economic growth, but by the dignity and gratitude with which a society treats its elderly. Youth must realize that honoring parents is both a divine religious commandment and a fundamental ethical obligation. When we protect, consult, and revere our elders, we enrich our homes with spiritual blessing and preserve the cultural wisdom essential for human flourishing.

reading.title: Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement
reading.theme: Civic Equality, National Struggle & Women Leadership
reading.author: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Textbook Board
reading.preReading:
Think and answer the pre-reading questions:
1. Do men and women have different roles in society, community, and at home? How?
2. What is the role of women in the socio-economic and political development of a nation?

passages.heading: The Awakening: From Domestic Seclusion to the Khilafat Movement
passages.text: At the dawn of the twentieth century, when the political destiny of Muslims in the Subcontinent was at a formative stage, most Muslim women led secluded lives within their homes. Bound by strict social conservatism and centuries-old cultural customs, they were largely excluded from public life and political discourse. A handful of visionary women, however, took the initial courageous steps during the Khilafat Movement (1919–1922)—a pan-Islamic mass movement launched for the restoration of the Ottoman Caliphate. The name of Abadi Begum, popularly revered as 'Bi Amma', stands foremost among these pioneering figures. As the courageous mother of Maulana Muhammad Ali Jauhar and Maulana Shaukat Ali, she cast aside traditional seclusion to address crowded political gatherings across India, inspiring both men and women to sacrifice their wealth and freedom for national honor.

summary.en: At the turn of the century, Muslim women lived secluded domestic lives until pioneers like Bi Amma emerged during the Khilafat Movement to inspire political awakening.
summary.ur: بیسویں صدی کے آغاز میں مسلمان خواتین گھریلو تنہائی کی زندگی گزارتی تھیں، لیکن تحریکِ خلافت کے دوران 'بی اماں' جیسی باہمت رہنماؤں نے سیاسی بیداری کی بنیاد رکھی۔

passages.heading: Quaid-e-Azam's Revolutionary Vision of Gender Equality
passages.text:
It was Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah who brought about a profound social revolution in the empowerment of Muslim women. Recognizing that no national liberation struggle could succeed while half the population remained marginalized, the Quaid tirelessly advocated for female emancipation. In a historic speech at Aligarh Muslim University in 1944, he declared with unshakeable conviction:

'No nation can rise to the height of glory unless your women are side by side with you; we are victims of evil customs. It is a crime against humanity that our women are shut up within the four walls of the houses as prisoners.'

Under his inspiring leadership, the All-India Muslim League established a Central Women's Subcommittee in 1938, creating formal provincial branches to mobilize women across urban and rural India.

summary.en: Quaid-e-Azam revolutionized women's status by declaring that no nation can rise unless women stand side-by-side with men, creating the Muslim League Women's Subcommittee.
summary.ur: قائد اعظم نے تاریخی انقلاب برپا کرتے ہوئے فرمایا کہ کوئی قوم اس وقت تک ترقی نہیں کر سکتی جب تک اس کی خواتین مردوں کے شانہ بشانہ کھڑی نہ ہوں۔

passages.heading: Pioneering Leaders and Nationwide Mobilization
passages.text:
Foremost among the towering personalities was the Quaid's devoted sister, Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah—affectionately titled 'Madar-e-Millat' (Mother of the Nation). As his constant companion, confidante, and adviser, she traveled the length and breadth of British India, rallying Muslim women under the banner of the Muslim League.

Other prominent leaders emerged across all regions: Begum Jahanara Shahnawaz, Begum Salma Tassaduq Hussain, and Begum Fatima from Lahore; Begum Shaista Ikramullah from Bengal; Miss Zari Sarfraz from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; and Lady Abdullah Haroon from Sindh. As the Pakistan Movement gained momentum, the Muslim Students Federation and its vibrant women's wing played an increasingly decisive role in mass mobilization. Young female students traveled even to the remote districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, defying deep-seated social conservatism to establish girl student committees. Begum Fatima, founder principal of the Jinnah Islamia College for Girls in Lahore, played a stellar role in training and inspiring female student cadres.

summary.en: Leaders like Fatima Jinnah, Jahanara Shahnawaz, Salma Tassaduq Hussain, Shaista Ikramullah, and Zari Sarfraz organized mass rallies and student federations across all provinces.
summary.ur: محترمہ فاطمہ جناح، بیگم جہان آرا شاہنواز، بیگم شائستہ اکرام اللہ اور زری سرفراز نے ملک گیر سطح پر خواتین اور طالبات کو منظم کر کے تحریک میں روح پھونکی۔

passages.heading: Diplomatic Missions, Civil Disobedience, and the Dawn of Independence
passages.text:
The diplomatic acumen of Muslim women proved instrumental on the world stage. In 1946, Quaid-e-Azam nominated Begum Jahanara Shahnawaz and M.A.H. Ispahani to undertake an international diplomatic mission to the United States. Their crucial mandate was to address delegations at the United Nations and dismantle hostile Congress propaganda that falsely portrayed the Pakistan demand as a reactionary theocratic movement. Begum Shahnawaz delivered eloquent, persuasive addresses that impressed international diplomats, winning global sympathy for the Muslim cause.

During the historic 1947 Punjab Civil Disobedience Movement, when male leaders were imprisoned, women took to the streets in fearless defiance of British tear gas, baton charges, and mass arrests. Begum Salma Tassaduq Hussain, Fatima Begum, and brave student activists famously scaled the walls of the Lahore Civil Secretariat, pulled down the Union Jack, and hoisted the Muslim League green flag. When the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan convened, Begum Shahnawaz and Begum Shaista Ikramullah took their seats as pioneering female legislators, ensuring that the new nation was founded upon the unshakeable bedrock of gender equality.

summary.en: Muslim women represented Pakistan diplomatically at the UN in 1946, faced colonial tear gas in Lahore, hoisted the League flag, and became foundational legislators.
summary.ur: خواتین رہنماؤں نے 1946 میں اقوام متحدہ میں سفارتی محاذ سنبھالا، لاہور سیکرٹریٹ پر لیگ کا پرچم لہرایا اور پاکستان کی پہلی دستور ساز اسمبلی کی رکن بنیں۔

glossary.meaning: The process of being set free from legal, social, or political restrictions and servitude; liberation.
glossary.sentence: Quaid-e-Azam championed the educational and political emancipation of Muslim women.

glossary.sentence: Female student organizers overcame intense social conservatism in frontier districts.

glossary.meaning: Sheltered, private, and removed from outside public activities or contact with society.
glossary.sentence: Early twentieth-century women largely led secluded lives within the domestic sphere.

glossary.meaning: An event, idea, or individual that causes a profound, transformative shift in the existing state of affairs.
glossary.sentence: The mass entry of female voters proved to be a decisive game changer in the 1946 elections.

glossary.meaning: Imbuing something with new life, vigor, energy, and strength.
glossary.sentence: Fatima Jinnah traveled tirelessly, revitalizing the political enthusiasm of Muslim youth.

glossary.meaning: The act of organizing, encouraging, and assembling large groups of people for active collective struggle.
glossary.sentence: The Muslim Students Federation spearheaded the mass mobilization of college girls.

glossary.sentence: Bi Amma was a passionate firebrand whose speeches electrified crowds during the Khilafat Movement.

questions.q: What was the social status of Muslim women at the dawn of the twentieth century?
questions.ans: At the start of the twentieth century, Muslim women led heavily secluded, restricted lives within their domestic homes. Strict social conservatism, illiteracy, and deep-rooted patriarchal traditions excluded them from higher education, political activism, employment, and public civic participation.

questions.q: What role did Bi Amma play in inspiring political consciousness among Muslims?
questions.ans: Abadi Begum ('Bi Amma'), the heroic mother of the Ali brothers, broke social barriers during the Khilafat Movement. She courageously stepped onto public platforms, addressed massive gatherings of men and women, and collected funds for the cause. She famously urged her sons to lay down their lives for truth and national self-respect, inspiring thousands of Muslim women to enter the national struggle.

questions.q: How did Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah advocate for women's active participation?
questions.ans: Quaid-e-Azam was a staunch champion of women's emancipation. He declared at Aligarh in 1944 that keeping women locked behind domestic walls like prisoners was a crime against humanity and that no nation could achieve greatness without women standing side by side with men. He established the Central Women's Subcommittee in the Muslim League, encouraging female leaders to organize rallies, negotiate with colonial officials, and represent Muslims internationally.

questions.q: Describe the role of women in the Pakistan Movement, highlighting their love and aspirations for the new homeland.
questions.ans: Muslim women demonstrated extraordinary heroism, love, and sacrifice. They established the women's wing of the Muslim Students Federation, canvassed voter support door-to-door during the 1946 elections, and organized public protests. During the 1947 Punjab Civil Disobedience Movement, brave women faced tear gas and lathi-charges, hoisted the League flag atop the Lahore Civil Secretariat, and provided emergency medical relief and food shelters to millions of wounded refugees arriving during Partition.

questions.q: Analyse the third paragraph of the lesson and identify the sentences that support the main idea through cause and effect.
questions.ans:
• Main Idea: Women's organizational mobilization accelerated rapidly across all provinces.
• Cause and Effect Sentences:
  1. Cause: Quaid-e-Azam mobilized women through provincial committees → Effect: Prominent figures like Begum Shahnawaz, Salma Tassaduq Hussain, and Zari Sarfraz established active grassroots units.
  2. Cause: The Pakistan Movement gained momentum → Effect: The Muslim Students Federation established women's wings that penetrated socially conservative rural areas like Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
  3. Cause: Begum Fatima founded Jinnah Islamia College for Girls → Effect: Female students received formal organizational training and led mass political marches.

questions.q: What ideas and issues have been explored in the fifth paragraph of the text?
questions.ans: The fifth paragraph highlights the diplomatic, legislative, and frontline civil disobedience achievements of female leaders. It explores: (1) Begum Shahnawaz's diplomatic mission to the United States and UN in 1946 to refute anti-Pakistan propaganda, (2) the direct street defiance of colonial laws where women were tear-gassed and arrested, (3) the historic hoisting of the national flag on the Lahore Secretariat, and (4) the election of female pioneers to the Constituent Assembly to shape the constitution.

mcqs.q: "Most of the Muslim women led secluded lives within their homes." By using contextual clues the word closest in meaning to 'secluded' is:
opts: involved little in outside social activities / isolated
involved too much in public politics
mcqs.exp: 'Secluded' means sheltered, private, and cut off from outside public life and social activities.

mcqs.q: Whom did Quaid-e-Azam nominate along with M.A.H. Ispahani to address international delegates at the United Nations in 1946?
mcqs.exp: The Quaid nominated Begum Jahanara Shahnawaz, an experienced parliamentarian, to represent Muslims at the UN in New York.

mcqs.q: Female student activists defied deep-seated social conservatism by traveling to organize student units in which province?
mcqs.exp: The text specifically highlights that girl students traveling to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was a remarkable feat given the province's traditional social conservatism.

mcqs.q: After reading the lesson, it can be concluded that the paragraphs are arranged in:
mcqs.exp: The text traces the historical progression from early seclusion (1900s) through the Khilafat Movement (1920s), the 1940s mobilization, and the 1947 independence.

mcqs.q: Abadi Begum, who inspired political consciousness during the Khilafat Movement, was popularly revered as:
mcqs.exp: Abadi Begum, mother of the Ali brothers, was affectionately known across the Subcontinent as 'Bi Amma'.

grammar.rule: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs, answering How? When? Where? or To what extent? Most adverbs of manner are formed by adding -ly to adjectives (quick → quickly). If ending in -y, change to -ily (heavy → heavily). If ending in -le, change to -ly (terrible → terribly). Irregular: good → well, hard → hard, fast → fast.
examples: perfect → perfectly
quick → quickly
heavy → heavily
good → well
terrible → terribly

exercises.q: Form adverbs from: perfect, quick, late, regular, heavy, good, fantastic, hard, nice, quiet, terrible, recent.
exercises.ans: perfect → perfectly | quick → quickly | late → late/lately | regular → regularly | heavy → heavily | good → well | fantastic → fantastically | hard → hard | nice → nicely | quiet → quietly | terrible → terribly | recent → recently

grammar.topic: Adjective vs Adverb in Sentence Context (Exercise C)
grammar.rule: Use an adjective to modify a noun or follow a linking verb (look, feel, seem, be). Use an adverb to modify an action verb, adjective, or another adverb.
examples: He walks hurriedly (adverb modifying action verb 'walks').
The library is always quiet (adjective following linking verb 'is').

exercises.q: He is always in a rush. I don't understand why he walks so ______ (hurry / hurriedly).
exercises.ans: hurriedly (adverb modifying verb 'walks').

exercises.q: I prefer studying in the library. It is always ______ (quiet / quietly).
exercises.ans: quiet (predicate adjective following linking verb 'is').

exercises.q: Masood ______ (happy / happily) took the assistant job.
exercises.ans: happily (adverb modifying verb 'took').

exercises.q: They speak Pashto very ______ (good / well).
exercises.ans: well (adverb modifying verb 'speak').

exercises.q: Please be ______ (careful / carefully) in the hallway. The walls have just been painted.
exercises.ans: careful (adjective following imperative linking verb 'be').

grammar.topic: Adverb Phrases and Adverb Clauses (Exercises D & E)
grammar.rule: An Adverb Phrase is a group of words without a subject-verb pair that modifies a verb (e.g. 'in spring', 'in a polite manner'). An Adverb Clause is a dependent clause beginning with a subordinating conjunction (when, although, because, in order that, if, wherever) that modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb.
examples: The flowers bloom in spring (Adverb phrase of time).
The lamb followed Maria wherever she went (Adverb clause of place).
Take a shawl because the night is cold (Adverb clause of reason).

exercises.q: Identify adverb phrase: 'Hamza did not go to school on account of the bad weather.'
exercises.ans: Adverb phrase of reason: 'on account of the bad weather'.

exercises.q: Identify adverb phrase: 'My brother spoke in a polite manner.'
exercises.ans: Adverb phrase of manner: 'in a polite manner'.

exercises.q: Identify adverb clause: 'Whether you like it or not, you have to go to bed now.'
exercises.ans: Adverb clause of concession: 'Whether you like it or not'.

exercises.q: Identify adverb clause: 'Take a shawl because the night is cold.'
exercises.ans: Adverb clause of reason: 'because the night is cold'.

exercises.q: Identify adverb clause: 'The lamb followed Maria wherever she went.'
exercises.ans: Adverb clause of place: 'wherever she went'.

writing.summary: This inspiring historical chapter chronicles the revolutionary transformation and indispensable contributions of Muslim women during the Pakistan Movement. In the early twentieth century, women in the Subcontinent were largely confined to secluded domestic spheres due to social conservatism. The initial spark of political awakening was ignited by pioneers like Bi Amma during the Khilafat Movement. Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah became the chief catalyst of their empowerment, passionately declaring that no nation could achieve greatness without women standing shoulder-to-shoulder with men. Under his guidance, the Muslim League formed dedicated women's subcommittees led by figures such as Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah, Begum Jahanara Shahnawaz, Begum Salma Tassaduq Hussain, Begum Shaista Ikramullah, and Miss Zari Sarfraz. Young female students actively mobilized conservative regions, organized protests, endured tear gas and imprisonment during the Punjab civil disobedience campaign, and heroically hoisted the Muslim League flag atop the Lahore Civil Secretariat. Their diplomatic brilliance at the UN and legislative presence in the first Constituent Assembly ensured that Pakistan was founded upon a bedrock of female leadership and gender equality.

essay.title: Patterns of Paragraph Organization in Historical Essays
essay.text:
Effective expository and historical writing relies upon deliberate, logical patterns of paragraph organization that guide the reader through complex events and arguments. Among the most fundamental organizational strategies are chronological order, order of importance, and spatial order.

Chronological order arranges events according to the precise timeline of their historical occurrence. This method is indispensable for historical narratives, biographies, and process analyses. For instance, the chapter 'Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement' follows chronological order: beginning with domestic seclusion in the early 1900s, progressing to the 1920 Khilafat Movement, advancing through the 1940s student mobilizations, and culminating in the 1947 independence. Chronological writing utilizes temporal transitions such as 'at the dawn of', 'subsequently', 'in 1946', and 'eventually'.

Order of importance structures information hierarchically, arranging ideas either from the most critical to least critical, or building progressively from minor points to a powerful, climactic central argument. This structure is ideal for persuasive essays and policy analyses where the author seeks to maximize rhetorical impact. Key transition words include 'foremost', 'principally', 'more importantly', and 'above all'.

Finally, spatial order organizes descriptive details according to physical location and geometric relationship—such as left to right, top to bottom, or inside to outside. It is commonly employed in architectural descriptions and scene-setting, enabling the reader to visualize a physical space with precision.

Mastering these organizational patterns empowers students to construct essays that are coherent, engaging, and logically persuasive.
