poet.name: Edgar Albert Guest
poet.bio: Edgar Albert Guest (August 20, 1881 – August 5, 1959) was a prolific English-born American poet who became known as the 'People's Poet'. Popular in the first half of the 20th century, his verses conveyed an inspirational, accessible, and optimistic view of everyday human life.

reading.title: Equipment
reading.theme: Self-Belief, Determination & Innate Human Equality
reading.author: Edgar Albert Guest (1881–1959)
reading.preReading:
Think and answer the pre-reading questions:
1. What are the essential inner qualities that one must possess to succeed in life?
2. How can we best utilize the physical and intellectual abilities Allah has blessed us with?

passages.heading: Stanza 1: The Common Heritage of Greatness
passages.text:
Figure it out for yourself, my lad,
You've all that the greatest of men have had,
Two arms, two hands, two legs, two eyes,
And a brain to use if you would be wise.
With this equipment they all began,
So start for the top and say "I can."

summary.en: The poet reminds the youth that he possesses the exact same biological and mental equipment—two arms, hands, legs, eyes, and a brain—as the greatest icons of history.
summary.ur: شاعر نوجوان کو یاد دلاتا ہے کہ اس کے پاس بھی وہی ہاتھ، پاؤں، آنکھیں اور دماغ ہے جو دنیا کے عظیم ترین انسانوں کے پاس تھا، اس لیے کامیابی کا عزم کرو۔

passages.heading: Stanza 2: The Ordinary Habits of Extraordinary Men
passages.text:
Look them over, the wise and great,
They take their food from a common plate,
And similar knives and forks they use,
With similar laces they tie their shoes,
The world considers them brave and smart,
But you've all they had when they made their start.

summary.en: The greatest leaders eat from common plates and tie their shoes just like anyone else; their beginning was identical to any ordinary person's.
summary.ur: دنیا کے عظیم لوگ بھی عام پلیٹوں سے کھانا کھاتے ہیں اور عام جوتے پہنتے ہیں؛ آغاز میں ان کے پاس بھی وہی کچھ تھا جو آج تمہارے پاس ہے۔

passages.heading: Stanza 3: Innate Capacity for Triumph
passages.text:
You can triumph and come to skill,
You can be great if only you will,
You're well equipped for what fight you choose,
You have legs and arms and a brain to use,
And the man who has risen, great deeds to do,
Began his life with no more than you.

summary.en: Greatness depends on will and determination, not on privileged starting equipment; anyone can triumph in any chosen field.
summary.ur: تم بھی ہر میدان میں فتح اور مہارت حاصل کر سکتے ہو بشرطیکہ تمہارے اندر عزم ہو، کیونکہ بڑے کام کرنے والوں نے بھی تم جتنے وسائل سے آغاز کیا۔

passages.heading: Stanza 4: Overcoming the Inner Handicap
passages.text:
You are the handicap you must face,
You are the one who must choose your place,
You must say where you want to go,
How much you will study the truth to know,
God has equipped you for life, but He
Lets you decide what you want to be.

summary.en: A person's only real handicap is their own self-doubt; God provided the tools, but grants human beings the free will to choose their destiny.
summary.ur: انسان کی سب سے بڑی رکاوٹ اس کا اپنا شک اور کاہلی ہے؛ اللہ نے تمام صلاحیتیں دے دیں مگر فیصلہ انسان پر چھوڑ دیا کہ وہ کیا بننا چاہتا ہے۔

passages.heading: Stanza 5: The Will to Win from Within
passages.text:
Courage must come from the soul within,
The man must furnish the will to win,
So figure it out for yourself, my lad,
You've all that the greatest of men have had,
With your equipment they all began,
Get hold of yourself, and say: "I can."

summary.en: True courage and the will to win must be generated from within the human soul; take command of yourself and declare 'I can.'
summary.ur: ہمت اور جیتنے کا جذبہ اندر کی روح سے پیدا ہونا چاہیے؛ خود پر قابو پاؤ اور بلند حوصلے سے کہو کہ 'میں یہ کر سکتا ہوں'۔

glossary.meaning: A boy or young man (often used as an affectionate form of address).
glossary.sentence: "Figure it out for yourself, my lad," advised the wise mentor.

glossary.meaning: The necessary items, tools, faculties, or physical/mental apparatus needed for a particular purpose.
glossary.sentence: God has endowed every human being with the physical and mental equipment needed for success.

glossary.meaning: To understand, solve, or discover the explanation of a problem through rational thought.
glossary.sentence: You must figure out your life goals through honest self-reflection.

glossary.meaning: A great victory, achievement, or overcoming of formidable odds.
glossary.sentence: Through disciplined effort, the determined student achieved a glorious academic triumph.

glossary.meaning: A circumstance, self-doubt, or condition that restricts progress or places one at a disadvantage.
glossary.sentence: Lack of self-confidence is the most crippling handicap that hinders youth.

glossary.meaning: To provide, supply, or generate something necessary from oneself.
glossary.sentence: Every ambitious individual must furnish the unyielding will to win.

vocabulary.title: Connotation vs Denotation in Everyday Objects
vocabulary.instruction: Analyze how mundane physical nouns assume profound symbolic connotations in the poem.

items.definition: Denotation: A standard porcelain dish for eating. Connotation: Shared human humility, ordinariness, and absence of innate biological superiority.
items.example: Eating from a common plate signifies that even heroes share basic mortal vulnerability.

items.definition: Denotation: Eating utensils and shoe cords. Connotation: The mundane, repetitive everyday routines common to both world leaders and ordinary laborers.
items.example: Great leaders tie their shoelaces one loop at a time, exactly like you.

items.definition: Denotation: Mechanical gear or sporting tools. Connotation: The God-given biological faculties—brain, senses, and limbs—given equally to all mankind.
items.example: Your physical body and intellect constitute your God-given equipment.

questions.q: Paraphrase the second stanza of the poem 'Equipment'.
questions.ans: Paraphrase of Stanza 2: Observe carefully the most celebrated and accomplished personalities throughout history; they are flesh-and-blood human beings who eat ordinary food from common dishes using everyday utensils, and tie their shoes with ordinary laces. Although society honors them as exceptionally courageous and brilliant, remember that when they first embarked upon their journeys, they possessed nothing more than the exact same biological and mental tools that you possess right now.

questions.q: Summarize the poem 'Equipment'.
questions.ans: Edgar Guest's 'Equipment' is an inspiring motivational poem asserting the fundamental equality of all human beings. The poet urges young individuals to realize that they possess the identical physical apparatus—two arms, hands, legs, eyes, and an intellect—as the greatest geniuses and conquerors of history. Exceptional achievers eat from common plates and begin with zero advantages. A person's only true handicap is their internal self-doubt and lack of initiative. Because God provides the equipment while granting free will to choose one's destiny, success requires summoning courage and the unyielding will to win from within one's own soul.

questions.q: Write down the rhyme scheme of the poem 'Equipment'.
questions.ans:
The rhyme scheme of every six-line stanza (sestet) in 'Equipment' is consistently AABBCC.
• Stanza 1: lad (A) / had (A), eyes (B) / wise (B), began (C) / can (C).
• Stanza 2: great (A) / plate (A), use (B) / shoes (B), smart (C) / start (C).
• Stanza 3: skill (A) / will (A), choose (B) / use (B), do (C) / you (C).
• Stanza 4: face (A) / place (A), go (B) / know (B), He (C) / be (C).
• Stanza 5: within (A) / win (A), lad (B) / had (B), began (C) / can (C).

questions.q: What is the theme of the poem 'Equipment'?
questions.ans: The central theme is self-belief, individual responsibility, and innate human equality. The poem teaches that greatness is not an exclusive privilege bestowed on a chosen elite; every human being is adequately equipped by God to achieve excellence. Victory is determined solely by moral resolve, continuous exertion, and the courage to proclaim 'I can'.

questions.q: 'All human beings are created equal'. Explain this statement in the light of the poem 'Equipment'.
questions.ans: The poem exemplifies this universal truth by pointing out that biologically and intellectually, all humans start from the same baseline: two hands, two arms, two legs, two eyes, and a thinking mind. History's titans were not born with supernatural limbs or divine utensils; they rose from ordinary origins by diligently harnessing their God-given potential. Disparities in achievement arise not from unequal divine endowment, but from whether an individual chooses to cultivate or neglect their inner faculties.

questions.q: How do you feel after reading the poem?
questions.ans: Reading 'Equipment' evokes a powerful surge of self-confidence, optimism, and personal accountability. It dispels paralyzing excuses of helplessness and replaces self-doubt with an empowering realization that the power to shape one's destiny lies firmly within one's own will.

mcqs.q: The word 'equipment' is used by the poet as a:
mcqs.exp: 'Equipment' is a metaphor comparing our natural physical limbs and intellect to tools given for life's struggle.

mcqs.q: The poem 'Equipment' by Edgar Guest is structured in the form of:
opts: loving paternal/mentor advice to a youth
mcqs.exp: The poem is framed as wise, encouraging counsel from a fatherly figure to 'my lad'.

mcqs.q: The everyday words 'forks', 'shoes', and 'laces' are used to highlight:
opts: the ordinary, common humanity of the great
mcqs.exp: These domestic items illustrate that even the most celebrated heroes perform the same simple human routines.

mcqs.q: The overall mood and tone of 'Equipment' is:
mcqs.exp: Edgar Guest, the 'People's Poet', is renowned for his vigorously optimistic and inspiring message.

mcqs.q: According to the poet, what must an individual supply from within his own soul to succeed?
mcqs.exp: The text explicitly declares: 'The man must furnish the will to win'.

grammar.topic: Prepositions of Movement and Direction (Exercise A)
grammar.rule: Prepositions of movement and direction describe movement toward, across, into, away from, or along a surface or space (to, across, away from, into, down, up, onto).
examples: He walked to the library (direction).
Walk across the bridge (movement from one side to the other).
Stay away from the dog (movement/distance from danger).

exercises.q: He walked ______ the library every evening. a) to b) across c) onto d) at
exercises.ans: a) to (indicates movement toward a destination).

exercises.q: You must walk ______ the bridge. a) into b) across c) away from d) down
exercises.ans: b) across (movement from one side of a surface to the other).

exercises.q: Stay ______ the dog. It bites! a) under b) into c) onto d) away from
exercises.ans: d) away from (indicates movement/posture maintaining safe distance).

exercises.q: Quick! Get the ball before it rolls ______ the hill. a) in b) down c) up d) across
exercises.ans: b) down (movement toward a lower elevation).

grammar.topic: Prepositions of Time and Place (Exercise B)
grammar.rule: Prepositions of time and place indicate when or where an event occurs: 'at' (precise clock times, specific points), 'in' (months, years, enclosed spaces), 'on' (days, dates, surfaces), 'since' (from a specific point in the past until now).
examples: What do you do at the weekend?
I haven't seen her since June.
His birthday is on the 6th of June.

exercises.q: What do you like to do ______ the weekend? a) up b) in c) on / at d) since
exercises.ans: c) at / on the weekend (British English prefers 'at', American English uses 'on').

exercises.q: I haven't seen her ______ June. a) at b) since c) on d) in
exercises.ans: b) since (indicates continuous time starting from a past month until now).

exercises.q: We will next meet ______ the middle of next month. a) at b) on c) in d) to
exercises.ans: c) in (used with periods of time like 'the middle of next month').

exercises.q: His birthday is ______ the 6th of June. a) at b) on c) in d) between

writing.summary: In 'Equipment', Edgar Albert Guest delivers a powerful motivational message asserting that every human being is endowed with the fundamental tools necessary for greatness. Through five structured sestets rhyming AABBCC, the poem speaks to a young man contemplating his prospects in life. The poet demonstrates that all historical icons—the wise, courageous, and great—started their lives with the exact same biological faculties: two arms, two legs, two eyes, and a brain. They lived ordinary mortal lives, eating from common plates and tying their shoelaces like everyone else. Therefore, failure cannot be attributed to deficient innate equipment. The only true handicap is internal: self-doubt, fear, and lack of discipline. God provides life's apparatus, but grants human beings free will to determine their own destiny. Success demands that an individual furnish the will to win from within their own soul, seize self-command, and courageously declare 'I can.'

essay.title: The Power of Self-Belief: Reflections on Edgar Guest's 'Equipment'
essay.text:
Human history is divided between those who resign themselves to mediocrity by lamenting supposed disadvantages, and those who recognize their innate potential and rise to achieve greatness. In 'Equipment', Edgar Guest cuts through the illusions of privilege and social elitism to deliver a profound egalitarian truth: all human beings are endowed with the same foundational biological apparatus needed to conquer adversity.

Too often, youth paralyze their ambitions under the false assumption that world-renowned achievers possess superhuman intellect or mystical fortune. Guest effectively demystifies greatness by reminding us that the greatest leaders, philosophers, and scientists eat from common dishes and tie their shoes with ordinary laces. Their triumph was not predetermined by luxury; it was forged through relentless will and purposeful exertion. When an individual realizes that their physical limbs and mental intellect match those of history's titans, excuses vanish.

The poem's deepest psychological insight is that 'you are the handicap you must face.' External barriers—poverty, prejudice, and harsh environments—are formidable, yet the only insurmountable obstacle is the defeatist attitude residing within one's own mind. When fear whispers that one is inadequate, ambition withers. Conversely, when an individual summons courage from the soul within and furnishes the disciplined will to win, obstacles transform into stepping stones.

In conclusion, Edgar Guest's 'Equipment' serves as a timeless clarion call to youth. God has equipped each of us with the sacred instruments of body and mind, leaving the choice of what we become entirely in our own hands. True victory begins the moment we overcome internal doubt and boldly proclaim: 'I can.'

passages.heading: Water Resources and the Three River Basins of Pakistan
passages.text:
Pakistan is a land gifted with lavish resources of water. It is a land where crystalline glacial water rolls down the mighty Himalayas, Karakoram, and Hindukush peaks to the fertile plains and breaks into an intricate web of canal systems that irrigates over 16 million hectares of land, out of 34 million hectares of cultivable land available. The other sources of water available in Pakistan are rainfall, surface water in rivers, and underground aquifers.

In surface water, Pakistan has three primary river drainage basins:
1. The Indus River Basin: Considered the lifeblood of Pakistan. Its water sources are snowfall, glacier melt, and monsoon rainfall. From the Indus River system, approximately 141.67 million acre feet (MAF) of water is received annually. In 1960, Pakistan signed a historic water treaty with India called the 'Indus Waters Treaty'. This treaty gave the rights of three eastern rivers—Beas, Sutlej, and Ravi—to India, whereas the waters of the three western rivers—Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab—were allocated exclusively to Pakistan.
2. The Closed Basin of the Kharan Desert: Consisting of mountain basins around Quetta and tributaries draining into the desert sinks, including the Pishin Lora and Bado rivers.
3. The Makran Coastal Basin: Comprising short coastal streams in Balochistan and Sindh, including the Malir, Hub, Porali, Kud, Hingol, and Dasht rivers.

summary.en: Pakistan is fed by three primary drainage basins: the Indus River Basin (yielding 141.67 MAF), the Kharan closed basin, and the Makran coastal basin.
summary.ur: پاکستان کے تین بڑے آبی طاس ہیں: دریائے سندھ کا طاس (جو ملک کی لائف لائن ہے)، خاران کا بند طاس، اور مکران کا ساحلی طاس۔

passages.heading: The Alarming Threat of Groundwater Depletion
passages.text:
Beneath the soil, groundwater serves as the second most vital reservoir for domestic, industrial, and agricultural use. Over 1.2 million private and public tube-wells pump groundwater relentlessly across the Punjab, Sindh, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa plains. However, unregulated over-pumping has triggered catastrophic groundwater depletion. Water tables that once lay 20 to 30 feet below ground level have plummeted to depths of several hundred feet in major cities like Quetta, Lahore, and Islamabad.

If current extraction rates continue, water demand will almost double by the year 2025, subjecting underground aquifers to irreversible saline contamination and exhaustion. Climate change, retreating glaciers in the northern highlands, and erratic rainfall patterns further compound this existential vulnerability.

summary.en: Unregulated extraction by over 1.2 million tube-wells has dropped water tables by hundreds of feet, threatening total aquifer depletion by 2025.
summary.ur: ٹیوب ویلوں کے بے دریغ استعمال سے زیرِ زمین پانی کی سطح سینکڑوں فٹ نیچے گر چکی ہے اور 2025 تک پانی کی طلب دگنی ہونے کا اندیشہ ہے۔

passages.heading: The Staggering $70 Billion Economic Waste
passages.text:
Despite facing severe water starvation, Pakistan suffers from a tragic lack of water storage infrastructure. According to authoritative research on Pakistan's water resources, freshwater of an economic value of $70 billion is dumped into the Arabian Sea every year unutilized due to the non-construction of major water storage reservoirs.

For a developing country whose foreign currency reserves often hover around $20 billion, throwing water worth $70 billion annually into the ocean is an unbearable national tragedy. Studies by the Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources (PCRWR) warn that Pakistan is rapidly transitioning from a 'water-stressed' country to a chronically 'water-scarce' nation. Per capita water availability has collapsed from over 5,000 cubic meters in 1951 to less than 1,000 cubic meters today—the international threshold of acute water poverty.

summary.en: Due to insufficient storage dams, water valued at $70 billion is lost to the sea each year, pushing Pakistan below the water-scarcity threshold of 1,000 m³ per capita.
summary.ur: ڈیموں کی کمی کے باعث ہر سال 70 ارب ڈالر کا قیمتی میٹھا پانی سمندر کی نذر ہو جاتا ہے جبکہ فی کس پانی کی دستیابی 5000 سے گر کر 1000 کیوبک میٹر رہ گئی ہے۔

passages.heading: Strategic Solutions: Modern Irrigation and Water Conservation
passages.text:
The problems faced by the water sector are acute, urgent, and complex. Therefore, constructing major and medium storage reservoirs, lining irrigation canals to eliminate seepage, and adopting effective water management policies are the paramount needs of the hour.

In agriculture, which consumes over 90% of our water, Pakistan must urgently transition from wasteful flood irrigation to conservation agriculture and micro-irrigation technologies:
1. Sprinkler Irrigation: A method of applying water similar to natural rainfall, distributed through pressurized pipes and sprayed uniformly over crops, cutting water waste by 40%.
2. Drip Irrigation: A high-efficiency technique where water flows through filters and dripper pipes directly to the plant root zones, saving up to 70% of water while boosting crop yields.
3. Laser Land Leveling and Rainwater Harvesting: Ensuring uniform water distribution in fields and capturing rooftop stormwater in cities.

It is widely acknowledged that the wars of the twenty-first century will be fought over water resources. We must save water now to secure our economic survival, guarantee food security, and prevent future geopolitical conflict.

summary.en: Sustainable survival requires building dams, lining canals, and shifting from flood irrigation to drip and sprinkler systems to prevent future water wars.
summary.ur: بقا کے لیے نئے ڈیم بنانا، نہروں کو پختہ کرنا، اور روایتی آبپاشی کے بجائے ڈرپ اور اسپرنکلر جیسے جدید نظام اپنانا وقت کی اہم ترین ضرورت ہے۔

questions.q: What are the major sources of water in Pakistan?
questions.ans: The major water sources in Pakistan include: (1) glacier and snow melt from the mighty Karakoram, Himalayan, and Hindukush mountain ranges, (2) seasonal monsoon and winter rainfall, (3) surface river flows across the three drainage basins, and (4) underground water aquifers tapped via tube-wells and open wells.

questions.q: What are the three surface water drainage basins in Pakistan?
questions.ans:
1. The Indus River Basin: The agricultural lifeblood of the nation, providing 141.67 MAF annually and feeding the world's largest contiguous canal irrigation network.
2. The Closed Basin of the Kharan Desert: Drained by interior mountain streams such as the Pishin Lora and Bado rivers in western Balochistan.
3. The Makran Coastal Basin: Comprising rivers that flow directly south into the Arabian Sea, such as the Malir, Hub, Porali, Kud, Hingol, and Dasht rivers.

questions.q: What were the key terms of the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty between Pakistan and India?
questions.ans: Brokered by the World Bank in 1960, the Indus Waters Treaty divided the six major rivers of the Indus basin between the two nations: India was granted exclusive unrestricted rights over the three eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej), while Pakistan received rights over the three western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab).

questions.q: Why is Pakistan facing a severe threat of water scarcity?
questions.ans: Pakistan is facing severe water scarcity due to: rapid population growth expanding demand, lack of large storage dams resulting in water dumping, massive canal seepage losses, climate change accelerating glacier retreat, wasteful conventional flood irrigation, and unregulated over-pumping of underground aquifers causing water tables to collapse.

questions.q: What economic loss does Pakistan suffer annually due to lack of water reservoirs?
questions.ans: Due to the absence of sufficient storage reservoirs, freshwater with an estimated economic value of $70 billion is discharged unutilized into the Arabian Sea every year. For a nation with foreign exchange reserves often around $20 billion, this represents a staggering and preventable national loss.

questions.q: What water-conserving agricultural techniques are recommended in the lesson?

grammar.rule: An Infinitive is the base form of a verb preceded by 'to' (to read, to care, to call). It can function as a noun (subject, direct object, predicate nominative), an adjective (modifying a noun), or an adverb (modifying a verb or adjective, expressing purpose).
examples: I wanted time to read (Adjective modifying 'time').
To finish will be a relief (Noun functioning as subject).
The wings must create lift to fly (Adverb expressing purpose).

exercises.q: To finish will be a relief. — Identify the infinitive and its function.
exercises.ans: Infinitive: 'To finish' | Function: Noun (grammatical subject of verb 'will be').

exercises.q: Do you agree with the decision to go? — Identify the infinitive and its function.

grammar.rule: A Gerund is a verb ending in -ing that functions as a noun (Subject, Direct Object, Predicate Nominative, or Object of a Preposition). A Gerund Phrase consists of a gerund plus its objects and modifiers.
examples: Swimming in the lake is good exercise (Subject).
Mrs. Noman enjoys playing bridge (Direct Object).
She was praised for volunteering at the hospital (Object of Preposition).

exercises.q: Underline gerund phrase: 'Swimming in the deep pool is Danial's favorite exercise.'
exercises.ans: Gerund phrase: 'Swimming in the deep pool' (Functions as subject of sentence).

exercises.q: Underline gerund phrase: 'Mrs. Noman enjoys playing bridge.'
exercises.ans: Gerund phrase: 'playing bridge' (Functions as direct object of 'enjoys').

exercises.q: Underline gerund phrase: 'I remember promising Sami my old bike.'

exercises.q: Underline gerund phrase: 'Standing during a two-hour train trip is not my idea of fun.'

exercises.q: Underline gerund phrase: 'Do you like sailing on the lake?'

exercises.q: Underline gerund phrase: 'Volunteering at the hospital is just one of Haleema's activities.'

writing.summary: This critical chapter explores Pakistan's escalating water crisis, analyzing its hydrological foundations, structural vulnerabilities, and vital solutions. Pakistan possesses magnificent water sources: snow and glacial runoff from the Himalayas and Karakoram feeding the 141.67 MAF Indus River Basin, alongside the Kharan desert closed basin and Makran coastal streams. Under the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, Pakistan received exclusive rights over the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab). Furthermore, over 1.2 million tube-wells extract groundwater for agriculture. However, unchecked over-extraction has caused water tables to collapse by hundreds of feet in urban and rural centers alike. Due to a tragic deficit of water storage dams, freshwater worth an estimated $70 billion is dumped unutilized into the sea every year. Consequently, per capita water availability has collapsed from 5,000 to below 1,000 cubic meters, thrusting Pakistan into severe water poverty. To avert catastrophic water wars, the chapter urges urgent dam construction, concrete canal lining, and a rapid transition to modern conservation agriculture, particularly drip and sprinkler irrigation technologies.

essay.title: Save a Drop Today and Reap an Ocean Tomorrow: The Urgent Imperative of Water Conservation
essay.text:
Water is the primordial essence of life and the foundational pillar of human civilization. In an agrarian nation like Pakistan, where ninety percent of food production depends on canal and tube-well irrigation, water security is indistinguishable from national sovereignty. Yet, heedless complacency and wasteful habits have brought our nation to the precipice of an unprecedented hydrological catastrophe. The adage 'Save a drop today and reap an ocean tomorrow' is no longer mere poetic rhetoric; it is a blueprint for national survival.

Pakistan's water crisis is primarily a crisis of management rather than absolute scarcity. Endowed with the colossal glaciers of the Karakoram and the vast Indus basin, our country receives over 140 million acre feet of water annually. Yet, because we lack adequate storage reservoirs, over $70 billion worth of life-giving freshwater is allowed to drain wastefully into the Arabian Sea each year. Meanwhile, farmers continue to employ primitive, Victorian-era flood irrigation methods, wasting over half of all diverted canal water through field evaporation and soil runoff. In urban domestic households, running faucets, power-washing driveways, and untreated municipal leaks deplete deep aquifers that took centuries to accumulate.

Averting this impending crisis requires immediate, concerted collective action at both policy and grassroots levels. The state must accelerate the construction of major storage dams, concrete-line canal networks to halt seepage, and subsidize high-efficiency drip and sprinkler irrigation for smallholder farmers. Simultaneously, individual citizens must cultivate an ethics of sacred stewardship toward water: installing low-flow aerators, harvesting monsoon rainwater from rooftops, and recycling graywater for gardens.

In conclusion, every single drop conserved today preserves the agricultural lifeline of tomorrow. If we continue our reckless squandering, our children will inherit an arid wasteland scarred by famine and conflict. By acting prudently today, we secure an abundant, green ocean of prosperity for future generations.

passages.heading: From Ancient Domestication to the Genetic Revolution
passages.text:
Several centuries ago, when human societies transitioned from nomadic foraging to settled farming, they began domesticating wild crops and animals. Early agriculturalists practiced selective breeding, initially unknowingly and later deliberately selecting parent plants and animals that exhibited superior vigor, sweeter fruits, or higher milk yields. Over thousands of years, farmers bred crops with desirable traits, such as increased resistance to blights, larger yields, and greater nutritional value.

While traditional selective breeding successfully molded our staple crops, it was fundamentally constrained: farmers could only crossbreed organisms belonging to the same or closely related biological species, a process that required tedious generations of trial and error. The true turning point in biology occurred with the discovery of the physical nature of heredity and the molecular architecture of the gene.

summary.en: Traditional selective breeding shaped domestic crops for millennia, but was limited to closely related species until molecular genetics unlocked the gene.
summary.ur: ہزاروں سال سے انسان فصلوں اور مویشیوں کی روایتی افزائشِ نسل کر رہا تھا، لیکن جدید جینیات نے جانداروں کے جینز میں براہِ راست تبدیلی کے راستے کھول دیے۔

passages.heading: The Breakthrough of Recombinant DNA Technology
passages.text:
Scientists first discovered in 1946 that genetic material (DNA) could be transferred between distinct organisms. It is now recognized that mechanisms of natural horizontal gene transfer occur in nature on a wide scale—most notably when bacteria exchange antibiotic-resistant plasmids. In the 1970s, molecular biologists developed recombinant DNA technology, enabling them to isolate a specific functional gene from one organism (even an animal, plant, or bacterium) and splice it directly into the genome of a totally unrelated species.

The world's first genetically engineered plant was successfully produced in 1983 using an antibiotic-resistant tobacco plant. In the early 1990s, China became the first country to commercialize transgenic crops by releasing virus-resistant tobacco to farmers. In 1994, the Flavr Savr tomato—genetically modified to delay rotting and maintain vine-ripened flavor—received regulatory approval in the United States, launching modern agricultural biotechnology into global commercial reality.

summary.en: Following the 1946 discovery of DNA transfer, the first transgenic plant was created in 1983, followed by commercialization in China and the US in the 1990s.
summary.ur: 1983 میں پہلی بار جینیاتی طور پر تبدیل شدہ پودا تیار ہوا اور 1990 کی دہائی میں چین اور امریکہ نے تجارتی پیمانے پر ایسی فصلیں متعارف کرائیں۔

passages.heading: Modern Agricultural and Biomedical Triumphs
passages.text:
Today, Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) touch nearly every facet of modern life. In agriculture, major crops like soybeans, maize, canola, and cotton have been genetically equipped with genes from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), enabling plants to produce their own natural insecticidal proteins that kill pests without chemical spraying. Drought-tolerant maize and flood-resistant 'scuba' rice allow harvests to survive extreme weather brought by climate change. Biofortified crops, such as 'Golden Rice' engineered to biosynthesize provitamin A (beta-carotene), prevent childhood blindness and malnutrition across developing nations.

In medicine, GMOs have achieved life-saving triumphs. Prior to genetic engineering, human diabetics relied on scarce insulin extracted from slaughterhouse animal pancreases, which frequently provoked allergic reactions. Today, harmless laboratory strains of Escherichia coli bacteria have been genetically modified with the human insulin gene, mass-producing pure, inexpensive human insulin. Similar transgenic techniques produce human growth hormones, life-saving blood-clotting factors, and recombinant vaccines.

summary.en: GMOs protect crops from pests (Bt cotton/corn), nourish malnourished children (Golden Rice), and produce pure human insulin via engineered bacteria.
summary.ur: بی ٹی کپاس، وٹامن اے والے گولڈن رائس اور شوگر کے مریضوں کے لیے مصنوعی جراثیم سے خالص انسولین کی تیاری جینیاتی ٹیکنالوجی کے بڑے کارنامے ہیں۔

passages.heading: The Bioethics Debate and Ecological Considerations
passages.text:
Despite these immense technological advances, the widespread adoption of GMOs has sparked intense global debate over environmental safety and bioethics. Critics and environmentalists express legitimate concerns regarding unintended ecological consequences: the potential transfer of herbicide-resistance genes to wild weeds through pollen drift, creating intractable 'superweeds'; the unintended harm to non-target beneficial insects; and the consolidation of global food supplies in the hands of a few multinational agribusiness corporations that patent genetically engineered seeds.

Health advocates emphasize rigorous, long-term testing for novel food allergens before commercialization. The scientific consensus, supported by the World Health Organization and the National Academy of Sciences, concludes that currently approved GM foods are as safe to consume as their conventional counterparts. Nevertheless, navigating this powerful technology requires strict biosafety regulations, transparent labeling, and ethical oversight to maximize human benefits while safeguarding the delicate balance of nature.

summary.en: The global debate focuses on ecological risks (superweeds, gene flow), corporate seed monopolies, and allergenicity, demanding strict regulatory oversight.
summary.ur: ماحولیاتی تحفظ اور کارپوریٹ اجارہ داری کے خدشات کے پیش نظر جینیاتی فصلوں کے شفاف تجزیے اور سخت حفاظتی ضوابط کی ضرورت پر زور دیا جاتا ہے۔

questions.q: What was the traditional method of improving crops and animals before modern genetics?
questions.ans: Before the advent of modern molecular genetics, humans practiced selective breeding (artificial selection) over thousands of years. Early farmers observed natural variations in plants and animals and intentionally bred those exhibiting favorable qualities—such as larger seeds, sweeter pulp, faster growth, or gentler temperament. However, this traditional method was slow and limited to interbreeding closely related species.

questions.q: What scientific discovery in 1946 revolutionized the understanding of DNA?
questions.ans: In 1946, scientists discovered that genetic material (DNA) could be transferred between distinct organisms naturally (horizontal gene transfer). This breakthrough proved that genetic boundaries between species in nature are permeable, paving the way for recombinant DNA technology in the 1970s.

questions.q: When and where was the first genetically modified plant produced and commercialized?
questions.ans: The world's first genetically engineered plant—an antibiotic-resistant tobacco variety—was produced in a research laboratory in 1983. In the early 1990s, China became the first nation to commercialize a transgenic crop by distributing virus-resistant tobacco to farmers, followed by the United States commercializing the Flavr Savr tomato in 1994.

questions.q: What are the key benefits of GMOs in agriculture and medicine?
questions.ans: In agriculture, GMOs enhance pest resistance (reducing pesticide spraying in Bt cotton/corn), confer tolerance to droughts and salinity, boost crop yields, and enhance nutrition (such as beta-carotene in Golden Rice). In medicine, genetically modified bacteria mass-produce pure human insulin for diabetics, human growth hormones, clotting factors for hemophiliacs, and novel vaccines.

questions.q: What are the major ethical and environmental concerns surrounding genetically modified organisms?
questions.ans: Major concerns include: (1) ecological disruption caused by gene flow to wild weeds, creating herbicide-tolerant 'superweeds', (2) unintended harm to non-target beneficial insects, (3) potential allergenicity in new GM foods, and (4) corporate consolidation where multinational agricultural firms hold intellectual property patents on seeds, creating dependency among smallholder farmers.

grammar.topic: Types of Sentences by Communicative Purpose (Exercise A)
grammar.rule: Sentences are classified by function into four categories: Declarative (makes a statement, ends with period), Interrogative (asks a question, ends with question mark), Imperative (gives a command, request, or instruction), and Exclamatory (expresses strong emotion, ends with exclamation mark).
examples: Declarative: Peshawar is a very big city.
Interrogative: Where is the school?
Imperative: Shut that door now.
Exclamatory: What a big city Peshawar is!

exercises.q: 'Yikes! I feel terrible that you got into an accident this morning.' — Classify sentence type.
exercises.ans: Exclamatory sentence (expresses strong emotion and starts with interjection).

exercises.q: 'Where is the school?' — Classify sentence type.
exercises.ans: Interrogative sentence (asks a question).

exercises.q: 'The smoke alarm battery should be changed at least once a year.' — Classify sentence type.
exercises.ans: Declarative sentence (makes an informative statement).

exercises.q: 'Shut that door now.' — Classify sentence type.
exercises.ans: Imperative sentence (issues a direct command).

exercises.q: Transform 'He is very generous' into Negative, Interrogative, and Exclamatory.
exercises.ans: Negative: He is not very generous. | Interrogative: Is he very generous? | Exclamatory: How generous he is!

exercises.q: Transform 'Gold is very precious' into Negative, Interrogative, and Exclamatory.
exercises.ans: Negative: Gold is not very precious. | Interrogative: Is gold very precious? | Exclamatory: How precious gold is!

grammar.topic: Sentence Structures: Simple, Compound, and Complex (Exercise B)
grammar.rule: A Simple Sentence has one independent clause. A Compound Sentence joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or a semicolon. A Complex Sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent (subordinate) clause joined by a subordinating conjunction (because, although, if, when, after).
examples: Simple: I like tea.
Compound: I like tea, and he likes coffee.
Complex: When the cake is brown, take it out of the oven.

exercises.q: 'The house was destroyed in the fire, but the whole family was saved.' — Classify structure.
exercises.ans: Compound sentence (two independent clauses joined by coordinating conjunction 'but').

exercises.q: 'Walking through the wood, he saw a fox that was following him.' — Classify structure.
exercises.ans: Complex sentence (independent clause modified by relative clause 'that was following him').

exercises.q: 'She likes to read historical novels in her spare time.' — Classify structure.
exercises.ans: Simple sentence (single independent clause with compound predicate phrase).

exercises.q: 'Although it rained heavily, the match continued.' — Classify structure.
exercises.ans: Complex sentence (dependent clause 'Although it rained heavily' + independent clause).

exercises.q: 'He worked hard, so he achieved first position in the board exam.' — Classify structure.
exercises.ans: Compound sentence (two independent clauses joined by coordinating conjunction 'so').

writing.summary: This informative chapter investigates the revolutionary science and social debates surrounding Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs). For millennia, mankind relied on traditional selective breeding to domesticate agricultural crops and livestock. However, the discovery of horizontal DNA transfer in 1946 and recombinant DNA technology in the 1970s enabled scientists to transfer individual functional genes across species barriers. The world's first genetically engineered plant was created in 1983, followed by commercialization in China and the United States in the 1990s. Today, GMOs solve critical global problems: Bt cotton and corn produce natural pest-fighting proteins, drought-resistant varieties withstand climate shocks, Golden Rice addresses childhood malnutrition, and genetically altered bacteria synthesize pure, life-saving human insulin for diabetics. Alongside these benefits, the chapter evaluates environmental concerns regarding herbicide-tolerant 'superweeds', gene flow, and corporate control of seed patents. The lesson emphasizes that strict biosafety standards, transparent food labeling, and ethical oversight are essential to harnessing biotechnology responsibly.

essay.title: Truth is Stranger than Fiction: The Miracles and Mysteries of Biotechnology
essay.text:
For centuries, science fiction authors captivated readers with fantastical tales of chimera creatures, glowing nocturnal flora, and magical elixirs that cured incurable plagues. Today, the astonishing breakthroughs of molecular genetics have demonstrated that truth is indeed stranger than fiction. In contemporary biotechnology laboratories, scenarios once dismissed as surreal fantasies have become everyday empirical reality.

Consider the remarkable reality of recombinant DNA technology. By isolating the bioluminescent luciferase gene from deep-sea jellyfish and splicing it into the embryos of ordinary zebrafish or tobacco plants, geneticists have created organisms that glow vivid neon green when illuminated with ultraviolet light. Even more astonishing is the medical synthesis of life-saving therapeutics: by inserting the human gene for insulin into microscopic Escherichia coli bacteria, scientists turn single-celled microbes into living biological factories that brew pure human medicine. Similarly, goats have been engineered to secrete spider silk proteins in their milk, producing materials stronger than steel and lighter than carbon fiber.

Yet, this technological power brings moral responsibilities that exceed ancient mythologies. Modifying the genetic blueprint of life challenges our understanding of nature. While biofortified crops like Golden Rice offer salvation from blindness for millions of impoverished children, the possibility of unintended gene transfer and ecological disruption cautions humanity against hubris.

In conclusion, modern biotechnology proves that human ingenuity continually outstrips literary fantasy. The marvels unfolding in molecular biology remind us that truth is not only stranger than fiction, but far more consequential for the future of our civilization.

reading.title: They Have Cut Down the Pines
reading.theme: Environmental Grief, Forest Conservation & Nature's Majesty
reading.author: Mary Lisle (1897–1973)
reading.preReading:
Discuss the title of the poem in groups and predict the content:
1. How does a landscape feel after majestic mature trees are chopped down?
2. Who suffers when a forest is destroyed for timber or fence posts?

passages.heading: Stanza 1: The Vanished Forest and the Mourning Wind
passages.text:
They have cut down the pines where they stood;
The wind will miss them, and the rain,
When its silver blind is down.
They have stripped the bark from the wood
The kind and friendly trees,
Where all day small winds sound,
And all day long the sun
Plays hide and seek with shadows
Till the flying shadows win-to-one
And night is here.

summary.en: The poet laments the felling of friendly pine trees, noting that the wind, rain, sun, and dancing shadows will deeply miss their sheltering presence.
summary.ur: شاعرہ صنوبر کے شفیق درختوں کے کاٹے جانے پر افسوس کرتی ہے جن کے ختم ہونے سے ہوا، بارش اور دھوپ کی چھاؤں ان کے سایے کو ترسیں گے۔

passages.heading: Stanza 2: The Severed Colloquy and Ghostly Trunks
passages.text:
They have cut down the trees and ended
The gentle colloquy of bough and bough.
They are making a fence by the creek,
And have cut the pines for the posts.
Wan in the sunlight, like ghosts,
The naked trunks lie.
A bird will seek in vain
A bough where she nested;
In vain, they have cut down the pines.

summary.en: Cut down merely to build mundane fence posts, the pale stripped trunks lie like ghosts while mother birds search in vain for their lost nests.
summary.ur: نہر کے کنارے باڑ بنانے کے لیے صنوبر کو کاٹ دیا گیا؛ اب تنے بھوتوں کی طرح پڑے ہیں اور پرندے اپنے گھونسلوں کے لیے شاخوں کو بے سود تلاش کرتے ہیں۔

vocabulary.title: Poetic Figurative Analysis & Connotative Diction
vocabulary.instruction: Analyze the figurative language and emotional resonance of poetic metaphors.

items.definition: A visual metaphor comparing sheets of falling monsoon rain to a drawn silver window shade.
items.example: When the rain's silver blind descends, the landscape is shrouded in gentle mist.

items.definition: A mournful simile comparing debarked, pale pine logs to haunting apparitions of the dead.
items.example: Wan in the sunlight, like ghosts, the naked trunks lie upon the barren dirt.

items.definition: Trampled, walked over heavily, or crushed beneath human footsteps.
items.example: The delicate forest wildflowers were trodden under the boots of woodcutters.

questions.q: Why were the pines cut down?
questions.ans: The majestic pines were cut down for an entirely mundane, utilitarian purpose: human farmers chopped them down to strip their bark and use the wooden trunks as fence posts along a nearby creek.

questions.q: Beside the poet, who will badly miss the company of the pines?
questions.ans: The elements of nature will mourn the pines: the wind that whistled softly through their needles, the rain that fell upon their canopy like a silver blind, the sun that played hide-and-seek with their shifting shadows, and the mother birds who will search in vain for the leafy branches where they once built their nests.

questions.q: Pick out the lines having personification.
questions.ans:
The poem abounds with poignant examples of personification:
1. 'The wind will miss them' (attributing emotional longing and grief to the wind).
2. 'The kind and friendly trees' (attributing human warmth and benevolence to trees).
3. 'All day long the sun plays hide and seek with shadows' (attributing human games to the sun and shadows).
4. 'The gentle colloquy of bough and bough' (portraying branches as intimate friends engaged in gentle conversation).

questions.q: How has the cutting down of the trees affected nature?
questions.ans: The felling of the pines has disrupted the entire ecological harmony of the landscape. The lively conversation of the forest canopy is permanently silenced, the interplay of light and shade is erased, the soil is exposed to erosion, and homeless songbirds flutter in distress, unable to find the vanished boughs where they raised their fledglings.

questions.q: What picture of the rain does the writer create?
questions.ans: The poet creates a delicate, visual picture of the rain through the metaphor 'When its silver blind is down'. She imagines sheets of falling rain as a shimmering silver window shade gently pulled down over the forest, creating an atmosphere of peaceful seclusion and natural intimacy.

questions.q: Explain the simile 'Wan in the sunlight, like ghosts, / The naked trunks lie'.
questions.ans: This powerful simile compares the debarked, pale pine logs lying on the ground to bloodless ghosts. Stripped of their vibrant green needles and protective bark, the lifeless white trunks resemble the haunting, pale corpses of living giants that were senselessly slaughtered for fence posts.

questions.q: What is the tone of the poem?
questions.ans: The tone of 'They Have Cut Down the Pines' is elegiac, mournful, tender, and deeply sorrowful. It expresses profound ecological grief and quiet indignation against mankind's callous destruction of living natural beauty.

mcqs.q: "And all day long the sun plays hide and seek with shadows." In these lines the poet has used the literary device of:
mcqs.exp: Attributing the human childhood game of 'hide and seek' to the sun and shadows is an example of personification.

mcqs.q: By using the contextual clue, the word closest in meaning to 'trodden' is:
mcqs.exp: 'Trodden' refers to being stepped on heavily, crushed, or trampled underfoot.

mcqs.q: "The gentle colloquy of bough and bough." In this line the poet uses the literary device of:
mcqs.exp: Describing tree branches as holding a 'gentle colloquy' (conversation) personifies them with human speech.

mcqs.q: "When its silver blind is down." In this line the phrase 'silver blind' is used as a:
mcqs.exp: 'Silver blind' is a direct metaphor equating the vertical curtain of falling rain to a drawn window blind.

mcqs.q: The overall tone of the poem 'They Have Cut Down the Pines' is:
mcqs.exp: The poem is an elegy expressing poignant sadness and sorrow over the destruction of the forest.

grammar.rule: The First Conditional expresses real or highly probable conditions in the present or future. Structure: If + Simple Present, ... will + base verb (or will + base verb ... if + Simple Present).
examples: If you wash the dishes, I will cook dinner.
If my dad has time next week, we will paint my room.
You will learn a lot if you visit the exhibition.

grammar.rule: The Second Conditional expresses hypothetical, imaginary, or improbable conditions in the present or future. Structure: If + Simple Past, ... would + base verb (Note: 'were' is conventionally used for all subjects with the verb 'to be').
examples: If I had more time, I would learn to play the guitar.
If she studied harder, she would get better marks.
If we were not afraid, we would explore the cave.

writing.summary: In 'They Have Cut Down the Pines', Australian poet Mary Lisle expresses intense sorrow over the senseless destruction of living trees for trivial human utility. The poem mourns the disappearance of a grove of mature pines, which the poet personifies as kind, benevolent companions. She laments that nature itself misses them: the wind that once whispered through their boughs, the rain that fell like a silver blind upon their needles, and the sun that played games of hide-and-seek with their dancing shadows. The felling of the pines has brought an end to the gentle, whispering colloquy between rustling branches. Now, cut down merely to serve as wooden fence posts along a creek, the stripped trunks lie pale and wan in the sun like ghostly corpses. The poem reaches an agonizing climax as a mother bird returns to the cleared clearing, searching in vain for the protective branch where she had lovingly nested.

essay.title: The Vital Importance of Planting Trees and Forest Conservation
essay.text:
Trees are the living lungs of planet Earth and the indispensable guardians of our biosphere. From producing the oxygen every creature breathes to stabilizing vulnerable soils, trees perform ecological functions that modern technology cannot replicate. Yet, rapid urbanization and industrial greed have caused catastrophic deforestation worldwide, turning Mary Lisle's poetic grief into a daily reality across continents.

The ecological consequences of logging are devastating. Trees absorb billions of tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, mitigating greenhouse gas accumulation and global warming. When forests are razed, this stored carbon is released into the atmosphere while destroying biodiversity habitats. Deforestation strips mountain hillsides of root anchors, causing catastrophic topsoil erosion, landslides, and silting up downstream water reservoirs. In urban environments, mature tree canopies cool temperatures by up to eight degrees Celsius, filtering dangerous airborne particulate matter and smog.

Tree plantation is therefore not merely an aesthetic civic project; it is an existential necessity. Pakistan, with less than five percent forest cover, is extraordinarily vulnerable to floods and droughts. Initiatives like the Billion Tree Tsunami demonstrate that large-scale afforestation can restore degraded watersheds and revive rural economies. Every citizen must actively plant native trees in gardens, schools, and roadsides, protecting our green heritage so future generations may hear the gentle colloquy of living boughs.

passages.heading: Early Life, Conversion, and Dedication to Islam
passages.text:
The Rasool of Islam (PBUH) had left behind a band of selfless people who dedicated themselves with singleness of purpose to the service of the new religion. One of these towering figures was Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA), who was great both in war and in peace. Few persons in the history of mankind have displayed better qualities of head and heart than Hazrat Umar (RA).

Hazrat Umar (RA) was born in Makkah in 40 B.H. (before Hijra). His ancestral lineage joined that of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) in the eighth generation. He was one of the literate few in Makkah when Muhammad (PBUH) was commissioned as the Rasool of Allah. He entered the fold of Islam at the age of 27. His conversion proved so momentous that Muslims, who previously offered prayers in secret for fear of persecution, prayed openly at the Holy Ka'aba for the very first time. For his unyielding discernment between truth and falsehood, the Holy Prophet (PBUH) bestowed upon him the revered title of 'Al-Farooq' (The One who Distinguishes Truth from Falsehood).

summary.en: Born in Makkah and accepting Islam at age 27, Hazrat Umar's conversion enabled Muslims to worship openly at the Ka'aba, earning him the title 'Al-Farooq'.
summary.ur: حضرت عمرؓ نے 27 سال کی عمر میں اسلام قبول کیا جس کے بعد مسلمانوں نے کعبہ میں اعلانیہ نماز ادا کی اور آپ کو 'فاروق' کا لقب عطا ہوا۔

passages.heading: Public Accountability and Custodianship of the Bait-ul-Mal
passages.text:
During his ten-year caliphate, Hazrat Umar (RA) established a vast, disciplined empire spanning Persia, the Levant, and Egypt, yet he led a life of utter simplicity. Everyone had easy, unrestricted access to Hazrat Umar (RA), and every citizen was entirely free to question his decisions and actions.

Once he stated publicly from the pulpit: 'I have no more authority over the Bait-ul-Mal (public treasury) than a custodian has over the property of an orphan. If I had been well-to-do, I would not accept any honorarium. If not, I draw merely a little to meet the ordinary necessities of life. Brothers! I am your servant, and you should neither unnecessarily hoard nor waste. I must work for the welfare and prosperity of our people.'

Once an ordinary citizen stood up in a public meeting and shouted boldly: 'O Umar, fear Allah!' The congregation wanted to silence the man for addressing the Caliph disrespectfully, but Hazrat Umar (RA) restrained them, saying: 'Let him speak! If such frankness is not exhibited by the people, they are of no good; and if we do not listen to them, we are of no good.'

summary.en: Hazrat Umar treated the public treasury like an orphan's trust, drew only a basic stipend, and welcomed public criticism with humility.
summary.ur: حضرت عمرؓ نے بیت المال کو یتیم کے مال کی طرح امانت سمجھا، انتہائی سادہ زندگی گزاری اور عام شہریوں کو برملا محاسبے کی اجازت دی۔

passages.heading: Night Patrols and the Weeping Mother
passages.text:
Hazrat Umar (RA) was deeply committed to the welfare of the disadvantaged. He frequently patrolled the streets of Madina during the dark hours of the night to see for himself whether anyone was in distress. On one bitterly cold night, accompanied by his servant Aslam, he observed a distant fire in the desert outskirts. Approaching the tent, he discovered a poor widow surrounded by weeping children. A pot filled with water sat upon the burning fire.

Hazrat Umar (RA) greeted the woman and inquired why the children were crying so bitterly. The mother explained that they were weeping from unbearable hunger, and that she had placed stones in the boiling water merely to pretend that food was cooking until the exhausted children fell asleep from exhaustion. She added in distress: 'Allah will judge between us and Umar on the Day of Judgment, for he neglects us!'

Hearing these words, tears welled up in Hazrat Umar's eyes. Without revealing his identity, he hurried back to the state warehouse in Madina. He packed a large sack with flour, dates, fat, and clothing. When his servant offered to carry the burden, Hazrat Umar (RA) replied sternly: 'Will you carry my burden of sins on the Day of Judgment?' He hoisted the heavy sack upon his own back and walked back to the woman's tent. There, he personally kneaded the dough, blew upon the fire until the hearth glowed, cooked a nourishing meal, and fed the starving children until they laughed with joy. Before departing, he arranged a permanent state dole (pension) for the family from the Bait-ul-Mal.

summary.en: During a night patrol, Hazrat Umar discovered a starving family, carried flour on his own back, cooked for the children, and granted them a permanent state pension.
summary.ur: رات کے گشت کے دوران بھوکے بچوں کو دیکھ کر آپؓ نے غلہ خود اپنی پیٹھ پر اٹھایا، اپنے ہاتھوں سے کھانا پکایا اور خاندان کے لیے مستقل وظیفہ مقرر کیا۔

passages.heading: Uncompromising Integrity and the Prophet's Praise
passages.text:
Honesty and uncompromising integrity were the highest virtues in the character of the Second Caliph. Once, during a severe illness, his physician prescribed honey as medicine. Tons of honey were stored in the public Bait-ul-Mal, yet Hazrat Umar (RA) refused to take a single drop until he had ascended the pulpit of the Prophet's Mosque and sought formal permission from the assembled citizens.

On another occasion, his wife, Umme Kulsum, sent a few modest bottles of rose perfume as a personal gift to the Empress of the Byzantine Roman Empire. The Empress graciously returned the bottles filled with precious jewels and pearls. When Hazrat Umar (RA) learned of the arrival of the gems, he immediately deposited every single jewel into the Bait-ul-Mal, explaining that the diplomatic courtesy had been accorded to her as the wife of the Caliph of Muslims, and therefore the treasure belonged to the Muslim public.

Hazrat Umar's extraordinary spiritual stature, unmatched justice, and moral greatness were celebrated by the Holy Prophet (PBUH), who stated in an authentic Hadith:

'If Allah had wished that there should have been another Nabi after me, he would have been Umar.' (Tirmidhi).

summary.en: Hazrat Umar refused public honey for his illness without public permission, deposited diplomatic jewels into the treasury, and earned supreme prophetic praise.
summary.ur: بیماری میں شہد کے لیے عوام سے اجازت لی، بیوی کو ملنے والے تحائف بیت المال میں جمع کروائے اور نبی کریم ﷺ نے فرمایا کہ میرے بعد نبی ہوتا تو عمر ہوتا۔

questions.q: Why did Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA) deposit the jewels, given by the Empress of Rome to Hazrat Umar's wife, in the Bait-ul-Mal?
questions.ans: Hazrat Umar (RA) deposited the precious jewels into the Bait-ul-Mal because he believed that the Roman Empress had presented the lavish gift solely due to Umme Kulsum's position as the wife of the Caliph of the Islamic state. Consequently, the gifts were public assets resulting from state diplomacy, belonging rightfully to the entire Muslim community rather than to his private family.

questions.q: Hazrat Umar (RA) was one of those people who served the new religion with singleness of purpose. Describe his services to Islam in the context of this statement.
questions.ans: Hazrat Umar (RA) demonstrated supreme dedication to Islam: his conversion brought courage to early Muslims to pray openly at the Ka'aba; he stood by the Holy Prophet (PBUH) in every battle; during his caliphate, he established an egalitarian welfare state with independent courts of justice, established public registries, constructed roadways and canals, organized regular armies, and expanded the frontiers of Islam with unmatched administrative brilliance.

questions.q: Humility and simplicity were the hallmarks of Hazrat Umar's rule. Support this view by giving evidence from the given text.
questions.ans:
Textual evidence illustrates his sublime humility:
1. He lived on coarse barley flour and vinegar, wearing garments bearing up to twelve patches.
2. He considered his authority over the Bait-ul-Mal equivalent only to an orphan's custodian.
3. He welcomed public accountability and refused to allow anyone to silence critics who told him to fear Allah.
4. He personally carried heavy sacks of grain on his own back at night to feed impoverished citizens.

questions.q: Why did Hazrat Umar not eat honey from the public treasury during his illness?
questions.ans: Hazrat Umar (RA) refused to consume honey from the Bait-ul-Mal because the public treasury belonged to all Muslims, and he held himself to the highest standard of moral accountability. He would not take a single drop of public medicine until he personally ascended the pulpit in the mosque and sought the unanimous consent and permission of the general Muslim assembly.

questions.q: Describe the incident of feeding the hungry children of the old woman by Hazrat Umar (RA).
questions.ans: While patrolling at night, Hazrat Umar found a poor widow whose weeping children were being lulled to sleep by boiling pebbles in a pot of water. Devastated by their suffering, Hazrat Umar rushed to the state storehouse, refused to let his servant carry the flour—asking who would carry his sins on Judgment Day—and carried the food on his own back to the tent. He personally cooked the meal, fed the starving children, and allocated an ongoing state pension for the family.

grammar.topic: Active and Passive Voice (Exercises A & B)
grammar.rule: In the Active Voice, the subject performs the action (Subject + Verb + Object). In the Passive Voice, the subject receives the action (Object + form of 'to be' + Past Participle + by Agent). Use the passive voice when the agent is unknown, obvious, or less important than the recipient.
examples: Active: Boys like to play soccer.
Passive: Cricket is played in Australia.
Passive: The report must be completed by next Friday.

exercises.q: 'Boys like to play soccer.' — Active or Passive?
exercises.ans: Active voice (subject 'Boys' performs the action 'like to play').

exercises.q: 'This room has been painted blue.' — Active or Passive?
exercises.ans: Passive voice (subject 'This room' receives the action; agent omitted).

exercises.q: 'Cricket is played in Australia.' — Active or Passive?
exercises.ans: Passive voice (verb form 'is played').

exercises.q: 'I am given a book.' — Active or Passive?
exercises.ans: Passive voice (verb form 'am given').

exercises.q: 'We have lost our keys.' — Active or Passive?
exercises.ans: Active voice (subject 'We' performs the action 'have lost').

exercises.q: 'Rewrite in Active Voice: We are taught grammar by Mrs. Sikandar.'
exercises.ans: Mrs. Sikandar teaches us grammar.

exercises.q: 'Rewrite in Active Voice: He was praised by the teacher.'
exercises.ans: The teacher praised him.

exercises.q: 'Rewrite in Active Voice: The injured were taken to the hospital by the firemen.'
exercises.ans: The firemen took the injured to the hospital.

exercises.q: 'Rewrite in Active Voice: The town was destroyed by an earthquake.'
exercises.ans: An earthquake destroyed the town.

writing.summary: This biographical chapter highlights the extraordinary life, exemplary governance, and moral integrity of Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA), the Second Caliph of Islam. Born in Makkah and embracing Islam at age 27, his conversion emboldened early Muslims to pray openly at the Ka'aba. During his decade-long caliphate, he established an empire spanning three continents, yet remained the ultimate model of simplicity, justice, and accountability. He regarded his authority over the public treasury (Bait-ul-Mal) merely as an orphan's trust, living on plain barley bread and wearing patched robes. He actively welcomed public criticism, stating that leaders who ignore the voices of their citizens are of no good. The lesson details his legendary night patrols, where he personally carried a heavy sack of flour on his own back to cook a meal for starving children whose mother was boiling stones in water. His honesty was absolute: he refused to take medicine honey from the state treasury without the public's consent, and deposited diplomatic jewels gifted to his wife into the public coffer. His sublime justice earned him the title 'Al-Farooq' and the highest prophetic praise.

essay.title: Hazrat Umar (RA): The Ruler as a Humble Public Servant
essay.text:
Throughout human history, political power has often corrupted leaders, transforming rulers into despots who exploit state wealth for personal vanity. In sharp contrast, Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA), the Second Caliph of Islam, established an administrative philosophy that redefined leadership as selfless servitude rather than sovereign privilege. By embodying the principle that a leader is the humble servant of his people, Hazrat Umar created the foundational blueprint for an incorruptible welfare state.

Hazrat Umar's governance was anchored in radical accountability and transparent stewardship. Although he commanded the mighty resources of an empire that eclipsed both the Roman and Persian domains, he refused all royal trappings. He dressed in garments bearing twelve patches, slept on plain palm-fiber mats under the open sky, and regarded the public treasury with the solemn reverence of a trustee guarding an orphan's inheritance. When citizens openly questioned his expenditures in public assemblies, he did not invoke royal immunity; rather, he celebrated their vigilance, asserting that a society lacking the courage to hold rulers accountable loses its moral purpose.

His compassion for the marginalized remains unmatched in the annals of governance. Rather than relying on sanitized intelligence reports, Hazrat Umar patrolled the dark streets of Madina himself to witness the hardships of ordinary citizens. His nocturnal journey to the tent of the impoverished widow—where he carried heavy grain sacks upon his own back, blew the hearth fires with his own breath, and fed weeping children—demonstrates that true greatness lies in personal empathy.

In conclusion, Hazrat Umar's legacy proves that righteous leadership is measured not by monuments or personal wealth, but by justice, humility, and the welfare of the poorest citizens. In an era troubled by political cynicism, his life remains an immortal beacon of ethical governance.

passages.heading: The Charming but Ineffectual Aristocrat
passages.text: Hughie Erskine was a wonderfully handsome, soft-hearted, and well-mannered young gentleman with brown curly hair, clear grey eyes, and a graceful profile. He was universally popular in London society because of his agreeable demeanor, generous heart, and unaffected simplicity. Intellectually, however, he was not of much importance: he had never said a brilliant or even an unkind thing in his life. Moreover, he was notoriously ineffectual in business. He had once been a tea merchant, but a sudden slump in the tea trade wiped out his capital. He then tried selling dry sherry, but that did not answer. Next, he attempted stock exchange speculation, but that ended in a fiasco. Ultimately, he became a charming young man with no profession, living upon an allowance of two hundred pounds a year made to him by an old aunt.

summary.en: Hughie Erskine is handsome, kind, and universally liked, but financially unsuccessful after failing in multiple commercial ventures.
summary.ur: ہیوگی ارسکن ایک خوش اخلاق، خوبصورت اور رحم دل نوجوان تھا مگر کاروبار میں مسلسل ناکام رہا اور قلیل وظیفے پر گزارا کرتا تھا۔

passages.heading: Love and the Colonel's Stern Ultimatum
passages.text: To make his predicament complete, Hughie was passionately in love with Laura Merton, the daughter of a retired Colonel. Laura adored him, and Hughie was ready to lay down his life for her; they were the handsomest couple in London, but neither had a penny. The Colonel was very fond of Hughie, but would not hear of any formal engagement. 'Come to me, my boy, when you have ten thousand pounds of your own,' the old warrior used to declare sternly, 'and we will see about it.' Hughie looked very glum on those days, and would often wander gloomily to the studio of his friend Alan Trevor to drown his sorrows.

summary.en: Hughie is in love with Laura Merton, but her father forbids marriage until Hughie acquires £10,000 of his own.
summary.ur: ہیوگی لورا مرٹن سے محبت کرتا تھا مگر اس کے والد ریٹائرڈ کرنل نے شرط رکھی کہ جب تک وہ 10,000 پاؤنڈ نہ لائے، شادی نہیں ہو سکتی۔

passages.heading: The Studio Visit and the Wretched Beggar Model
passages.text:
Alan Trevor was an artistic painter of rare genius, whose masterful pictures were eagerly sought after by art collectors. When Hughie came into Trevor's studio one morning, he found the artist putting the finishing touches to a remarkable life-sized canvas of a beggar-man. The beggar model was standing upon a raised platform in a corner of the room: a wizened, stooping old man of eighty, with wrinkled face like parchment, sad brown eyes, a battered tattered brown coat, and torn boots. Over his shoulder hung a coarse ragged cloak, and with one gnarled hand he leaned upon a rough stick, while with the other he held out a battered hat for alms.

'What an amazing model!' whispered Hughie, taking a seat on a divan. 'How miserable he looks! But I suppose, to you painters, his face is his fortune?'
'Certainly,' replied Trevor cheerfully. 'You don't want a beggar to look happy, do you?'
'How much does a model get for sitting?' asked Hughie.
'A shilling an hour,' answered Trevor.
'And how much do you get for the picture, Alan?'
'Oh, for this canvas I get two thousand guineas!'
'Well, I think the model should have a percentage,' cried Hughie, laughing; 'they work quite as hard as you do.'

summary.en: At Alan Trevor's studio, Hughie observes a wretched, wrinkled old beggar model posing for a portrait worth 2,000 guineas.
summary.ur: ایلن ٹریور کے اسٹوڈیو میں ایک جھریوں والا بوڑھا بھکاری ماڈل کے طور پر کھڑا تھا جسے دیکھ کر ہیوگی کو دلی ہمدردی محسوس ہوئی۔

passages.heading: A Sovereign of True Compassion
passages.text:
Presently, Trevor's servant came in to inform him that the frame-maker wished to speak with him in the hallway. When Trevor stepped out, the old beggar took advantage of the artist's absence to rest for a moment on a wooden bench behind him. He looked so lonely, forlorn, and wretched that Hughie could not help feeling deep pity for him. He reached into his pockets to see what money he had. All he could find was a single gold sovereign and some small copper coins.

'The poor old fellow needs it more than I do,' thought Hughie. 'It means having no carriage rides for a fortnight, but he must have it.' He walked quietly across the studio and slipped the golden sovereign into the beggar's trembling palm. The old man started in surprise, his wrinkled eyes looked up in astonishment, and a faint smile flitted across his withered lips. 'Thank you, sir,' he muttered in a quavering voice; 'thank you.' Then Trevor returned, and Hughie took his leave, blushing slightly at what he had done.

summary.en: Touched by pity, Hughie gives his last gold sovereign to the beggar, who smiles with quiet gratitude.
summary.ur: ہیوگی نے ترس کھا کر اپنی جیب کا آخری سونے کا سکہ (سوورن) بوڑھے کے ہاتھ پر رکھ دیا، جس پر اس نے حیرت اور مسکراہٹ سے شکریہ ادا کیا۔

passages.heading: The Astonishing Revelation at the Palette Club
passages.text:
That night at eleven o'clock, Hughie strolled into the Palette Club and found Alan Trevor enjoying a cup of black coffee in the smoking-room. 'Well, Alan, did you get the picture finished?' asked Hughie.

'Finished and framed, my boy!' answered Trevor. 'And, by the bye, you made a complete conquest! That old model you saw kept asking all about you—who you were, where you lived, what your income was, and what your prospects were.'
'My dear Alan,' cried Hughie, 'I shall probably find him waiting on my doorstep! But the poor old chap looked so wretched that I gave him a sovereign.'

'Gave him a sovereign!' shouted Trevor, bursting into a roar of laughter that echoed through the club. 'My dear boy, you gave a sovereign to Baron Hausberg, one of the richest men in Europe! He owns all the railways in the Balkans, has an empire in Paris, and bought my painting with cash!'

Hughie sank into an armchair in horror and dismay. 'Baron Hausberg!' he gasped. 'Good heavens! What will he think of me?'
'He was vastly interested in your generosity,' laughed Trevor. 'He knows all about Laura, all about the stern Colonel, and all about your ten thousand pounds!'

summary.en: Trevor reveals that the beggar model was actually Baron Hausberg, one of Europe's wealthiest financiers, leaving Hughie horrified.
summary.ur: رات کو ٹریور نے انکشاف کیا کہ وہ بھکاری دراصل یورپ کا امیر ترین شخص 'بیرن ہاؤس برگ' تھا، جس پر ہیوگی شرمندگی سے پریشان ہو گیا۔

passages.heading: The Wedding Gift of the Model Millionaire
passages.text:
The next morning, while Hughie was breakfasting in deep dejection, his servant brought him a visiting card bearing the name 'Monsieur Gustave Naudin, on behalf of Baron Hausberg.' An elderly gentleman with gold spectacles and gray hair entered the room.

'I have come from Baron Hausberg,' the visitor said with formal courtesy. 'I believe you had an encounter with him yesterday at Mr. Trevor's studio.'
'I beg of you, sir,' stammered Hughie, 'to convey my sincere apologies to the Baron. I had no idea who he was!'

'The Baron commissioned me to deliver this letter to you personally,' smiled the visitor, placing a sealed envelope into Hughie's hand. On the outside was inscribed: 'A wedding present to Hughie Erskine and Laura Merton, from an old beggar.' When Hughie opened the envelope, there lay inside a certified cheque for ten thousand pounds!

When Hughie and Laura were married, Alan Trevor was the best man, and Baron Hausberg made a magnificent speech at the wedding breakfast. 'Millionaire models,' remarked Alan Trevor with a smile, 'are rare enough; but, by Jove, model millionaires are rarer still!'

summary.en: Baron Hausberg sends Hughie an envelope containing a £10,000 cheque as a wedding gift, fulfilling the Colonel's condition.
summary.ur: اگلی صبح بیرن نے ہیوگی کو شادی کے تحفے کے طور پر 10,000 پاؤنڈ کا چیک بھیج دیا، جس سے اس کی لورا سے دھوم دھام سے شادی ہو گئی۔
