subtopics.name: Axial Skeleton (80 Bones)
subtopics.desc: 1. Skull (28 bones): Cranium (8 flat bones enclosing the brain) and Facial bones (14 bones, only the mandible/lower jaw is movable), plus 6 auditory ossicles. 2. Vertebral Column (33 vertebrae): 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (chest), 5 lumbar (lower back), 5 sacral (fused into sacrum), and 4 coccygeal (fused into coccyx/tailbone). 3. Rib Cage (25 bones): 12 pairs of ribs (7 pairs of true ribs attaching directly to sternum, 3 pairs of false ribs, and 2 pairs of floating ribs) and 1 Sternum (breastbone).
subtopics.sciNote: The first cervical vertebra is the Atlas, which articulates with the skull for nodding, and the second is the Axis, which allows head rotation.
subtopics.sq: Differentiate between true ribs, false ribs, and floating ribs.

mcq.q: How many pairs of ribs are called 'floating ribs' in the human rib cage?

subtopics.name: Appendicular Skeleton (126 Bones)
subtopics.desc: 1. Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs (64 bones): Each side has Clavicle (collarbone) and Scapula (shoulder blade), leading to Humerus (arm), Radius and Ulna (forearm), 8 Carpals (wrist), 5 Metacarpals (palm), and 14 Phalanges (fingers). 2. Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs (62 bones): Pelvis composed of two coxal bones (ilium, ischium, pubis fused), articulating with Femur (thigh, longest and strongest bone), Patella (kneecap), Tibia and Fibula (shank), 7 Tarsals (ankle), 5 Metatarsals (sole), and 14 Phalanges (toes).
subtopics.sciNote: The femur withstands pressures up to 1,800 to 2,500 pounds per square inch during running and jumping.
subtopics.sq: Name the bones comprising the human pectoral girdle and upper limb.

summary.en: Bone and cartilage are specialized connective tissues. Bone is hard, rigid, and calcified, containing osteocytes in Haversian systems. Cartilage is softer, flexible, and avascular, containing chondrocytes embedded in a collagen matrix. Cartilage exists as Hyaline, Elastic, and Fibrocartilage.
summary.ur: ہڈی اور کرکری ہڈی (کارٹیلیج) جاندار کنیکٹیو ٹشوز ہیں۔ ہڈی کیلشیم اور فاسفیٹ کی وجہ سے سخت ہوتی ہے جبکہ کارٹیلیج لچکدار اور خون کی نالیوں سے خالی ہوتی ہے۔
summary.ps: هډوکی سخت او کلک جوړښت لري پداسې حال کې چې غضروف (کارټیلیج) نرم او انعطاف منونکی دی.

subtopics.name: Bone Histology: Compact and Spongy Bone
subtopics.desc: Outer layer is dense Compact Bone, structured into cylindrical structural units called Osteons (Haversian systems) containing concentric lamellae, osteocytes within lacunae, and a central Haversian canal for blood vessels and nerves. Inner layer is Spongy (Cancellous) Bone, consisting of an open latticework of trabeculae filled with red bone marrow where red and white blood cells are manufactured (hematopoiesis).
subtopics.sciNote: Bone is living tissue that undergoes continuous remodeling throughout life by bone-forming osteoblasts and bone-resorbing osteoclasts.
subtopics.sq: Differentiate between compact bone and spongy bone.

mcq.q: Red bone marrow responsible for blood cell production is located inside:

subtopics.name: Cartilage Types and Distribution
subtopics.desc: Cartilage cells (chondrocytes) reside in lacunae within an extracellular matrix rich in collagen fibers and proteoglycans. Avascular (nutrients diffuse from surrounding perichondrium). Three types: 1. Hyaline Cartilage: Glassy, translucent with fine collagen; found at articulating ends of long bones, nose, trachea, larynx, bronchi. 2. Elastic Cartilage: Rich in elastic fibers; found in pinna of external ear and epiglottis. 3. Fibrocartilage: Tough with dense collagen bundles; found in intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis.
subtopics.sciNote: Because cartilage lacks blood vessels, damaged cartilage heals very slowly compared to bone.
subtopics.sq: Identify the locations of hyaline, elastic, and fibrocartilage in the human body.

summary.en: A joint is the site of junction between two or more bones. Joints are classified structurally and functionally into: Immovable (Fibrous) joints, Slightly movable (Cartilaginous) joints, and Freely movable (Synovial) joints such as Hinge and Ball-and-Socket joints.
summary.ur: جوڑ وہ مقام ہے جہاں دو یا دو سے زیادہ ہڈیاں آپس میں ملتی ہیں۔ ان کی تین بنیادی اقسام ہیں: غیر متحرک جوڑ (کھوپڑی کے سیوچرز)، جزوی متحرک جوڑ اور مکمل متحرک (سائنوویل) جوڑ جیسے قبضہ نما اور گیند اور پیالہ نما جوڑ۔

subtopics.name: Classification of Joints
subtopics.desc: 1. Immovable (Fibrous) Joints: Bones held tightly together by dense fibrous connective tissue sutures allowing no movement (e.g., skull bones). 2. Slightly Movable (Cartilaginous) Joints: Bones separated by pads of fibrocartilage allowing restricted movement (e.g., joints between adjacent vertebrae, pubic symphysis). 3. Freely Movable (Synovial) Joints: Separated by a fluid-filled synovial cavity allowing wide range of movement. Examples: Hinge joints (elbow, knee - movement in one plane) and Ball-and-Socket joints (shoulder, hip - movement in all three planes).
subtopics.sciNote: A synovial joint is enclosed by a fibrous articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane that secretes viscous synovial fluid to lubricate the joint and reduce friction.
subtopics.sq: Compare a hinge joint with a ball-and-socket joint with examples.

summary.en: Skeletal muscles contract to pull bones; they cannot push. Therefore, muscles work in antagonistic pairs where one contracts (flexor) to bend the joint while the other relaxes, and the other contracts (extensor) to straighten it. Tendons connect muscle to bone, while ligaments connect bone to bone at joints.
summary.ur: عضلات ہڈیوں کو کھینچ کر حرکت پیدا کرتے ہیں۔ عضلات جوڑوں پر مخالفانہ (اینٹاگونیسٹک) جوڑوں کی صورت میں کام کرتے ہیں جیسے بائیسپس (فلیکسر) اور ٹرائی سیپس (ایکسٹینسر)۔ ٹینڈنز عضلات کو ہڈی سے جوڑتے ہیں جبکہ لگامنٹس ہڈی کو ہڈی سے جوڑتے ہیں۔

subtopics.name: Antagonistic Muscles: Biceps and Triceps
subtopics.desc: The biceps brachii is on the anterior upper arm and acts as a Flexor: when it contracts, it pulls the radius and ulna upward, bending the elbow joint, while the triceps relaxes. The triceps brachii is on the posterior upper arm and acts as an Extensor: when it contracts, it pulls the ulna downward, straightening the elbow joint, while the biceps relaxes.
subtopics.sciNote: Tendons are tough, non-elastic fibrous cords with high tensile strength that transmit muscular pulling force directly to bone. Ligaments are tough, elastic bands that hold bones together at joints, preventing dislocation.
subtopics.sq: Differentiate between tendons and ligaments.

summary.en: Common skeletal disorders include Osteoporosis (reduction in bone mineral density leading to fragile, porous bones susceptible to fractures) and Arthritis (inflammation of joints, including Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid arthritis, and Gout).

subtopics.name: Osteoporosis and Types of Arthritis
subtopics.desc: 1. Osteoporosis: Age-related loss of bone mass and calcium, making bones brittle and prone to spontaneous fractures (hips, wrists, vertebrae). Highly prevalent in postmenopausal women due to decreased estrogen levels, sedentary lifestyle, and calcium/vitamin D deficiency. 2. Arthritis: Joint inflammation causing pain, swelling, and stiffness. - Osteoarthritis: Degeneration of articular cartilage due to wear and tear. - Rheumatoid Arthritis: Autoimmune disorder where immune cells attack the synovial membrane. - Gout: Deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints (especially big toe) due to hyperuricemia.
subtopics.sciNote: Regular weight-bearing exercise and adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D promote osteoblast activity, preventing osteoporosis.
subtopics.sq: What is osteoporosis and why are postmenopausal women more prone to it?

mcqs.q: The total number of bones in the human axial skeleton is:
mcqs.expl: The axial skeleton comprises 80 bones: skull (28), vertebral column (26/33), ribs (24), and sternum (1).

mcqs.q: The longest, heaviest, and strongest bone in the human body is the:
mcqs.expl: The femur (thigh bone) is the largest and strongest bone in the human skeleton.

mcqs.q: A joint that allows movement in only one single plane is a:
mcqs.expl: Hinge joints (such as the elbow and knee) permit movement primarily in one plane (flexion and extension).

mcqs.q: Which tissue connects bone to another bone at a joint?
mcqs.expl: Ligaments are strong elastic bands of fibrous connective tissue that connect bones to bones across joints.

mcqs.q: The muscle that bends a limb at a joint during contraction is known as a:
mcqs.expl: A flexor muscle contracts to bend a joint (e.g. biceps bending the elbow), whereas an extensor contracts to straighten it.

mcqs.q: The matrix of bone is hardened by deposits of:
mcqs.expl: Inorganic mineral salts, predominantly calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) and calcium carbonate, give bone its hardness.

opts: Loss of bone mineral density and brittle bones
mcqs.expl: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone mass, microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, and fragility.

mcqs.q: The first cervical vertebra that supports the skull is called the:
mcqs.expl: The atlas (C1) articulates superiorly with the occipital condyles of the skull to support the head.

mcqs.q: Hyaline cartilage is present in all of the following EXCEPT the:
mcqs.expl: The pinna of the external ear is composed of elastic cartilage, not hyaline cartilage.

mcqs.q: Rheumatoid arthritis is categorized as an:
mcqs.expl: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disorder in which the body's immune system attacks its own synovial membranes.

sq.q: Differentiate between the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton.
sq.ans: The axial skeleton forms the central longitudinal axis of the human body and consists of 80 bones (skull, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum), primarily functioning to protect vital organs like the brain, spinal cord, heart, and lungs. The appendicular skeleton consists of 126 bones associated with the appendages (pectoral girdle with arms, and pelvic girdle with legs), primarily functioning to facilitate locomotion and manual manipulation.

sq.q: Explain how biceps and triceps muscles act antagonistically to move the human forearm.
sq.ans: Biceps brachii and triceps brachii work as an antagonistic pair. When the biceps contracts, it pulls on the radius and ulna, flexing (bending) the elbow joint, while the triceps relaxes. To straighten the arm, the triceps contracts, pulling on the olecranon process of the ulna to extend the joint, while the biceps relaxes.

sq.q: Describe the microscopic structure of an osteon (Haversian system) in compact bone.
sq.ans: An osteon consists of a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves. Around this canal are concentric rings of hard mineralized bone matrix called lamellae. Embedded between the lamellae are small spaces called lacunae, each housing a mature bone cell (osteocyte). Radiating from lacunae are microscopic canals called canaliculi, through which osteocyte processes connect for nutrient exchange.

sq.q: What is the structural difference between a tendon and a ligament?
sq.ans: A tendon is a tough, dense, non-elastic cord of parallel collagen fibers that attaches a skeletal muscle to a bone, transmitting tensile contractile force. A ligament is a tough, elastic band of collagen and elastin fibers that connects one bone to another across a joint, stabilizing the joint and preventing dislocation while permitting normal range of motion.

sq.q: What is arthritis? Name its three common forms.
sq.ans: Arthritis is an inflammatory condition affecting one or more joints, characterized by pain, swelling, stiffness, and reduced mobility. Its three major types are: 1. Osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear degeneration of articular cartilage), 2. Rheumatoid Arthritis (autoimmune destruction of synovial membrane), and 3. Gout (deposition of needle-like uric acid crystals in synovial joints).

lq.q: Give a detailed classification and account of the human skeleton, detailing the bones in both axial and appendicular divisions.
lq.ans:
The adult human skeleton comprises 206 bones divided into:
1. Axial Skeleton (80 Bones):
- Skull (28 bones): Cranium (8 bones: frontal, 2 parietal, 2 temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid), Facial bones (14 bones: 2 maxillae, 2 zygomatic, 2 nasal, 2 lacrimal, 2 palatine, 2 inferior conchae, vomer, mandible), and 6 middle ear ossicles (2 malleus, 2 incus, 2 stapes), plus 1 hyoid bone.
- Vertebral Column (26 bones in adult / 33 vertebrae in child): 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum (5 fused), 1 coccyx (4 fused).
- Thoracic Cage (25 bones): 12 pairs of ribs (7 pairs true ribs 1–7; 3 pairs false ribs 8–10; 2 pairs floating ribs 11–12) and 1 sternum.

2. Appendicular Skeleton (126 Bones):
- Pectoral Girdle (4 bones): 2 clavicles and 2 scapulae.
- Upper Limbs (60 bones): 2 humeri, 2 radii, 2 ulnae, 16 carpals (wrist), 10 metacarpals (palm), and 28 phalanges (fingers).
- Pelvic Girdle (2 bones): 2 coxal (hip) bones, each formed by fusion of ilium, ischium, and pubis.
- Lower Limbs (60 bones): 2 femora (thigh), 2 patellae (kneecap), 2 tibiae (shin), 2 fibulae, 14 tarsals (ankle), 10 metatarsals (sole), and 28 phalanges (toes).

lq.q: Describe the structure of a synovial joint with the aid of a diagrammatic explanation, and classify synovial joints with examples.
lq.ans:
Structure of a Synovial Joint:
- Articular Cartilage: Both bone ends are capped with smooth hyaline cartilage that absorbs shock and eliminates friction.
- Articular Capsule: A tough double-layered fibrous capsule that envelops the joint, holding the bones together.
- Synovial Membrane: Inner lining of the capsule composed of vascular connective tissue that secretes slippery, albuminous synovial fluid.
- Synovial Cavity: The fluid-filled space between articulating bones that lubricates joint surfaces and nourishes chondrocytes.
- Ligaments & Tendons: Extracapsular and intracapsular ligaments reinforce and stabilize the joint structure.

Classification of Synovial Joints:
1. Hinge Joint: Resembles a door hinge; allows movement in only one plane (flexion and extension). Examples: Elbow joint (between humerus and ulna) and Knee joint.
2. Ball-and-Socket Joint: A spherical head of one bone fits into a cup-like socket of another; allows universal rotational movement in all planes (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction, rotation). Examples: Shoulder joint (glenoid cavity and humerus) and Hip joint (acetabulum and femur).

lq.q: Write comprehensive notes on the causes, symptoms, and preventive measures of Osteoporosis and Arthritis.
lq.ans:
1. Osteoporosis:
- Causes: Progressive imbalance where bone resorption by osteoclasts exceeds bone formation by osteoblasts. Risk factors include postmenopausal drop in estrogen, insufficient dietary calcium and vitamin D, lack of physical weight-bearing exercise, hyperparathyroidism, smoking, and chronic corticosteroid use.
- Symptoms: Often asymptomatic until a bone breaks ('silent disease'). Later signs include gradual loss of height, stooped posture (kyphosis / 'dowager's hump'), back pain from collapsed vertebrae, and pathological fractures of wrist, hip, or spine.
- Prevention & Treatment: Adequate calcium (1000–1200 mg/day) and vitamin D intake, regular resistance and weight-bearing exercises, hormone replacement therapy (HRT) where indicated, and bisphosphonate medications.

2. Arthritis:
- Causes: 1. Osteoarthritis (wear and tear of cartilage in weight-bearing joints due to aging, obesity, joint injury); 2. Rheumatoid Arthritis (autoimmune attack producing inflammatory pannus that erodes cartilage and bone); 3. Gout (hyperuricemia causing needle-like sodium urate crystals to deposit in joint synovium).
- Symptoms: Joint pain, swelling, warmth, morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes, crackling sounds (crepitus), and progressive joint deformity with loss of mobility.
- Prevention & Treatment: Maintaining healthy body weight to reduce stress on joints, physical therapy, NSAIDs and analgesics for pain relief, DMARDs for rheumatoid arthritis, allopurinol and low-purine diet for gout, and total joint replacement surgery (arthroplasty) in end-stage disease.

topics.title: Concept of Reproduction & Asexual vs Sexual Reproduction

summary.en: Reproduction is the biological process by which organisms produce offspring of their own kind, ensuring the continuity of life. In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces genetically identical offspring by mitosis without gamete fusion. In sexual reproduction, two parents produce genetically diverse offspring through gamete formation by meiosis and subsequent fertilization.
summary.ur: تولید وہ حیاتیاتی عمل ہے جس کے ذریعے جاندار اپنی ہی نوع کے نئے افراد پیدا کرتے ہیں۔ غیر جنسی تولید میں ایک ہی جاندار بغیر گیمیٹس کے ہو بہو اپنی نقل پیدا کرتا ہے جبکہ جنسی تولید میں مائیوسس اور فرٹیلائزیشن کے ذریعے جینیاتی تنوع پیدا ہوتا ہے۔

subtopics.name: Asexual Reproduction Methods
subtopics.desc: 1. Binary Fission: Parent organism divides into two equal daughter cells (e.g. Bacteria, Amoeba). 2. Multiple Fission: Parent divides into many daughter cells simultaneously under harsh conditions inside a protective cyst (e.g. Amoeba, Plasmodium). 3. Budding: A small outgrowth (bud) develops on the parent body, matures, and detaches (e.g. Yeast, Hydra). 4. Spore Formation: Production of microscopic, resistant spores inside sporangia that disperse and germinate (e.g. Rhizopus / bread mold). 5. Fragmentation: Organism breaks into fragments, each regenerating a complete organism (e.g. Spirogyra, Planaria). 6. Parthenogenesis: Development of an unfertilized egg into an adult (e.g. drone honeybees).
subtopics.sciNote: A single bacterium reproducing by binary fission every 20 minutes can theoretically produce over 68 billion cells in 12 hours.
subtopics.sq: Differentiate between binary fission and multiple fission.

subtopics.name: Vegetative Propagation in Plants
subtopics.desc: Reproduction from vegetative parts (stem, root, leaves) rather than seeds. 1. Natural Methods: Bulbs (condensed underground stem with fleshy scale leaves, e.g. Onion, Garlic), Corms (solid swollen underground stem, e.g. Colocasia), Rhizomes (horizontal underground stems with nodes/buds, e.g. Ginger, Ferns), Stem Tubers (swollen stem tips with 'eyes', e.g. Potato), Suckers (underground shoots arising from stem base, e.g. Mint, Banana), and Leaves (adventitious buds in leaf notches, e.g. Bryophyllum). 2. Artificial Methods: Stem Cuttings (Rose, Sugarcane), Grafting (joining Scion shoot onto Stock root, e.g. Apple, Mango), Layering, and Tissue Culture (Micropropagation).
subtopics.sciNote: Tissue culture enables the propagation of thousands of disease-free, identical clones from a few cells of a desirable plant in a sterile nutrient agar medium.

summary.en: Angiosperms reproduce sexually through flowers. Flowers contain Calyx (sepals), Corolla (petals), Androecium (stamens: anther and filament producing microspores/pollen grains), and Gynoecium (carpels: stigma, style, and ovary enclosing ovules). Pollination transfers pollen to stigma. Double fertilization produces a diploid zygote (forming the embryo) and a triploid endosperm nucleus (forming nutritive tissue).
summary.ur: پھولدار پودوں میں جنسی تولید پھول کے ذریعے ہوتی ہے۔ پھول کے چار گھیرے ہوتے ہیں: کیلکس، کورولا، اینڈروشیم (نر حصہ) اور گائینوشیم (مادہ حصہ)۔ پولینیشن کے بعد ڈبل فرٹیلائزیشن ہوتی ہے جس سے بیج اور پھل بنتے ہیں۔

subtopics.name: Pollination and Adaptations
subtopics.desc: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma. Self-pollination: Pollen transferred to stigma of same flower or another flower on same plant (Pea, Wheat). Cross-pollination: Pollen transferred to stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species (Rose, Maize). Adaptations: Insect-pollinated flowers have large, brightly colored petals, sweet nectar, pleasant fragrance, and rough, sticky pollen. Wind-pollinated flowers have small, dull petals, no nectar/scent, long feathery stigmas, and copious, lightweight, smooth pollen grains.
subtopics.sciNote: Cross-pollination results in genetic recombination and increased environmental adaptability of offspring compared to self-pollination.
subtopics.sq: List four distinguishing features between insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers.

mcq.q: Which characteristic is typical of wind-pollinated flowers?
opts: Feathery protruding stigmas and smooth light pollen

subtopics.name: Double Fertilization and Seed Structure
subtopics.desc: On the stigma, a pollen grain germinates to form a pollen tube that grows down the style into the ovule through the micropyle, carrying two sperm nuclei. Double Fertilization: 1. One sperm nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form a 2n diploid zygote (embryo). 2. The second sperm nucleus fuses with the diploid fusion nucleus (central cell) to form a 3n triploid Endosperm Nucleus that develops into nutritive endosperm tissue. Post-fertilization: Ovule becomes the Seed; Ovary matures into the Fruit.
subtopics.sciNote: Double fertilization is a unique diagnostic feature exclusive to angiosperms (flowering plants).
subtopics.sq: What is meant by double fertilization in flowering plants?

mcq.q: The triploid (3n) tissue formed in flowering plants after double fertilization is the:

subtopics.name: Seed Structure and Germination
subtopics.desc: A mature seed has: 1. Seed Coat (Testa: outer thick layer; Tegmen: inner thin layer), 2. Embryo consisting of Radicle (future root), Plumule (future shoot), and Cotyledons (seed leaves). Germination types: 1. Epigeal Germination: Hypocotyl elongates rapidly, curving and pulling the cotyledons above ground (Bean, Castor, Cotton, Papaya). 2. Hypogeal Germination: Epicotyl elongates while hypocotyl does not, leaving cotyledons below ground (Pea, Gram, Maize). Conditions required: Water, Oxygen, and Suitable Temperature.
subtopics.sciNote: Water imbibition softens the seed coat, hydrates protoplasm, and activates hydrolytic enzymes like amylase to digest stored starches.
subtopics.sq: Differentiate between epigeal and hypogeal germination with examples.

mcq.q: In which type of germination do the cotyledons remain below the ground?

topics.title: Sexual Reproduction in Animals & Human Reproductive System

summary.en: Animals reproduce sexually through gamete formation: Spermatogenesis (sperm in testes) and Oogenesis (ova in ovaries). Fertilization may be external (amphibians, fish) or internal (reptiles, birds, mammals). The human reproductive system comprises specialized male and female anatomical organs coordinated by pituitary and gonadal hormones.
summary.ur: جانوروں میں سپرم اور بیضہ بننے کے عمل کو سپرمیٹوجینیسس اور اوجینیسس کہتے ہیں۔ انسانی تولیدی نظام نر اور مادہ اعضاء پر مشتمل ہوتا ہے جن کی نشوونما ہارمونز کے کنٹرول میں ہوتی ہے۔
summary.ps: په حیواناتو کې سپرماتوجینیسس او اوجینیسس د القاح لپاره ګیمیټونه جوړوي چې په انسانانو کې داخلي القاح صورت نیسي.

subtopics.name: Male and Female Reproductive Systems
subtopics.desc: 1. Male System: Testes located in scrotum (2–3°C cooler than body for spermatogenesis); Seminiferous Tubules produce sperm; Epididymis stores sperm; Vas Deferens conducts sperm; Accessory glands (Seminal Vesicles, Prostate Gland, Bulbourethral Glands) add seminal fluid; Urethra and Penis deliver semen. 2. Female System: Ovaries produce ova, estrogen, and progesterone; Fallopian Tubes (Oviducts) where fertilization occurs; Uterus (thick muscular organ lined by vascular endometrium where the blastocyst implants); Cervix and Vagina (birth canal).
subtopics.sciNote: A single ejaculation in healthy adult human males contains between 200 and 400 million sperm cells.
subtopics.sq: What is the function of the scrotum in the human male reproductive system?

subtopics.name: Sexually Transmitted Diseases: AIDS
subtopics.desc: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), a retrovirus that infects and destroys helper T lymphocytes (CD4+ cells), collapsing the immune system. Transmission: Unprotected sexual contact, transfusion of contaminated blood/blood products, sharing unsterilized needles, and mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding. Prevention: Safe sexual practices, screening blood before transfusion, using sterilized disposable syringes, and antiretroviral therapy (ART).
subtopics.sciNote: HIV cannot be transmitted through casual social contact, shaking hands, hugging, sharing food or utensils, coughing, or mosquito bites.
subtopics.sq: Explain how HIV affects the human immune system and list two modes of transmission.

mcq.q: HIV primarily attacks and destroys which cells of the human body?

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of natural vegetative propagation through leaves?
mcqs.expl: Bryophyllum develops adventitious buds in the notches along its leaf margins that drop off to form independent plants.

mcqs.q: The product of double fertilization that provides nourishment to the developing plant embryo is:
mcqs.expl: The triploid (3n) endosperm tissue stores nutrients for the embryo during seed development.

mcqs.q: In epigeal germination, which part of the seedling elongates rapidly to pull the cotyledons above the soil?
mcqs.expl: In epigeal germination, the hypocotyl elongates into an arch, lifting the cotyledons into the sunlight.

mcqs.q: The swollen underground horizontal stem bearing nodes, internodes, and buds found in ginger is a:
mcqs.expl: A rhizome is a prostrate underground stem with distinct nodes, internodes, scale leaves, and axillary buds.

mcqs.q: Fertilization in humans takes place in the:
mcqs.expl: Sperm encounters and fertilizes the secondary oocyte in the ampulla of the fallopian tube.

mcqs.q: Asexual reproduction in bread mold (Rhizopus) occurs by the formation of:
mcqs.expl: Rhizopus produces asexual, non-motile spores within rounded structures called sporangia atop aerial sporangiophores.

mcqs.q: Which part of the flower develops into the fruit after fertilization?
mcqs.expl: After fertilization, the ovary wall thickens and ripens to become the pericarp of the fruit, while the ovules become seeds.

mcqs.q: The production of offspring from an unfertilized egg is called:
mcqs.expl: Parthenogenesis is a form of asexual reproduction where an egg develops into an embryo without fertilization, as in drone bees.

mcqs.q: The primary male sex hormone responsible for secondary sexual characteristics is:
mcqs.expl: Testosterone produced by Leydig cells in the testes stimulates spermatogenesis and develops male secondary sexual traits.

mcqs.q: AIDS is caused by:
mcqs.expl: AIDS is caused by the retrovirus HIV, which destroys CD4+ T lymphocytes.

sq.q: Compare asexual reproduction with sexual reproduction in terms of parents, cell division, and genetic variation.
sq.ans: Asexual reproduction involves a single parent, relies exclusively on mitosis, produces genetically identical offspring (clones), and occurs rapidly. Sexual reproduction involves two parents, involves meiosis during gametogenesis and fertilization, produces genetically diverse offspring with novel gene combinations, and provides the raw material for adaptation and evolution.

sq.q: What is double fertilization and in which group of plants does it occur?
sq.ans: Double fertilization is a unique reproductive process found exclusively in angiosperms (flowering plants). One sperm nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid (2n) zygote that develops into the embryo, while the second sperm nucleus fuses with the central diploid fusion nucleus to form a triploid (3n) endosperm nucleus that develops into nutritive endosperm tissue.

sq.q: Explain the difference between epigeal and hypogeal germination.
sq.ans: In epigeal germination, the hypocotyl elongates rapidly and forms an arch that pushes the cotyledons above the ground, where they often turn green and photosynthetic (e.g. bean, castor, sunflower). In hypogeal germination, the epicotyl elongates rapidly while the hypocotyl remains short, so the cotyledons remain buried beneath the soil surface (e.g. pea, maize, gram).

sq.q: Define grafting and mention its economic importance.
sq.ans: Grafting is an artificial method of vegetative propagation in which a shoot cutting with buds (scion) from a superior, high-yield plant is inserted and bound onto the rooted stem (stock) of a hardy, disease-resistant plant so their vascular cambiums unite. It is widely used in commercial fruit orchards (apples, peaches, citrus) to propagate desired cultivars rapidly without loss of quality.

sq.q: State three major ways through which HIV can be transmitted.
sq.ans:
1. Unprotected sexual intercourse with an HIV-infected person.
2. Transfusion of unscreened, contaminated blood or blood products, or using unsterilized contaminated needles and surgical instruments.
3. Vertical transmission from an infected mother to her fetus across the placenta, during delivery, or through breastfeeding.

lq.q: Describe the structure of a typical flower and explain the process of pollination and fertilization in angiosperms.
lq.ans:
1. Structure of a Flower:
- Calyx: Outermost whorl of green sepals that protect the flower bud.
- Corolla: Whorl of colorful, scented petals that attract animal pollinators.
- Androecium (Male whorl): Composed of stamens, each having a slender filament and a terminal anther containing four microsporangia (pollen sacs) where microspore mother cells undergo meiosis to produce haploid pollen grains.
- Gynoecium (Female whorl): Composed of one or more carpels (pistil), consisting of a receptive sticky Stigma, an elongated Style, and a basal Ovary containing one or more ovules.

2. Pollination:
- The transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma via wind, water, insects, or birds.

3. Fertilization:
- Once on the stigma, the pollen grain absorbs sugar-rich secretions and germinates, producing a pollen tube.
- The pollen tube grows down through the style into the ovary, guided biochemically toward the micropyle of the ovule.
- The generative cell inside divides by mitosis into two non-motile male gametes (sperm cells).
- Upon entering the embryo sac, one sperm fertilizes the egg (forming the 2n zygote), and the other fertilizes the 2n polar nuclei (forming the 3n endosperm), completing double fertilization.

lq.q: Explain the natural and artificial methods of vegetative propagation in plants with suitable examples.
lq.ans:
1. Natural Methods of Vegetative Propagation:
- Bulbs: Condensed underground shoots with fleshy, food-storing scale leaves enclosing an apical bud; axillary buds grow into daughter bulbs (e.g., Onion, Garlic, Tulip).
- Corms: Short, solid, upright swollen underground stems storing food with distinct nodes and buds (e.g., Colocasia / Arvi, Gladiolus).
- Rhizomes: Thick, horizontal underground stems bearing nodes, internodes, scale leaves, and terminal buds (e.g., Ginger, Turmeric, Ferns).
- Stem Tubers: Swollen underground stem tips with dormant buds ('eyes') that sprout into new plants (e.g., Potato).
- Suckers: Underground shoots originating from parent roots or stem bases that emerge above ground (e.g., Mint, Banana, Chrysanthemum).
- Leaves: Leaves of Bryophyllum possess adventitious buds in marginal notches that sprout into plantlets when detached.

2. Artificial Methods:
- Stem Cuttings: A healthy stem section with nodes is cut and planted in moist soil; adventitious roots form at the cut end (e.g., Rose, Sugarcane, Grapevine).
- Grafting: Joining a scion (twig with desirable fruit/flower traits) onto a stock (rooted plant providing hardy root system) ensuring cambial contact; the two heal into a single plant (e.g., Mango, Citrus, Apple).
- Layering: A flexible branch is bent down and covered with soil while still attached to the parent plant until adventitious roots develop, after which it is severed (e.g., Jasmine, Raspberry).
- Micropropagation (Tissue Culture): Culturing tiny explants on sterile nutrient media with plant growth regulators to generate millions of clones (e.g., Orchids, Oil palm).

lq.q: Describe the human male and female reproductive systems and discuss the role of sex hormones in human reproduction.
lq.ans:
1. Male Reproductive System:
- Testes: Paired oval organs housed inside the external scrotal sac, maintaining a temperature 2–3°C below core body temperature essential for spermatogenesis.
- Seminiferous Tubules: Highly coiled tubules where spermatogenic cells produce millions of spermatozoa under FSH stimulation, while interstitial Leydig cells produce testosterone under LH stimulation.
- Epididymis: Coiled tube atop each testis where sperm mature and gain motility.
- Vas Deferens: Muscular duct that conducts sperm into the ejaculatory duct.
- Accessory Glands: Seminal vesicles (secrete alkaline fructose-rich fluid), Prostate gland (milky fluid neutralizing vaginal acidity), and Bulbourethral glands (lubricating mucus).
- Penis: Copulatory organ enclosing the urethra.

2. Female Reproductive System:
- Ovaries: Paired almond-shaped organs in the pelvic cavity that produce secondary oocytes via oogenesis and secrete estrogen and progesterone.
- Fallopian Tubes (Oviducts): Ciliated muscular tubes with fimbriated funnels that capture the ovulated oocyte and provide the site for fertilization.
- Uterus (Womb): Pear-shaped muscular organ with an inner vascular lining (endometrium) that prepares monthly for blastocyst implantation and supports embryonic development.
- Cervix & Vagina: Muscular canal receiving sperm and serving as the birth canal during parturition.

3. Hormonal Roles:
- FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone): Stimulates spermatogenesis in males and follicle maturation in females.
- LH (Luteinizing Hormone): Triggers testosterone secretion in males and ovulation/corpus luteum formation in females.
- Estrogen: Develops female secondary sexual characteristics and promotes endometrial proliferation.
- Progesterone: Secreted by corpus luteum; maintains the vascularized endometrium for pregnancy and inhibits uterine contractions.

activities.title: Dissection and Study of the Floral Whorls of Brassica / Hibiscus Flower
activities.desc: Take a fresh flower (Brassica campestris or China rose). Dissect the four concentric whorls carefully using forceps and needle. Observe and count: Sepals (Calyx), Petals (Corolla), Stamens (Anther and Filament under dissecting microscope to observe pollen), and Carpel/Pistil (Stigma, Style, and transverse section of Ovary showing ovules).

activities.title: Observation of Germinating Seeds (Epigeal vs Hypogeal)
activities.desc: Soak bean seeds and pea/maize seeds in water overnight. Plant them in moist sawdust in two separate pots. Observe daily for 7–10 days: note that in bean seedlings, the green cotyledons emerge above the sawdust (epigeal), whereas in pea/maize seedlings, the cotyledons stay buried below the surface (hypogeal).

topics.title: Introduction to Genetics, Chromosomes and DNA

summary.en: Genetics is the branch of biology dealing with heredity (transmission of traits from parents to offspring) and variations. Chromosomes in eukaryotic nuclei consist of chromatin material (DNA tightly wrapped around histone proteins). DNA is the molecule of heredity, structured as a double helix of antiparallel polynucleotide chains discovered by Watson and Crick.

subtopics.name: Chromatin and Chromosome Structure
subtopics.desc: In non-dividing cells, genetic material exists as diffuse Chromatin. During cell division, chromatin condenses into visible Chromosomes. Each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at a primary constriction called the Centromere. Chromatin is composed of DNA (approx. 40%) and basic Histone proteins (approx. 60%). DNA winds around octamers of histone proteins to form repeating bead-like units called Nucleosomes.
subtopics.sciNote: Human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes (23 homologous pairs): 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males).

subtopics.name: The Watson-Crick Model of DNA
subtopics.desc: James Watson and Francis Crick (1953) elucidated the double helix structure of DNA: 1. DNA is composed of two polynucleotide strands coiled around a central axis in a right-handed double helix. 2. The strands are antiparallel (one runs 5' to 3', the other 3' to 5'). 3. The backbone consists of alternating deoxyribose sugar and phosphate groups. 4. Nitrogenous bases face inward: Adenine (A) pairs with Thymine (T) via 2 hydrogen bonds (A=T); Guanine (G) pairs with Cytosine (C) via 3 hydrogen bonds (G=C).
subtopics.sciNote: Chargaff's rules state that in double-stranded DNA, the molar ratio of adenine equals thymine (A=T) and guanine equals cytosine (G=C).

topics.title: Genes, Alleles, and Protein Synthesis (Central Dogma)

summary.en: A gene is a specific sequence of nucleotides on DNA that codes for a functional polypeptide or RNA. Alternative forms of a gene occupying the same locus on homologous chromosomes are alleles. The Central Dogma describes genetic information flow: DNA -> mRNA (Transcription in nucleus) -> Protein (Translation at ribosomes in cytoplasm).

subtopics.name: Genotype vs Phenotype & Dominant vs Recessive
subtopics.desc: Genotype is the specific genetic constitution of an organism (e.g., TT, Tt, tt). Phenotype is the observable physical or physiological expression of the genotype (e.g., Tall vs Short). Homozygous: An organism with two identical alleles (TT or tt). Heterozygous: An organism with two different alleles (Tt). In heterozygotes, the allele that fully expresses itself is Dominant (represented by a capital letter, T), while the allele that is masked is Recessive (lowercase, t).
subtopics.sciNote: A recessive allele expresses its phenotype only when present in homozygous state (tt).

subtopics.name: The Central Dogma: Transcription and Translation
subtopics.desc: 1. Transcription: Inside the nucleus, RNA Polymerase reads the template strand of DNA to synthesize a complementary single strand of messenger RNA (mRNA), replacing thymine with uracil. 2. Translation: The mRNA exits through nuclear pores into the cytoplasm and binds to a ribosome. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry specific amino acids matching the mRNA codons (triplet nucleotide codes) to assemble a polypeptide chain.
subtopics.sciNote: The genetic code is universal, triplet, and non-overlapping: 64 codons code for 20 standard amino acids, including 1 start codon (AUG) and 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA).

summary.en: Gregor Johann Mendel (Father of Genetics) deduced the fundamental principles of inheritance through hybridizing garden pea plants (Pisum sativum). He formulated two universal laws: The Law of Segregation (monohybrid cross, 3:1 phenotypic ratio) and The Law of Independent Assortment (dihybrid cross, 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio).

subtopics.name: Mendel's Law of Segregation (Monohybrid Cross)
subtopics.desc: Mendel crossed pure-breeding tall pea plants (TT) with pure-breeding dwarf plants (tt). All F1 offspring were tall (Tt). In the F2 generation, self-pollination yielded tall and dwarf plants in a 3:1 phenotypic ratio (1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt genotypic ratio). Law of Segregation: 'In every organism, traits are determined by pairs of distinct factors (alleles). During gamete formation, the members of a pair segregate (separate) from each other so that each gamete carries only one allele of the pair.'
subtopics.sciNote: Mendel chose garden peas because they are easy to cultivate, have a short life cycle, possess sharp contrasting traits, and are naturally self-pollinating but can be easily cross-pollinated.
subtopics.sq: State Mendel's Law of Segregation.

subtopics.name: Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment (Dihybrid Cross)
subtopics.desc: Mendel crossed pea plants differing in two traits: Round Yellow seeds (RRYY) with Wrinkled Green seeds (rryy). F1 plants were all Round Yellow (RrYy). In F2, four distinct phenotypes emerged in a 9:3:3:1 ratio: 9 Round Yellow, 3 Round Green, 3 Wrinkled Yellow, 1 Wrinkled Green. Law of Independent Assortment: 'When two pairs of contrasting traits are followed in a cross, the alleles of one pair segregate independently of the alleles of the other pair during gamete formation.'
subtopics.sciNote: Independent assortment occurs during Metaphase-I of meiosis when homologous chromosome pairs align randomly at the equatorial plate.

summary.en: Variations are differences among individuals of the same species. They are classified as Continuous (gradual range, e.g. human height/weight) and Discontinuous (distinct categories without intermediates, e.g. ABO blood groups). Charles Darwin proposed the Theory of Natural Selection to explain organic evolution: organisms produce excess offspring, struggle for survival, adapt through advantageous variations, and the fittest survive and reproduce.

subtopics.name: Continuous vs Discontinuous Variations
subtopics.desc: 1. Continuous Variation: Shows a complete gradient/spectrum of phenotypes from one extreme to another without sharp dividing lines; influenced by multiple genes (polygenic inheritance) and environmental factors. Examples: Human skin color, height, body mass, intelligence. 2. Discontinuous Variation: Exhibits distinct, discrete, mutually exclusive phenotypic categories with no intermediate forms; controlled by one or a few genes and unaffected by the environment. Examples: ABO blood groups (A, B, AB, O), tongue rolling, free vs attached earlobes, sickle-cell anemia.
subtopics.sciNote: Crossing over during prophase-I of meiosis, random assortment of chromosomes, and random fertilization are major sources of genetic variation.

subtopics.name: Darwin's Theory of Natural Selection
subtopics.desc: Charles Darwin (1859, On the Origin of Species) proposed: 1. Overproduction: Species produce far more offspring than the environment can support. 2. Struggle for Existence: Competition for limited food, territory, and mates. 3. Variations and Adaptations: Individuals possess heritable variations; those with favorable traits adapt better. 4. Survival of the Fittest (Natural Selection): Better-adapted individuals survive, reproduce, and pass their advantageous alleles to the next generation. 5. Speciation: Over many generations, accumulation of adaptations leads to the origin of new species.
subtopics.sciNote: Artificial selection (selective breeding) carried out by humans in dogs, cattle, and wheat provided Darwin with compelling analogous evidence for natural selection.

sq.q: Define the terms 'gene' and 'allele'.
sq.ans: A gene is the fundamental physical and functional unit of heredity, consisting of a specific linear sequence of nucleotides on a DNA molecule that encodes a particular functional polypeptide or RNA. An allele is an alternative, variable form of a gene located at the same specific locus on homologous chromosomes (e.g. T and t for plant height).

sq.q: State Mendel's Law of Segregation and illustrate it with genotypes.
sq.ans: Mendel's Law of Segregation states that every individual possesses a pair of alleles for any particular trait. During gamete formation (meiosis), these alleles segregate (separate) from each other so that each gamete receives only one allele. Illustration: Crossing homozygous tall (TT) with homozygous dwarf (tt) gives F1 heterozygous tall (Tt). When F1 forms gametes, 50% carry 'T' and 50% carry 't'. Random fertilization produces F2 genotypes in the ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.

sq.q: How does transcription differ from translation?
sq.ans: Transcription is the synthesis of a complementary single strand of messenger RNA (mRNA) from a DNA template strand inside the nucleus by RNA polymerase. Translation is the synthesis of a specific polypeptide chain at ribosomes in the cytoplasm, where transfer RNA (tRNA) decodes the triplet codons of the mRNA into a linear sequence of amino acids.

sq.q: Differentiate between continuous and discontinuous variations.
sq.ans: Continuous variations exhibit a smooth, unbroken spectrum of intermediate phenotypes between two extremes without sharp demarcations (e.g., human height, weight, skin color), are polygenic, and are influenced by the environment. Discontinuous variations show distinct, discrete, mutually exclusive phenotypic categories with no intermediate forms (e.g., ABO blood groups, tongue rolling), are controlled by a single gene or few genes, and are unaffected by environmental factors.

sq.q: What is meant by 'Survival of the Fittest' in Darwin's theory?
sq.ans: 'Survival of the Fittest' means that individuals possessing advantageous heritable variations that are better suited to their specific environment have a higher probability of surviving, reproducing, and transmitting those favorable alleles to the subsequent generation, while less suited individuals leave fewer or no offspring.

lq.q: Describe the Watson-Crick double helix model of DNA with details on its chemical components and bonding.
lq.ans:
1. Chemical Components of DNA:
- Deoxyribose Sugar: A 5-carbon pentose sugar lacking an oxygen atom at the 2' carbon position.
- Phosphate Group: Linked to the 5' carbon of one sugar and the 3' carbon of the preceding sugar, forming a phosphodiester backbone.
- Nitrogenous Bases: Purines with double rings (Adenine [A] and Guanine [G]) and Pyrimidines with single rings (Thymine [T] and Cytosine [C]).

2. Double Helix Architecture:
- Two antiparallel polynucleotide chains: One strand runs in the 5' -> 3' direction, while the complementary strand runs in the 3' -> 5' direction.
- Right-handed helical spiral: The sugar-phosphate backbones form the outer structural rails, while the nitrogenous bases point inward like the rungs of a twisted ladder.
- Complementary Base Pairing: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine. Adenine forms two hydrogen bonds with Thymine (A = T), and Guanine forms three hydrogen bonds with Cytosine (G ≡ C).
- Helical Dimensions: One complete helical turn has a pitch of 3.4 nm (34 Å) and contains 10 base pairs (0.34 nm between adjacent pairs). The diameter of the double helix is uniform at 2.0 nm (20 Å).
- The complementary nature explains DNA replication: each strand serves as a template to synthesize an identical daughter duplex (semiconservative replication).

lq.q: Explain Mendel's experiments on dihybrid crosses and explain how they led to the formulation of the Law of Independent Assortment.
lq.ans:
1. Dihybrid Cross Experiment:
- Mendel crossed true-breeding pea plants possessing two pairs of contrasting traits: Round Yellow seeds (RRYY) with Wrinkled Green seeds (rryy).
- Round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r); Yellow (Y) is dominant over green (y).
- Gametes: RRYY produced 'RY' gametes; rryy produced 'ry' gametes.
- F1 Generation: All offspring had the genotype RrYy and exhibited the Round Yellow phenotype.

2. F2 Generation (Selfing of F1):
- F1 plants formed four types of gametes in equal proportions (25% each): RY, Ry, rY, ry.
- Using a 4x4 Punnett square (16 combinations), the resulting F2 phenotypes appeared in the ratio:
  * 9 Round Yellow (R_Y_)
  * 3 Round Green (R_yy)
  * 3 Wrinkled Yellow (rrY_)
  * 1 Wrinkled Green (rryy)
- The appearance of recombinant phenotypes (Round Green and Wrinkled Yellow) demonstrated that seed shape and seed color are inherited independently.

3. Law of Independent Assortment:
- 'When two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, the segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters during gamete formation.'
- This occurs biologically because non-homologous chromosome pairs align randomly at the metaphase plate during Meiosis I.

lq.q: Discuss Charles Darwin's Theory of Natural Selection, explaining its five core observations and deductions.
lq.ans:
Darwin's Theory of Evolution by Natural Selection (1859) rests on five key observations and deductions:
1. Overproduction (High Reproductive Potential):
- Living organisms have an immense innate capacity to reproduce and multiply geometrically. A single oyster can release 100 million eggs in one spawning.

2. Constancy of Population Size:
- Despite high reproductive potential, the adult populations of species remain relatively stable over time because resources (food, water, space) in any environment are finite.

3. Struggle for Existence (Deduction 1):
- Since more individuals are born than can possibly survive on limited resources, intense competition ensues: intraspecific competition (among members of the same species), interspecific competition (between different species), and environmental struggle (against drought, cold, predators, disease).

4. Universal Variations and Heredity:
- No two individuals within a sexually reproducing population are completely identical. Organisms exhibit widespread morphological, physiological, and behavioral variations, many of which are heritable.

5. Survival of the Fittest / Natural Selection (Deduction 2):
- Individuals possessing variations that give them an advantage in obtaining food, evading predators, or enduring climatic extremes are more likely to survive, reach reproductive maturity, and produce fertile offspring.

6. Speciation (Deduction 3):
- Over countless generations, favorable variations accumulate while unfavorable ones are eliminated. Over evolutionary time, populations diverge sufficiently from their ancestral forms to become entirely new species.

activities.title: Survey and Recording of Discontinuous Variations (Tongue Rolling and Earlobe Attachment)

Tally the numbers into distinct categories and display as a bar chart. Confirms that discontinuous variations exhibit discrete categories with no intermediates.

activities.title: Measurement and Graphical Representation of Continuous Variation (Student Height)
activities.desc: Measure the height of 50 students in centimeters. Group the measurements into continuous class intervals (e.g. 140–144 cm, 145–149 cm, 150–154 cm, etc.). Plot a frequency histogram and observe the characteristic bell-shaped normal distribution curve representing continuous variation.

topics.title: Levels of Ecological Organization & Ecosystem Components

summary.en: Ecology is the study of relationships between living organisms and their environment. The levels of organization range from species to population, community, ecosystem, and the biosphere. An ecosystem consists of Abiotic (non-living: sunlight, temperature, water, air, soil) and Biotic (living: producers, consumers, and decomposers) components.
summary.ur: ایکولوجی جانداروں اور ان کے ماحول کے باہمی تعلق کے مطالعے کا نام ہے۔ اس کے درجے آبادی، کمیونٹی، ایکو سسٹم اور بائیوسفیئر ہیں۔ ایکو سسٹم جاندار (پروڈیوسرز، کنزیومرز، ڈی کمپوزرز) اور غیر جاندار اجزاء پر مشتمل ہوتا ہے۔
summary.ps: ایکالوجي د ژوندیو موجوداتو او د هغوی د چاپیریال ترمنځ اړیکې مطالعه کوي او ایکوسیستم ژوندي او غیر ژوندي عناصر لري.

subtopics.name: Levels of Ecological Organization
subtopics.desc: 1. Species: A group of morphologically similar organisms capable of interbreeding to produce fertile offspring. 2. Population: A group of individuals of the same species living in a specific geographical area at a given time. 3. Community: An assemblage of all populations of different species living and interacting in a common habitat. 4. Ecosystem: A self-sustaining structural and functional unit of the biosphere where living organisms interact with each other and their physical environment. 5. Biosphere: The global zone of life on Earth, extending from deep ocean trenches to the upper atmosphere.
subtopics.sciNote: The biosphere is approximately 20 kilometers thick, supporting all known life in the universe.
subtopics.sq: Define an ecosystem and differentiate between a population and a community.

mcq.q: A group of individuals of the same species inhabiting a specific geographical area at the same time is called a:

subtopics.name: Biotic Components: Producers, Consumers & Decomposers
subtopics.desc: 1. Producers (Autotrophs): Green plants, algae, and cyanobacteria that capture solar energy through chlorophyll and synthesize organic food via photosynthesis. 2. Consumers (Heterotrophs): Organisms that obtain energy by feeding on other organisms. Classified as Primary consumers (Herbivores: cattle, deer, grasshoppers), Secondary consumers (Primary carnivores: frogs, foxes), and Tertiary consumers (Top carnivores: lions, eagles, sharks). 3. Decomposers (Saprotrophs): Heterotrophic fungi and bacteria that secrete extracellular digestive enzymes to break down dead organic matter, releasing inorganic nutrients back into soil and air.
subtopics.sciNote: Without decomposers, the Earth would be buried under accumulated organic detritus and essential nutrients would be permanently locked up.
subtopics.sq: What is the ecological role of decomposers in an ecosystem?

mcq.q: Organisms that break down dead bodies and recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem are:

summary.en: Energy flows unidirectionally through an ecosystem from the sun to producers and consumers, diminishing by roughly 90% at each trophic level (10% law). Unlike energy, chemical elements cycle continuously through Biogeochemical Cycles such as the Carbon Cycle and Nitrogen Cycle.
summary.ur: ایکو سسٹم میں توانائی کا بہاؤ یک طرفہ ہوتا ہے جو ہر ٹرافک لیول پر ۱۰ فیصد کے قانون کے تحت کم ہوتا جاتا ہے۔ جبکہ غذائی مادے بائیو جیو کیمیکل سائیکلز (کاربن اور نائٹروجن سائیکلز) کے ذریعے بار بار گھومتے ہیں۔
summary.ps: په ایکوسیستم کې د انرژۍ جریان یو طرفه دی پداسې حال کې چې کیمیاوي مواد د کاربن او نایتروجن دورانونو له لارې بیا بیا کارول کیږي.

subtopics.name: Food Chains, Food Webs and Ecological Pyramids
subtopics.desc: A Food Chain is a linear feeding sequence showing who eats whom in an ecosystem (e.g. Grass -> Grasshopper -> Frog -> Snake -> Hawk). A Food Web is a network of interconnected food chains reflecting natural feeding complexity. Ecological Pyramids graphically represent trophic structures: 1. Pyramid of Numbers (usually upright, inverted in parasites), 2. Pyramid of Biomass (total dry mass of organic matter at each level), and 3. Pyramid of Energy (always upright because energy is lost as metabolic heat at every step).
subtopics.sciNote: According to Lindeman's 10% Rule, only approximately 10% of the energy entering a trophic level is incorporated into biomass to be transferred to the next trophic level.
subtopics.sq: Why is an ecological pyramid of energy always upright?

mcq.q: What percentage of energy is approximately transferred from one trophic level to the next?

subtopics.name: Biogeochemical Cycles: Carbon and Nitrogen
subtopics.desc: 1. Carbon Cycle: CO2 is fixed by plants in photosynthesis to produce carbohydrates. Carbon returns to the atmosphere through cellular respiration, decomposition of dead organisms by bacteria/fungi, and combustion of fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas). 2. Nitrogen Cycle: Atmospheric N2 (78%) cannot be directly utilized. - Nitrogen Fixation: Conversion of N2 into ammonia by lightning or symbiotic Rhizobium bacteria in legumes. - Ammonification: Breakdown of nitrogenous wastes into ammonia. - Nitrification: Oxidation of ammonia into nitrites (NO2-) by Nitrosomonas, then into nitrates (NO3-) by Nitrobacter. - Assimilation: Plants absorb nitrates to make proteins. - Denitrification: Conversion of nitrates back into N2 gas by Pseudomonas bacteria in waterlogged soils.
subtopics.sciNote: Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter bacteria are chemoautotrophs that derive chemical energy by oxidizing nitrogen compounds.
subtopics.sq: Describe the stages of nitrification in the nitrogen cycle.

mcq.q: The conversion of ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates by soil bacteria is called:

summary.en: Organisms interact in various ecological relationships: Predation (predator kills and eats prey), Parasitism (parasite lives on/in host and causes harm), Symbiosis including Mutualism (both species benefit) and Commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected), and Competition (struggle for limited resources).
summary.ur: ایکو سسٹم میں جانداروں کے باہمی تعلقات میں شکاری اور شکار، طفیلی تعلق (پیراسیٹزم)، باہمی ہمزیستی (میوچولزم اور کمنسلزم) اور مسابقت شامل ہیں۔
summary.ps: په ایکوسیستم کې د ژوندیو موجوداتو ترمنځ اړیکې لکه ښکار کول، پرازیتي ژوند، او دوه اړخیزه ګټه اخیستنه (Symbiosis) شامل دي.

subtopics.name: Symbiosis: Mutualism and Commensalism
subtopics.desc: 1. Mutualism: An obligatory or facultative relationship in which both partner species benefit. Examples: Lichens (fungus provides water, minerals, and shelter; alga/cyanobacterium provides photosynthesized food); Mycorrhizae (fungus assists plant root in mineral/water absorption; plant supplies carbohydrates); Nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium in root nodules of leguminous plants; Pollination of flowers by bees. 2. Commensalism: A relationship in which one species benefits while the other is neither harmed nor helped. Examples: Epiphytes (orchids) growing on tree branches for sunlight; Remora fish attaching to sharks for transportation and scraps.
subtopics.sciNote: In lichens, the fungal partner is termed the mycobiont and the photosynthetic partner is the photobiont.
subtopics.sq: Differentiate between mutualism and commensalism with an example of each.

mcq.q: The association between a fungus and an alga in a lichen is an example of:

subtopics.name: Predation, Parasitism, and Competition
subtopics.desc: 1. Predation: One organism (predator) captures, kills, and consumes another (prey). E.g. Lion hunting zebra, insectivorous plants (pitcher plant, sundew) trapping insects for nitrogen in nutrient-poor soils. 2. Parasitism: The parasite derives food and shelter from the living host, causing damage. Ectoparasites live on host surface (lice, ticks, fleas, Cuscuta/dodder plant); Endoparasites live inside host tissues (Plasmodium, Ascaris, tapeworm). 3. Competition: Struggle between organisms for limited resources (food, light, territory, mates). Intraspecific (same species) is more intense than Interspecific (different species).
subtopics.sciNote: Cuscuta (Amerbel) is a non-green parasitic angiosperm that penetrates host vascular tissues using specialized root-like structures called haustoria.
subtopics.sq: What are haustoria and what is their role in parasitic plants?

mcq.q: Which of the following is an ectoparasitic plant that lacks chlorophyll?

summary.en: Human population growth, urbanization, and industrialization cause pollution (Air, Water, and Land). Major global concerns include the Greenhouse Effect, Global Warming, Acid Rain, and Ozone Depletion. Conservation requires adopting the 3Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle), reforestation, and renewable energy.
summary.ur: انسانی آبادی، صنعت کاری اور شہری پھیلاؤ سے ماحولیاتی آلودگی (ہوا، پانی، زمین)، گلوبل وارمنگ، تیزابی بارش اور اوزون کی تباہی ہو رہی ہے۔ اس کے تدارک کے لیے تھری آرز اور شجرکاری ضروری ہے۔
summary.ps: د انساني فعالیتونو له امله هوا، اوبه او خاوره ککړیږي چې د نړیوالې تودوخې او تیزابي باران لامل کیږي او د ژغورنې لپاره یې ونې کرل اړین دي.

subtopics.name: Global Environmental Issues: Acid Rain, Global Warming & Ozone Depletion
subtopics.desc: 1. Acid Rain: SO2 and NOx from burning fossil fuels combine with atmospheric water vapour to form sulfuric and nitric acids, falling as rain with pH below 5.6. Damaging to aquatic life, leaches soil nutrients, and corrodes marble/metals. 2. Greenhouse Effect & Global Warming: Excessive greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, CFCs) trap outgoing infrared radiation, elevating Earth's average temperature, melting glaciers, raising sea levels, and causing erratic weather. 3. Ozone Layer Depletion: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere that catalyze the breakdown of ozone (O3) molecules into O2, forming an ozone hole that allows dangerous UV radiation to cause skin cancer and cataracts.
subtopics.sciNote: A single chlorine atom released from CFCs can destroy up to 100,000 ozone molecules before being deactivated.
subtopics.sq: Explain how acid rain is formed and state two of its damaging effects.

mcq.q: The primary greenhouse gas contributing to global warming is:

subtopics.name: Conservation of Nature: The 3Rs and Reforestation
subtopics.desc: Conservation strategies: 1. Reduce: Minimize consumption of raw resources and energy. 2. Reuse: Utilize items repeatedly instead of discarding after single use. 3. Recycle: Collect and reprocess waste materials (paper, glass, metals, plastics) into new products, conserving energy and reducing landfill volume. 4. Reforestation & Afforestation: Planting trees restores biodiversity, stabilizes soil against erosion, replenishes water tables, and acts as a massive carbon sink to combat climate change.
subtopics.sciNote: Recycling one ton of paper saves approximately 17 mature trees, 7,000 gallons of water, and 4,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity.
subtopics.sq: What are the 3Rs in environmental conservation? Explain each briefly.

mcq.q: The strategy of collecting and reprocessing discarded materials into new items is:

mcqs.q: All the populations of different species living and interacting in a particular area form a:
mcqs.expl: A biological community is composed of all the interacting populations of diverse species sharing a specific habitat.

mcqs.q: Which of the following organisms is an autotroph that converts solar energy into chemical energy?
mcqs.expl: Phytoplankton and green plants are primary producers capable of photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: In an ecosystem, the flow of energy is always:
mcqs.expl: Energy enters as solar radiation, flows through trophic levels, and dissipates into space as heat; it does not cycle.

mcqs.q: The bacteria that convert nitrates in soil into free atmospheric nitrogen gas are called:
mcqs.expl: Denitrifying bacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas) reduce nitrates to molecular nitrogen gas under anaerobic conditions.

mcqs.q: An interaction where one organism benefits while the other organism is harmed is known as:
mcqs.expl: Parasitism is an ecological relationship where the parasite gains nourishment and shelter at the physiological expense of the host.

mcqs.q: Lichens represent a mutualistic partnership between a fungus and a/an:
mcqs.expl: In lichens, the fungus provides structure, water, and minerals, while the alga or cyanobacterium photosynthesizes organic nutrients.

mcqs.q: Acid rain is primarily caused by emissions of which gases into the atmosphere?
mcqs.expl: Sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) react with atmospheric moisture to form sulfuric and nitric acids.

mcqs.q: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are primarily responsible for:
opts: Depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer
mcqs.expl: CFCs release reactive chlorine free radicals in the stratosphere that catalyze the destruction of ozone molecules.

mcqs.q: Insectivorous plants like the Venus flytrap catch insects mainly to obtain:
mcqs.expl: Insectivorous plants grow in acidic, nitrogen-deficient bogs and digest insects to fulfill their nitrogen requirements.

mcqs.q: The graphical representation of the total weight of living tissue at each trophic level is the:
mcqs.expl: The pyramid of biomass shows the total dry mass of all organisms present at each successive trophic level.

sq.q: Differentiate between a food chain and a food web.
sq.ans: A food chain is a single linear pathway illustrating the transfer of food energy from producers through a sequence of consumers (e.g. grass -> deer -> tiger). A food web is a complex, interconnected network of multiple food chains in an ecosystem, reflecting that most organisms consume and are consumed by more than one species, thereby providing ecosystem stability.

sq.q: Explain the ecological significance of the 10% law of energy transfer.
sq.ans: The 10% law states that only about 10% of the energy stored as biomass in one trophic level is transferred to the next trophic level; the remaining 90% is lost during cellular respiration, heat dissipation, and incomplete digestion. Because available energy diminishes drastically with each transfer, food chains rarely exceed four or five trophic levels.

sq.q: What is nitrogen fixation? Name two ways by which it occurs naturally.
sq.ans: Nitrogen fixation is the process of converting inert molecular atmospheric nitrogen gas (N2) into usable nitrogenous compounds such as ammonia (NH3) or nitrates (NO3-). It occurs naturally via: 1. Biological Nitrogen Fixation by symbiotic bacteria (Rhizobium in legume root nodules) and free-living bacteria (Azotobacter, cyanobacteria); and 2. Atmospheric/Physical Nitrogen Fixation by high-voltage lightning strikes.

sq.q: What is the greenhouse effect and how does it lead to global warming?
sq.ans: The greenhouse effect is the natural trapping of outgoing infrared thermal radiation by atmospheric gases (CO2, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide), keeping the Earth habitable. However, human activities such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation increase greenhouse gas concentrations, trapping excessive heat and causing an abnormal rise in global mean temperatures, a phenomenon termed global warming.

sq.q: Define the 3Rs of environmental conservation.
sq.ans: The 3Rs represent three sustainable environmental practices: 1. Reduce (lowering resource consumption and waste generation), 2. Reuse (using items multiple times instead of discarding them after a single use), and 3. Recycle (reprocessing waste materials into new usable products).

lq.q: Describe the Nitrogen Cycle in detail with all its major biological and chemical steps and an explanatory flow diagram.
lq.ans:
The Nitrogen Cycle consists of five major cyclical steps:
1. Nitrogen Fixation:
- Atmospheric N2 gas (78% of air) is converted into reactive ammonia (NH3/NH4+).
- Biological fixation: Performed by Rhizobium bacteria living symbiotically in root nodules of legumes, and free-living soil bacteria (Azotobacter, Clostridium, Nostoc).
- Atmospheric fixation: Lightning and thunderstorm energy forces N2 and O2 to combine, forming nitrates washed down by rain.
- Industrial fixation: Haber process synthesizes ammonia fertilizers.

2. Ammonification:
- Decomposers (saprophytic bacteria and fungi) break down complex organic nitrogenous compounds (proteins, nucleic acids) from dead plants, animals, and excretion products (urea) into ammonia.

3. Nitrification:
- A two-step aerobic biological oxidation of ammonia into nitrates:
  * Step 1: Ammonia is oxidized to Nitrite (NO2-) by Nitrosomonas bacteria: 2NH3 + 3O2 -> 2NO2- + 2H+ + 2H2O.
  * Step 2: Nitrite is oxidized to Nitrate (NO3-) by Nitrobacter bacteria: 2NO2- + O2 -> 2NO3-.

4. Assimilation:
- Plant roots absorb soluble nitrates and ammonium ions from soil water and incorporate them into plant amino acids, proteins, and nucleotides. Herbivores and carnivores obtain organic nitrogen by consuming plants.

5. Denitrification:
- In waterlogged or anaerobic soils, denitrifying bacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas denitrificans) reduce nitrates back into gaseous nitrous oxide (N2O) and molecular nitrogen (N2), which returns to the atmosphere, completing the global cycle.

lq.q: Discuss the types of symbiotic relationships (Mutualism and Commensalism) and contrast them with Predation and Parasitism, giving two examples for each.
lq.ans:
1. Mutualism (+/+):
- A close, intimate relationship between two different species in which both organisms derive mutual benefit.
- Example 1: Lichens — A partnership between a fungus (ascomycete) that provides structural protection, moisture, and minerals, and an alga/cyanobacterium that produces carbohydrates through photosynthesis.
- Example 2: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) living inside root nodules of legumes (peas, beans) — bacteria supply fixed nitrogen to the plant, while the plant provides carbohydrates and shelter.

2. Commensalism (+/0):
- A relationship in which one species benefits while the other partner is neither harmed nor helped.
- Example 1: Epiphytes (such as orchids) that grow on the branches of tall rainforest trees to reach sunlight without absorbing nutrients from the host tree.
- Example 2: Remora (suckerfish) attached to the belly of a shark, obtaining transportation and leftover food particles without affecting the shark.

3. Parasitism (+/-):
- A relationship where one organism (the parasite) lives on or inside another living organism (the host), deriving nourishment and shelter while causing physiological damage or disease.
- Example 1: Plasmodium (endoparasite) living in human red blood cells and liver, causing malaria.
- Example 2: Cuscuta (dodder plant, ectoparasite) lacking chlorophyll, wrapping around host stems and penetrating vascular bundles via haustoria to siphon sugars and sap.

4. Predation (+/-):
- An active interaction where one organism (the predator) hunts, kills, and consumes another organism (the prey).
- Example 1: Lion hunting and killing a zebra on the savannah.
- Example 2: Pitcher plant trapping insects with slippery digestive fluid to obtain nitrogen in acidic soils.

lq.q: Explain the causes, catastrophic consequences, and remedial measures for Air Pollution, Acid Rain, and Global Warming.
lq.ans:
1. Air Pollution:
- Causes: Combustion of fossil fuels in motor vehicles, thermal power plants, and industrial boilers releasing carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx), unburnt hydrocarbons, soot, and particulate matter (PM2.5).
- Consequences: Respiratory diseases (asthma, chronic bronchitis, lung cancer), cardiovascular disorders, photochemical smog reducing visibility and causing eye irritation.
- Remedial Measures: Installing catalytic converters in vehicles, electrostatic precipitators in industrial chimneys, transitioning to electric vehicles, and using clean renewable energy (solar, wind, hydroelectric).

2. Acid Rain:
- Causes: Atmospheric emission of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides reacting with water, oxygen, and oxidants to produce sulfuric acid (H2SO4) and nitric acid (HNO3), yielding precipitation with pH below 5.6.
- Consequences: Destroys aquatic ecosystems by lowering lake pH (killing fish eggs and gills); leaches essential soil nutrients (calcium, magnesium) while mobilizing toxic aluminum; corrodes historical stone monuments (e.g. marble) and metal bridges.
- Remedial Measures: Flue-gas desulfurization (scrubbers) in power plants, low-sulfur fuels, and liming acidified lakes.

3. Global Warming:
- Causes: Excessive accumulation of greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide from burning coal/oil and deforestation; methane from livestock and rice paddies; CFCs and nitrous oxide).
- Consequences: Rapid melting of polar ice caps and Himalayan glaciers; rising sea levels threatening coastal cities; extreme weather events (prolonged droughts, catastrophic floods, intense heatwaves); loss of biodiversity.
- Remedial Measures: Massive global afforestation and reforestation; reducing carbon emissions under international climate agreements; adopting the 3Rs; improving energy efficiency.

activities.title: Field Study: Construction of a Food Chain and Food Web in a Local Ecosystem
activities.desc: Visit a local school garden, pond, or park. Observe and record all living organisms: green plants, grasses, insects, birds, frogs, snails, earthworms. Construct at least two distinct food chains (e.g. Grass -> Caterpillar -> Sparrow -> Falcon; Algae -> Water flea -> Small fish -> Kingfisher) and interconnect them into a functional food web diagram.

slos: Define biotechnology and distinguish between classical and modern biotechnology.

summary.en: Biotechnology is the application of biological organisms, systems, or processes to manufacture products for the benefit of humanity. Classical biotechnology encompasses traditional fermentation processes like making bread, cheese, yogurt, and vinegar. Modern biotechnology involves recombinant DNA technology, genetic engineering, and molecular cloning.
summary.ur: بائیو ٹیکنالوجی جانداروں، ان کے اجزاء یا حیاتیاتی طریقہ کار کو انسانی فائدے کے لیے استعمال کرنے کی سائنس ہے۔ قدیم بائیو ٹیکنالوجی میں خمیر کے ذریعے دہی، پنیر اور روٹی بنانا شامل تھا جبکہ جدید بائیو ٹیکنالوجی جینیٹک انجینئرنگ پر مبنی ہے۔
summary.ps: بایوټیکنالوجي د انسانانو د ګټې لپاره د ژوندیو موجوداتو کارول دي چې په دودیزه او عصري (جینیټیک انجینرۍ) ویشل شوې ده.

subtopics.name: Scope and History of Biotechnology
subtopics.desc: The term 'biotechnology' was coined by Hungarian agricultural engineer Karl Ereky in 1919. It integrates microbiology, biochemistry, genetics, and chemical engineering. While prehistoric humans inadvertently utilized yeast and lactic acid bacteria for bread, cheese, and beer, modern biotechnology emerged in the 1970s with the invention of recombinant DNA techniques, allowing the direct transfer of genes across species barriers.
subtopics.sciNote: In 1978, scientists at Genentech successfully produced the first genetically engineered human insulin using transformed Escherichia coli bacteria.
subtopics.sq: Who coined the term biotechnology and what is its modern scope?

mcq.q: The term 'biotechnology' was first coined in 1919 by:

summary.en: Fermentation is the anaerobic microbial breakdown of organic substrates (primarily sugars) to generate energy and commercially valuable products. The two primary types are Alcoholic Fermentation (yeast produces ethanol and CO2) and Lactic Acid Fermentation (bacteria produce lactic acid). Industrial fermenters (bioreactors) optimize growth conditions (pH, temperature, oxygen, nutrients) to maximize microbial yields.
summary.ur: خمیر کا عمل (فرمینٹیشن) آکسیجن کے بغیر مائیکرو آرگنزمز کے ذریعے کاربوہائیڈریٹس کے ٹوٹنے کا عمل ہے۔ الکوحلک فرمینٹیشن اور لیکٹک ایسڈ فرمینٹیشن اس کی دو بنیادی اقسام ہیں۔ بڑے پیمانے پر مصنوعات بنانے کے لیے انڈسٹریل فرمنٹرز استعمال کیے جاتے ہیں۔
summary.ps: فرمینټیشن د مایکرو ارګانیزمونو په واسطه د اکسیجن پرته د موادو تجزیه ده چې په بیوریکټرونو کې په لویه کچه ترسره کیږي.

subtopics.name: Alcoholic and Lactic Acid Fermentation
subtopics.desc: 1. Alcoholic Fermentation: Performed by yeasts (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) under anaerobic conditions. Glucose is converted into pyruvate via glycolysis, which is then decarboxylated and reduced to ethanol and carbon dioxide: C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2 + 2 ATP. Used in brewing, winemaking, and baking (CO2 gas makes bread dough rise). 2. Lactic Acid Fermentation: Performed by lactic acid bacteria (Lactobacillus, Streptococcus). Pyruvate is reduced directly to lactic acid: C6H12O6 -> 2 CH3CH(OH)COOH + 2 ATP. Used in dairy industries for yogurt, cheese, and in pickling.
subtopics.sciNote: During intense physical exertion when muscle cells experience oxygen debt, muscle glycogen undergoes lactic acid fermentation, causing temporary muscle fatigue and cramps.
subtopics.sq: Differentiate between alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation.

mcq.q: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast converts glucose into:

subtopics.name: Industrial Fermenters (Bioreactors)
subtopics.desc: A fermenter is a large closed stainless steel vessel engineered to cultivate microorganisms under strictly controlled aseptic conditions to produce antibiotics, enzymes, hormones, and vitamins on an industrial scale. Features: 1. Agitator/Impeller for uniform mixing, 2. Sparger for aerating sterile air bubbles, 3. Cooling jacket to dissipate metabolic heat, 4. Automated sensors and probes to monitor pH, temperature, and dissolved oxygen. Types: Batch Fermentation (closed system, substrate added at start, harvested when completed) and Continuous Fermentation (open system, nutrients added continuously while spent medium and product are continuously harvested).
subtopics.sciNote: Fermenters can range in capacity from a few liters in research laboratories to over 500,000 liters in commercial biotechnology plants.
subtopics.sq: Compare batch fermentation with continuous fermentation.

mcq.q: A closed system fermentation where nutrients are added at the start and products harvested at the end is called:

summary.en: Genetic engineering (recombinant DNA technology) is the artificial modification of an organism's genome by cutting, inserting, or modifying genes. The fundamental steps include: isolating the gene of interest, cutting a vector plasmid with restriction enzymes, joining them using DNA ligase, transforming host cells (e.g. E. coli), and culturing transgenic organisms to extract desired products.
summary.ur: جینیٹک انجینئرنگ میں کسی جاندار کے ڈی این اے میں من پسند جین داخل کر کے نئی خصوصیات پیدا کی جاتی ہیں۔ اس میں مالیکیولر قینچی (ریسٹرکشن انزائمز) اور ویکٹر (پلازمڈ) کا استعمال کیا جاتا ہے۔
summary.ps: جینیټیک انجینرۍ د ژوندیو موجوداتو د جینونو بدلول دي چې د درملو، انسولین، او ښه حاصل لرونکو بوټو په تولید کې کارول کیږي.

subtopics.name: Basic Steps in Genetic Engineering
subtopics.desc: 1. Isolation of Gene of Interest: Identified and cut out from donor chromosomal DNA using Restriction Endonucleases ('molecular scissors') that recognize specific palindromic sequences. 2. Selection and Preparation of Cloning Vector: Bacterial Plasmids (circular extrachromosomal DNA) or bacteriophages are cut with the same restriction enzyme, creating compatible sticky ends. 3. Formation of Recombinant DNA: The gene of interest and vector plasmid are joined together by DNA Ligase ('molecular glue'). 4. Transformation: Recombinant plasmid is introduced into a host bacterium (Escherichia coli) through chemical or electrical permeabilization. 5.
